A company uses Amazon CloudFront for its website. The company has enabled logging for the CloudFront distribution, and the logs are stored in one of the company’s Amazon S3 buckets. The company needs to perform advanced analysis on the logs and create visualizations.  
  
What should a solutions architect do to meet these requirements?

options.text: Use standard SQL queries in Amazon Athena to analyze the CloudFront logs in the S3 bucket. Visualize the results with AWS Glue.
Use standard SQL queries in Amazon Athena to analyze the CloudFront logs in the S3 bucket. Visualize the results with Amazon QuickSight.
Use standard SQL queries in Amazon DynamoDB to analyze the CloudFront logs in the S3 bucket. Visualize the results with AWS Glue.
Use standard SQL queries in Amazon DynamoDB to analyze the CloudFront logs in the S3 bucket. Visualize the results with Amazon QuickSight.

questions.explanation:
Amazon Athena is the appropriate service to run standard SQL queries directly against CloudFront log files stored in Amazon S3, and AWS provides documented support for analyzing CloudFront logs with Athena. For dashboards and visual analytics, Amazon QuickSight is the AWS business intelligence service that can visualize data queried through Athena. AWS Glue is not a visualization service, and DynamoDB is not used to run standard SQL queries over CloudFront log files in S3.

**Learn more:** [Amazon CloudFront logs - Amazon Athena](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/athena/latest/ug/cloudfront-logs.html) · [Create a table for CloudFront standard logs (legacy) - Amazon Athena](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/athena/latest/ug/create-cloudfront-table-standard-logs.html)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],A company has an on-premises server that uses an Oracle database to process and store customer information. The company wants to use an AWS database service to achieve higher availability and improve application performance. The company also wants to offload reporting from its primary database system.  
  
Which solution will meet these requirements in the **MOST operationally efficient** way?

options.text: Use AWS Database Migration Service (AWS DMS) to create an Amazon RDS DB instance in multiple AWS Regions. Point the reporting functions toward a separate DB instance from the primary DB instance.
Use Amazon RDS in a Single-AZ deployment to create an Oracle database. Create a read replica in the same zone as the primary DB instance. Direct the reporting functions to the read replica.
Use Amazon RDS deployed in a Multi-AZ cluster deployment to create an Oracle database. Direct the reporting functions to use the reader instance in the cluster deployment.
Use Amazon RDS deployed in a Multi-AZ instance deployment to create an Amazon Aurora database. Direct the reporting functions to the reader instances.

questions.explanation:
Amazon RDS for Oracle supports Multi-AZ instance deployments (not DB clusters, which are unavailable for Oracle). Multi-AZ instance deployment provides automatic failover and high availability. RDS read replicas allow reporting workloads to be offloaded from the primary database instance. This configuration provides both high availability and reporting scalability with minimal operational overhead compared to self-managed Oracle on EC2.

**Learn more:** [Reader endpoints for Amazon Aurora](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonRDS/latest/AuroraUserGuide/Aurora.Endpoints.Reader.html) · [High availability for Amazon Aurora](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonRDS/latest/AuroraUserGuide/Concepts.AuroraHighAvailability.html)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],An application running on an Amazon EC2 instance in VPC-A must access files on another EC2 instance in VPC-B. Both VPCs are in separate AWS accounts.  
  
The network administrator must design a solution to provide secure access to the EC2 instance in VPC-B from VPC-A. The connectivity must not introduce a single point of failure or bandwidth concerns.  
  
Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Set up a VPC peering connection between VPC-A and VPC-B.
Set up VPC gateway endpoints for the EC2 instance running in VPC-B.
Attach a virtual private gateway to VPC-B and set up routing from VPC-A.
Create a private virtual interface (VIF) for the EC2 instance running in VPC-B and add appropriate routes from VPC-A.

questions.explanation:
A VPC peering connection provides private IP connectivity between two VPCs and supports peering across different AWS accounts. It is the appropriate AWS-native option for direct EC2-to-EC2 communication between VPC-A and VPC-B without relying on an intermediary device that could become a single point of failure or bandwidth bottleneck. Gateway endpoints do not connect to EC2 instances, a virtual private gateway is used for VPN or Direct Connect termination rather than VPC-to-VPC peering, and a private VIF is an AWS Direct Connect construct for on-premises connectivity.

**Learn more:** [Connect VPCs using VPC peering - Amazon VPC](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/userguide/vpc-peering.html) · [Create a VPC peering connection - Amazon VPC](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/peering/create-vpc-peering-connection.html)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],A social media company wants to let its users upload images in an application hosted in the AWS Cloud. The company needs a solution that automatically resizes the images so they can be displayed on multiple device types. The application has unpredictable traffic patterns throughout the day. The company wants a highly available solution that maximizes scalability.  
  
What should a solutions architect do to meet these requirements?

options.text: Create a static website hosted in Amazon S3 that invokes AWS Lambda functions to resize the images and store the images in an Amazon S3 bucket.
Create a static website hosted in Amazon CloudFront that invokes AWS Step Functions to resize the images and store the images in an Amazon RDS database.

Create a dynamic website hosted on a web server that runs on an Amazon EC2 instance. Configure a process that runs on the EC2 instance to resize the images and store the images in an Amazon S3 bucket.

Create a dynamic website hosted on an automatically scaling Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) cluster that creates a resize job in Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS). Set up an image-resizing program that runs on an Amazon EC2 instance to process the resize jobs.

questions.explanation:
A serverless design with Amazon S3 and AWS Lambda best fits automatic image resizing under unpredictable demand because Lambda can be invoked by Amazon S3 events and scales automatically without managing servers. Amazon S3 provides durable, highly available object storage for the original and resized images. This is the standard AWS event-driven pattern for image processing, whereas EC2-based solutions require instance management and do not maximize elasticity, and Amazon RDS is not an appropriate destination for image objects. Official AWS documentation describes S3 as an event source for Lambda and AWS guidance shows image optimization and resizing architectures built from Amazon S3 and AWS Lambda.

**Learn more:** [Creating event-driven architectures with Lambda - AWS Lambda Developer Guide](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/lambda/latest/dg/concepts-event-driven-architectures.html) · [Enabling website hosting - Amazon Simple Storage Service](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/EnableWebsiteHosting.html)

A company runs an application on five Amazon EC2 instances. An Application Load Balancer (ALB) sends traffic to the instances by using a target group. The average CPU utilization on each instance stays below 10% most of the time, with occasional spikes to 65%.  
  
A solutions architect must implement a solution to automate the application's scalability. The solution must optimize architectural cost and must ensure that the application has sufficient CPU resources when surges occur.  
  
Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Create an Amazon CloudWatch alarm that enters the ALARM state when the CPUUtilization metric is less than 20%. Create an AWS Lambda function that the CloudWatch alarm invokes to terminate one of the EC2 instances in the ALB target group.

Create an EC2 Auto Scaling group. Select the existing ALB as the load balancer and the existing target group as the target group. Set a target tracking scaling policy that is based on the ASGAverageCPUUtilization metric. Set the minimum instances to 2, the desired capacity to 3, the maximum instances to 6, and the target value to 50%. Add the EC2 instances to the Auto Scaling group.

Create an EC2 Auto Scaling group. Select the existing ALB as the load balancer and the existing target group as the target group. Set the minimum instances to 2, the desired capacity to 3, and the maximum instances to 6. Add the EC2 instances to the Auto Scaling group.

Create two Amazon CloudWatch alarms. Configure the first CloudWatch alarm to enter the ALARM state when the average CPUUtilization metric is below 20%. Configure the second CloudWatch alarm to enter the ALARM state when the average CPUUtilization matric is above 50%. Configure the alarms to publish to an Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS) topic to send an email message. After receiving the message, log in to decrease or increase the number of EC2 instances that are running.

questions.explanation:
An EC2 Auto Scaling group with a target tracking scaling policy based on `ASGAverageCPUUtilization` automatically adjusts capacity to keep average CPU near the configured target. That reduces cost during long periods of low utilization by allowing scale-in, and it adds instances during spikes so enough CPU capacity is available. AWS also supports attaching the existing instances to the Auto Scaling group and registering them with the existing ALB target group. Simply creating an Auto Scaling group without a scaling policy does not automate scale adjustments, and CloudWatch alarms plus Lambda or email-driven manual changes are not the appropriate managed scaling solution.

**Learn more:** [Detach or attach instances from your Auto Scaling group - Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/autoscaling/ec2/userguide/ec2-auto-scaling-detach-attach-instances.html) · [AttachInstances - Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling API Reference](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/autoscaling/ec2/APIReference/API_AttachInstances.html)

A company stores 700 terabytes of data on a large network-attached storage (NAS) system in its corporate data center. The company operates in a hybrid environment with a 10 Gbps AWS Direct Connect connection.  
  
After a regulator's audit, the company has 90 days to move the data to the cloud. The company must move the data efficiently and without disruption. The company must also continue to access and update the data during the transfer window.  
  
Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Create an AWS DataSync agent in the corporate data center. Create a data transfer task Start the transfer to an Amazon S3 bucket.
Back up the data to AWS Snowball Edge Storage Optimized devices. Ship the devices to an AWS data center. Mount a target Amazon S3 bucket on the on-premises file system.
Use rsync to copy the data directly from local storage to a designated Amazon S3 bucket over the Direct Connect connection.
Back up the data on tapes. Ship the tapes to an AWS data center. Mount a target Amazon S3 bucket on the on-premises file system.

questions.explanation:
AWS DataSync is built to transfer data from on-premises NAS environments, including NFS and SMB file servers, to Amazon S3. It uses an on-premises agent, works over existing network connectivity such as Direct Connect, and supports recurring incremental transfers so that after the initial copy, only changed data and metadata are moved. DataSync can transfer open files, and if a file changes during transfer, rerunning the task captures the latest version. That makes it the appropriate managed service for migrating a large active dataset while users continue to read and update the source data.

**Learn more:** [Transferring to or from on-premises storage with AWS DataSync](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/en_us/datasync/latest/userguide/transferring-on-premises-storage.html) · [How AWS DataSync works](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/datasync/latest/userguide/how-datasync-transfer-works.html)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],A company receives **10 TB of instrumentation data each day** from several machines located at a single factory. The data consists of **JSON files** stored on a **storage area network (SAN)** in an **on-premises data center** within the factory.  
  
The company wants to send this data to **Amazon S3**, where it can be accessed by several additional systems that provide critical **near-real-time analytics**. A **secure transfer** is important because the data is considered sensitive.  
  
Which solution provides the **MOST reliable** data transfer?

options.text: AWS DataSync over public internet
AWS DataSync over AWS Direct Connect
AWS Database Migration Service (AWS DMS) over public internet
AWS Database Migration Service (AWS DMS) over AWS Direct Connect

questions.explanation:
AWS DataSync is the correct service because it is built for secure, reliable, high-speed transfer of file data between on-premises storage and AWS storage services such as Amazon S3. AWS DMS is intended for migrating and replicating databases, not bulk transfer of JSON files from a SAN. For the connection method, AWS Direct Connect is more reliable than the public internet because it uses a dedicated network path with more consistent throughput and lower dependence on internet conditions, which better fits a sustained 10 TB-per-day sensitive data transfer requirement.

**Learn more:** [What is AWS DataSync?](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/datasync/latest/userguide/what-is-datasync.html) · [Transferring to or from on-premises storage with AWS DataSync](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/en_us/datasync/latest/userguide/transferring-on-premises-storage.html)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],A medical research lab generates data for a new study. The lab wants to provide the data to clinics nationwide with minimum latency for their on-premises, file-based applications. The data files are stored in an Amazon S3 bucket that grants each clinic read-only permissions.  
  
What should a solutions architect recommend to meet these requirements?

options.text: Deploy an AWS Storage Gateway file gateway as a virtual machine (VM) on premises at each clinic
Migrate the files to each clinic’s on-premises applications by using AWS DataSync for processing.
Deploy an AWS Storage Gateway volume gateway as a virtual machine (VM) on premises at each clinic.
Attach an Amazon Elastic File System (Amazon EFS) file system to each clinic’s on-premises servers.

questions.explanation:
AWS Storage Gateway S3 File Gateway is the correct fit because it presents data stored in Amazon S3 to on-premises applications through standard file protocols such as NFS or SMB, and it is deployed locally as a virtual machine at each site. Its local cache is designed to provide low-latency access to frequently or recently accessed data, which matches the requirement for minimum latency at each clinic. Volume Gateway provides iSCSI block storage rather than file shares, AWS DataSync is for data transfer rather than application-facing file access, and Amazon EFS is a separate file system service rather than a way to expose an existing S3 bucket to on-premises file-based applications.

**Learn more:** [How Amazon S3 File Gateway works - AWS Storage Gateway](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/filegateway/latest/files3/file-gateway-concepts.html) · [Maximizing S3 File Gateway throughput - AWS Storage Gateway](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/filegateway/latest/files3/Performance-Throughput.html)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],A company plans to migrate its on-premises data center to AWS. Per the company's compliance requirements, it may use only the `ap-northeast-3` Region. Company administrators must not be allowed to connect VPCs to the internet.  
  
Which solutions meet these requirements? **(Choose two.)**

options.text: Use AWS Control Tower to implement data residency guardrails to deny internet access and deny access to all AWS Regions except ap-northeast-3.
Use rules in AWS WAF to prevent internet access. Deny access to all AWS Regions except ap-northeast-3 in the AWS account settings.
Use AWS Organizations to configure service control policies (SCPS) that prevent VPCs from gaining internet access. Deny access to all AWS Regions except ap-northeast-3.
Create an outbound rule for the network ACL in each VPC to deny all traffic from 0.0.0.0/0. Create an IAM policy for each user to prevent the use of any AWS Region other than ap-northeast-3.
Use AWS Config to activate managed rules to detect and alert for internet gateways and to detect and alert for new resources deployed outside of ap-northeast-3.

questions.explanation:
AWS Control Tower provides preventive controls for data residency, including a Region deny control to block access to nonapproved AWS Regions and a preventive control that disallows internet access for customer-managed Amazon VPC instances. AWS Organizations service control policies (SCPs) can also enforce organization-wide guardrails by denying API actions outside `ap-northeast-3` with the `aws:RequestedRegion` condition and by denying VPC internet-enabling actions such as internet gateway–related operations. By contrast, AWS WAF protects web applications rather than VPC connectivity, and AWS Config rules are detective controls that only report noncompliance instead of preventing it.

**Learn more:** [Configure the Region deny control - AWS Control Tower](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/controltower/latest/userguide/region-deny.html) · [Data residency controls with preventive behavior - AWS Control Tower](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/controltower/latest/controlreference/data-residency-preventive-controls.html)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],A company has developed a new video game as a web application. The application uses a three-tier architecture in a VPC with Amazon RDS for MySQL in the database layer. Several players will compete online at the same time. The game's developers want to:  
  
- display a top-10 scoreboard in near real time, and  
- provide the ability to stop and restore the game while preserving the current scores.  
  
What should a solutions architect do to meet these requirements?

options.text: Set up an Amazon ElastiCache for Memcached cluster to cache the scores for the web application to display.
Set up an Amazon ElastiCache for Redis cluster to compute and cache the scores for the web application to display.
Place an Amazon CloudFront distribution in front of the web application to cache the scoreboard in a section of the application.
Create a read replica on Amazon RDS for MySQL to run queries to compute the scoreboard and serve the read traffic to the web application.

questions.explanation:
Amazon ElastiCache for Redis is designed for real-time leaderboards by using sorted sets, which automatically maintain unique members in score order and support efficient top-N and rank queries as scores change. AWS documentation specifically identifies gaming leaderboards as a Redis/Valkey use case. Redis-based ElastiCache also supports persistence-oriented durability and backup/restore capabilities needed to preserve scores when the game is stopped and restored, whereas Memcached is only a volatile cache. CloudFront is not appropriate for highly dynamic, low-cacheability leaderboard data, and an RDS read replica only offloads database reads rather than providing an in-memory ranking data structure optimized for concurrent score updates.

**Learn more:** [Common ElastiCache Use Cases and How ElastiCache Can Help - Gaming Leaderboards](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonElastiCache/latest/dg/elasticache-use-cases.html) · [Supported and restricted Valkey, Memcached, and Redis OSS commands](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonElastiCache/latest/dg/SupportedCommands.html)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],An ecommerce application uses a PostgreSQL database that runs on an Amazon EC2 instance. During a monthly sales event, database usage increases and causes database connection issues for the application. Traffic is unpredictable for future monthly sales events, which affects the sales forecast.  
  
The company needs to maintain performance when traffic increases unpredictably.  
  
Which solution resolves this issue in the **MOST cost-effective** way?

options.text: Migrate the PostgreSQL database to Amazon Aurora Serverless v2.
Enable auto scaling for the PostgreSQL database on the EC2 instance to accommodate increased usage.
Migrate the PostgreSQL database to Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL with a larger instance type.
Migrate the PostgreSQL database to Amazon Redshift to accommodate increased usage.

questions.explanation:
Amazon Aurora Serverless v2 is designed for applications with variable or unpredictable workloads and can automatically scale compute and memory capacity up during traffic spikes and back down afterward. AWS documentation specifically cites ecommerce sales or promotional surges as a use case and notes that you pay only for the database resources consumed, which avoids the overprovisioning required by a larger fixed RDS instance. Amazon Redshift is intended for analytics/data warehousing rather than OLTP ecommerce transactions, and keeping PostgreSQL on EC2 does not provide the same managed, automatic database scaling behavior.

**Learn more:** [Using Aurora serverless - Amazon Aurora](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonRDS/latest/AuroraUserGuide/aurora-serverless-v2.html) · [How Aurora Serverless v2 works - Amazon Aurora](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/en_en/AmazonRDS/latest/AuroraUserGuide/aurora-serverless-v2.how-it-works.html)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],A company uses AWS Cost Explorer to track its AWS costs. The company notices that Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) storage and snapshot costs rise every month. However, the company does not buy additional EBS storage each month. The company wants to optimize monthly costs for its current storage usage.  
  
Which solution will meet these requirements with the **LEAST operational overhead**?

options.text: Use logs in Amazon CloudWatch Logs to monitor the storage utilization of Amazon EBS. Use Amazon EBS Elastic Volumes to reduce the size of the EBS volumes.
Use a custom script to monitor space usage. Use Amazon EBS Elastic Volumes to reduce the size of the EBS volumes.
Delete all expired and unused snapshots to reduce snapshot costs.
Delete all nonessential snapshots. Use Amazon Data Lifecycle Manager to create and manage the snapshots according to the company's snapshot policy requirements.

questions.explanation:
Amazon EBS snapshot costs commonly grow over time as snapshots accumulate, even when active volume capacity does not increase. Amazon EBS Elastic Volumes does not support shrinking an existing volume, so options based on reducing EBS volume size are not valid. Deleting unnecessary snapshots can reduce snapshot-related cost, and using Amazon Data Lifecycle Manager is the lowest-overhead way to automate snapshot retention and deletion according to policy so snapshot sprawl does not keep increasing.

**Learn more:** [Modify an Amazon EBS volume using Elastic Volumes operations - Amazon EBS](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/ebs/latest/userguide/ebs-modify-volume.html) · [Delete an Amazon EBS snapshot - Amazon EBS](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/ebs/latest/userguide/ebs-deleting-snapshot.html)

options.text: Increase the minimum capacity for the Auto Scaling group.
Increase the maximum capacity for the Auto Scaling group.
Configure scheduled scaling to scale up to the desired compute level.
Change the scaling policy to add more EC2 instances during each scaling operation.

questions.explanation:
Scheduled scaling is the correct approach for predictable demand that occurs at a known time. Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling scheduled actions can set the group's desired capacity at specific times, so the Auto Scaling group can scale out before the 1 AM batch job begins and scale in after the job completes. That satisfies both the fast availability requirement and the cost-control requirement. Raising minimum capacity would leave excess instances running continuously, raising maximum capacity only changes the upper limit without proactively adding instances, and adding more instances per scaling step remains a reactive policy rather than a time-based pre-scaling method.

**Learn more:** [Scheduled scaling for Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/autoscaling/ec2/userguide/ec2-auto-scaling-scheduled-scaling.html) · [Choose your scaling method - Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/autoscaling/ec2/userguide/scaling-overview.html)

A company operates its production workload on an Amazon Aurora MySQL DB cluster that has six Aurora Replicas. The company needs near-real-time reporting queries from one department to be automatically distributed across three Aurora Replicas. Those three replicas use different compute and memory specifications than the rest of the DB cluster.  
  
Which solution satisfies these requirements?

options.text: Create and use a custom endpoint for the workload
Create a three-node cluster clone and use the reader endpoint
Use any of the instance endpoints for the selected three nodes
Use the reader endpoint to automatically distribute the read-only workload

questions.explanation:
An Aurora custom endpoint can be associated with a selected subset of DB instances and balances connections across that group. It is intended for clusters containing DB instances with different capacities or configurations, allowing reporting traffic to be directed only to the three designated Aurora Replicas.

**Learn more:** [Custom endpoints for Amazon Aurora](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonRDS/latest/AuroraUserGuide/Aurora.Endpoints.Custom.html) · [Amazon Aurora endpoint connections](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonRDS/latest/AuroraUserGuide/Aurora.Overview.Endpoints.html)

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],A social media company is creating a feature for its website that will let users upload photos. The company anticipates major surges in demand during large events and must make sure the website can support user upload traffic.  
  
Which solution satisfies these requirements with the **MOST scalability**?

options.text: Upload files from the user's browser to the application servers. Transfer the files to an Amazon S3 bucket.
Provision an AWS Storage Gateway file gateway. Upload files directly from the user's browser to the file gateway.
Generate Amazon S3 presigned URLs in the application. Upload files directly from the user's browser into an S3 bucket.
Provision an Amazon Elastic File System (Amazon EFS) file system. Upload files directly from the user's browser to the file system.

questions.explanation:
Generating Amazon S3 presigned URLs in the application and having the user's browser upload directly to Amazon S3 provides the greatest scalability because it offloads file transfer from the application servers and uses S3 as the upload endpoint. AWS documentation states that presigned URLs can allow a user to upload a specific object directly to an S3 bucket without requiring AWS security credentials, which is the standard pattern for direct-to-S3 uploads and avoids the application tier becoming a bottleneck.

**Learn more:** [Uploading objects with presigned URLs - Amazon S3 User Guide](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/PresignedUrlUploadObject.html) · [Download and upload objects with presigned URLs - Amazon S3 User Guide](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/using-presigned-url.html)

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],An image hosting company stores its large assets in Amazon S3 Standard buckets. The company uploads by using parallel multipart upload through S3 APIs and overwrites objects if the same object is uploaded again.  
  
For the first 30 days after upload, the objects will be accessed frequently. After 30 days, the objects will be accessed less often, but each object's access pattern will be inconsistent. The company must optimize S3 storage costs while maintaining high availability and resiliency for the stored assets.  
  
Which combination of actions should a solutions architect recommend to meet these requirements? **(Choose two.)**

options.text: Move assets to S3 Intelligent-Tiering after 30 days.
Configure an S3 Lifecycle policy to clean up incomplete multipart uploads.
Configure an S3 Lifecycle policy to clean up expired object delete markers.
Move assets to S3 Standard-Infrequent Access (S3 Standard-IA) after 30 days.
Move assets to S3 One Zone-Infrequent Access (S3 One Zone-IA) after 30 days.

questions.explanation:
S3 Intelligent-Tiering is the appropriate storage class after 30 days because it is intended for data with changing or unknown access patterns and automatically moves objects between access tiers without reducing the multi-Availability Zone availability and resiliency of the data. For multipart uploads, incomplete uploaded parts continue to incur storage charges until they are completed or aborted, so an S3 Lifecycle rule that aborts incomplete multipart uploads is a direct cost-optimization best practice. S3 One Zone-IA does not satisfy the resiliency requirement because it stores data in a single Availability Zone, and S3 Standard-IA is less suitable than Intelligent-Tiering when access is inconsistent rather than predictably infrequent.

**Learn more:** [Understanding and managing Amazon S3 storage classes](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/storage-class-intro.html) · [Data protection in Amazon S3](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/DataDurability.html)

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],A marketing team wants to create a campaign for an upcoming multi-sport event. The team has news reports from the past five years in PDF format. The team needs a solution to extract insights about the content and the sentiment of the news reports. The solution must use Amazon Textract to process the news reports.  
  
Which solution will meet these requirements with the **LEAST operational overhead**?

options.text: Provide the extracted insights to Amazon Athena for analysis. Store the extracted insights and analysis in an Amazon S3 bucket.
Store the extracted insights in an Amazon DynamoDB table. Use Amazon SageMaker to build a sentiment model.
Provide the extracted insights to Amazon Comprehend for analysis. Save the analysis to an Amazon S3 bucket.
Store the extracted insights in an Amazon S3 bucket. Use Amazon QuickSight to visualize and analyze the data.

questions.explanation:
Amazon Textract can extract text from PDF documents, and Amazon Comprehend is the AWS managed natural language processing service that can analyze document text for sentiment and other content insights such as entities and key phrases. Using Comprehend avoids building and training a custom model in SageMaker, which would add unnecessary operational overhead. Storing the analysis output in Amazon S3 provides simple managed persistence for the results.

**Learn more:** [Detecting Document Text with Amazon Textract](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/textract/latest/dg/detecting-document-text.html) · [Amazon Comprehend Documentation](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/comprehend/)

A company runs its core network services, including directory services and DNS, in an on-premises data center. The data center connects to the AWS Cloud through AWS Direct Connect (DX). More AWS accounts are planned and will need fast, cost-effective, and consistent access to these network services.  
  
What should a solutions architect implement to satisfy these requirements with the **LEAST** operational overhead?

options.text: Create a DX connection in each new account. Route the network traffic to the on-premises servers.
Configure VPC endpoints in the DX VPC for all required services. Route the network traffic to the on-premises servers.
Create a VPN connection between each new account and the DX VPRoute the network traffic to the on-premises servers.
Configure AWS Transit Gateway between the accounts. Assign DX to the transit gateway and route network traffic to the on-premises servers.

questions.explanation:
AWS Transit Gateway centrally connects VPCs across accounts and on-premises networks. Associating a Direct Connect gateway with the transit gateway through a transit virtual interface lets multiple attached VPCs use one Direct Connect connection and provides centralized routing, avoiding separate Direct Connect connections or VPNs for each account.

**Learn more:** [Transit gateway attachments to a Direct Connect gateway in AWS Transit Gateway](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/tgw/tgw-dcg-attachments.html) · [Direct Connect gateways](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/directconnect/latest/UserGuide/direct-connect-gateways-intro.html)

A company operates database workloads on AWS as the backend for its customer portals. The company uses a Multi-AZ database cluster on Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL.  
  
The company must implement a 30-day backup retention policy. It currently has both automated RDS backups and manual RDS backups. The company wants to retain both types of existing RDS backups that are less than 30 days old.  
  
Which solution will meet these requirements in the MOST cost-effective manner?

options.text: Configure the RDS backup retention policy to 30 days for automated backups by using AWS Backup. Manually delete manual backups that are older than 30 days.
Disable RDS automated backups. Delete automated backups and manual backups that are older than 30 days. Configure the RDS backup retention policy to 30 days for automated backups.
Configure the RDS backup retention policy to 30 days for automated backups. Manually delete manual backups that are older than 30 days.

Disable RDS automated backups. Delete automated backups and manual backups that are older than 30 days automatically by using AWS CloudFormation. Configure the RDS backup retention policy to 30 days for automated backups.

questions.explanation:
For an RDS Multi-AZ DB cluster, configuring a 30-day backup retention period causes Amazon RDS to retain automated backups for that period. Manual snapshots are retained until explicitly deleted, so manually deleting only those older than 30 days preserves existing manual snapshots that are less than 30 days old without adding AWS Backup or custom automation costs.

**Learn more:** [Backup retention period - Amazon RDS](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonRDS/latest/UserGuide/USER_WorkingWithAutomatedBackups.BackupRetention.html) · [Introduction to backups - Amazon RDS](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonRDS/latest/UserGuide/USER_WorkingWithAutomatedBackups.html)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],A company is implementing new data retention policies for all databases running on Amazon RDS DB instances. The company must keep daily backups for a minimum of 2 years. The backups must be consistent and capable of being restored.  
  
Which solution should a solutions architect recommend to meet these requirements?

options.text: Create a backup vault in AWS Backup to retain RDS backups. Create a new backup plan with a daily schedule and an expiration period of 2 years after creation. Assign the RDS DB instances to the backup plan.

Configure a backup window for the RDS DB instances for daily snapshots. Assign a snapshot retention policy of 2 years to each RDS DB instance. Use Amazon Data Lifecycle Manager (Amazon DLM) to schedule snapshot deletions.
Configure database transaction logs to be automatically backed up to Amazon CloudWatch Logs with an expiration period of 2 years.

Configure an AWS Database Migration Service (AWS DMS) replication task. Deploy a replication instance, and configure a change data capture (CDC) task to stream database changes to Amazon S3 as the target. Configure S3 Lifecycle policies to delete the snapshots after 2 years.

questions.explanation:
AWS Backup can protect Amazon RDS with scheduled backup plans and lifecycle retention measured in years, so a daily backup plan with 2-year expiration meets the retention requirement. Those AWS Backup recovery points for RDS are snapshot-based and are restorable. By contrast, Amazon RDS automated backups are limited to a maximum retention period of 35 days, so native RDS backup retention alone cannot meet a 2-year requirement. Amazon DLM does not manage RDS snapshot retention, and DMS CDC to Amazon S3 or exporting logs to CloudWatch Logs does not create native, consistent, restorable RDS backups.

**Learn more:** [Amazon Relational Database Service backups - AWS Backup](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/aws-backup/latest/devguide/rds-backup.html) · [Backup retention period - Amazon Relational Database Service](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonRDS/latest/UserGuide/USER_WorkingWithAutomatedBackups.BackupRetention.html)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],A company wants to configure its Amazon CloudFront distribution to use SSL/TLS certificates. The company does not want to use the default domain name for the distribution. Instead, the company wants to use a different domain name for the distribution.  
  
Which solution will deploy the certificate without incurring any additional costs?

options.text: Request an Amazon issued private certificate from AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) in the us-east-1 Region.
Request an Amazon issued private certificate from AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) in the us-west-1 Region.
Request an Amazon issued public certificate from AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) in the us-east-1 Region.
Request an Amazon issued public certificate from AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) in the us-west-1 Region.

questions.explanation:
For Amazon CloudFront with an alternate domain name, the viewer certificate must be an ACM public certificate requested or imported in the US East (N. Virginia) Region (`us-east-1`). AWS states that ACM public certificates used with integrated services such as CloudFront are provided at no additional charge. A private certificate is the wrong certificate type for this internet-facing custom domain scenario, and a certificate in `us-west-1` cannot be attached to CloudFront for viewer HTTPS.

**Learn more:** [Requirements for using SSL/TLS certificates with CloudFront](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonCloudFront/latest/DeveloperGuide/cnames-and-https-requirements.html) · [AWS Certificate Manager FAQs](https://aws.amazon.com/certificate-manager/faqs/)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],A gaming company uses Amazon DynamoDB to store user information such as geographic location, player data, and leaderboards.  
  
The company needs to configure continuous backups to an Amazon S3 bucket with a minimal amount of coding. The backups must not affect availability of the application and must not affect the read capacity units (RCUs) that are defined for the table.  
  
Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Use an Amazon EMR cluster. Create an Apache Hive job to back up the data to Amazon S3.
Export the data directly from DynamoDB to Amazon S3 with continuous backups. Turn on point-in-time recovery for the table.
Configure Amazon DynamoDB Streams. Create an AWS Lambda function to consume the stream and export the data to an Amazon S3 bucket.
Create an AWS Lambda function to export the data from the database tables to Amazon S3 on a regular basis. Turn on point-in-time recovery for the table.

questions.explanation:
Amazon DynamoDB Export to Amazon S3 is the managed feature designed for this use case. It uses point-in-time recovery (PITR) backups as the export source, so PITR must be enabled on the table. The export runs asynchronously, does not consume RCUs, and does not affect table performance or application availability. That makes the direct export-to-S3 option the best fit with the least custom code.

**Learn more:** [DynamoDB data export to Amazon S3: how it works](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/amazondynamodb/latest/developerguide/S3DataExport.HowItWorks.html) · [Point-in-time backups for DynamoDB](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/amazondynamodb/latest/developerguide/Point-in-time-recovery.html)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],A company is moving its on-premises Oracle database to an Amazon RDS for Oracle database. The company must retain data for 90 days to satisfy regulatory requirements. The company must also be able to restore the database to a particular point in time for up to 14 days.  
  
Which solution meets these requirements with the **LEAST** operational overhead?

options.text: Create Amazon RDS automated backups. Set the retention period to 90 days.
Create an Amazon RDS manual snapshot every day. Delete manual snapshots that are older than 90 days.
Use the Amazon Aurora Clone feature for Oracle to create a point-in-time restore. Delete clones that are older than 90 days.
Create a backup plan that has a retention period of 90 days by using AWS Backup for Amazon RDS.

questions.explanation:
AWS Backup centrally automates Amazon RDS backup scheduling and lifecycle retention, allowing backup recovery points to be retained for 90 days without manually creating and deleting snapshots. RDS continuous/automated backups provide point-in-time recovery within their configured retention period, so a 14-day PITR window can be maintained alongside the longer-lived AWS Backup snapshots. Native RDS automated backups alone cannot use a 90-day retention period because their maximum retention is 35 days.

**Learn more:** [Amazon Relational Database Service backups - AWS Backup](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/aws-backup/latest/devguide/rds-backup.html) · [Backing up and restoring your Amazon RDS DB instance](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonRDS/latest/gettingstartedguide/managing-backup-restore.html)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],A company recently announced the deployment of its retail website to a global audience. The website runs on multiple Amazon EC2 instances behind an Elastic Load Balancer. The instances run in an Auto Scaling group across multiple Availability Zones.  
  
The company wants to provide its customers with different versions of content based on the devices that the customers use to access the website.  
  
Which combination of actions should a solutions architect take to meet these requirements? **(Choose two.)**

options.text: Configure Amazon CloudFront to cache multiple versions of the content.
Configure a host header in a Network Load Balancer to forward traffic to different instances.
Configure a Lambda@Edge function to send specific objects to users based on the User-Agent header.
Configure AWS Global Accelerator. Forward requests to a Network Load Balancer (NLB). Configure the NLB to set up host-based routing to different EC2 instances.
Configure AWS Global Accelerator. Forward requests to a Network Load Balancer (NLB). Configure the NLB to set up path-based routing to different EC2 instances.

questions.explanation:
Amazon CloudFront can cache separate versions of the same content for different device types, using CloudFront device headers that are derived from the viewer’s `User-Agent`. Lambda@Edge can then inspect request information such as the `User-Agent` header and direct viewers to the appropriate device-specific objects. This combination satisfies the requirement to deliver different content versions by device. The Network Load Balancer options are not suitable because NLB operates at Layer 4 and does not provide host-based or path-based routing for this use case; those are Application Load Balancer capabilities.

**Learn more:** [Cache content based on request headers - Amazon CloudFront](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonCloudFront/latest/DeveloperGuide/header-caching.html) · [Add CloudFront request headers - Amazon CloudFront](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonCloudFront/latest/DeveloperGuide/adding-cloudfront-headers.html)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],A company has an on-premises MySQL database that the global sales team uses, with infrequent access patterns. The sales team requires minimal downtime for the database. A database administrator wants to migrate this database to AWS without choosing a specific instance type in anticipation of more users in the future.  
  
Which service should a solutions architect recommend?

options.text: Amazon Aurora MySQL
Amazon Aurora Serverless for MySQL
Amazon Redshift Spectrum
Amazon RDS for MySQL

questions.explanation:
Amazon Aurora Serverless for MySQL is the best fit because it supports MySQL compatibility while avoiding the need to choose a fixed DB instance class up front. Aurora Serverless is intended for variable or infrequent usage patterns and automatically adjusts database capacity as demand changes, which aligns with expected future growth. By contrast, Amazon RDS for MySQL and provisioned Amazon Aurora MySQL require selecting DB instance classes, and Amazon Redshift Spectrum is an analytics feature for querying data in Amazon S3 rather than a managed MySQL transactional database service.

**Learn more:** [Amazon Aurora Serverless](https://aws.amazon.com/rds/aurora/serverless/) · [What is Amazon Relational Database Service (Amazon RDS)?](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonRDS/latest/UserGuide/Welcome.html)

A company is moving a legacy application to AWS. The application runs a batch job once every hour and is CPU-intensive. On an on-premises server, the batch job takes 15 minutes on average. That server has 64 virtual CPUs (vCPUs) and 512 GiB of memory.  
  
Which solution will execute the batch job within 15 minutes with the **LEAST operational overhead**?

options.text: Use AWS Lambda with functional scaling.
Use Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) with AWS Fargate.
Use Amazon Lightsail with AWS Auto Scaling.
Use AWS Batch on Amazon EC2.

questions.explanation:
AWS Batch is the AWS service designed specifically for batch and compute-intensive jobs. It is a fully managed batch computing service that plans, schedules, and runs containerized batch workloads, and it can scale compute capacity for those jobs automatically. The Amazon EC2 compute option in AWS Batch can provide the larger CPU and memory capacity that a workload comparable to a 64-vCPU, 512-GiB server may require. Lambda does not provide that class of per-job compute capacity, and ECS with Fargate is a general container runtime rather than a purpose-built batch scheduler. Therefore, AWS Batch on Amazon EC2 best satisfies the performance target with the least operational overhead among the listed choices.

**Learn more:** [What is AWS Batch?](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/batch/latest/userguide/what-is-batch.html) · [Managed compute environments - AWS Batch](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/batch/latest/userguide/managed_compute_environments.html)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],A company plans to move its data to an Amazon S3 bucket. The data must be encrypted while stored in the S3 bucket. In addition, the encryption key must be rotated automatically every year.  
  
Which solution will meet these requirements with the **LEAST operational overhead**?

options.text: Move the data to the S3 bucket. Use server-side encryption with Amazon S3 managed encryption keys (SSE-S3). Use the built-in key rotation behavior of SSE-S3 encryption keys.

Create an AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) customer managed key. Enable automatic key rotation. Set the S3 bucket’s default encryption behavior to use the customer managed KMS key. Move the data to the S3 bucket.

Create an AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) customer managed key. Set the S3 bucket’s default encryption behavior to use the customer managed KMS key. Move the data to the S3 bucket. Manually rotate the KMS key every year.

Encrypt the data with customer key material before moving the data to the S3 bucket. Create an AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) key without key material. Import the customer key material into the KMS key. Enable automatic key rotation.

questions.explanation:
Using Amazon S3 default encryption with SSE-KMS and an AWS KMS customer managed key satisfies both requirements: the objects are encrypted at rest in S3, and AWS KMS can automatically rotate a customer managed symmetric key on a 365-day schedule. This is the lowest-overhead option that directly gives customer-configurable annual automatic rotation. SSE-S3 does not provide a customer-managed annual rotation setting for this requirement, manual KMS rotation adds administration, and KMS keys with imported key material do not support automatic rotation.

**Learn more:** [Rotate AWS KMS keys - AWS Key Management Service](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/kms/latest/developerguide/rotate-keys.html) · [Enable automatic key rotation - AWS Key Management Service](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/kms/latest/developerguide/rotating-keys-enable.html)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],A company has multiple AWS accounts that use consolidated billing. The company runs several active, high-performance Amazon RDS for Oracle On-Demand DB instances for 90 days. The company’s finance team has access to AWS Trusted Advisor in the consolidated billing account and in all other AWS accounts.  
  
The finance team needs to use the correct AWS account to access the Trusted Advisor check recommendations for RDS. The team must review the appropriate Trusted Advisor check to reduce RDS costs.  
  
Which combination of steps should the finance team take to meet these requirements? **(Choose two.)**

options.text: Use the Trusted Advisor recommendations from the account where the RDS instances are running.
Use the Trusted Advisor recommendations from the consolidated billing account to see all RDS instance checks at the same time.
Review the Trusted Advisor check for Amazon RDS Reserved Instance Optimization.
Review the Trusted Advisor check for Amazon RDS Idle DB Instances.
Review the Trusted Advisor check for Amazon Redshift Reserved Node Optimization.

questions.explanation:
AWS Trusted Advisor recommendations for service resources are generally viewed in the account that owns and runs those resources, so the finance team should use the account where the Amazon RDS instances are running. To reduce cost for active Amazon RDS for Oracle On-Demand DB instances that have been running for an extended period, the relevant Trusted Advisor cost check is **Amazon RDS Reserved Instance Optimization**, which identifies long-running On-Demand DB instances that are good candidates for Reserved DB instances. Consolidated billing can share Reserved Instance benefits across accounts for billing, but that does not make the consolidated billing account the correct place to view every member account’s normal RDS Trusted Advisor recommendation.

**Learn more:** [Organizational view for AWS Trusted Advisor](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/awssupport/latest/user/organizational-view.html) · [Consolidating billing for AWS Organizations](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/awsaccountbilling/latest/aboutv2/consolidated-billing.html)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],A company has an application that customers use to upload images to an Amazon S3 bucket. Each night, the company starts an Amazon EC2 Spot Fleet to process all images that were received that day. Processing each image takes 2 minutes and requires 512 MB of memory.  
  
A solutions architect needs to modify the application so the images are processed when they are uploaded.  
  
Which change will meet these requirements **MOST cost-effectively**?

options.text: Use S3 Event Notifications to write a message with image details to an Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) queue. Configure an AWS Lambda function to read the messages from the queue and to process the images.

Use S3 Event Notifications to write a message with image details to an Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) queue. Configure an EC2 Reserved Instance to read the messages from the queue and to process the images.

Use S3 Event Notifications to publish a message with image details to an Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS) topic. Configure a container instance in Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) to subscribe to the topic and to process the images.

Use S3 Event Notifications to publish a message with image details to an Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS) topic. Configure an AWS Elastic Beanstalk application to subscribe to the topic and to process the images.

questions.explanation:
AWS Lambda is the most cost-effective fit for per-upload, event-driven image processing because it runs only when needed and the stated workload fits within Lambda’s limits: 2 minutes of processing is well below the 15-minute maximum execution time. Amazon S3 supports event notifications to Amazon SQS, and Lambda can consume from SQS to process each uploaded image asynchronously without maintaining always-on servers. Using Reserved Instances, ECS container instances, or Elastic Beanstalk would require provisioned compute and would generally cost more for this short, sporadic processing pattern.

**Learn more:** [Event notification types and destinations - Amazon S3](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/notification-how-to-event-types-and-destinations.html) · [Configure Lambda function timeout - AWS Lambda](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/lambda/latest/dg/configuration-timeout.html)

A company has built an application by using Docker containers and must run the application in the AWS Cloud by using a managed service to host it.  
  
The solution must:  
  
- scale in and out appropriately based on demand for the individual container services  
- avoid creating additional operational overhead or infrastructure to manage  
  
Which solutions meet these requirements? **(Choose two.)**

options.text: Use Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) with AWS Fargate.
Use Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS) with AWS Fargate.
Provision an Amazon API Gateway API. Connect the API to AWS Lambda to run the containers.
Use Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) with Amazon EC2 worker nodes.
Use Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS) with Amazon EC2 worker nodes.

questions.explanation:
AWS Fargate is a serverless compute option for containers that removes the need to provision and manage underlying servers. With Amazon ECS on AWS Fargate, containerized services can be deployed and scaled without managing EC2 container instances. With Amazon EKS on AWS Fargate, Kubernetes Pods run on Fargate without managing worker nodes. The EC2-based ECS and EKS options add infrastructure management overhead, and API Gateway with Lambda is not the managed container-service model described for independently scaling container services.

**Learn more:** [What is Amazon Elastic Container Service?](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonECS/latest/developerguide/Welcome.html) · [Amazon ECS launch types and capacity providers](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonECS/latest/developerguide/capacity-launch-type-comparison.html)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],A company runs a monolithic web application on an Amazon EC2 instance. Application users have recently reported degraded performance at particular times. Analysis of Amazon CloudWatch metrics indicates that CPU utilization reaches 100% during the periods of poor performance.  
  
The company needs to resolve this performance problem and improve application availability.  
  
Which combination of steps will satisfy these requirements in the MOST cost-effective manner? (Choose two.)

options.text: Use AWS Compute Optimizer to obtain a recommendation for an instance type to scale vertically.
Create an Amazon Machine Image (AMI) from the web server. Reference the AMI in a new launch template.
Create an Auto Scaling group and an Application Load Balancer to scale vertically.
Use AWS Compute Optimizer to obtain a recommendation for an instance type to scale horizontally.
Create an Auto Scaling group and an Application Load Balancer to scale horizontally.

questions.explanation:
An AMI captured from the existing web server and referenced by a launch template provides the consistent instance configuration required for an Auto Scaling group. An Auto Scaling group scales out by launching additional EC2 instances, and an Application Load Balancer distributes requests across healthy instances, preventing one instance from being overwhelmed and eliminating the single-instance availability dependency. AWS documents that launch templates for Auto Scaling include the AMI configuration, and that Elastic Load Balancing distributes application traffic across the EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group.

**Learn more:** [Create a launch template for an Auto Scaling group](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/autoscaling/ec2/userguide/create-launch-template.html) · [Use Elastic Load Balancing to distribute incoming application traffic in your Auto Scaling group](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/autoscaling/ec2/userguide/autoscaling-load-balancer.html)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],A company manages AWS accounts by using AWS Organizations. AWS IAM Identity Center (AWS Single Sign-On) and AWS Control Tower are configured for the accounts. The company wants to manage permissions for multiple users across all the accounts.  
  
The permissions will be used by multiple IAM users and must be separated between the developer and administrator teams. Each team needs different permissions. The company wants a solution that will also accommodate new users who are hired for either team.  
  
Which solution will meet these requirements with the **LEAST operational overhead**?

options.text: Create individual users in IAM Identity Center for each account. Create separate developer and administrator groups in IAM Identity Center. Assign the users to the appropriate groups. Create a custom IAM policy for each group to set fine-grained permissions.

Create individual users in IAM Identity Center for each account. Create separate developer and administrator groups in IAM Identity Center. Assign the users to the appropriate groups. Attach AWS managed IAM policies to each user as needed for fine-grained permissions.

Create individual users in IAM Identity Center. Create new developer and administrator groups in IAM Identity Center. Create new permission sets that include the appropriate IAM policies for each group. Assign the new groups to the appropriate accounts. Assign the new permission sets to the new groups. When new users are hired, add them to the appropriate group.

Create individual users in IAM Identity Center. Create new permission sets that include the appropriate IAM policies for each user. Assign the users to the appropriate accounts. Grant additional IAM permissions to the users from within specific accounts. When new users are hired, add them to IAM Identity Center and assign them to the accounts.

questions.explanation:
The lowest-overhead approach is to use AWS IAM Identity Center groups together with permission sets. Permission sets are the IAM Identity Center mechanism for defining permissions across one or more AWS accounts, and AWS recommends assigning access to groups rather than directly to individual users. By creating developer and administrator groups, creating permission sets with the appropriate IAM policies, assigning those permission sets to the groups for the required accounts, and then adding new hires to the correct group, the company gets centralized, reusable, team-based access management across all accounts with minimal ongoing administration.

**Learn more:** [Assign user or group access to AWS accounts - AWS IAM Identity Center](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/singlesignon/latest/userguide/assignusers.html) · [Manage AWS accounts with permission sets - AWS IAM Identity Center](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/singlesignon/latest/userguide/permissionsetsconcept.html)

A company is designing a web application on AWS. The application will use a VPN connection between the company’s existing data centers and the company's VPCs.  
  
The company uses Amazon Route 53 as its DNS service. The application must use private DNS records to communicate with the on-premises services from a VPC.  
  
Which solution will meet these requirements in the **MOST secure** manner?

options.text: Create a Route 53 Resolver outbound endpoint. Create a resolver rule. Associate the resolver rule with the VPC.
Create a Route 53 Resolver inbound endpoint. Create a resolver rule. Associate the resolver rule with the VPC.
Create a Route 53 private hosted zone. Associate the private hosted zone with the VPC.
Create a Route 53 public hosted zone. Create a record for each service to allow service communication

questions.explanation:
To let workloads in a VPC resolve private DNS names for on-premises services, Amazon Route 53 Resolver must forward matching DNS queries from the VPC to the on-premises DNS servers. AWS documents that this pattern uses a **Route 53 Resolver outbound endpoint** and **Resolver rules** associated with the VPC. Inbound endpoints are for the reverse direction, when on-premises resolvers need to resolve AWS private DNS names. Public hosted zones are internet-facing, and a private hosted zone does not by itself forward VPC DNS queries to authoritative DNS servers in the on-premises environment.

**Learn more:** [Resolving DNS queries between VPCs and your network - Amazon Route 53](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/Route53/latest/DeveloperGuide/resolver-overview-DSN-queries-to-vpc.html) · [How Resolver endpoints forward DNS queries from your VPCs to your network - Amazon Route 53](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/Route53/latest/DeveloperGuide/resolver-overview-forward-vpc-to-network.html)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],A company's near-real-time streaming application runs on AWS. As data is ingested, a job runs against the data and requires 30 minutes to finish. The workload often experiences high latency because of large volumes of incoming data. A solutions architect must design a scalable, serverless solution to improve performance.  
  
Which combination of steps should the solutions architect take? *(Choose two.)*

options.text: Use Amazon Kinesis Data Firehose to ingest the data.
Use AWS Lambda with AWS Step Functions to process the data.
Use AWS Database Migration Service (AWS DMS) to ingest the data.
Use Amazon EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group to process the data.
Use AWS Fargate with Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) to process the data.

questions.explanation:
Amazon Data Firehose is a fully managed service for ingesting and delivering real-time streaming data, which makes it suitable for the serverless ingestion layer. The processing component cannot rely on AWS Lambda because Lambda invocations are limited to 15 minutes, while the job runs for 30 minutes. AWS Fargate with Amazon ECS provides serverless container-based compute that can scale without managing servers, making it a better fit for longer-running stream-processing tasks.

**Learn more:** [What is Amazon Data Firehose?](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/firehose/latest/dev/what-is-this-service.html) · [Configure Lambda function timeout - AWS Lambda](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/lambda/latest/dg/configuration-timeout.html)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],A media company gathers and analyzes user activity data on premises and wants to move this capability to AWS.  
  
The user activity data store will keep growing and will be **petabytes** in size. The company must build a **highly available** data ingestion solution that supports **on-demand analytics** of both **existing data** and **new data** by using **SQL**.  
  
Which solution will meet these requirements with the **LEAST operational overhead**?

options.text: Send activity data to an Amazon Kinesis data stream. Configure the stream to deliver the data to an Amazon S3 bucket.
Send activity data to an Amazon Kinesis Data Firehose delivery stream. Configure the stream to deliver the data to an Amazon Redshift cluster.
Place activity data in an Amazon S3 bucket. Configure Amazon S3 to run an AWS Lambda function on the data as the data arrives in the S3 bucket.
Create an ingestion service on Amazon EC2 instances that are spread across multiple Availability Zones. Configure the service to forward data to an Amazon RDS Multi-AZ database.

questions.explanation:
Amazon Kinesis Data Firehose is a fully managed streaming delivery service that automatically scales to deliver large volumes of data to Amazon S3 with minimal operational overhead. Amazon Redshift is a fully managed, petabyte-scale data warehouse designed for SQL analytics. This combination provides managed infrastructure for both ingestion and analytics without requiring manual scaling or complex consumer logic.

**Learn more:** [Amazon Data Firehose destination settings (Redshift)](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/firehose/latest/dev/create-destination.html) · [What is Amazon Data Firehose?](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/firehose/latest/dev/what-is-this-service.html)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],A company is moving an application from an on-premises environment to Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS). To meet requirements, the company must use a custom subnet for pods in the company’s VPC. The company must also ensure that pods can communicate securely within the pods’ VPC.  
  
Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Configure AWS Transit Gateway to directly manage custom subnet configurations for the pods in Amazon EKS.
Create an AWS Direct Connect connection from the company's on-premises IP address ranges to the EKS pods.
Use the Amazon VPC CNI plugin for Kubernetes. Define custom subnets in the VPC cluster for the pods to use.
Implement a Kubernetes network policy that has pod anti-affinity rules to restrict pod placement to specific nodes that are within custom subnets.

questions.explanation:
The Amazon VPC CNI plugin for Kubernetes supports custom networking for Amazon EKS. Custom networking uses ENIConfig resources to specify alternate VPC subnets and security groups for pod network interfaces, giving pods VPC-routable IP addresses from the required custom subnet while allowing VPC security controls to protect their traffic.

**Learn more:** [Deploy Pods in alternate subnets with custom networking - Amazon EKS](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/eks/latest/userguide/cni-custom-network.html) · [Custom Networking - Amazon EKS Best Practices Guide](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/eks/latest/best-practices/custom-networking.html)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],A company recently migrated its web application to the AWS Cloud. The company uses an Amazon EC2 instance to run multiple processes that host the application. The processes include an Apache web server that serves static content. The Apache web server sends requests to a PHP application that uses a local Redis server for user sessions.  
  
The company wants to redesign the architecture to be highly available and to use AWS managed solutions.  
  
Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Use AWS Elastic Beanstalk to host the static content and the PHP application. Configure Elastic Beanstalk to deploy its EC2 instance into a public subnet. Assign a public IP address.

Use AWS Lambda to host the static content and the PHP application. Use an Amazon API Gateway REST API to proxy requests to the Lambda function. Set the API Gateway CORS configuration to respond to the domain name. Configure Amazon ElastiCache for Redis to handle session information.

Keep the backend code on the EC2 instance. Create an Amazon ElastiCache for Redis cluster that has Multi-AZ enabled. Configure the ElastiCache for Redis cluster in cluster mode. Copy the frontend resources to Amazon S3. Configure the backend code to reference the EC2 instance.

Configure an Amazon CloudFront distribution with an Amazon S3 endpoint to an S3 bucket that is configured to host the static content. Configure an Application Load Balancer that targets an Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) service that runs AWS Fargate tasks for the PHP application. Configure the PHP application to use an Amazon ElastiCache for Redis cluster that runs in multiple Availability Zones.

questions.explanation:
A highly available managed redesign should decouple the web tier into managed services: Amazon S3 with Amazon CloudFront is the standard managed pattern for static content, Amazon ECS with AWS Fargate behind an Application Load Balancer provides highly available managed compute for the PHP application across Availability Zones, and Amazon ElastiCache for Redis can provide managed session storage with Multi-AZ capabilities. Keeping the application on a single EC2 instance does not satisfy high availability, and Lambda plus API Gateway is not the appropriate direct replacement for hosting this kind of stateful PHP web tier with separate static assets. Therefore the architecture in choice D is the one that meets both requirements.

**Learn more:** [Get started with a secure static website - Amazon CloudFront](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonCloudFront/latest/DeveloperGuide/getting-started-secure-static-website-cloudformation-template.html) · [What is Amazon ElastiCache?](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonElastiCache/latest/dg/WhatIs.html)

options.text: Create an S3 bucket lifecycle policy to move files from S3 Standard to S3 Glacier 30 days from object creation. Delete the files 4 years after object creation.
Create an S3 bucket lifecycle policy to move files from S3 Standard to S3 One Zone-Infrequent Access (S3 One Zone-IA) 30 days from object creation. Delete the files 4 years after object creation.
Create an S3 bucket lifecycle policy to move files from S3 Standard to S3 Standard-Infrequent Access (S3 Standard-IA) 30 days from object creation. Delete the files 4 years after object creation.

Create an S3 bucket lifecycle policy to move files from S3 Standard to S3 Standard-Infrequent Access (S3 Standard-IA) 30 days from object creation. Move the files to S3 Glacier 4 years after object creation.

questions.explanation:
Amazon S3 Standard-IA is the best fit for data that becomes infrequently accessed after 30 days but still must remain available with millisecond access. It also preserves multi-Availability Zone resiliency, which is appropriate for critical data that is not easy to recreate. S3 One Zone-IA is cheaper but is intended for re-creatable data in a single AZ, and S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval does not provide immediate access. An S3 Lifecycle rule that transitions objects from S3 Standard to S3 Standard-IA after 30 days and expires them after 4 years matches both the access pattern and the retention requirement.

**Learn more:** [Understanding and managing Amazon S3 storage classes - Amazon S3 User Guide](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/storage-class-intro.html) · [Transitioning objects using Amazon S3 Lifecycle - Amazon S3 User Guide](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/lifecycle-transition-general-considerations.html)

A company is deploying an application in three AWS Regions by using an Application Load Balancer. Amazon Route 53 will distribute traffic across these Regions.  
  
Which Route 53 configuration should a solutions architect use to deliver the **MOST** high-performing experience?

options.text: Create an A record with a latency policy.
Create an A record with a geolocation policy.
Create a CNAME record with a failover policy.
Create a CNAME record with a geoproximity policy.

questions.explanation:
Latency-based routing is the Route 53 policy intended to direct users to the AWS Region that provides the lowest latency, which is the best fit when the goal is maximum performance across multiple regional deployments. For an Application Load Balancer, Route 53 should use an alias A record rather than a CNAME for the load balancer target. Geolocation and geoproximity policies are based on geographic location, not measured latency, and failover is for resilience rather than performance.

**Learn more:** [Transitioning to latency-based routing in Amazon Route 53](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/Route53/latest/DeveloperGuide/TutorialTransitionToLBR.html) · [Routing traffic to an ELB load balancer](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/Route53/latest/DeveloperGuide/routing-to-elb-load-balancer.html)

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],A company has built a multi-tier application for its ecommerce website. The website uses:  
  
- an Application Load Balancer in the public subnets,  
- a web tier in the public subnets, and  
- a MySQL cluster hosted on Amazon EC2 instances in the private subnets.  
  
The MySQL database must retrieve product catalog and pricing information that is hosted on the internet by a third-party provider.  
  
A solutions architect must design a strategy that maximizes security without increasing operational overhead.  
  
What should the solutions architect do to meet these requirements?

options.text: Deploy a NAT instance in the VPC. Route all the internet-based traffic through the NAT instance.
Deploy a NAT gateway in the public subnets. Modify the private subnet route table to direct all internet-bound traffic to the NAT gateway.
Configure an internet gateway and attach it to the VPModify the private subnet route table to direct internet-bound traffic to the internet gateway.
Configure a virtual private gateway and attach it to the VPC. Modify the private subnet route table to direct internet-bound traffic to the virtual private gateway.

questions.explanation:
A NAT gateway in a public subnet lets instances in private subnets initiate outbound internet connections while preventing unsolicited inbound connections, which preserves the security posture of the private MySQL tier. AWS documentation recommends NAT gateways over NAT instances because NAT gateways are managed by AWS and require less administration, while a virtual private gateway is for private network connectivity and an internet gateway does not provide secure outbound access for private-subnet instances by itself.

**Learn more:** [NAT gateways - Amazon VPC](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/userguide/vpc-nat-gateway.html) · [Connect to the internet or other networks using NAT devices - Amazon VPC](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/userguide/vpc-nat.html)

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],A company runs an application on AWS. The application receives inconsistent levels of usage. The application uses AWS Direct Connect to connect to an on-premises MySQL-compatible database. The on-premises database consistently uses a minimum of 2 GiB of memory.  
  
The company wants to migrate the on-premises database to a managed AWS service. The company wants to use auto scaling capabilities to handle unexpected workload increases.  
  
Which solution will meet these requirements with the **LEAST administrative overhead**?

options.text: Provision an Amazon DynamoDB database with default read and write capacity settings.
Provision an Amazon Aurora database with a minimum capacity of 1 Aurora capacity unit (ACU).
Provision an Amazon Aurora Serverless v2 database with a minimum capacity of 1 Aurora capacity unit (ACU).
Provision an Amazon RDS for MySQL database with 2 GiB of memory.

questions.explanation:
Amazon Aurora Serverless v2 is a managed relational service for Aurora MySQL-compatible databases that automatically scales compute capacity up and down based on demand, which minimizes administration for variable workloads. AWS documentation states that Aurora Serverless v2 uses Aurora capacity units (ACUs) and that each ACU provides approximately 2 GiB of memory, so configuring a minimum of 1 ACU matches the stated 2 GiB baseline while still allowing automatic scaling for spikes. Amazon RDS for MySQL does not automatically scale database compute for workload increases, and DynamoDB is not a drop-in MySQL-compatible replacement.

**Learn more:** [How Aurora Serverless v2 works - Amazon Aurora](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/en_en/AmazonRDS/latest/AuroraUserGuide/aurora-serverless-v2.how-it-works.html) · [Requirements and limitations for Aurora Serverless v2 - Amazon Aurora](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonRDS/latest/AuroraUserGuide/aurora-serverless-v2.requirements.html)
