A company has an on-premises application that generates a large volume of time-sensitive data and backs it up to Amazon S3. The application has grown, and users are complaining about internet bandwidth constraints.  
  
A solutions architect must design a **long-term** solution that provides both:  
  
- timely backups to Amazon S3, and  
- minimal impact on internet connectivity for internal users.  
  
Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Establish AWS VPN connections and proxy all traffic through a VPC gateway endpoint.
Establish a new AWS Direct Connect connection and direct backup traffic through this new connection.
Order daily AWS Snowball devices. Load the data onto the Snowball devices and return the devices to AWS each day.
Submit a support ticket through the AWS Management Console. Request the removal of S3 service limits from the account.

questions.explanation:
AWS Direct Connect is the correct long-term design because it provides a dedicated network connection from the on-premises environment to AWS and can use a public virtual interface to reach Amazon S3. This moves backup traffic off the company’s regular internet path, reducing contention for internal users while still supporting ongoing, time-sensitive transfers. A VPN with an S3 gateway endpoint does not solve this because gateway endpoints are for VPC traffic, not direct on-premises access. Snowball is intended for offline bulk transfer rather than continuous daily time-sensitive backups, and increasing S3 limits would not change the available internet bandwidth between the company and AWS.

**Learn more:** [What is Direct Connect?](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/directconnect/latest/UserGuide/prefix-controls.html) · [Create a Direct Connect public virtual interface](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/directconnect/latest/UserGuide/create-public-vif.html)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],A company needs to share accounting data with an external auditor. The data is stored in an Amazon RDS DB instance in a private subnet. The auditor has a separate AWS account and needs its own copy of the database.  
  
What is the **MOST secure** way for the company to share the database with the auditor?

options.text: Create a read replica of the database. Configure IAM standard database authentication to grant the auditor access.
Export the database contents to text files. Store the files in an Amazon S3 bucket. Create a new IAM user for the auditor. Grant the user access to the S3 bucket.
Copy a snapshot of the database to an Amazon S3 bucket. Create an IAM user. Share the user's keys with the auditor to grant access to the object in the S3 bucket.
Create an encrypted snapshot of the database. Share the snapshot with the auditor. Allow access to the AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) encryption key.

questions.explanation:
Amazon RDS supports sharing manual DB snapshots with specific AWS accounts, which lets the recipient create its own copy and restore its own DB instance. For sensitive accounting data, using an encrypted snapshot is the most secure approach. When the snapshot is encrypted, the source account must also allow the target account to use the relevant AWS KMS key so the auditor can copy or restore the snapshot in its own account. This matches AWS guidance for cross-account sharing of encrypted RDS snapshots.

**Learn more:** [Sharing a DB snapshot for Amazon RDS](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonRDS/latest/UserGuide/USER_ShareSnapshot.html) · [Sharing encrypted snapshots for Amazon RDS](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonRDS/latest/UserGuide/share-encrypted-snapshot.html)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],A company recently began using Amazon Aurora as the data store for its global ecommerce application. When large reports are executed, developers say that the ecommerce application performs poorly. After reviewing Amazon CloudWatch metrics, a solutions architect determines that the `ReadIOPS` and `CPUUtilization` metrics spike when the monthly reports run.  
  
What is the **MOST cost-effective** solution?

options.text: Migrate the monthly reporting to Amazon Redshift.
Migrate the monthly reporting to an Aurora Replica.
Migrate the Aurora database to a larger instance class.
Increase the Provisioned IOPS on the Aurora instance.

questions.explanation:
Aurora Replicas are designed to scale read workloads by serving read-only traffic from the same cluster volume, making them a good fit for reporting queries that are driving up `ReadIOPS` and `CPUUtilization` on the writer instance. Redirecting monthly reports to an Aurora Replica offloads the read contention from the primary database while requiring far less cost and change than migrating the reporting stack to Amazon Redshift or vertically scaling the database instance. Increasing Provisioned IOPS would not solve the CPU bottleneck and is not the primary optimization for this Aurora read-scaling scenario.

**Learn more:** [Replication with Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonRDS/latest/AuroraUserGuide/AuroraPostgreSQL.Replication.html) · [Amazon RDS Read Replicas](https://aws.amazon.com/rds/features/read-replicas/)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],An international company has one subdomain for each country in which it operates. The subdomains use the formats `example.com`, `country1.example.com`, and `country2.example.com`. The company's workloads are behind an Application Load Balancer. The company wants to encrypt website data while it is in transit.  
  
Which combination of steps will satisfy these requirements? **(Choose two.)**

options.text: Use the AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) console to request a public certificate for the apex top domain example com and a wildcard certificate for *.example.com.
Use the AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) console to request a private certificate for the apex top domain example.com and a wildcard certificate for *.example.com.
Use the AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) console to request a public and private certificate for the apex top domain example.com.
Validate domain ownership by email address. Switch to DNS validation by adding the required DNS records to the DNS provider.
Validate domain ownership for the domain by adding the required DNS records to the DNS provider.

questions.explanation:
For HTTPS on an Application Load Balancer, you attach an ACM certificate to the HTTPS listener. A wildcard certificate for `*.example.com` secures first-level subdomains such as `country1.example.com`, but it does not secure the apex domain `example.com`. To cover both, ACM should issue certificates including the apex domain and the wildcard domain as public certificates. ACM public certificates also require domain validation, and adding the required DNS records to the DNS provider is the correct validation method. Private ACM certificates are for private PKI use cases and are not the right choice for a public website behind an ALB.

**Learn more:** [Request a public certificate in AWS Certificate Manager](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/acm/latest/userguide/acm-public-certificates.html) · [AWS Certificate Manager public certificate characteristics and limitations](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/acm/latest/userguide/acm-certificate-characteristics.html)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],A company is building a new application that uses a relational database to retain user data and application configurations. The company anticipates steady growth in application users. Database use is expected to be variable and read-heavy, with occasional writes.  
  
The company needs to cost-optimize the database solution while using an AWS managed database service that supplies the required performance.  
  
Which solution will satisfy these requirements in the **MOST** cost-effective way?

options.text: Deploy the database on Amazon RDS. Use Provisioned IOPS SSD storage to ensure consistent performance for read and write operations.
Deploy the database on Amazon Aurora Serverless to automatically scale the database capacity based on actual usage to accommodate the workload.
Deploy the database on Amazon DynamoDB. Use on-demand capacity mode to automatically scale throughput to accommodate the workload.
Deploy the database on Amazon RDS. Use magnetic storage and use read replicas to accommodate the workload.

questions.explanation:
Amazon Aurora Serverless is a managed relational database configuration that automatically adjusts database capacity to match application demand. Its consumption-based capacity model avoids maintaining provisioned capacity that is not needed, while its scalable writer and reader capacity can support variable, read-heavy workloads.

**Learn more:** [Using Aurora Serverless](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonRDS/latest/AuroraUserGuide/aurora-serverless-v2.html) · [How Aurora Serverless works](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonRDS/latest/AuroraUserGuide/aurora-serverless-v2.how-it-works.html)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],A company wants to run an in-memory database for a latency-sensitive application on Amazon EC2 instances. The application handles more than 100,000 transactions per minute and requires high network throughput. A solutions architect must provide a cost-effective network design that minimizes data transfer charges.  
  
Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Launch all EC2 instances in the same Availability Zone within the same AWS Region. Specify a placement group with cluster strategy when launching EC2 instances.
Launch all EC2 instances in different Availability Zones within the same AWS Region. Specify a placement group with partition strategy when launching EC2 instances.
Deploy an Auto Scaling group to launch EC2 instances in different Availability Zones based on a network utilization target.
Deploy an Auto Scaling group with a step scaling policy to launch EC2 instances in different Availability Zones.

questions.explanation:
A cluster placement group places EC2 instances close together within a single Availability Zone, which is the AWS-recommended design for workloads that need low network latency and high network throughput. Keeping all instances in the same Availability Zone also avoids the regional data transfer charges that apply when traffic moves between Availability Zones in the same Region. That combination best fits a latency-sensitive, high-throughput in-memory database at the lowest network transfer cost.

**Learn more:** [Placement strategies for your placement groups - Amazon EC2](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSEC2/latest/UserGuide/placement-strategies.html) · [Placement groups for your Amazon EC2 instances - Amazon EC2](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSEC2/latest/UserGuide/placement-groups.html)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],A company hosts a website behind multiple Application Load Balancers. The company has different distribution rights for its content in various parts of the world. A solutions architect must ensure that users receive the correct content without violating those distribution rights.  
  
Which configuration should the solutions architect choose to meet these requirements?

options.text: Configure Amazon CloudFront with AWS WAF.
Configure Application Load Balancers with AWS WAF
Configure Amazon Route 53 with a geolocation policy
Configure Amazon Route 53 with a geoproximity routing policy

questions.explanation:
Amazon Route 53 geolocation routing is designed to route users based on their geographic location, and AWS documentation specifically states that it can be used to restrict distribution of content to only the locations where you have distribution rights. Geoproximity routing instead routes according to the locations of resources and optional bias, while AWS WAF controls request filtering rather than region-based content selection.

**Learn more:** [Geolocation routing - Amazon Route 53](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/Route53/latest/DeveloperGuide/routing-policy-geo.html) · [Choosing a routing policy - Amazon Route 53](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/Route53/latest/DeveloperGuide/routing-policy.html)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],A financial services company intends to launch a new application on AWS to process sensitive financial transactions. The company will deploy the application on Amazon EC2 instances and use Amazon RDS for MySQL as the database. Company security policies require data encryption both at rest and in transit.  
  
Which solution satisfies these requirements with the **LEAST** operational overhead?

options.text: Configure encryption at rest for Amazon RDS for MySQL by using AWS KMS managed keys. Configure AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) SSL/TLS certificates for encryption in transit.
Configure encryption at rest for Amazon RDS for MySQL by using AWS KMS managed keys. Configure IPsec tunnels for encryption in transit.
Implement third-party application-level data encryption before storing data in Amazon RDS for MySQL. Configure AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) SSL/TLS certificates for encryption in transit.
Configure encryption at rest for Amazon RDS for MySQL by using AWS KMS managed keys. Configure a VPN connection to enable private connectivity to encrypt data in transit.

questions.explanation:
Amazon RDS can encrypt a MySQL DB instance, including its storage, automated backups, read replicas, logs, and snapshots, by using an AWS KMS key. RDS for MySQL also supports SSL/TLS to encrypt application-client connections in transit. These managed service controls avoid the additional implementation and maintenance required for application-level encryption, IPsec tunnels, or VPN connectivity.

**Learn more:** [Encrypting Amazon RDS resources](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonRDS/latest/UserGuide/Overview.Encryption.html) · [Encrypting client connections with SSL/TLS to MySQL DB instances on Amazon RDS](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonRDS/latest/UserGuide/mysql-ssl-connections.html)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],A company has an application that processes customer orders. The company hosts the application on an Amazon EC2 instance that stores the orders in an Amazon Aurora database. Occasionally, when traffic is high, the workload cannot process orders quickly enough.  
  
What should a solutions architect do to ensure the orders are written to the database reliably and as fast as possible?

options.text: Increase the instance size of the EC2 instance when traffic is high. Write orders to Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS). Subscribe the database endpoint to the SNS topic.

Write orders to an Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) queue. Use EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group behind an Application Load Balancer to read from the SQS queue and process orders into the database.

Write orders to Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS). Subscribe the database endpoint to the SNS topic. Use EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group behind an Application Load Balancer to read from the SNS topic.

Write orders to an Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) queue when the EC2 instance reaches CPU threshold limits. Use scheduled scaling of EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group behind an Application Load Balancer to read from the SQS queue and process orders into the database.

questions.explanation:
Amazon SQS is a durable message queue used to decouple producers from consumers and absorb traffic spikes so requests are not lost while downstream processing catches up. A fleet of EC2 worker instances in an Auto Scaling group can scale out to read from the queue and write orders into Aurora at higher throughput. Amazon SNS is a pub/sub service, not a database write mechanism, and its supported subscription endpoints include services such as SQS, Lambda, HTTP/S, and Firehose—not an Aurora database endpoint. Using SQS plus scalable consumers is therefore the correct architecture for reliable, fast order processing under bursty load.

**Learn more:** [What is Amazon Simple Queue Service?](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSSimpleQueueService/latest/SQSDeveloperGuide/welcome.html) · [Amazon SQS queue types](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSSimpleQueueService/latest/SQSDeveloperGuide/sqs-queue-types.html)

A company that uses AWS is building an application to transfer data to a product manufacturer. The company has its own identity provider (IdP). The company wants the IdP to authenticate application users while the users use the application to transfer data. The company must use Applicability Statement 2 (AS2) protocol.  
  
Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Use AWS DataSync to transfer the data. Create an AWS Lambda function for IdP authentication.
Use Amazon AppFlow flows to transfer the data. Create an Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) task for IdP authentication.
Use AWS Transfer Family to transfer the data. Create an AWS Lambda function for IdP authentication.
Use AWS Storage Gateway to transfer the data. Create an Amazon Cognito identity pool for IdP authentication.

questions.explanation:
AWS Transfer Family is the AWS service that supports the AS2 protocol. AWS Transfer Family also provides custom identity provider integration, including AWS Lambda-based authentication flows for integrating an external IdP. The other services listed do not provide AS2-based managed file transfer for this use case, so the matching solution is AWS Transfer Family with Lambda-based IdP authentication.

**Learn more:** [Create an AS2 server - AWS Transfer Family](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/transfer/latest/userguide/create-as2-transfer-server.html) · [Using AWS Lambda to integrate your identity provider - AWS Transfer Family](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/transfer/latest/userguide/custom-lambda-idp.html)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],A company runs an application on Amazon EC2 instances. The company must implement a disaster recovery (DR) solution for the application.  
  
The DR solution must meet these requirements:  
  
- have a recovery time objective (RTO) of less than 4 hours  
- use the fewest possible AWS resources during normal operations  
  
Which solution will meet these requirements in the **MOST operationally efficient** way?

options.text: Create Amazon Machine Images (AMIs) to back up the EC2 instances. Copy the AMIs to a secondary AWS Region. Automate infrastructure deployment in the secondary Region by using AWS Lambda and custom scripts.
Create Amazon Machine Images (AMIs) to back up the EC2 instances. Copy the AMIs to a secondary AWS Region. Automate infrastructure deployment in the secondary Region by using AWS CloudFormation.
Launch EC2 instances in a secondary AWS Region. Keep the EC2 instances in the secondary Region active at all times.
Launch EC2 instances in a secondary Availability Zone. Keep the EC2 instances in the secondary Availability Zone active at all times.

questions.explanation:
The best fit is a backup-and-restore style DR approach that keeps only backups in a secondary Region during normal operations and provisions compute there only during recovery. That minimizes steady-state AWS resource usage while still aligning with an hours-level RTO. Using Amazon Machine Images copied to a secondary Region and deploying the recovery infrastructure with AWS CloudFormation is more operationally efficient than using Lambda with custom scripts because CloudFormation is AWS’s infrastructure-as-code service for predictable, repeatable provisioning. Keeping EC2 instances always running in another Region or Availability Zone consumes more resources continuously, and an additional Availability Zone is primarily a high-availability design rather than the best disaster recovery choice for a regional failure scenario.

**Learn more:** [Disaster recovery options in the cloud - AWS](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/whitepapers/latest/disaster-recovery-workloads-on-aws/disaster-recovery-options-in-the-cloud.html) · [Defining your disaster recovery strategy - AWS Prescriptive Guidance](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/prescriptive-guidance/latest/strategy-database-disaster-recovery/defining.html)

A company wants to host a scalable web application on AWS. The application will be accessed by users from multiple geographic regions around the world. Application users will be able to upload and download unique data that can be up to gigabytes in size. The development team wants a cost-effective solution that minimizes upload and download latency and maximizes performance.  
  
What should a solutions architect do to achieve this?

options.text: Use Amazon S3 with Transfer Acceleration to host the application.
Use Amazon S3 with CacheControl headers to host the application.
Use Amazon EC2 with Auto Scaling and Amazon CloudFront to host the application.
Use Amazon EC2 with Auto Scaling and Amazon ElastiCache to host the application.

questions.explanation:
Amazon S3 with Transfer Acceleration is the best fit because it is built to accelerate uploads and downloads to S3 for globally dispersed users by using AWS edge locations and the AWS backbone network. AWS documentation specifically describes S3 Transfer Acceleration as effective for minimizing latency caused by geographic distance and as ideal for applications that transfer large objects or have a lot of content to upload. That matches the need for unique multi-GB user data from worldwide regions more closely than CloudFront caching, Cache-Control headers, or ElastiCache.

**Learn more:** [Configuring fast, secure file transfers using Amazon S3 Transfer Acceleration](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/transfer-acceleration.html) · [Performance design patterns for Amazon S3](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/optimizing-performance-design-patterns.html)

options.text: Dedicated Reserved Hosts
Dedicated On-Demand Hosts
Dedicated Reserved Instances
Dedicated On-Demand Instances

questions.explanation:
Amazon EC2 Dedicated Hosts are the correct platform for software licensed by socket or core because they provide host-level visibility into physical sockets and cores and support bring-your-own-license for per-socket and per-core licenses. Since the workload has steady, predictable usage, reserving the host is more cost-effective than paying On-Demand rates. Dedicated Instances are not the best choice because BYOL support there is only partial and they do not provide the socket/core visibility required for this licensing model.

**Learn more:** [Bring your own software licenses to Amazon EC2 Dedicated Hosts](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSEC2/latest/UserGuide/dedicated-hosts-BYOL.html) · [Amazon EC2 Dedicated Hosts](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSEC2/latest/UserGuide/dedicated-hosts-overview.html)

A company runs a containerized application on a Kubernetes cluster in an on-premises data center. The company uses a MongoDB database for data storage. The company wants to migrate some of these environments to AWS, but no code changes or deployment-method changes are possible at this time. The company needs a solution that minimizes operational overhead.  
  
Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Use Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) with Amazon EC2 worker nodes for compute and MongoDB on EC2 for data storage.
Use Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) with AWS Fargate for compute and Amazon DynamoDB for data storage
Use Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS) with Amazon EC2 worker nodes for compute and Amazon DynamoDB for data storage.
Use Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS) with AWS Fargate for compute and Amazon DocumentDB (with MongoDB compatibility) for data storage.

questions.explanation:
Amazon EKS is the AWS service that preserves Kubernetes as the deployment platform, so the existing Kubernetes-based deployment method can remain in place. Using AWS Fargate with Amazon EKS minimizes operational overhead because AWS manages the compute infrastructure for pods instead of requiring the company to operate EC2 worker nodes. For the database layer, Amazon DocumentDB is a fully managed document database with MongoDB compatibility, making it the closest fit to an existing MongoDB application when code changes are not allowed. By contrast, ECS would require changing away from Kubernetes, DynamoDB would require application redesign, and EC2-based options increase operational management.

**Learn more:** [Get started with AWS Fargate for your cluster - Amazon EKS](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/eks/latest/userguide/fargate-getting-started.html) · [What is Amazon DocumentDB (with MongoDB compatibility)](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/documentdb/latest/devguide/what-is.html)

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],A company runs production and nonproduction workloads in multiple AWS accounts.  
  
The accounts are part of an organization in AWS Organizations.  
  
The company needs to design a solution that prevents modification of cost usage tags.  
  
Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Create a custom AWS Config rule to prevent tag modification except by authorized principals.
Create a custom trail in AWS CloudTrail to prevent tag modification.
Create a service control policy (SCP) to prevent tag modification except by authorized principals.
Create custom Amazon CloudWatch logs to prevent tag modification.

questions.explanation:
A service control policy (SCP) is the AWS Organizations mechanism used to apply preventive permission guardrails across multiple member accounts. By using an SCP with deny statements for tag-modification actions, and exempting only authorized principals through conditions, the organization can stop unauthorized changes before they occur. AWS Config, AWS CloudTrail, and Amazon CloudWatch Logs can detect, record, or monitor changes, but they do not enforce preventive access control. AWS documentation states that SCPs restrict what principals in affected accounts can do, while cost allocation tags are user-defined tags used for cost tracking and can be activated for billing purposes.

**Learn more:** [Restrict access using AWS Organizations service control policies](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/accounts/latest/reference/using-orgs-example-scps.html) · [Authorization policies in AWS Organizations](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/organizations/latest/userguide/orgs_manage_policies_authorization_policies.html)

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],A company has an on-premises MySQL database that manages transactional data. The company is migrating this database to the AWS Cloud. The migrated database must preserve compatibility with the company's applications that use the database. The migrated database also must scale automatically during periods of increased demand.  
  
Which migration solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Use native MySQL tools to migrate the database to Amazon RDS for MySQL. Configure elastic storage scaling.
Migrate the database to Amazon Redshift by using the mysqldump utility. Turn on Auto Scaling for the Amazon Redshift cluster.
Use AWS Database Migration Service (AWS DMS) to migrate the database to Amazon Aurora. Turn on Aurora Auto Scaling.
Use AWS Database Migration Service (AWS DMS) to migrate the database to Amazon DynamoDB. Configure an Auto Scaling policy.

questions.explanation:
Amazon Aurora is the correct fit because Aurora MySQL is compatible with MySQL applications, and Aurora Auto Scaling can automatically add or remove Aurora Replicas to respond to increases in workload. AWS Database Migration Service (AWS DMS) is a standard AWS service for migrating databases into AWS-managed database platforms such as Aurora. Amazon Redshift is intended for analytics rather than as a MySQL-compatible transactional database, and DynamoDB is a NoSQL service that would require application changes. Amazon RDS for MySQL storage autoscaling increases storage only, not database processing capacity.

**Learn more:** [Amazon Aurora Auto Scaling with Aurora Replicas](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonRDS/latest/AuroraUserGuide/Aurora.Integrating.AutoScaling.html) · [Aurora MySQL version 3 compatible with MySQL 8.0](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonRDS/latest/AuroraUserGuide/AuroraMySQL.MySQL80.html)

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],A company that runs its web application on AWS wants to make sure that all Amazon EC2 instances, Amazon RDS DB instances, and Amazon Redshift clusters have tags configured.  
  
The company wants to minimize the effort required to configure and operate this check.  
  
What should a solutions architect do to achieve this?

options.text: Use AWS Config rules to define and detect resources that are not properly tagged.
Use Cost Explorer to display resources that are not properly tagged. Tag those resources manually.
Write API calls to check all resources for proper tag allocation. Periodically run the code on an EC2 instance.
Write API calls to check all resources for proper tag allocation. Schedule an AWS Lambda function through Amazon CloudWatch to periodically run the code.

questions.explanation:
AWS Config managed rules are the lowest-effort way to evaluate whether AWS resources have required tags. The AWS Config `REQUIRED_TAGS` rule checks specified resources for tag keys you define, and AWS documentation lists support for `AWS::EC2::Instance`, `AWS::RDS::DBInstance`, and `AWS::Redshift::Cluster`. That satisfies the tagging-compliance requirement without building and operating custom API-based code.

**Learn more:** [required-tags - AWS Config](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/config/latest/developerguide/required-tags.html) · [Supported Resource Types for AWS Config - AWS Config](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/config/latest/developerguide/resource-config-reference.html)

A company operates an employee web portal. Employees sign in to the portal to view payroll details. The company is developing a new system that lets employees upload scanned documents for reimbursement. The company runs a program that extracts text-based data from the documents and attaches the extracted information to each employee’s reimbursement IDs for processing.  
  
The employee web portal requires 100% uptime. The document-extraction program runs infrequently throughout the day on an on-demand basis. The company wants to build a scalable, cost-effective new system that requires minimal changes to the existing web portal. The company does not want to make any code changes.  
  
Which solution meets these requirements with the **LEAST** implementation effort?

options.text: Run Amazon EC2 On-Demand Instances in an Auto Scaling group for the web portal. Use an AWS Lambda function to run the document extract program. Invoke the Lambda function when an employee uploads a new reimbursement document.

Run Amazon EC2 Spot Instances in an Auto Scaling group for the web portal. Run the document extract program on EC2 Spot Instances. Start document extract program instances when an employee uploads a new reimbursement document.
Purchase a Savings Plan to run the web portal and the document extract program. Run the web portal and the document extract program in an Auto Scaling group.

Create an Amazon S3 bucket to host the web portal. Use Amazon API Gateway and an AWS Lambda function for the existing functionalities. Use the Lambda function to run the document extract program. Invoke the Lambda function when the API that is associated with a new document upload is called.

questions.explanation:
On-Demand EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group provide a suitable highly available, scalable hosting approach for the existing portal, while AWS Lambda is cost-effective for infrequent event-driven document extraction because it runs only when invoked. Spot Instances can be interrupted and are not appropriate for a workload requiring uninterrupted availability. Replacing the portal with an S3, API Gateway, and Lambda architecture would require substantially more implementation effort. Amazon S3 can invoke a Lambda function in response to object events, and Lambda can process S3 event notifications.

**Learn more:** [Process Amazon S3 event notifications with Lambda](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/lambda/latest/dg/with-s3.html) · [Best practices for Amazon EC2 Spot](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSEC2/latest/UserGuide/spot-best-practices.html)

An image-hosting company keeps its objects in Amazon S3 buckets. The company wants to prevent accidental public exposure of the objects in those S3 buckets. All S3 objects across the entire AWS account must stay private.  
  
Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Use Amazon GuardDuty to monitor S3 bucket policies. Create an automatic remediation action rule that uses an AWS Lambda function to remediate any change that makes the objects public.

Use AWS Trusted Advisor to find publicly accessible S3 buckets. Configure email notifications in Trusted Advisor when a change is detected. Manually change the S3 bucket policy if it allows public access.

Use AWS Resource Access Manager to find publicly accessible S3 buckets. Use Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS) to invoke an AWS Lambda function when a change is detected. Deploy a Lambda function that programmatically remediates the change.

Use the S3 Block Public Access feature on the account level. Use AWS Organizations to create a service control policy (SCP) that prevents IAM users from changing the setting. Apply the SCP to the account.

questions.explanation:
Amazon S3 Block Public Access is designed to centrally prevent public access to S3 resources at the account level, including future buckets and objects. AWS documentation states that S3 evaluates account-level Block Public Access settings and that these settings override permissions that would otherwise make buckets or objects public. Using an AWS Organizations service control policy to deny changes to the Block Public Access configuration ensures IAM users in the account cannot disable or weaken that protection. This is the only option that provides preventive, account-wide enforcement instead of detection followed by remediation.

**Learn more:** [Blocking public access to your Amazon S3 storage - Amazon S3 User Guide](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/access-control-block-public-access.html) · [Configuring block public access settings for your S3 buckets - Amazon S3 User Guide](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/configuring-block-public-access-bucket.html)

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],A solutions architect needs all newly created users to have specific complexity requirements and required rotation periods for IAM user passwords.  
  
What should the solutions architect do to achieve this?

options.text: Set an overall password policy for the entire AWS account.
Set a password policy for each IAM user in the AWS account.
Use third-party vendor software to set password requirements.
Attach an Amazon CloudWatch rule to the Create_newuser event to set the password with the appropriate requirements.

questions.explanation:
In AWS Identity and Access Management, password strength rules and password expiration settings for IAM users are controlled by the account password policy. That policy applies across the AWS account rather than being configured separately for each IAM user. This is the AWS-native mechanism for enforcing complexity requirements and mandatory rotation periods for new and existing IAM user passwords.

**Learn more:** [Set an account password policy for IAM users - AWS Identity and Access Management](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/id_credentials_passwords_account-policy.html) · [GetAccountPasswordPolicy - AWS Identity and Access Management](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/APIReference/API_GetAccountPasswordPolicy.html)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],A company hosts a web application on Amazon EC2 instances across multiple Availability Zones. The EC2 instances reside in private subnets. A solutions architect deploys an internet-facing Application Load Balancer (ALB) and configures the EC2 instances as the target group. However, internet traffic is not reaching the EC2 instances.  
  
How should the solutions architect reconfigure the architecture to fix this issue?

options.text: Replace the ALB with a Network Load Balancer. Configure a NAT gateway in a public subnet to allow internet traffic.
Move the EC2 instances to public subnets. Add a rule to the EC2 instances’ security groups to allow outbound traffic to 0.0.0.0/0.

Update the route tables for the EC2 instances’ subnets to send 0.0.0.0/0 traffic through the internet gateway route. Add a rule to the EC2 instances’ security groups to allow outbound traffic to 0.0.0.0/0.
Create public subnets in each Availability Zone. Associate the public subnets with the ALB. Update the route tables for the public subnets with a route to the private subnets.

questions.explanation:
An internet-facing Application Load Balancer must be deployed in public subnets (subnets with routes to an internet gateway) to receive inbound internet traffic. The EC2 instances can remain in private subnets because the ALB communicates with targets through the local VPC network. The route tables for public subnets need a route to send 0.0.0.0/0 to the internet gateway, while private subnet route tables can route to the targets directly via local routes.

**Learn more:** [Subnets for your Application Load Balancer](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/elasticloadbalancing/latest/application/application-load-balancers.html) · [Update Availability Zones for your ALB](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/elasticloadbalancing/latest/application/load-balancer-subnets.html)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],A solutions architect is designing a highly available Amazon ElastiCache for Redis–based solution. The solutions architect must ensure that failures do not cause performance degradation or data loss locally and within an AWS Region. The solution must provide high availability at both:  
  
- the node level  
- the Region level  
  
Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Use Multi-AZ Redis replication groups with shards that contain multiple nodes.
Use Redis shards that contain multiple nodes with Redis append only files (AOF) turned on.
Use a Multi-AZ Redis cluster with more than one read replica in the replication group.
Use Redis shards that contain multiple nodes with Auto Scaling turned on.

questions.explanation:
Amazon ElastiCache for Redis achieves high availability within an AWS Region by using Multi-AZ replication groups with automatic failover, so if a primary node fails, a replica in another Availability Zone can be promoted. Using shards that contain multiple nodes adds node-level resilience for a Redis deployment that is distributed across node groups. Append-only files improve persistence but do not provide automatic high availability, and Auto Scaling does not address failover or data redundancy. AWS documentation states that Redis replication groups with replicas provide Multi-AZ and automatic failover, which is the feature set that satisfies these requirements.

**Learn more:** [Minimizing downtime in ElastiCache by using Multi-AZ with Valkey and Redis OSS](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonElastiCache/latest/dg/AutoFailover.html) · [Replication: Valkey and Redis OSS Cluster Mode Disabled vs. Enabled](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonElastiCache/latest/dg/Replication.Redis-RedisCluster.html)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],A large media company runs a web application on AWS. The company wants to begin caching confidential media files so that users worldwide will have reliable access to the files. The content is stored in Amazon S3 buckets. The company must deliver the content rapidly, regardless of the geographic location from which requests originate.  
  
Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Use AWS DataSync to connect the S3 buckets to the web application.
Deploy AWS Global Accelerator to connect the S3 buckets to the web application.
Deploy Amazon CloudFront to connect the S3 buckets to CloudFront edge servers.
Use Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) to connect the S3 buckets to the web application.

questions.explanation:
Amazon CloudFront is the AWS content delivery network designed to cache content at global edge locations so users can retrieve S3-hosted media with low latency from anywhere in the world. For confidential files, CloudFront can restrict access to private content by using signed URLs or signed cookies and by preventing direct access to the underlying S3 objects. That combination satisfies both the global performance requirement and the confidentiality requirement.

**Learn more:** [Restrict access to files - Amazon CloudFront](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonCloudFront/latest/DeveloperGuide/private-content-overview.html) · [Use signed URLs - Amazon CloudFront](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonCloudFront/latest/DeveloperGuide/private-content-signed-urls.html)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],A company is building a new application that will store a large volume of data. The data will be analyzed every hour and modified by several Amazon EC2 Linux instances deployed across multiple Availability Zones. The required storage capacity will keep increasing for the next 6 months.  
  
Which storage solution should a solutions architect recommend to meet these requirements?

options.text: Store the data in Amazon S3 Glacier. Update the S3 Glacier vault policy to allow access to the application instances.
Store the data in an Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) volume. Mount the EBS volume on the application instances.
Store the data in an Amazon Elastic File System (Amazon EFS) file system. Mount the file system on the application instances.
Store the data in an Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) Provisioned IOPS volume shared between the application instances.

questions.explanation:
Amazon Elastic File System (Amazon EFS) is the best fit because it provides elastic shared file storage for Linux workloads and can be mounted concurrently by multiple Amazon EC2 instances across multiple Availability Zones. It is designed to scale as storage grows without needing to provision capacity in advance. Amazon EBS volumes are limited to instances in the same Availability Zone, and even Multi-Attach Provisioned IOPS volumes are only supported within a single Availability Zone. Amazon S3 Glacier storage classes are intended for infrequently accessed archival data with longer retrieval times, not for data that is modified regularly and analyzed hourly.

**Learn more:** [How Amazon EFS works](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/efs/latest/ug/how-it-works.html) · [Use Amazon EFS with Amazon EC2 Linux instances](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSEC2/latest/UserGuide/AmazonEFS.html)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],A financial services company has launched a new application that uses an Amazon RDS for MySQL database. The company uses the application to track stock market trends. The company needs to run the application for only 2 hours at the end of each week. The company needs to optimize the cost of running the database.  
  
Which solution will meet these requirements **MOST cost-effectively**?

options.text: Migrate the existing RDS for MySQL database to an Aurora Serverless v2 MySQL database cluster.
Migrate the existing RDS for MySQL database to an Aurora MySQL database cluster.
Migrate the existing RDS for MySQL database to an Amazon EC2 instance that runs MySQL. Purchase an instance reservation for the EC2 instance.
Migrate the existing RDS for MySQL database to an Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) cluster that uses MySQL container images to run tasks.

questions.explanation:
Amazon Aurora Serverless v2 for Aurora MySQL is designed for workloads with long idle periods because it can automatically pause and resume, and it can scale down to 0 ACUs so you are not charged for database instance capacity while paused. That makes it more cost-effective for a database needed only briefly each week than provisioned Aurora, an EC2-hosted MySQL instance with a reservation, or a MySQL deployment in ECS.

**Learn more:** [Scaling to Zero ACUs with automatic pause and resume for Aurora serverless](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonRDS/latest/AuroraUserGuide/aurora-serverless-v2-auto-pause.html) · [Using Aurora Serverless v2](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonRDS/latest/AuroraUserGuide/aurora-serverless-v2.html)

A company runs a serverless application on AWS. The application uses Amazon API Gateway, AWS Lambda, and an Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL database. The company observes an increase in application errors caused by database connection timeouts during periods of peak traffic or unpredictable traffic.  
  
The company needs a solution that reduces application failures with the least amount of code change.  
  
What should a solutions architect do to meet these requirements?

options.text: Reduce the Lambda concurrency rate.
Enable RDS Proxy on the RDS DB instance.
Resize the RDS DB instance class to accept more connections.
Migrate the database to Amazon DynamoDB with on-demand scaling.

questions.explanation:
Amazon RDS Proxy is designed to help serverless applications such as AWS Lambda avoid exhausting database connections by pooling and reusing connections to Amazon RDS. AWS documentation states that RDS Proxy can handle unpredictable surges in database traffic and can be enabled for most applications with no code changes, which directly matches the requirement to reduce connection-timeout failures with minimal code modification.

**Learn more:** [Amazon RDS Proxy - Amazon RDS User Guide](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonRDS/latest/UserGuide/rds-proxy.html) · [Planning where to use RDS Proxy - Amazon RDS User Guide](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonRDS/latest/UserGuide/rds-proxy-planning.html)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],A company uses AWS Organizations to run workloads across multiple AWS accounts. A tagging policy adds `department` tags to AWS resources when the company creates tags.  
  
An accounting team needs to identify spending for Amazon EC2 consumption. The accounting team must determine which departments are responsible for the costs regardless of AWS account. The accounting team has access to AWS Cost Explorer for all AWS accounts in the organization and needs to access all reports from Cost Explorer.  
  
Which solution meets these requirements in the **MOST operationally efficient** way?

options.text: From the Organizations management account billing console, activate a user-defined cost allocation tag named department. Create one cost report in Cost Explorer grouping by tag name, and filter by EC2.

From the Organizations management account billing console, activate an AWS-defined cost allocation tag named department. Create one cost report in Cost Explorer grouping by tag name, and filter by EC2.

From the Organizations member account billing console, activate a user-defined cost allocation tag named department. Create one cost report in Cost Explorer grouping by the tag name, and filter by EC2.
From the Organizations member account billing console, activate an AWS-defined cost allocation tag named department. Create one cost report in Cost Explorer grouping by tag name, and filter by EC2.

questions.explanation:
A `department` tag that the company creates is a user-defined cost allocation tag. For AWS Organizations, cost allocation tags must be activated in the Billing and Cost Management console from the organization management account to make them available for consolidated cost reporting. After activation, Cost Explorer can filter costs to Amazon EC2 and group them by the `department` tag, allowing the accounting team to see EC2 costs by department across all member accounts from a single report.

**Learn more:** [Using user-defined cost allocation tags - AWS Billing](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/awsaccountbilling/latest/aboutv2/custom-tags.html) · [Activating user-defined cost allocation tags - AWS Billing](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/awsaccountbilling/latest/aboutv2/activating-tags.html)

A company migrated its on-premises PostgreSQL database to an Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL DB instance. The company successfully launched a new product, and the database workload has increased. The company wants to support the larger workload without adding infrastructure.  
  
Which solution will meet these requirements **MOST cost-effectively**?

options.text: Buy reserved DB instances for the total workload. Make the Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL DB instance larger.
Make the Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL DB instance a Multi-AZ DB instance.
Buy reserved DB instances for the total workload. Add another Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL DB instance.
Make the Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL DB instance an on-demand DB instance.

questions.explanation:
Scaling up the existing Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL DB instance increases database capacity without introducing another DB instance, so it satisfies the requirement to avoid adding infrastructure. Reserved DB instances are a billing discount for committed usage and are more cost-effective than on-demand pricing for steady workloads. A Multi-AZ DB instance deployment is primarily for high availability and failover, not workload scaling, because its standby instance does not serve read traffic. Adding another RDS DB instance would add infrastructure, and switching to on-demand pricing would not improve performance. Official AWS documentation describes Reserved DB instances as discounted compared with on-demand pricing and states that a Multi-AZ DB instance standby does not serve read traffic.

**Learn more:** [Reserved DB instances for Amazon RDS](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonRDS/latest/UserGuide/USER_WorkingWithReservedDBInstances.html) · [Configuring and managing a Multi-AZ deployment for Amazon RDS](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonRDS/latest/UserGuide/Concepts.MultiAZ.html)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],A company has built an image analysis application in which users can upload photos and add photo frames to those images. Users upload the images and metadata that indicates which photo frames they want to apply to their images. The application uses a single Amazon EC2 instance and Amazon DynamoDB to store the metadata.  
  
The application is growing in popularity, and the number of users is increasing. The company expects the number of concurrent users to vary significantly depending on the time of day and the day of the week. The company must ensure that the application can scale to meet the needs of the expanding user base.  
  
Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Use AWS Lambda to process the photos. Store the photos and metadata in DynamoDB.
Use Amazon Kinesis Data Firehose to process the photos and to store the photos and metadata.
Use AWS Lambda to process the photos. Store the photos in Amazon S3. Retain DynamoDB to store the metadata.
Increase the number of EC2 instances to three. Use Provisioned IOPS SSD (io2) Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) volumes to store the photos and metadata.

questions.explanation:
AWS Lambda provides serverless compute that can scale automatically with fluctuating request volume, making it well suited for variable concurrent image-processing workloads. Amazon S3 is the correct service for storing uploaded photo objects at scale, while Amazon DynamoDB should continue to store the structured metadata. AWS documentation specifically recommends storing large items such as images in Amazon S3 instead of DynamoDB and keeping related metadata or object references in DynamoDB.

**Learn more:** [Best practices for storing large items and attributes in DynamoDB](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/amazondynamodb/latest/developerguide/bp-use-s3-too.html) · [What is Amazon S3?](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],A company is building an application in the AWS Cloud. The application's HTTP API includes critical information and is published through Amazon API Gateway. The critical information must be accessible only from a limited set of trusted IP addresses within the company's internal network.  
  
Which solution satisfies these requirements?

options.text: Set up an API Gateway private integration to restrict access to a predefined set of IP addresses.
Create a resource policy for the API that denies access to any IP address that is not specifically allowed.
Directly deploy the API in a private subnet. Create a network ACL. Set up rules to allow the traffic from specific IP addresses.
Modify the security group that is attached to API Gateway to allow inbound traffic from only the trusted IP addresses.

questions.explanation:
An API Gateway resource policy can restrict invocation by source IP address. An explicit deny using an IP-address condition for every source address outside the approved ranges prevents untrusted clients from invoking the API, while requests from the trusted internal IP ranges can be allowed. [Control access to a REST API with API Gateway resource policies](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/apigateway/latest/developerguide/apigateway-resource-policies.html)

**Learn more:** [Control access to a REST API with API Gateway resource policies](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/apigateway/latest/developerguide/apigateway-resource-policies.html) · [API Gateway resource policy examples](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/apigateway/latest/developerguide/apigateway-resource-policies-examples.html)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],A company has a service that generates event data. The company wants to use AWS to process the event data as it arrives. The data is written in a specific order that must be preserved throughout processing. The company wants to implement a solution that minimizes operational overhead.  
  
How should a solutions architect accomplish this?

options.text: Create an Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) FIFO queue to hold messages. Set up an AWS Lambda function to process messages from the queue.
Create an Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS) topic to deliver notifications containing payloads to process. Configure an AWS Lambda function as a subscriber.
Create an Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) standard queue to hold messages. Set up an AWS Lambda function to process messages from the queue independently.
Create an Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS) topic to deliver notifications containing payloads to process. Configure an Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) queue as a subscriber.

questions.explanation:
Amazon SQS FIFO queues are built for workloads that require first-in, first-out message handling, and AWS Lambda can process messages from an SQS FIFO queue while maintaining order within each message group. That satisfies the requirement to preserve the event order during processing and keeps operational overhead low by using fully managed, serverless services. Standard SNS or standard SQS do not guarantee ordered delivery, and an SNS topic with an SQS subscriber would need explicit FIFO topic and FIFO queue configuration to preserve order.

**Learn more:** [Amazon SQS FIFO queue and Lambda concurrency behavior](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSSimpleQueueService/latest/SQSDeveloperGuide/fifo-queue-lambda-behavior.html) · [Amazon SNS message ordering details for FIFO topics](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sns/latest/dg/fifo-topic-message-ordering.html)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],A company's containerized application runs on an Amazon EC2 instance. The application must download security certificates before it can communicate with other business applications. The company wants a highly secure solution to encrypt and decrypt the certificates in near real time. The solution must also store the data in highly available storage after the data is encrypted.  
  
Which solution meets these requirements with the **LEAST operational overhead**?

options.text: Create AWS Secrets Manager secrets for encrypted certificates. Manually update the certificates as needed. Control access to the data by using fine-grained IAM access.
Create an AWS Lambda function that uses the Python cryptography library to receive and perform encryption operations. Store the function in an Amazon S3 bucket.
Create an AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) customer managed key. Allow the EC2 role to use the KMS key for encryption operations. Store the encrypted data on Amazon S3.

Create an AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) customer managed key. Allow the EC2 role to use the KMS key for encryption operations. Store the encrypted data on Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) volumes.

questions.explanation:
AWS KMS provides managed encryption and decryption operations using a customer managed key, so the EC2 instance role can securely call KMS without building and maintaining custom cryptography code. After encryption, Amazon S3 is the better storage target because it is managed object storage designed for high availability and durability, which gives less operational overhead than managing encrypted data on EBS volumes. AWS documentation also positions KMS, not Secrets Manager, as the recommended service for encryption keys. 

**Learn more:** [What is AWS Secrets Manager?](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/secretsmanager/latest/userguide/intro.html) · [Encrypt - AWS Key Management Service API Reference](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/kms/latest/APIReference/API_Encrypt.html)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],A company wants to migrate its application to a serverless solution.  
  
The serverless solution must analyze existing and new data by using SQL. The company stores the data in an Amazon S3 bucket. The data must be encrypted and replicated to a different AWS Region.  
  
Which solution will meet these requirements with the **LEAST operational overhead**?

options.text: Create a new S3 bucket. Load the data into the new S3 bucket. Use S3 Cross-Region Replication (CRR) to replicate encrypted objects to an S3 bucket in another Region. Use server-side encryption with AWS KMS multi-Region kays (SSE-KMS). Use Amazon Athena to query the data.

Create a new S3 bucket. Load the data into the new S3 bucket. Use S3 Cross-Region Replication (CRR) to replicate encrypted objects to an S3 bucket in another Region. Use server-side encryption with AWS KMS multi-Region keys (SSE-KMS). Use Amazon RDS to query the data.

Load the data into the existing S3 bucket. Use S3 Cross-Region Replication (CRR) to replicate encrypted objects to an S3 bucket in another Region. Use server-side encryption with Amazon S3 managed encryption keys (SSE-S3). Use Amazon Athena to query the data.

Load the data into the existing S3 bucket. Use S3 Cross-Region Replication (CRR) to replicate encrypted objects to an S3 bucket in another Region. Use server-side encryption with Amazon S3 managed encryption keys (SSE-S3). Use Amazon RDS to query the data.

questions.explanation:
Amazon Athena is the serverless service for running SQL queries directly against data in Amazon S3, so it satisfies the serverless analytics requirement with minimal administration. Amazon S3 Cross-Region Replication can replicate objects to a bucket in another Region, and Amazon S3 managed encryption keys (SSE-S3) provide encryption with less setup than SSE-KMS. AWS documentation also notes that replicating SSE-KMS objects requires additional configuration, and that Amazon S3 treats multi-Region KMS keys as single-Region keys for this purpose, so SSE-KMS multi-Region keys do not reduce operational effort here. Using the existing S3 bucket also avoids the extra work of creating and migrating to a new bucket.

**Learn more:** [What is Amazon Athena?](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/athena/latest/ug/what-is.html) · [Replicating objects within and across Regions](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/replication.html)

A company is designing a containerized application that will use Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS). The application must access a shared file system that is highly durable and can recover data to another AWS Region with a recovery point objective (RPO) of 8 hours. The file system must provide a mount target in each Availability Zone within a Region.  
  
A solutions architect wants to use AWS Backup to manage replication to another Region.  
  
Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Amazon FSx for Windows File Server with a Multi-AZ deployment
Amazon FSx for NetApp ONTAP with a Multi-AZ deployment
Amazon Elastic File System (Amazon EFS) with the Standard storage class
Amazon FSx for OpenZFS

questions.explanation:
Amazon Elastic File System (Amazon EFS) with the Standard storage class is the best fit because a Regional EFS file system is built for shared access by containerized workloads and supports a mount target in each Availability Zone in the Region. EFS Standard stores data across multiple Availability Zones for high durability and availability, and AWS Backup supports Amazon EFS with cross-Region copy for disaster recovery, which can satisfy an 8-hour RPO when backups are scheduled appropriately.

**Learn more:** [Managing mount targets - Amazon Elastic File System](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/efs/latest/ug/accessing-fs.html) · [Features of Amazon EFS - Amazon Elastic File System](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/efs/latest/ug/features.html)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],A company runs applications on Amazon EC2 instances in one AWS Region. The company needs to back up the EC2 instances to a second Region. The company also wants to provision EC2 resources in the second Region and centrally manage the EC2 instances from a single AWS account.  
  
Which solution meets these requirements **MOST cost-effectively**?

options.text: Create a disaster recovery (DR) plan that has a similar number of EC2 instances in the second Region. Configure data replication.
Create point-in-time Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) snapshots of the EC2 instances. Copy the snapshots to the second Region periodically.
Create a backup plan by using AWS Backup. Configure cross-Region backup to the second Region for the EC2 instances.
Deploy a similar number of EC2 instances in the second Region. Use AWS DataSync to transfer the data from the source Region to the second Region.

questions.explanation:
AWS Backup is the centrally managed service for protecting EC2 instances and supports scheduled cross-Region copies through a backup plan. It creates recovery points without the ongoing expense of pre-provisioning duplicate EC2 capacity in the second Region, while avoiding the manual snapshot-copy process in option B.

**Learn more:** [Creating backup copies across AWS Regions](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/aws-backup/latest/devguide/cross-region-backup.html) · [AWS Backup feature availability](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/aws-backup/latest/devguide/backup-feature-availability.html)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],A company has hired a new employee as a deployment engineer. The deployment engineer will use AWS CloudFormation templates to provision multiple AWS resources. A solutions architect wants the deployment engineer to carry out job duties while adhering to the principle of least privilege.  
  
Which combination of actions should the solutions architect take to achieve this goal? **(Choose two.)**

options.text: Have the deployment engineer use AWS account root user credentials for performing AWS CloudFormation stack operations.
Create a new IAM user for the deployment engineer and add the IAM user to a group that has the PowerUsers IAM policy attached.
Create a new IAM user for the deployment engineer and add the IAM user to a group that has the AdministratorAccess IAM policy attached.
Create a new IAM user for the deployment engineer and add the IAM user to a group that has an IAM policy that allows AWS CloudFormation actions only.
Create an IAM role for the deployment engineer to explicitly define the permissions specific to the AWS CloudFormation stack and launch stacks using that IAM role.

questions.explanation:
Least privilege in this situation means the deployment engineer should have only the permissions needed to work with AWS CloudFormation, while CloudFormation itself uses a separate service role that grants only the specific permissions required to create, update, or delete the resources defined in the stack. AWS documentation states that if a service role is specified, CloudFormation uses that role's credentials instead of the user's credentials, and recommends defining that role with only the permissions needed for the template. That makes an IAM policy allowing AWS CloudFormation actions only appropriate for the engineer, together with an IAM role explicitly scoped to the stack's required permissions for stack launches.

**Learn more:** [CloudFormation service role - AWS CloudFormation](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSCloudFormation/latest/UserGuide/using-iam-servicerole.html) · [Service roles for CloudFormation - AWS Prescriptive Guidance](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/prescriptive-guidance/latest/least-privilege-cloudformation/service-roles-for-cloudformation.html)

A company gathers temperature, humidity, and atmospheric pressure data in cities on multiple continents. The average amount of data collected from each site each day is 500 GB. Every site has a high-speed internet connection.  
  
The company wants to consolidate the data from all of these global sites as fast as possible into a single Amazon S3 bucket. The solution must minimize operational complexity.  
  
Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Turn on S3 Transfer Acceleration on the destination S3 bucket. Use multipart uploads to directly upload site data to the destination S3 bucket.
Upload the data from each site to an S3 bucket in the closest Region. Use S3 Cross-Region Replication to copy objects to the destination S3 bucket. Then remove the data from the origin S3 bucket.
Schedule AWS Snowball Edge Storage Optimized device jobs daily to transfer data from each site to the closest Region. Use S3 Cross-Region Replication to copy objects to the destination S3 bucket.

Upload the data from each site to an Amazon EC2 instance in the closest Region. Store the data in an Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) volume. At regular intervals, take an EBS snapshot and copy it to the Region that contains the destination S3 bucket. Restore the EBS volume in that Region.

questions.explanation:
Amazon S3 Transfer Acceleration is built for fast uploads to a centralized S3 bucket from geographically distributed locations by sending data to the nearest AWS edge location and then across the AWS optimized network path to Amazon S3. With high-speed internet already available at each site, direct multipart uploads to the destination bucket provide the quickest and simplest design. Using intermediate buckets with Cross-Region Replication, Snowball Edge devices, or EC2/EBS snapshot workflows adds extra steps, extra services, and more operational overhead without being faster for this connected, continuous-ingest use case.

**Learn more:** [Configuring fast, secure file transfers using Amazon S3 Transfer Acceleration](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/transfer-acceleration.html) · [Performance design patterns for Amazon S3](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/optimizing-performance-design-patterns.html)

options.text: Run a query with Amazon Athena to generate the report.
Create a report in Cost Explorer and download the report.
Access the bill details from the billing dashboard and download the bill.
Modify a cost budget in AWS Budgets to alert with Amazon Simple Email Service (Amazon SES).

questions.explanation:
AWS Cost Explorer is the most direct and operationally efficient option for creating a filtered or grouped cost report and downloading its data as a CSV file. Athena would require first configuring a Cost and Usage Report in Amazon S3 and then maintaining a query, which is unnecessary for this reporting request. The billing dashboard and AWS Budgets do not provide the requested user-oriented downloadable analysis.

**Learn more:** [Exploring your data using Cost Explorer](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/cost-management/latest/userguide/ce-exploring-data.html)

A company has an ecommerce checkout workflow that writes an order to a database and calls a service to process the payment. Users are experiencing timeouts during the checkout process. When users resubmit the checkout form, multiple unique orders are created for the same intended transaction.  
  
How should a solutions architect refactor this workflow to prevent the creation of multiple orders?

options.text: Configure the web application to send an order message to Amazon Kinesis Data Firehose. Set the payment service to retrieve the message from Kinesis Data Firehose and process the order.

Create a rule in AWS CloudTrail to invoke an AWS Lambda function based on the logged application path request. Use Lambda to query the database, call the payment service, and pass in the order information.

Store the order in the database. Send a message that includes the order number to Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS). Set the payment service to poll Amazon SNS, retrieve the message, and process the order.

Store the order in the database. Send a message that includes the order number to an Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) FIFO queue. Set the payment service to retrieve the message and process the order. Delete the message from the queue.

questions.explanation:
An Amazon SQS FIFO queue is the appropriate refactor because FIFO queues are built for workflows where duplicates cannot be tolerated and provide exactly-once processing with deduplication. Persisting the order first, then sending a message that contains the order number to an SQS FIFO queue, lets the payment service process the order asynchronously and delete the message after successful processing. This removes the synchronous timeout dependency from checkout and prevents duplicate order processing when retries occur. SNS is not polled directly by consumers, CloudTrail is not an application integration mechanism for this pattern, and Kinesis Data Firehose is for data delivery to destinations rather than transactional work-queue processing.

**Learn more:** [Exactly-once processing in Amazon SQS](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSSimpleQueueService/latest/SQSDeveloperGuide/FIFO-queues-exactly-once-processing.html) · [Amazon SQS FIFO queues](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSSimpleQueueService/latest/SQSDeveloperGuide/sqs-fifo-queues.html)

A solutions architect needs to design a highly available infrastructure for a website. The website is powered by Windows web servers running on Amazon EC2 instances. The solutions architect must implement a solution that can mitigate a large-scale DDoS attack originating from thousands of IP addresses. Downtime is not acceptable for the website.  
  
Which actions should the solutions architect take to protect the website from this type of attack? **(Choose two.)**

options.text: Use AWS Shield Advanced to stop the DDoS attack.
Configure Amazon GuardDuty to automatically block the attackers.
Configure the website to use Amazon CloudFront for both static and dynamic content.
Use an AWS Lambda function to automatically add attacker IP addresses to VPC network ACLs.
Use EC2 Spot Instances in an Auto Scaling group with a target tracking scaling policy that is set to 80% CPU utilization.

questions.explanation:
For a public website that must remain available during a large, distributed DDoS event, the correct design is to place the application behind Amazon CloudFront and use AWS Shield Advanced. CloudFront provides access to the AWS global edge network, which is specifically recommended for mitigating large volumetric attacks while serving both static and dynamic web content. Shield Advanced adds expanded DDoS detection and mitigation for protected resources and is part of AWS guidance for building DDoS-resilient web architectures. By contrast, GuardDuty is for threat detection rather than automatic DDoS blocking, manually or programmatically blocking thousands of source IPs in network ACLs is not an effective large-scale mitigation strategy, and Spot-based Auto Scaling does not provide DDoS protection or guaranteed availability.

**Learn more:** [AWS Shield Documentation](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/shield/) · [Building basic DDoS resilient architectures with Shield Advanced](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/waf/latest/developerguide/ddos-resiliency.html)

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],A company has a mobile game that reads most of its metadata from an Amazon RDS DB instance. As the game's popularity increased, developers observed slowdowns related to metadata load times. Performance metrics indicate that simply scaling the database will not help. A solutions architect must evaluate all options that include capabilities for snapshots, replication, and sub-millisecond response times.  
  
What should the solutions architect recommend to resolve these issues?

options.text: Migrate the database to Amazon Aurora with Aurora Replicas.
Migrate the database to Amazon DynamoDB with global tables.
Add an Amazon ElastiCache for Redis layer in front of the database.
Add an Amazon ElastiCache for Memcached layer in front of the database.

questions.explanation:
Amazon ElastiCache for Redis is designed to sit in front of databases such as Amazon RDS to offload frequent reads with sub-millisecond latency, and Redis supports replication groups plus backup and restore through snapshots. That combination matches all of the stated requirements. ElastiCache for Memcached is missing snapshot and replication features, Aurora Replicas do not provide in-memory sub-millisecond cache access, and DynamoDB global tables are a different database pattern with typical single-digit millisecond performance rather than the required cache-oriented sub-millisecond response time.

**Learn more:** [Amazon ElastiCache for Redis Documentation](https://aws.amazon.com/documentation-overview/redis/) · [Exporting a backup - Amazon ElastiCache](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonElastiCache/latest/dg/backups-exporting.html)

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],An Amazon EC2 instance resides in a private subnet in a new VPC. The subnet has no outbound internet connectivity, but the EC2 instance must be able to download monthly security updates from an external vendor.  
  
What should a solutions architect do to satisfy these requirements?

options.text: Create an internet gateway, and attach it to the VPC. Configure the private subnet route table to use the internet gateway as the default route.
Create a NAT gateway, and place it in a public subnet. Configure the private subnet route table to use the NAT gateway as the default route.
Create a NAT instance, and place it in the same subnet where the EC2 instance is located. Configure the private subnet route table to use the NAT instance as the default route.

Create an internet gateway, and attach it to the VPC. Create a NAT instance, and place it in the same subnet where the EC2 instance is located. Configure the private subnet route table to use the internet gateway as the default route.

questions.explanation:
A private-subnet EC2 instance that needs to initiate outbound internet connections without allowing unsolicited inbound internet access should use a NAT gateway. AWS documentation states that instances in private subnets can connect to the internet through a public NAT gateway, and the NAT gateway must be created in a public subnet; the private subnet then uses the NAT gateway as its default route. An internet gateway alone is for public subnet routing, and a NAT instance must also be placed in a public subnet, not in the same private subnet as the workload instance.

**Learn more:** [Connect to the internet or other networks using NAT devices - Amazon VPC](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/userguide/vpc-nat.html) · [NAT gateways - Amazon Virtual Private Cloud](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/userguide/vpc-nat-gateway.html)

An Amazon SQS FIFO queue is the appropriate refactor because FIFO queues are built for workflows where duplicates cannot be tolerated and provide exactly-once processing with deduplication. Persisting the order first, then sending a message that contains the order number to an SQS FIFO queue, lets the payment service process the order asynchronously and delete the message after successful processing. This removes the synchronous timeout dependency from checkout and prevents duplicate order processing when retries occur. SNS is not polled directly by consumers, CloudTrail is not an application integration mechanism for this pattern, and Kinesis Data Firehose is for data delivery to destinations rather than transactional work-queue processing.

For a public website that must remain available during a large, distributed DDoS event, the correct design is to place the application behind Amazon CloudFront and use AWS Shield Advanced. CloudFront provides access to the AWS global edge network, which is specifically recommended for mitigating large volumetric attacks while serving both static and dynamic web content. Shield Advanced adds expanded DDoS detection and mitigation for protected resources and is part of AWS guidance for building DDoS-resilient web architectures.
