A company is building a microservices-based application that will be deployed on Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS). The microservices will communicate with one another. The company wants to make sure the application is observable so that it can identify performance issues in the future.  
  
Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Configure the application to use Amazon ElastiCache to reduce the number of requests that are sent to the microservices.
Configure Amazon CloudWatch Container Insights to collect metrics from the EKS clusters. Configure AWS X-Ray to trace the requests between the microservices.
Configure AWS CloudTrail to review the API calls. Build an Amazon QuickSight dashboard to observe the microservice interactions.
Use AWS Trusted Advisor to understand the performance of the application.

questions.explanation:
Amazon CloudWatch Container Insights provides observability for Amazon EKS by collecting and summarizing metrics and logs from containerized applications and clusters, which helps monitor health and performance. AWS X-Ray adds distributed tracing for requests flowing between microservices, making it possible to analyze service dependencies and pinpoint latency or other performance problems across the application. Together, these services satisfy the need to observe both EKS workload performance and inter-service request paths.

**Learn more:** [Container Insights - Amazon CloudWatch](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonCloudWatch/latest/monitoring/ContainerInsights.html) · [What is AWS X-Ray? - AWS X-Ray](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/xray/latest/devguide/aws-xray.html)

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],A solutions architect is designing a data processing job that runs once each day and can take as long as 2 hours to finish. If the job is interrupted, it must restart from the beginning.  
  
How should the solutions architect solve this in the **MOST cost-effective** way?

options.text: Create a script that runs locally on an Amazon EC2 Reserved Instance that is triggered by a cron job.
Create an AWS Lambda function triggered by an Amazon EventBridge scheduled event.
Use an Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) Fargate task triggered by an Amazon EventBridge scheduled event.
Use an Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) task running on Amazon EC2 triggered by an Amazon EventBridge scheduled event.

questions.explanation:
AWS Lambda is not suitable because its maximum execution timeout is 15 minutes. A daily batch process that can run for 2 hours is a better fit for a scheduled Amazon ECS task. Using Amazon ECS on AWS Fargate with an Amazon EventBridge scheduled event is more cost-effective than keeping Amazon EC2 capacity running or committed through Reserved Instances for a workload that runs only once per day, and standard Fargate avoids interruption-related restarts that would be unacceptable for this job.

**Learn more:** [Configure Lambda function timeout - AWS Lambda](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/lambda/latest/dg/configuration-timeout.html) · [Amazon EC2 billing and purchasing options - Amazon EC2](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSEC2/latest/UserGuide/instance-purchasing-options.html)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],A company runs container applications by using Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS). The company's workload is not consistent throughout the day. The company wants Amazon EKS to scale in and out based on the workload.  
  
Which combination of steps will meet these requirements with the **LEAST operational overhead**? **(Choose two.)**

options.text: Use an AWS Lambda function to resize the EKS cluster.
Use the Kubernetes Metrics Server to activate horizontal pod autoscaling.
Use the Kubernetes Cluster Autoscaler to manage the number of nodes in the cluster.
Use Amazon API Gateway and connect it to Amazon EKS.
Use AWS App Mesh to observe network activity.

questions.explanation:
For Amazon EKS, the low-overhead way to scale with changing demand is to combine Horizontal Pod Autoscaler for adjusting the number of pod replicas with Cluster Autoscaler for adjusting the number of worker nodes. HPA uses workload metrics, typically provided through Kubernetes Metrics Server, to scale application pods up or down. Cluster Autoscaler increases node count when pods cannot be scheduled and removes underutilized nodes when demand drops. AWS guidance recommends HPA for replica scaling and a node autoscaler such as Cluster Autoscaler for cluster capacity management.

**Learn more:** [Scale pod deployments with Horizontal Pod Autoscaler - Amazon EKS](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/eks/latest/userguide/horizontal-pod-autoscaler.html) · [View resource usage with the Kubernetes Metrics Server - Amazon EKS](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/eks/latest/userguide/metrics-server.html)

options.text: Configure the security group for the EC2 instances.
Configure the security group on the Application Load Balancer.
Configure AWS WAF on the Application Load Balancer in a VPC.
Configure the network ACL for the subnet that contains the EC2 instances.

questions.explanation:
AWS WAF supports geographic match rules that inspect the request's country of origin based on IP address and can allow or block traffic accordingly. AWS WAF can be associated with an Application Load Balancer, making it the appropriate control for restricting access to a single country. Security groups and network ACLs do not provide country-based filtering; they operate on IP addresses, ports, and protocols instead.

**Learn more:** [Geographic match rule statement - AWS WAF Developer Guide](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/waf/latest/developerguide/waf-rule-statement-type-geo-match.html) · [Configuring protection in AWS WAF](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/waf/latest/developerguide/web-acl.html)

A financial services company wants to close two data centers and migrate more than 100 TB of data to AWS. The data has a complex directory structure with millions of small files stored in deep subfolder hierarchies. Most of the data is unstructured, and the company’s file storage uses SMB-based storage types from multiple vendors. The company does not want to modify its applications to access the data after the migration.  
  
What should a solutions architect do to meet these requirements with the **LEAST operational overhead**?

options.text: Use AWS Direct Connect to migrate the data to Amazon S3.
Use AWS DataSync to migrate the data to Amazon FSx for Lustre.
Use AWS DataSync to migrate the data to Amazon FSx for Windows File Server.
Use AWS Direct Connect to migrate the data on-premises file storage to an AWS Storage Gateway volume gateway.

questions.explanation:
AWS DataSync is designed to transfer data from SMB file servers into AWS managed storage, including Amazon FSx for Windows File Server. Amazon FSx for Windows File Server provides fully managed native Windows file storage with SMB support, so the company can preserve file-share access patterns and avoid changing applications. Amazon S3 would change access semantics from SMB file storage to object storage, and FSx for Lustre is a Lustre-based file system rather than the natural target for SMB-dependent applications.

**Learn more:** [Configuring AWS DataSync transfers with an SMB file server](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/datasync/latest/userguide/create-smb-location.html) · [Configuring transfers with FSx for Windows File Server](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/datasync/latest/userguide/create-fsx-location.html)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],A company has several VPCs in AWS Regions to support and run workloads that are isolated from workloads in other Regions.  
  
Because of a recent application launch requirement, the company's VPCs now must communicate with every other VPC across all Regions.  
  
Which solution will meet these requirements with the **LEAST** amount of administrative effort?

options.text: Use VPC peering to manage VPC communication in a single Region. Use VPC peering across Regions to manage VPC communications.
Use AWS Direct Connect gateways across all Regions to connect VPCs across regions and manage VPC communications.
Use AWS Transit Gateway to manage VPC communication in a single Region and Transit Gateway peering across Regions to manage VPC communications.
Use AWS PrivateLink across all Regions to connect VPCs across Regions and manage VPC communications

questions.explanation:
AWS Transit Gateway is designed to centrally connect multiple VPCs and supports transitive routing, which makes it the scalable, low-administration choice for multi-VPC networking. For connectivity across Regions, Transit Gateway peering connects regional transit gateways so VPCs in different Regions can communicate through those hubs. By contrast, VPC peering requires direct connections between each pair of VPCs and does not support transitive routing, which increases management overhead substantially. AWS PrivateLink is intended for private access to specific services rather than general VPC-to-VPC mesh connectivity, and Direct Connect gateways are primarily for on-premises-to-AWS connectivity rather than connecting AWS VPCs to each other. Official AWS guidance identifies Transit Gateway as the best practice for managing multi-VPC infrastructure at scale.

**Learn more:** [Communicating across VPCs and AWS Regions - AWS Prescriptive Guidance](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/prescriptive-guidance/latest/secure-outbound-network-traffic/vpc-region-communication.html) · [What is AWS Transit Gateway for Amazon VPC?](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/tgw/what-is-transit-gateway.html)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],A security team needs to restrict access to certain services or actions in all of the team's AWS accounts. All accounts are part of a large organization in AWS Organizations. The solution must scale, and permissions must be maintained from a single central location.  
  
What should a solutions architect do to achieve this?

options.text: Create an ACL to provide access to the services or actions.
Create a security group to allow accounts and attach it to user groups.
Create cross-account roles in each account to deny access to the services or actions.
Create a service control policy in the root organizational unit to deny access to the services or actions.

questions.explanation:
AWS Organizations service control policies (SCPs) provide centralized permission guardrails for member accounts in an organization. An SCP can deny specified AWS services or actions and, when attached at the organization root or an organizational unit, it applies across all affected accounts, which makes the solution scalable and centrally managed. ACLs and security groups do not control AWS service-level permissions across accounts, and creating separate cross-account roles in every account would be decentralized and harder to maintain.

**Learn more:** [Service control policies (SCPs) - AWS Organizations](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/organizations/latest/userguide/orgs_manage_policies_scps.html) · [SCP evaluation - AWS Organizations](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/organizations/latest/userguide/orgs_manage_policies_scps_evaluation.html)

options.text: Create IAM users for the employees in the required AWS accounts. Connect IAM users to the existing IdP. Configure federated authentication for the IAM users.
Set up AWS account root users with user email addresses and passwords that are synchronized from the existing IdP.

Use AWS Resource Access Manager (AWS RAM) to share access to the AWS accounts with the users in the existing IdP.

questions.explanation:
AWS IAM Identity Center is integrated with AWS Organizations so access to multiple AWS accounts can be managed centrally. It also supports connecting an external identity provider for authentication and provisioning users and groups from that IdP, which fits a large workforce using existing corporate identities. IAM users in each account would be operationally heavy at this scale, root users are not appropriate for employee access, and AWS RAM is for sharing AWS resources rather than providing sign-in access to accounts.

AWS Transit Gateway is designed to centrally connect multiple VPCs and supports transitive routing, which makes it the scalable, low-administration choice for multi-VPC networking. For connectivity across Regions, Transit Gateway peering connects regional transit gateways so VPCs in different Regions can communicate through those hubs. By contrast, VPC peering requires direct connections between each pair of VPCs and does not support transitive routing, which increases management overhead substantially. AWS Application Discovery Service is designed for migration planning by collecting configuration, utilization, and dependency information from on-premises servers. AWS Migration Hub must have a home Region configured before discovery begins, because discovery and planning data is stored there. That combination satisfies the need to assess on-premises workloads and plan their migration to AWS.

**Learn more:** [Discovery with AWS Migration Hub requires the home Region](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/migrationhub/latest/ug/home-region-with-discovery.html) · [What is AWS Application Discovery Service?](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/application-discovery/latest/userguide/what-is-appdiscovery.html)

A company wants to run its payment application on AWS. The application receives payment notifications from mobile devices. Payment notifications need a basic validation step before they are sent for additional processing.  
  
The backend processing application is long-running and requires compute and memory to be adjustable. The company does not want to manage the infrastructure.  
  
Which solution will meet these requirements with the **LEAST operational overhead**?

options.text: Create an Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) queue. Integrate the queue with an Amazon EventBridge rule to receive payment notifications from mobile devices. Configure the rule to validate payment notifications and send the notifications to the backend application. Deploy the backend application on Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS) Anywhere. Create a standalone cluster.

Create an Amazon API Gateway API. Integrate the API with an AWS Step Functions state machine to receive payment notifications from mobile devices. Invoke the state machine to validate payment notifications and send the notifications to the backend application. Deploy the backend application on Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS). Configure an EKS cluster with self-managed nodes.

Create an Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) queue. Integrate the queue with an Amazon EventBridge rule to receive payment notifications from mobile devices. Configure the rule to validate payment notifications and send the notifications to the backend application. Deploy the backend application on Amazon EC2 Spot Instances. Configure a Spot Fleet with a default allocation strategy.

Create an Amazon API Gateway API. Integrate the API with AWS Lambda to receive payment notifications from mobile devices. Invoke a Lambda function to validate payment notifications and send the notifications to the backend application. Deploy the backend application on Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS). Configure Amazon ECS with an AWS Fargate launch type.

questions.explanation:
Amazon API Gateway provides a fully managed way to receive requests from mobile devices, and AWS Lambda is well suited for lightweight validation without managing servers. For the long-running backend, Amazon ECS on AWS Fargate is the lowest-operations container option because Fargate is serverless and lets you define task-level CPU and memory for the workload. By contrast, EKS Anywhere, EKS with self-managed nodes, and EC2 Spot fleets all require significantly more infrastructure management. AWS documentation also notes that Standard Step Functions can support long-running workflows, but option B still relies on self-managed EKS nodes, so it does not offer the least operational overhead.

**Learn more:** [Amazon ECS task definition differences for Fargate](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonECS/latest/developerguide/fargate-tasks-services.html) · [AWS Decision Guide: Choosing an AWS container service](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/pdfs/decision-guides/latest/containers-on-aws-how-to-choose/containers-on-aws-how-to-choose.pdf)

A company needs a way to analyze the log files for its proprietary application. The logs are stored in JSON format in an Amazon S3 bucket. Queries will be simple and run on demand.  
  
A solutions architect must perform the analysis with minimal changes to the existing architecture.  
  
What should the solutions architect do to meet these requirements with the **LEAST** operational overhead?

options.text: Use Amazon Redshift to load all the content into one place and run the SQL queries as needed.
Use Amazon CloudWatch Logs to store the logs. Run SQL queries as needed from the Amazon CloudWatch console.
Use Amazon Athena directly with Amazon S3 to run the queries as needed.
Use AWS Glue to catalog the logs. Use a transient Apache Spark cluster on Amazon EMR to run the SQL queries as needed.

questions.explanation:
Amazon Athena is the best fit because it can run standard SQL queries directly against data stored in Amazon S3, supports querying JSON data, and is serverless, which minimizes operational overhead. This meets the requirement for simple, on-demand analysis with minimal changes to the existing architecture because the logs can remain in S3 instead of being loaded into and managed by another analytics platform.

**Learn more:** [What is Amazon Athena?](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/athena/latest/ug/what-is.html) · [Query JSON data - Amazon Athena](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/athena/latest/ug/querying-JSON.html)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],A company wants to analyze and create reports to track usage of its mobile app. The app is popular and has a global user base. The company uses a custom report-building program to analyze application usage.  
  
The program generates multiple reports during the last week of each month. The program takes less than 10 minutes to produce each report. The company rarely uses the program to generate reports outside the last week of each month. The company wants to generate reports in the least amount of time when the reports are requested.  
  
Which solution will meet these requirements **MOST cost-effectively**?

options.text: Run the program by using Amazon EC2 On-Demand Instances. Create an Amazon EventBridge rule to start the EC2 instances when reports are requested. Run the EC2 instances continuously during the last week of each month.
Run the program in AWS Lambda. Create an Amazon EventBridge rule to run a Lambda function when reports are requested.
Run the program in Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS). Schedule Amazon ECS to run the program when reports are requested.

Run the program by using Amazon EC2 Spot Instances. Create an Amazon EventBndge rule to start the EC2 instances when reports are requested. Run the EC2 instances continuously during the last week of each month.

questions.explanation:
AWS Lambda is the best fit for a short, infrequent, event-driven reporting workload because it runs code on demand without requiring servers to remain provisioned between report requests. Lambda supports executions up to 15 minutes, so a job that completes in less than 10 minutes fits within its limits. Using Amazon EventBridge to invoke the function when reports are requested provides fast startup with pay-per-use pricing, making it more cost-effective than keeping EC2 instances running during the last week of each month or using Spot capacity that can be interrupted.

**Learn more:** [What is AWS Lambda?](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/lambda/latest/dg/welcome.html) · [Configure scheduled rules for Amazon EventBridge](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/eventbridge/latest/userguide/eb-create-rule-schedule.html)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],A company has a web server running on an Amazon EC2 instance in a public subnet with an Elastic IP address. The default security group is attached to the EC2 instance. The default network ACL has been changed to block all traffic. A solutions architect must make the web server reachable from anywhere on port 443.  
  
Which combination of steps will accomplish this task? (Choose two.)

options.text: Create a security group with a rule to allow TCP port 443 from source 0.0.0.0/0.
Create a security group with a rule to allow TCP port 443 to destination 0.0.0.0/0.
Update the network ACL to allow TCP port 443 from source 0.0.0.0/0.
Update the network ACL to allow inbound/outbound TCP port 443 from source 0.0.0.0/0 and to destination 0.0.0.0/0.
Update the network ACL to allow inbound TCP port 443 from source 0.0.0.0/0 and outbound TCP port 32768-65535 to destination 0.0.0.0/0.

questions.explanation:
An internet-facing EC2 web server needs a security group rule that permits inbound HTTPS traffic on TCP port 443 from `0.0.0.0/0`. Because network ACLs are stateless, they must also allow both the inbound HTTPS request and the outbound return traffic. For client connections to a web server, the return traffic goes to the client’s ephemeral port range, so the correct network ACL change is to allow inbound TCP 443 from `0.0.0.0/0` and outbound TCP `32768-65535` to `0.0.0.0/0`.

**Learn more:** [Security group rules for different use cases - Amazon EC2](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSEC2/latest/UserGuide/security-group-rules-reference.html) · [Custom network ACLs for your VPC - Amazon VPC](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/userguide/custom-network-acl.html)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],A research company runs experiments that are powered by a simulation application and a visualization application. The simulation application runs on Linux and writes intermediate data to an NFS share every 5 minutes. The visualization application is a Windows desktop application that shows the simulation output and requires an SMB file system.  
  
The company maintains two synchronized file systems. This approach is causing duplicated data and inefficient use of resources. The company must migrate the applications to AWS without making code changes to either application.  
  
Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Migrate both applications to AWS Lambda. Create an Amazon S3 bucket to exchange data between the applications.
Migrate both applications to Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS). Configure Amazon FSx File Gateway for storage.

Migrate the simulation application to Linux Amazon EC2 instances. Migrate the visualization application to Windows EC2 instances. Configure Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) to exchange data between the applications.
Migrate the simulation application to Linux Amazon EC2 instances. Migrate the visualization application to Windows EC2 instances. Configure Amazon FSx for NetApp ONTAP for storage.

questions.explanation:
Amazon FSx for NetApp ONTAP is the correct choice because it supports multiprotocol access, including concurrent NFS and SMB access to the same volume. That allows the Linux simulation application and the Windows visualization application to use one shared file system instead of two synchronized copies, while preserving the file-access methods the applications already require. Running the applications on Linux and Windows Amazon EC2 instances avoids code changes and matches their existing operating system dependencies.

**Learn more:** [Managing FSx for ONTAP volumes](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/fsx/latest/ONTAPGuide/managing-volumes.html) · [Accessing your FSx for ONTAP data](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/fsx/latest/ONTAPGuide/supported-fsx-clients.html)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],A company must run a critical application on AWS. The company needs to use Amazon EC2 for the application's database. The database must be highly available and must automatically fail over if a disruptive event occurs.  
  
Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Launch two EC2 instances, each in a different Availability Zone in the same AWS Region. Install the database on both EC2 instances. Configure the EC2 instances as a cluster. Set up database replication.

Launch an EC2 instance in an Availability Zone. Install the database on the EC2 instance. Use an Amazon Machine Image (AMI) to back up the data. Use AWS CloudFormation to automate provisioning of the EC2 instance if a disruptive event occurs.
Launch two EC2 instances, each in a different AWS Region. Install the database on both EC2 instances. Set up database replication. Fail over the database to a second Region.

Launch an EC2 instance in an Availability Zone. Install the database on the EC2 instance. Use an Amazon Machine Image (AMI) to back up the data. Use EC2 automatic recovery to recover the instance if a disruptive event occurs.

questions.explanation:
High availability for a self-managed database on Amazon EC2 is achieved by deploying redundant database instances in different Availability Zones within the same AWS Region and configuring clustering and replication so a standby can take over when the primary fails. AWS Regions are designed with multiple isolated Availability Zones for resiliency, while EC2 automatic recovery only restores an impaired instance on underlying hardware and does not provide a second database node for automatic failover. Cross-Region replication is generally a disaster recovery pattern rather than the primary high-availability design for automatic failover of an EC2-hosted database.

**Learn more:** [Resilience in Amazon EC2 - Amazon EC2 User Guide](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSEC2/latest/UserGuide/disaster-recovery-resiliency.html) · [Amazon EC2 now performs automatic recovery of instances by default](https://aws.amazon.com/about-aws/whats-new/2022/03/amazon-ec2-default-automatic-recovery/)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],A company needs to store contract documents. A contract lasts for 5 years. During the 5-year period, the company must ensure that the documents cannot be overwritten or deleted. The company needs to encrypt the documents at rest and rotate the encryption keys automatically every year.  
  
Which combination of steps should a solutions architect take to meet these requirements with the **LEAST operational overhead**? *(Choose two.)*

options.text: Store the documents in Amazon S3. Use S3 Object Lock in governance mode.
Store the documents in Amazon S3. Use S3 Object Lock in compliance mode.
Use server-side encryption with Amazon S3 managed encryption keys (SSE-S3). Configure key rotation.
Use server-side encryption with AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) customer managed keys. Configure key rotation.
Use server-side encryption with AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) customer provided (imported) keys. Configure key rotation.

questions.explanation:
Amazon S3 Object Lock **compliance mode** provides WORM protection for the retention period, preventing object versions from being overwritten or deleted until the retention date expires. Governance mode is weaker because authorized users can bypass retention controls. For encryption, **AWS KMS customer managed keys** support automatic key rotation on a yearly schedule, which satisfies the annual rotation requirement with low operational overhead. S3-managed keys do not give you a configurable rotation setting for this requirement, and KMS keys with imported key material do not support automatic rotation. Official AWS documentation for S3 Object Lock and AWS KMS key rotation supports these behaviors.

**Learn more:** [Locking objects with Object Lock - Amazon S3 User Guide](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/object-lock.html) · [Rotate AWS KMS keys - AWS Key Management Service](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/kms/latest/developerguide/rotate-keys.html)

A company runs a containerized application on Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS). The application includes microservices that manage customers and place orders. The company must route incoming requests to the correct microservices.  
  
Which solution will meet this requirement **MOST cost-effectively**?

options.text: Use the AWS Load Balancer Controller to provision a Network Load Balancer.
Use the AWS Load Balancer Controller to provision an Application Load Balancer.
Use an AWS Lambda function to connect the requests to Amazon EKS.
Use Amazon API Gateway to connect the requests to Amazon EKS.

questions.explanation:
An Application Load Balancer provisioned by the AWS Load Balancer Controller is the appropriate EKS ingress solution for HTTP/HTTPS microservices because it provides Layer 7 routing, including directing requests to different services based on rules such as paths or hosts. AWS documentation distinguishes this from a Network Load Balancer, which is primarily for Layer 4 TCP/UDP traffic, and using API Gateway or Lambda would add unnecessary components and cost for straightforward microservice request routing into EKS.

**Learn more:** [Route internet traffic with AWS Load Balancer Controller - Amazon EKS](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/eks/latest/userguide/aws-load-balancer-controller.html) · [Load Balancing - Amazon EKS Best Practices](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/eks/latest/best-practices/load-balancing.html)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],A company runs an online transaction processing (OLTP) workload on AWS. The workload uses an unencrypted Amazon RDS DB instance in a Multi-AZ deployment. Daily database snapshots are taken from this instance.  
  
What should a solutions architect do to ensure that the database and snapshots are always encrypted going forward?

options.text: Encrypt a copy of the latest DB snapshot. Replace existing DB instance by restoring the encrypted snapshot.
Create a new encrypted Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) volume and copy the snapshots to it. Enable encryption on the DB instance.
Copy the snapshots and enable encryption using AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) Restore encrypted snapshot to an existing DB instance.
Copy the snapshots to an Amazon S3 bucket that is encrypted using server-side encryption with AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) managed keys (SSE-KMS).

questions.explanation:
Amazon RDS encryption must be enabled when the DB instance is created; you cannot enable encryption on an existing unencrypted RDS DB instance in place. AWS supports encrypting a copy of an unencrypted DB snapshot with AWS KMS and then restoring a new DB instance from that encrypted snapshot. Once the replacement DB instance is encrypted, its storage, automated backups, and snapshots are encrypted as well.

**Learn more:** [Copying a DB snapshot for Amazon RDS](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonRDS/latest/UserGuide/USER_CopySnapshot.html) · [Encrypting Amazon RDS resources](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonRDS/latest/UserGuide/Overview.Encryption.html)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],A company is expecting rapid growth in the near future. A solutions architect needs to configure existing users and grant permissions to new users on AWS. The solutions architect has decided to create IAM groups. The solutions architect will add the new users to IAM groups based on department.  
  
Which additional action is the **MOST secure** way to grant permissions to the new users?

options.text: Apply service control policies (SCPs) to manage access permissions
Create IAM roles that have least privilege permission. Attach the roles to the IAM groups
Create an IAM policy that grants least privilege permission. Attach the policy to the IAM groups
Create IAM roles. Associate the roles with a permissions boundary that defines the maximum permissions

questions.explanation:
The most secure approach is to create a least-privilege IAM policy and attach that policy to the appropriate IAM groups. In AWS, permissions for IAM groups are granted by attaching identity-based policies to the group, and all users in the group inherit those permissions. This matches the department-based group design and applies least privilege. SCPs only set maximum guardrails for accounts in AWS Organizations and do not grant permissions, and IAM roles are not attached to IAM groups for this purpose.

**Learn more:** [IAM user groups - AWS Identity and Access Management](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/id_groups.html) · [Attach a policy to an IAM user group - AWS Identity and Access Management](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/id_groups_manage_attach-policy.html)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],A company's data platform uses an Amazon Aurora MySQL database. The database has multiple read replicas and multiple DB instances across different Availability Zones. Users have recently reported database errors indicating that there are too many connections.  
  
The company wants to reduce the failover time by 20% when a read replica is promoted to the primary writer.  
  
Which solution will meet this requirement?

options.text: Switch from Aurora to Amazon RDS with Multi-AZ cluster deployment.
Use Amazon RDS Proxy in front of the Aurora database.
Switch to Amazon DynamoDB with DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) for read connections.
Switch to Amazon Redshift with relocation capability.

questions.explanation:
Amazon RDS Proxy is the correct solution because it provides connection pooling and sharing for Amazon Aurora, which helps prevent connection exhaustion, and it improves failover behavior by preserving application connections and bypassing DNS caching. AWS documents that RDS Proxy can reduce failover times by up to 66% for Aurora Multi-AZ databases, which exceeds the required 20% reduction.

**Learn more:** [Planning where to use RDS Proxy - Amazon Aurora](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/en_us/AmazonRDS/latest/AuroraUserGuide/rds-proxy-planning.html) · [Amazon RDS Proxy for Aurora - Amazon Aurora](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonRDS/latest/AuroraUserGuide/rds-proxy.html)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],A solutions architect is designing the cloud architecture for a new application that will be deployed on AWS.  
  
The process must run in parallel while adding and removing application nodes as needed, based on the number of jobs to be processed. The processor application is stateless.  
  
The solutions architect must ensure that the application is loosely coupled and that the job items are durably stored.  
  
Which design should the solutions architect use?

options.text: Create an Amazon SNS topic to send the jobs that need to be processed. Create an Amazon Machine Image (AMI) that consists of the processor application. Create a launch configuration that uses the AMI. Create an Auto Scaling group using the launch configuration. Set the scaling policy for the Auto Scaling group to add and remove nodes based on CPU usage.

Create an Amazon SQS queue to hold the jobs that need to be processed. Create an Amazon Machine Image (AMI) that consists of the processor application. Create a launch configuration that uses the AMI. Create an Auto Scaling group using the launch configuration. Set the scaling policy for the Auto Scaling group to add and remove nodes based on network usage.

Create an Amazon SQS queue to hold the jobs that need to be processed. Create an Amazon Machine Image (AMI) that consists of the processor application. Create a launch template that uses the AMI. Create an Auto Scaling group using the launch template. Set the scaling policy for the Auto Scaling group to add and remove nodes based on the number of items in the SQS queue.

Create an Amazon SNS topic to send the jobs that need to be processed. Create an Amazon Machine Image (AMI) that consists of the processor application. Create a launch template that uses the AMI. Create an Auto Scaling group using the launch template. Set the scaling policy for the Auto Scaling group to add and remove nodes based on the number of messages published to the SNS topic.

questions.explanation:
A durable, loosely coupled worker architecture on AWS uses Amazon SQS to hold job messages while stateless processing nodes poll and process them independently. Amazon SQS is specifically designed to decouple distributed components and provides durable message storage. For elastic worker fleets, Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling should scale according to SQS backlog or queue depth so capacity tracks the amount of pending work, rather than indirect signals such as CPU or network usage. Using a launch template with an Auto Scaling group fits the current EC2 Auto Scaling design pattern for queue-based workers.

**Learn more:** [What is Amazon Simple Queue Service?](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSSimpleQueueService/latest/SQSDeveloperGuide/welcome.html) · [Scaling policy based on Amazon SQS - Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/autoscaling/ec2/userguide/as-using-sqs-queue.html)

A company runs its critical storage application in the AWS Cloud. The application uses Amazon S3 in two AWS Regions. The company wants the application to send remote user data to the nearest S3 bucket with no public network congestion. The company also wants the application to fail over with the least amount of management of Amazon S3.  
  
Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Implement an active-active design between the two Regions. Configure the application to use the regional S3 endpoints closest to the user.
Use an active-passive configuration with S3 Multi-Region Access Points. Create a global endpoint for each of the Regions.
Send user data to the regional S3 endpoints closest to the user. Configure an S3 cross-account replication rule to keep the S3 buckets synchronized.
Set up Amazon S3 to use Multi-Region Access Points in an active-active configuration with a single global endpoint. Configure S3 Cross-Region Replication.

questions.explanation:
Amazon S3 Multi-Region Access Points provide a single global endpoint that routes requests over the AWS global network to the closest active S3 bucket, which avoids relying on congested public internet paths and minimizes application-side routing management. In an active-active configuration, requests automatically go to the nearest active Region and can be redirected if a disruption occurs. To keep data available in both Regions behind that endpoint, S3 Cross-Region Replication must be configured, because Multi-Region Access Points do not replicate objects by themselves.

**Learn more:** [Managing multi-Region traffic with Multi-Region Access Points - Amazon S3](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/en_en/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/MultiRegionAccessPoints.html) · [Amazon S3 Multi-Region Access Points routing states](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/FailoverConfiguration.html)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],A company hosts a data lake on Amazon S3. The data lake ingests data in Apache Parquet format from multiple data sources. The company uses several transformation steps to prepare the ingested data. These steps include:  
  
- filtering anomalies  
- normalizing data to standard date and time values  
- generating aggregates for analysis  
  
The company must store the transformed data in S3 buckets that data analysts can access. The company needs a prebuilt data transformation solution that does not require code. The solution must provide data lineage and data profiling. The company also needs to share the data transformation steps with employees across the company.  
  
Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Configure an AWS Glue Studio visual canvas to transform the data. Share the transformation steps with employees by using AWS Glue jobs.
Configure Amazon EMR Serverless to transform the data. Share the transformation steps with employees by using EMR Serverless jobs.
Configure AWS Glue DataBrew to transform the data. Share the transformation steps with employees by using DataBrew recipes.
Create Amazon Athena tables for the data. Write Athena SQL queries to transform the data. Share the Athena SQL queries with employees.

questions.explanation:
AWS Glue DataBrew is a visual, no-code data preparation service for cleaning, normalizing, and transforming data, including data stored in Amazon S3. It provides built-in data profiling and visual data lineage, and it stores transformation logic as reusable recipes that can be published and shared. DataBrew recipe jobs can write transformed output back to Amazon S3, which satisfies the requirement to make transformed data available to analysts.

**Learn more:** [What is AWS Glue DataBrew?](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/databrew/latest/dg/what-is.html) · [Core concepts and terms in AWS Glue DataBrew](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/databrew/latest/dg/core-concepts-and-terms.html)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],A company designed a stateless two-tier application that uses Amazon EC2 in a single Availability Zone and an Amazon RDS Multi-AZ DB instance. New company management wants to ensure that the application is highly available.  
  
What should a solutions architect do to meet this requirement?

options.text: Configure the application to use Multi-AZ EC2 Auto Scaling and create an Application Load Balancer
Configure the application to take snapshots of the EC2 instances and send them to a different AWS Region
Configure the application to use Amazon Route 53 latency-based routing to feed requests to the application
Configure Amazon Route 53 rules to handle incoming requests and create a Multi-AZ Application Load Balancer

questions.explanation:
For a stateless application tier, high availability is achieved by running EC2 instances across multiple Availability Zones and placing them behind an Application Load Balancer so traffic can be distributed to healthy targets if one Availability Zone fails. The database tier is already protected by Amazon RDS Multi-AZ, so the missing requirement is Multi-AZ resilience for the EC2 tier. AWS documentation states that Application Load Balancers use subnets in at least two Availability Zones, and EC2 Auto Scaling can span multiple Availability Zones to maintain capacity across them.

**Learn more:** [Create an Application Load Balancer - Elastic Load Balancing](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/elasticloadbalancing/latest/application/create-application-load-balancer.html) · [How Elastic Load Balancing works - Elastic Load Balancing](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/elasticloadbalancing/latest/userguide/how-elastic-load-balancing-works.html)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],A company uses AWS Organizations. A member account has purchased a Compute Savings Plan. Because of workload changes inside the member account, the account no longer receives the full benefit of the Compute Savings Plan commitment. The company is using less than 50% of its purchased compute power.

options.text: Turn on discount sharing from the Billing Preferences section of the account console in the member account that purchased the Compute Savings Plan.
Turn on discount sharing from the Billing Preferences section of the account console in the company's Organizations management account.
Migrate additional compute workloads from another AWS account to the account that has the Compute Savings Plan.
Sell the excess Savings Plan commitment in the Reserved Instance Marketplace.

questions.explanation:
In an AWS Organizations consolidated billing family, a Compute Savings Plan is applied to the purchasing account first and then can apply to eligible usage in other organization accounts only when discount sharing is enabled. AWS Billing documentation states that the management account controls Reserved Instance and Savings Plans discount sharing preferences for accounts in the organization. Because the member account is underutilizing its commitment, enabling discount sharing in the management account allows the remaining Savings Plan benefit to be used by other eligible member accounts instead of going unused. Savings Plans also cannot be sold in the Reserved Instance Marketplace.

**Learn more:** [Understanding how Savings Plans apply to your usage](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/savingsplans/latest/userguide/sp-applying.html) · [Reserved Instances and Savings Plans discount sharing](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/awsaccountbilling/latest/aboutv2/ri-turn-off.html)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],A company wants to move its three-tier application from on premises to AWS. The web tier and the application tier run on third-party virtual machines (VMs). The database tier runs on MySQL.  
  
The company must migrate the application while making the fewest possible changes to the architecture. The company also requires a database solution that can restore data to a specific point in time.  
  
Which solution will meet these requirements with the **LEAST operational overhead**?

options.text: Migrate the web tier and the application tier to Amazon EC2 instances in private subnets. Migrate the database tier to Amazon RDS for MySQL in private subnets.
Migrate the web tier to Amazon EC2 instances in public subnets. Migrate the application tier to EC2 instances in private subnets. Migrate the database tier to Amazon Aurora MySQL in private subnets.
Migrate the web tier to Amazon EC2 instances in public subnets. Migrate the application tier to EC2 instances in private subnets. Migrate the database tier to Amazon RDS for MySQL in private subnets.
Migrate the web tier and the application tier to Amazon EC2 instances in public subnets. Migrate the database tier to Amazon Aurora MySQL in public subnets.

questions.explanation:
Using Amazon EC2 for the web and application tiers preserves the existing VM-based architecture with minimal change, and placing the web tier in public subnets while keeping the application tier in private subnets matches the standard three-tier AWS design. Amazon RDS for MySQL provides a managed MySQL service with point-in-time restore capability, which satisfies the recovery requirement without introducing an unnecessary database engine change to Aurora. This combination minimizes both rearchitecture effort and ongoing database administration.

**Learn more:** [An overview of traditional web hosting - Web Application Hosting in the AWS Cloud](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/whitepapers/latest/web-application-hosting-best-practices/an-overview-of-traditional-web-hosting.html) · [Amazon RDS for MySQL - Amazon Relational Database Service](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonRDS/latest/UserGuide/CHAP_MySQL.html)

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],A company operates a Node.js function on a server in its on-premises data center. The data center holds data in a PostgreSQL database. The company keeps the credentials in a connection string within an environment variable on the server. The company wants to migrate its application to AWS and replace the Node.js application server with AWS Lambda. The company also wants to migrate to Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL and ensure that database credentials are managed securely.  
  
Which solution meets these requirements with the **LEAST** operational overhead?

options.text: Store the database credentials as a parameter in AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store Configure Parameter Store to automatically rotate the secrets every 30 days. Update the Lambda function to retrieve the credentials from the parameter.

Store the database credentials as a secret in AWS Secrets Manager. Configure Secrets Manager to automatically rotate the credentials every 30 days. Update the Lambda function to retrieve the credentials from the secret.
Store the database credentials as an encrypted Lambda environment variable. Write a custom Lambda function to rotate the credentials. Schedule the Lambda function to run every 30 days.
Store the database credentials as a key in AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS). Configure automatic rotation for the key. Update the Lambda function to retneve the credentials from the KMS key.

questions.explanation:
AWS Secrets Manager is designed to store database credentials securely and can automatically rotate credentials for supported Amazon RDS databases, including RDS for PostgreSQL. A Lambda function can retrieve the secret at runtime using IAM authorization, avoiding a custom credential-rotation implementation.

**Learn more:** [AWS Secrets Manager User Guide: Rotate AWS Secrets Manager secrets](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/secretsmanager/latest/userguide/rotate-secrets_turn-on-for-db.html)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],An ecommerce company needs a disaster recovery solution for its Amazon RDS DB instances that use Microsoft SQL Server Enterprise Edition. The company's current recovery point objective (RPO) and recovery time objective (RTO) are 24 hours.  
  
Which solution will meet these requirements **MOST cost-effectively**?

options.text: Create a cross-Region read replica and promote the read replica to the primary instance.
Use AWS Database Migration Service (AWS DMS) to create RDS cross-Region replication.
Use cross-Region replication every 24 hours to copy native backups to an Amazon S3 bucket.
Copy automatic snapshots to another Region every 24 hours.

questions.explanation:
For an Amazon RDS for SQL Server workload with a 24-hour RPO and 24-hour RTO, the most cost-effective disaster recovery approach is to copy automated snapshots to another Region on a daily basis. This avoids the ongoing cost of a continuously running cross-Region read replica while still allowing the database to be restored in the secondary Region within the stated recovery objectives. AWS documentation also indicates that native SQL Server backup and restore to Amazon S3 is supported, but it is not intended to replace the cross-Region snapshot copy feature for recovery. Official RDS documentation supports cross-Region snapshot and automated backup replication for SQL Server, making snapshot copy the appropriate low-cost DR choice here.

**Learn more:** [Copying a DB snapshot for Amazon RDS](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonRDS/latest/UserGuide/USER_CopySnapshot.html) · [Replicating automated backups to another AWS Region](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonRDS/latest/UserGuide/USER_ReplicateBackups.html)

options.text: Store the video archives in Amazon S3 Glacier and use Expedited retrievals.
Store the video archives in Amazon S3 Glacier and use Standard retrievals.
Store the video archives in Amazon S3 Standard-Infrequent Access (S3 Standard-IA).
Store the video archives in Amazon S3 One Zone-Infrequent Access (S3 One Zone-IA).

questions.explanation:
Amazon S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval is designed for archive data that is accessed rarely and optimized for low storage cost. Its Expedited retrieval option typically makes archived objects available in 1–5 minutes, which meets the five-minute restore requirement. Standard retrieval is too slow at 3–5 hours, while S3 Standard-IA and S3 One Zone-IA provide immediate access but are not the lowest-cost archival choice for rarely restored archives.

**Learn more:** [Understanding archive retrieval options - Amazon S3](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/restoring-objects-retrieval-options.html) · [Understanding S3 Glacier storage classes for long-term data storage - Amazon S3](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/glacier-storage-classes.html)

A company is building a new furniture inventory application. The company has deployed the application on a fleet of Amazon EC2 instances across multiple Availability Zones. The EC2 instances run behind an Application Load Balancer (ALB) in their VPC.  
  
A solutions architect has observed that incoming traffic seems to favor one EC2 instance, resulting in latency for some requests.  
  
What should the solutions architect do to resolve this issue?

options.text: Disable session affinity (sticky sessions) on the ALB
Replace the ALB with a Network Load Balancer
Increase the number of EC2 instances in each Availability Zone
Adjust the frequency of the health checks on the ALB's target group

questions.explanation:
For an Application Load Balancer, requests are distributed independently across healthy targets by default. If sticky sessions (session affinity) are enabled, the ALB uses cookies to keep sending a client's requests to the same EC2 instance, which can make one instance appear to receive disproportionately more traffic and increase latency. Disabling sticky sessions removes that target binding and allows the ALB to spread requests normally across the instances in the target group.

**Learn more:** [Edit target group attributes for your Application Load Balancer - Elastic Load Balancing](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/elasticloadbalancing/latest/application/edit-target-group-attributes.html) · [Which stickiness strategy is right for you? - AWS Prescriptive Guidance](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/prescriptive-guidance/latest/load-balancer-stickiness/options.html)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],A company stores sensitive data in Amazon S3. A solutions architect must design an encryption solution. The company needs to fully control users' ability to create, rotate, and disable encryption keys with minimal effort for any data that must be encrypted.  
  
Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Use default server-side encryption with Amazon S3 managed encryption keys (SSE-S3) to store the sensitive data.
Create a customer managed key by using AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS). Use the new key to encrypt the S3 objects by using server-side encryption with AWS KMS keys (SSE-KMS).
Create an AWS managed key by using AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS). Use the new key to encrypt the S3 objects by using server-side encryption with AWS KMS keys (SSE-KMS).
Download S3 objects to an Amazon EC2 instance. Encrypt the objects by using customer managed keys. Upload the encrypted objects back into Amazon S3.

questions.explanation:
Using a customer managed AWS KMS key with Amazon S3 SSE-KMS provides customer control over the key lifecycle and permissions, including the ability to create keys, enable or disable them, and configure or perform rotation, while still using native server-side encryption in S3. SSE-S3 does not provide customer control of the encryption keys, AWS managed KMS keys are not fully customer-configurable, and client-side re-encryption through EC2 adds unnecessary operational effort.

**Learn more:** [Using server-side encryption with AWS KMS keys (SSE-KMS) - Amazon S3](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/UsingKMSEncryption.html) · [Specifying server-side encryption with AWS KMS (SSE-KMS) - Amazon S3](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/specifying-kms-encryption.html)

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],A company hosts a high-traffic static website on Amazon S3 behind an Amazon CloudFront distribution with a default TTL of 0 seconds. The company wants to enable caching to improve website performance.  
  
However, the company also needs to ensure that stale content is not served for more than a few minutes after a deployment.  
  
Which combination of caching methods should a solutions architect implement to meet these requirements? **(Choose two.)**

options.text: Set the CloudFront default TTL to 2 minutes.
Set a default TTL of 2 minutes on the S3 bucket.
Add a Cache-Control private directive to the objects in Amazon S3.
Create an AWS Lambda@Edge function to add an Expires header to HTTP responses. Configure the function to run on viewer response.
Add a Cache-Control max-age directive of 24 hours to the objects in Amazon S3. On deployment, create a CloudFront invalidation to clear any changed files from edge caches.

questions.explanation:
CloudFront uses the cache behavior's default TTL when the origin does not return `Cache-Control` or `Expires`, and AWS documentation notes that setting the TTLs to 0 disables caching. Setting the CloudFront default TTL to 2 minutes enables caching while limiting stale content to only a few minutes for objects without explicit cache headers. For static website content, AWS also supports using long-lived object cache headers such as `Cache-Control: max-age` together with a CloudFront invalidation after deployment so that changed files are removed from edge caches immediately instead of waiting for the full TTL to expire. This combination satisfies both performance and freshness requirements.

**Learn more:** [Manage how long content stays in the cache (expiration) - Amazon CloudFront](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonCloudFront/latest/DeveloperGuide/Expiration.html) · [Understand cache policies - Amazon CloudFront](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonCloudFront/latest/DeveloperGuide/cache-key-understand-cache-policy.html)

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],A company runs an application in the AWS Cloud that generates sensitive archival data files. The company wants to redesign the application's data storage. The company needs to encrypt the data files and ensure that third parties cannot access the data before it is encrypted and sent to AWS. The company has already created an Amazon S3 bucket.  
  
Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Configure the S3 bucket to use client-side encryption with an Amazon S3 managed encryption key. Configure the application to use the S3 bucket to store the archival files.
Configure the S3 bucket to use server-side encryption with AWS KMS keys (SSE-KMS). Configure the application to use the S3 bucket to store the archival files.
Configure the S3 bucket to use dual-layer server-side encryption with AWS KMS keys (SSE-KMS). Configure the application to use the S3 bucket to store the archival files.
Configure the application to use client-side encryption with a key stored in AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS). Configure the application to store the archival files in the S3 bucket.

questions.explanation:
Client-side encryption is required because the data must be encrypted before it is sent to Amazon S3. AWS states that with client-side encryption, objects are encrypted locally before being passed to S3, and S3 receives them already encrypted, so the data is not exposed to AWS or other third parties prior to encryption. Server-side options such as SSE-KMS and DSSE-KMS encrypt data only after Amazon S3 receives it. Using client-side encryption with a key stored in AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) satisfies the requirement.

**Learn more:** [What is the Amazon S3 Encryption Client?](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/amazon-s3-encryption-client/latest/developerguide/what-is-s3-encryption-client.html) · [Client-side and server-side encryption - Amazon S3 Encryption Client](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/amazon-s3-encryption-client/latest/developerguide/client-server-side.html)

A company has multiple AWS accounts in an organization in AWS Organizations that are used by different business units. The company also has multiple offices worldwide. It needs to update security group rules to allow new office CIDR ranges or remove old CIDR ranges across the organization. The company wants to centralize management of the security group rules to minimize the administrative overhead required for CIDR range updates.  
  
Which solution will meet these requirements **MOST cost-effectively**?

options.text: Create VPC security groups in the organization's management account. Update the security groups when a CIDR range update is necessary.

Create a VPC customer managed prefix list that contains the list of CIDRs. Use AWS Resource Access Manager (AWS RAM) to share the prefix list across the organization. Use the prefix list in the security groups across the organization.

Create an AWS managed prefix list. Use an AWS Security Hub policy to enforce the security group update across the organization. Use an AWS Lambda function to update the prefix list automatically when the CIDR ranges change.

Create security groups in a central administrative AWS account. Create an AWS Firewall Manager common security group policy for the whole organization. Select the previously created security groups as primary groups in the policy.

questions.explanation:
A customer-managed prefix list lets the company keep the office CIDR ranges in one centrally managed list and reference that list in security group rules instead of maintaining individual CIDRs in each account. AWS RAM can share a customer-managed prefix list with an AWS Organizations organization, so accounts across the organization can use the same prefix list in their security groups. Updating the prefix list once centrally is the lowest-overhead and most cost-effective way to propagate CIDR changes. AWS-managed prefix lists cannot be created or modified by customers, and Firewall Manager common security group policies are a heavier, less cost-effective solution for this use case than simply sharing a customer-managed prefix list.

**Learn more:** [Share customer-managed prefix lists - Amazon VPC](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/userguide/sharing-managed-prefix-lists.html) · [Consolidate and manage network CIDR blocks with managed prefix lists - Amazon VPC](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/userguide/managed-prefix-lists.html)

A company has recently released a new application for its customers. The application runs on multiple Amazon EC2 instances in two Availability Zones. End users communicate with the application using TCP.  
  
The application must be highly available and automatically scale as the user count grows.  
  
Which combination of steps will satisfy these requirements **MOST** cost-effectively? *(Choose two.)*

options.text: Add a Network Load Balancer in front of the EC2 instances.
Configure an Auto Scaling group for the EC2 instances.
Add an Application Load Balancer in front of the EC2 instances.
Manually add more EC2 instances for the application.
Add a Gateway Load Balancer in front of the EC2 instances.

questions.explanation:
A Network Load Balancer operates at the transport layer and supports TCP traffic. It distributes traffic across healthy EC2 targets in enabled Availability Zones. An Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling group automatically adjusts instance capacity as demand changes, maintaining availability while avoiding the cost of manually keeping excess instances running. When attached to the load balancer’s target group, instances launched and terminated by the Auto Scaling group are registered and deregistered automatically.

**Learn more:** [What is a Network Load Balancer?](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/elasticloadbalancing/latest/network/introduction.html) · [What is Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling?](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/autoscaling/ec2/userguide/what-is-amazon-ec2-auto-scaling.html)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],A retail company has several businesses. The IT team for each business manages its own AWS account. Each team account belongs to an organization in AWS Organizations. Each team tracks its product inventory levels in an Amazon DynamoDB table in that team's own AWS account.  
  
The company is deploying a central inventory reporting application in a shared AWS account. The application must be able to read items from all the teams' DynamoDB tables.  
  
Which authentication option will meet these requirements **MOST securely**?

options.text: Integrate DynamoDB with AWS Secrets Manager in the inventory application account. Configure the application to use the correct secret from Secrets Manager to authenticate and read the DynamoDB table. Schedule secret rotation for every 30 days.

In every business account, create an IAM user that has programmatic access. Configure the application to use the correct IAM user access key ID and secret access key to authenticate and read the DynamoDB table. Manually rotate IAM access keys every 30 days.

In every business account, create an IAM role named BU_ROLE with a policy that gives the role access to the DynamoDB table and a trust policy to trust a specific role in the inventory application account. In the inventory account, create a role named APP_ROLE that allows access to the STS AssumeRole API operation. Configure the application to use APP_ROLE and assume the crossaccount role BU_ROLE to read the DynamoDB table.

Integrate DynamoDB with AWS Certificate Manager (ACM). Generate identity certificates to authenticate DynamoDB. Configure the application to use the correct certificate to authenticate and read the DynamoDB table.

questions.explanation:
Using a cross-account IAM role with AWS STS AssumeRole is the most secure choice because it gives the central application temporary credentials to access each business unit's DynamoDB table, instead of requiring long-term stored secrets or IAM user access keys. In this design, each business account creates a role with least-privilege permissions to its table and a trust policy that allows only the application role in the shared account to assume it. AWS IAM best practices recommend temporary credentials through IAM roles for workloads, and STS AssumeRole is the standard mechanism for cross-account access.

**Learn more:** [Security best practices in IAM](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/best-practices.html) · [Secure access keys](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/securing_access-keys.html)

A company runs an application by using Amazon EC2 instances and AWS Lambda functions. The EC2 instances run in private subnets in a VPC. The Lambda functions require direct network access to the EC2 instances for the application to function.  
  
The application will run for 1 year. The number of Lambda functions that the application uses will increase during the 1-year period. The company must minimize costs for all application resources.  
  
Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Purchase an EC2 Instance Savings Plan. Connect the Lambda functions to the private subnets that contain the EC2 instances.
Purchase an EC2 Instance Savings Plan. Connect the Lambda functions to new public subnets in the same VPC where the EC2 instances run.
Purchase a Compute Savings Plan. Connect the Lambda functions to the private subnets that contain the EC2 instances.
Purchase a Compute Savings Plan. Keep the Lambda functions in the Lambda service VPC.

questions.explanation:
AWS Lambda functions that need to reach Amazon EC2 instances in private subnets should be attached to the VPC through private subnets, which gives them private network connectivity to those resources. To minimize 1-year compute costs when the environment uses both Amazon EC2 and AWS Lambda and Lambda usage is expected to grow, a Compute Savings Plan is the correct pricing model because it covers both EC2 and Lambda usage, whereas an EC2 Instance Savings Plan covers only EC2. This makes Compute Savings Plans with Lambda connected to the private subnets the cost-optimized and technically valid solution.

**Learn more:** [Giving Lambda functions access to resources in an Amazon VPC - AWS Lambda](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/lambda/latest/dg/configuration-vpc.html) · [Enable internet access for VPC-connected Lambda functions - AWS Lambda](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/lambda/latest/dg/configuration-vpc-internet.html)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],A company has created a new AWS account. The account has just been provisioned, and no default settings have been changed. The company is concerned about securing the AWS account root user.  
  
What should be done to protect the root user?

options.text: Create IAM users for daily administrative tasks. Disable the root user.
Create IAM users for daily administrative tasks. Enable multi-factor authentication on the root user.
Generate an access key for the root user. Use the access key for daily administration tasks instead of the AWS Management Console.
Provide the root user credentials to the most senior solutions architect. Have the solutions architect use the root user for daily administration tasks.

questions.explanation:
AWS recommends securing the account root user by enabling multi-factor authentication and not using the root user for routine administration. Daily administrative work should be performed with IAM users or other administrative identities instead. In a newly provisioned default AWS account, disabling the root user is not the standard action, while creating root access keys or sharing root credentials are both contrary to AWS security best practices.

**Learn more:** [Using the AWS account root user](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/accounts/latest/reference/root-user.html) · [Root user best practices for your AWS account](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/root-user-best-practices.html)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],A company runs a web application on Amazon EC2 instances that are deployed in the private subnet of a VPC. An Application Load Balancer (ALB) spanning the public subnets sends web traffic to the EC2 instances. The company wants to add new security controls to limit inbound traffic from the ALB to the EC2 instances, while preventing access from any other source inside or outside the EC2 instances' private subnet.  
  
Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Configure a route in a route table to direct traffic from the internet to the private IP addresses of the EC2 instances.
Configure the security group for the EC2 instances to only allow traffic that comes from the security group for the ALB.
Move the EC2 instances into the public subnet. Give the EC2 instances a set of Elastic IP addresses.
Configure the security group for the ALB to allow any TCP traffic on any port.

questions.explanation:
An EC2 security group can allow inbound traffic by referencing the ALB's security group as the source. That permits traffic only from the load balancer to the instances and denies other inbound sources unless separately allowed. This matches the requirement to restrict instance access to ALB-originated traffic only.

**Learn more:** [Amazon EC2 security groups for your EC2 instances](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/us_en/AWSEC2/latest/UserGuide/ec2-security-groups.html) · [Create a security group for your Amazon EC2 instance](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSEC2/latest/UserGuide/creating-security-group.html)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],A company has migrated a two-tier application from its on-premises data center to the AWS Cloud. The data tier is a Multi-AZ deployment of Amazon RDS for Oracle with 12 TB of General Purpose SSD Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) storage. The application is built to process and store documents in the database as binary large objects (BLOBs), with an average document size of 6 MB.  
  
Over time, the database has increased in size, which has reduced performance and raised storage costs. The company must improve database performance and needs a solution that is highly available and resilient.  
  
Which solution will meet these requirements **MOST cost-effectively**?

options.text: Reduce the RDS DB instance size. Increase the storage capacity to 24 TiB. Change the storage type to Magnetic.
Increase the RDS DB instance size. Increase the storage capacity to 24 TiChange the storage type to Provisioned IOPS.
Create an Amazon S3 bucket. Update the application to store documents in the S3 bucket. Store the object metadata in the existing database.
Create an Amazon DynamoDB table. Update the application to use DynamoDB. Use AWS Database Migration Service (AWS DMS) to migrate data from the Oracle database to DynamoDB.

questions.explanation:
Amazon S3 is the most cost-effective place to store large document binaries because it is highly durable, highly available object storage, while Amazon RDS storage is optimized for database workloads and becomes more expensive as large BLOB data grows. Keeping only object metadata in Oracle reduces the database size, lowers RDS storage and I/O pressure, and improves database performance without requiring a full database platform migration. AWS documentation also indicates that Provisioned IOPS is for I/O-intensive database workloads, but that would only improve performance at higher cost rather than addressing the root cause, and magnetic storage is deprecated for Amazon RDS.

**Learn more:** [Amazon RDS DB instance storage](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonRDS/latest/UserGuide/CHAP_Storage.html) · [Best practices for Amazon RDS](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonRDS/latest/UserGuide/CHAP_BestPractices.html)

A company wants to analyze and troubleshoot **Access Denied** errors and **Unauthorized** errors that are related to IAM permissions. The company has AWS CloudTrail turned on.  
  
Which solution will meet these requirements with the **LEAST effort**?

options.text: Use AWS Glue and write custom scripts to query CloudTrail logs for the errors.
Use AWS Batch and write custom scripts to query CloudTrail logs for the errors.
Search CloudTrail logs with Amazon Athena queries to identify the errors.
Search CloudTrail logs with Amazon QuickSight. Create a dashboard to identify the errors.

questions.explanation:
Amazon Athena is the simplest fit because AWS supports querying AWS CloudTrail logs in Amazon S3 directly with SQL, including example CloudTrail queries for analysis and troubleshooting. Since CloudTrail is already enabled, Athena can search those logs for IAM-related Access Denied or Unauthorized events without building custom ETL or batch-processing scripts. AWS Glue and AWS Batch add unnecessary implementation effort, and Amazon QuickSight is oriented to dashboards rather than the lowest-effort log investigation workflow.

**Learn more:** [Query AWS CloudTrail logs - Amazon Athena](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/athena/latest/ug/cloudtrail-logs.html) · [Example CloudTrail log queries - Amazon Athena](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/athena/latest/ug/query-examples-cloudtrail-logs.html)
