A company wants to give data scientists near real-time, read-only access to the company's production Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL database. The database is currently configured as a Single-AZ database. The data scientists run complex queries that will not affect the production database. The company requires a highly available solution.  
  
Which solution will meet these requirements **MOST cost-effectively**?

options.text: Scale the existing production database in a maintenance window to provide enough power for the data scientists.
Change the setup from a Single-AZ to a Multi-AZ instance deployment with a larger secondary standby instance. Provide the data scientists access to the secondary instance.
Change the setup from a Single-AZ to a Multi-AZ instance deployment. Provide two additional read replicas for the data scientists.
Change the setup from a Single-AZ to a Multi-AZ cluster deployment with two readable standby instances. Provide read endpoints to the data scientists.

questions.explanation:
An Amazon RDS Multi-AZ DB cluster is designed for high availability and read scaling together: it provides one writer instance and two readable standby instances in separate Availability Zones, and a reader endpoint can route the data scientists' read-only connections to those standby instances. By contrast, a standard Multi-AZ DB instance deployment has a standby that cannot serve read traffic, and adding separate read replicas to a Multi-AZ instance would add extra instances beyond what is needed here. Therefore, the Multi-AZ DB cluster with readable standbys is the best fit and the most cost-effective of the listed options.

**Learn more:** [Configuring and managing a Multi-AZ deployment for Amazon RDS](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonRDS/latest/UserGuide/Concepts.MultiAZ.html) · [Multi-AZ DB instance deployments for Amazon RDS](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonRDS/latest/UserGuide/Concepts.MultiAZSingleStandby.html)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],A company is deploying a new application to Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS) on an AWS Fargate cluster. The application requires a storage solution for persistent data.  
  
The solution must be:  
  
- highly available  
- fault tolerant  
- shared across multiple application containers  
  
Which solution will meet these requirements with the **LEAST operational overhead**?

options.text: Create Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) volumes in the same Availability Zones where EKS worker nodes are placed. Register the volumes in a StorageClass object on an EKS cluster. Use EBS Multi-Attach to share the data between containers.
Create an Amazon Elastic File System (Amazon EFS) file system. Register the file system in a StorageClass object on an EKS cluster. Use the same file system for all containers.
Create an Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) volume. Register the volume in a StorageClass object on an EKS cluster. Use the same volume for all containers.

Create Amazon Elastic File System (Amazon EFS) file systems in the same Availability Zones where EKS worker nodes are placed. Register the file systems in a StorageClass object on an EKS cluster. Create an AWS Lambda function to synchronize the data between file systems.

questions.explanation:
Amazon EFS is the correct choice because it provides managed shared file storage that can be mounted by multiple containers and is designed to be highly available and fault tolerant across Availability Zones. For Amazon EKS on AWS Fargate, Amazon EBS volumes cannot be mounted to Fargate Pods, which eliminates the EBS options. A single EFS file system used through Kubernetes storage integration satisfies persistence and shared access while minimizing administration compared with building and synchronizing multiple file systems.

**Learn more:** [Use elastic file system storage with Amazon EFS - Amazon EKS](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/eks/latest/userguide/efs-csi.html) · [Use Kubernetes volume storage with Amazon EBS - Amazon EKS](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/eks/latest/userguide/ebs-csi.html)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],A company's compliance team needs to move its file shares to AWS. The shares run on a Windows Server SMB file share. A self-managed on-premises Active Directory controls access to the files and folders.  
  
The company wants to use Amazon FSx for Windows File Server as part of the solution. The company must ensure that the on-premises Active Directory groups restrict access to the FSx for Windows File Server SMB compliance shares, folders, and files after the move to AWS. The company has created an FSx for Windows File Server file system.  
  
Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Create an Active Directory Connector to connect to the Active Directory. Map the Active Directory groups to IAM groups to restrict access.
Assign a tag with a Restrict tag key and a Compliance tag value. Map the Active Directory groups to IAM groups to restrict access.
Create an IAM service-linked role that is linked directly to FSx for Windows File Server to restrict access.
Join the file system to the Active Directory to restrict access.

questions.explanation:
Amazon FSx for Windows File Server provides SMB authentication through Microsoft Active Directory and enforces share-, file-, and folder-level permissions with standard Windows ACLs. When the file system is joined to the self-managed Active Directory domain, users can access the shares with their existing AD identities and groups, and existing ACL-based authorization can continue to control access. IAM groups, tags, and service-linked roles do not control Windows SMB share or NTFS permissions for FSx for Windows File Server.

**Learn more:** [Working with Microsoft Active Directory - Amazon FSx for Windows File Server](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/fsx/latest/WindowsGuide/aws-ad-integration-fsxW.html) · [Best practices for FSx for Windows File Server - Amazon FSx for Windows File Server](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/fsx/latest/WindowsGuide/windows-best-practices.html)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],A company runs multiple Amazon EC2 Linux instances in a VPC across two Availability Zones. The instances host applications that use a hierarchical directory structure. The applications must read from and write to shared storage rapidly and concurrently.  
  
What should a solutions architect do to meet these requirements?

options.text: Create an Amazon S3 bucket. Allow access from all the EC2 instances in the VPC.
Create an Amazon Elastic File System (Amazon EFS) file system. Mount the EFS file system from each EC2 instance.
Create a file system on a Provisioned IOPS SSD (io2) Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) volume. Attach the EBS volume to all the EC2 instances.
Create file systems on Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) volumes that are attached to each EC2 instance. Synchronize the EBS volumes across the different EC2 instances.

questions.explanation:
Amazon Elastic File System (Amazon EFS) is the correct service because it provides shared file storage for Linux workloads, supports concurrent read and write access from multiple EC2 instances, and is accessible across multiple Availability Zones in the same Region. That matches an application that needs a shared hierarchical file system. Amazon S3 is object storage rather than a shared file system, and Amazon EBS volumes are Availability Zone scoped block storage; even io2 Multi-Attach does not solve this here because it is limited to instances in the same Availability Zone and standard file systems are not designed for simultaneous access by multiple servers. Official AWS documentation states that Amazon EFS supports concurrent access from multiple EC2 instances and is accessible from all Availability Zones in the Region, while EBS Multi-Attach is same-AZ only and requires special clustered file-system considerations.

**Learn more:** [Creating and managing EFS resources - Amazon Elastic File System](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/efs/latest/ug/creating-using.html) · [How Amazon EFS works - Amazon Elastic File System](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/efs/latest/ug/how-it-works.html)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],A robotics company is creating a solution for medical surgery. The robots will use advanced sensors, cameras, and AI algorithms to perceive their environment and complete surgeries.  
  
The company requires a public load balancer in the AWS Cloud to ensure seamless communication with backend services. The load balancer must be able to route traffic to different target groups based on the query strings. The traffic must also be encrypted.  
  
Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Use a Network Load Balancer with a certificate attached from AWS Certificate Manager (ACM). Use query parameter-based routing.
Use a Gateway Load Balancer. Import a generated certificate in AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM). Attach the certificate to the load balancer. Use HTTP path-based routing.
Use an Application Load Balancer with a certificate attached from AWS Certificate Manager (ACM). Use query parameter-based routing.
Use a Network Load Balancer. Import a generated certificate in AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM). Attach the certificate to the load balancer. Use query parameter-based routing.

questions.explanation:
An Application Load Balancer is the Elastic Load Balancing option that supports advanced HTTP/HTTPS request routing, including listener rules that match on query strings and forward requests to different target groups. It also supports HTTPS listeners using AWS Certificate Manager certificates for encrypted traffic. Network Load Balancers do not provide query string-based routing, and Gateway Load Balancers are intended for network appliances rather than application-layer request routing. Official AWS documentation states that ALB supports routing based on the query string and that query string conditions can be used in listener rules. It also supports HTTPS listeners with ACM-managed certificates.

**Learn more:** [Condition types for listener rules - Elastic Load Balancing](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/elasticloadbalancing/latest/application/rule-condition-types.html) · [Application Load Balancer - AWS Prescriptive Guidance](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/prescriptive-guidance/latest/choosing-the-right-aws-service-for-your-microservice-endpoints/app-load-balancer.html)

A company operates a multi-tier web application. The application's internal service components run on Amazon EC2 instances. Those internal components must access third-party software-as-a-service (SaaS) APIs hosted on AWS.  
  
The company must provide secure, private connectivity from the application's internal services to the third-party SaaS application while keeping public internet exposure to a minimum.  
  
Which solution will satisfy these requirements?

options.text: Implement an AWS Site-to-Site VPN to establish a secure connection with the third-party SaaS provider.
Deploy AWS Transit Gateway to manage and route traffic between the application's VPC and the third-party SaaS provider.
Configure AWS PrivateLink to allow only outbound traffic from the VPC without enabling the third-party SaaS provider to establish.
Use AWS PrivateLink to create a private connection between the application's VPC and the third-party SaaS provider.

questions.explanation:
AWS PrivateLink lets a service consumer create an interface VPC endpoint to privately connect resources in its VPC to a provider's endpoint service, including supported SaaS products. The traffic stays on the AWS network and does not require an internet gateway, NAT device, public IP address, or Site-to-Site VPN, thereby minimizing public internet exposure.

**Learn more:** [Access SaaS products through AWS PrivateLink](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/privatelink/privatelink-access-saas.html) · [What is AWS PrivateLink?](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/privatelink/what-is-privatelink.html)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],A company has hired an external vendor to perform work in the company’s AWS account. The vendor uses an automated tool that is hosted in an AWS account the vendor owns. The vendor does not have IAM access to the company’s AWS account.  
  
How should a solutions architect grant this access to the vendor?

options.text: Create an IAM role in the company’s account to delegate access to the vendor’s IAM role. Attach the appropriate IAM policies to the role for the permissions that the vendor requires.

Create an IAM user in the company’s account with a password that meets the password complexity requirements. Attach the appropriate IAM policies to the user for the permissions that the vendor requires.

Create an IAM group in the company’s account. Add the tool’s IAM user from the vendor account to the group. Attach the appropriate IAM policies to the group for the permissions that the vendor requires.

Create a new identity provider by choosing “AWS account” as the provider type in the IAM console. Supply the vendor’s AWS account ID and user name. Attach the appropriate IAM policies to the new provider for the permissions that the vendor requires.

questions.explanation:
The correct approach for a third party that operates from its own AWS account is cross-account role assumption. Create an IAM role in the company account, attach only the permissions the vendor needs, and configure the role’s trust policy to allow the vendor’s AWS account or specific IAM role to assume it. AWS documents third-party access as using IAM roles rather than sharing long-term IAM user credentials, and IAM groups cannot include users from another account. An IAM identity provider is also not the mechanism for trusting another AWS account for this scenario.

**Learn more:** [Access to AWS accounts owned by third parties - AWS IAM](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/en_en/IAM/latest/UserGuide/id_roles_common-scenarios_third-party.html) · [IAM tutorial: Delegate access across AWS accounts using IAM roles - AWS IAM](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/en_en/IAM/latest/UserGuide/tutorial_cross-account-with-roles.html)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],A company sees an increase in Amazon EC2 costs on its most recent bill. The billing team notices unwanted vertical scaling of instance types for a couple of EC2 instances. A solutions architect must create a graph that compares the last 2 months of EC2 costs and perform an in-depth analysis to determine the root cause of the vertical scaling.  
  
How should the solutions architect generate this information with the **LEAST operational overhead**?

options.text: Use AWS Budgets to create a budget report and compare EC2 costs based on instance types.
Use Cost Explorer's granular filtering feature to perform an in-depth analysis of EC2 costs based on instance types.
Use graphs from the AWS Billing and Cost Management dashboard to compare EC2 costs based on instance types for the last 2 months.
Use AWS Cost and Usage Reports to create a report and send it to an Amazon S3 bucket. Use Amazon QuickSight with Amazon S3 as a source to generate an interactive graph based on instance types.

questions.explanation:
AWS Cost Explorer is the lowest-overhead way to analyze this because it provides built-in charts, month-to-month cost comparison, and grouping/filtering by dimensions such as instance types for Amazon EC2. Its Cost Comparison capability is specifically intended to identify cost changes and their drivers between two months, which matches the need to compare the last 2 months and investigate why costs increased. AWS Budgets is mainly for budget tracking and alerts, the Billing dashboard is only a higher-level summary, and Cost and Usage Reports with Amazon S3 and Amazon QuickSight require more setup and maintenance than needed for this analysis.

**Learn more:** [Comparing your costs between time periods - AWS Cost Management](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/cost-management/latest/userguide/ce-cost-comparison.html) · [Performing a cost comparison - AWS Cost Management](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/cost-management/latest/userguide/ce-perform-cost-comparison.html)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],A company wants to create a logging solution for multiple AWS accounts. The company currently keeps logs from all accounts in a centralized account. It has created an Amazon S3 bucket in the centralized account to store VPC flow logs and AWS CloudTrail logs.  
  
All logs must be:  
  
- highly available for 30 days for frequent analysis,  
- retained for an additional 60 days for backup purposes, and  
- deleted 90 days after creation.  
  
Which solution will meet these requirements **MOST cost-effectively**?

options.text: Transition objects to the S3 Standard storage class 30 days after creation. Write an expiration action that directs Amazon S3 to delete objects after 90 days.

Transition objects to the S3 Standard-Infrequent Access (S3 Standard-IA) storage class 30 days after creation. Move all objects to the S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval storage class after 90 days. Write an expiration action that directs Amazon S3 to delete objects after 90 days.
Transition objects to the S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval storage class 30 days after creation. Write an expiration action that directs Amazon S3 to delete objects after 90 days.

Transition objects to the S3 One Zone-Infrequent Access (S3 One Zone-IA) storage class 30 days after creation. Move all objects to the S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval storage class after 90 days. Write an expiration action that directs Amazon S3 to delete objects after 90 days.

questions.explanation:
For the first 30 days, the logs need frequent access, so keeping them in S3 Standard fits that access pattern. After that, the logs are only being kept as backup until day 90, so transitioning them to S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval is the lowest-cost option among the choices that still maintains multi-AZ resilience. AWS documents that S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval is for archive and backup data, is not for real-time access, and has a 90-day minimum storage duration, which aligns exactly with storing the objects there from day 30 through day 90 before expiration. S3 One Zone-IA is less resilient because it stores data in only one Availability Zone, so it does not satisfy the highly available requirement. Keeping the objects in S3 Standard after day 30 is more expensive than necessary, and moving them again at day 90 is pointless if they are deleted at day 90.

**Learn more:** [Understanding and managing Amazon S3 storage classes](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/storage-class-intro.html) · [Understanding S3 Glacier storage classes for long-term data storage](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/glacier-storage-classes.html)

A law firm must share information with the public. The information includes hundreds of files that need to be publicly readable. No one may modify or delete the files before a specified future date.  
  
Which solution will meet these requirements in the **MOST secure** way?

options.text: Upload all files to an Amazon S3 bucket that is configured for static website hosting. Grant read-only IAM permissions to any AWS principals that access the S3 bucket until the designated date.

Create a new Amazon S3 bucket with S3 Versioning enabled. Use S3 Object Lock with a retention period in accordance with the designated date. Configure the S3 bucket for static website hosting. Set an S3 bucket policy to allow read-only access to the objects.

Create a new Amazon S3 bucket with S3 Versioning enabled. Configure an event trigger to run an AWS Lambda function in case of object modification or deletion. Configure the Lambda function to replace the objects with the original versions from a private S3 bucket.

Upload all files to an Amazon S3 bucket that is configured for static website hosting. Select the folder that contains the files. Use S3 Object Lock with a retention period in accordance with the designated date. Grant read-only IAM permissions to any AWS principals that access the S3 bucket.

questions.explanation:
Amazon S3 Object Lock provides write-once-read-many protection by preventing object versions from being deleted or overwritten until the retention period expires, and S3 Object Lock works only on buckets with S3 Versioning enabled. For public readability of static content in Amazon S3, the normal approach is to use a bucket policy that allows read access to the objects. That makes the versioned, Object-Locked S3 bucket with a public read bucket policy the most secure option for allowing public access while prohibiting modification or deletion until the designated date.

**Learn more:** [Locking objects with Object Lock - Amazon S3 User Guide](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/object-lock.html) · [Setting permissions for website access - Amazon S3 User Guide](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/WebsiteAccessPermissionsReqd.html)

A solutions architect operates a web application on multiple Amazon EC2 instances, with the instances placed in separate target groups behind an Application Load Balancer (ALB). Users access the application through a public website.  
  
The solutions architect needs to let engineers use a development version of the website to reach one specific development EC2 instance for testing new application features. The solutions architect wants to use an Amazon Route 53 hosted zone to provide the engineers with access to the development instance. The solution must automatically route to the development instance even if that development instance is replaced.  
  
Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Create an A Record for the development website that has the value set to the ALB. Create a listener rule on the ALB that forwards requests for the development website to the target group that contains the development instance.
Recreate the development instance with a public IP address. Create an A Record for the development website that has the value set to the public IP address of the development instance.

Create an A Record for the development website that has the value set to the ALB. Create a listener rule on the ALB to redirect requests for the development website to the public IP address of the development instance.

Place all the instances in the same target group. Create an A Record for the development website. Set the value to the ALB. Create a listener rule on the ALB that forwards requests for the development website to the target group.

questions.explanation:
The correct design is to create a Route 53 alias A record for the development hostname that points to the ALB, and then use an ALB host-based listener rule to forward requests for that hostname to the target group containing the development instance. Route 53 officially supports alias records to an Application Load Balancer, and an ALB listener rule can route requests based on the host header to a specific target group. This preserves a stable DNS name while allowing the backend instance to be replaced without changing DNS, as long as the replacement instance is registered in the same target group.

**Learn more:** [Routing traffic to an ELB load balancer - Amazon Route 53](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/Route53/latest/DeveloperGuide/routing-to-elb-load-balancer.html) · [Register targets with your Application Load Balancer target group - Elastic Load Balancing](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/elasticloadbalancing/latest/application/target-group-register-targets.html)

A company measures customer satisfaction through surveys hosted on its website. At times, the surveys reach thousands of customers each hour. Survey results are currently delivered to the company by email, where employees manually review the results and evaluate customer sentiment.  
  
The company wants to automate the customer-survey process. Survey results must remain available for the preceding 12 months.  
  
Which solution satisfies these requirements in the **MOST** scalable way?

options.text: Send the survey results data to an Amazon API Gateway endpoint that is connected to an Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) queue. Create an AWS Lambda function to poll the SQS queue, call Amazon Comprehend for sentiment analysis, and save the results to an Amazon DynamoDB table. Set the TTL for all records to 365 days in the future.

Send the survey results data to an API that is running on an Amazon EC2 instance. Configure the API to store the survey results as a new record in an Amazon DynamoDB table, call Amazon Comprehend for sentiment analysis, and save the results in a second DynamoDB table. Set the TTL for all records to 365 days in the future.

Write the survey results data to an Amazon S3 bucket. Use S3 Event Notifications to invoke an AWS Lambda function to read the data and call Amazon Rekognition for sentiment analysis. Store the sentiment analysis results in a second S3 bucket. Use S3 lifecycle policies on each bucket to expire objects after 365 days.

Send the survey results data to an Amazon API Gateway endpoint that is connected to an Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) queue. Configure the SQS queue to invoke an AWS Lambda function that calls Amazon Lex for sentiment analysis and saves the results to an Amazon DynamoDB table. Set the TTL for all records to 365 days in the future.

questions.explanation:
Amazon Comprehend detects sentiment in text. API Gateway and Amazon SQS provide a decoupled, scalable ingestion buffer for high-volume survey submissions, while a Lambda SQS event source mapping polls and processes queued messages. DynamoDB scales the stored results, and a TTL value set 365 days ahead makes each record eligible for expiration after the required retention period. Amazon Rekognition is not a text-sentiment service, and Amazon Lex is intended for conversational interfaces rather than sentiment analysis.

**Learn more:** [Sentiment - Amazon Comprehend](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/comprehend/latest/dg/how-sentiment.html) · [Using Lambda with Amazon SQS](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/lambda/latest/dg/with-sqs.html)

options.text: Create an S3 bucket policy that permits access to the bucket from the public IP address range of the company’s on-premises data center.
Use IAM Roles Anywhere to obtain security credentials in IAM Identity Center that grant access to the S3 bucket. Configure the virtual machines to assume the role by using the AWS CLI.
Install the AWS CLI on the virtual machine. Configure the AWS CLI with access keys from an IAM user that has access to the bucket.

Create an IAM user and policy that grants access to the bucket. Store the access key and secret key for the IAM user in AWS Secrets Manager. Configure the application to retrieve the access key and secret key at startup.

questions.explanation:
IAM Roles Anywhere enables workloads that run outside AWS, including on-premises virtual machines, to authenticate with X.509 certificates and receive temporary credentials for an IAM role. Granting that role the necessary S3 permissions provides secure, short-lived access without distributing long-term IAM-user access keys.

**Learn more:** [Access for non-AWS workloads](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/id_roles_common-scenarios_non-aws.html) · [Get temporary security credentials from IAM Roles Anywhere](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/rolesanywhere/latest/userguide/credential-helper.html)

A company runs its application on Oracle Database Enterprise Edition. The company needs to migrate the application and the database to AWS. The company can use the Bring Your Own License (BYOL) model during the migration to AWS. The application uses third-party database features that require privileged access.  
  
A solutions architect must design a solution for the database migration.  
  
Which solution will meet these requirements **MOST cost-effectively**?

options.text: Migrate the database to Amazon RDS for Oracle by using native tools. Replace the third-party features with AWS Lambda.
Migrate the database to Amazon RDS Custom for Oracle by using native tools. Customize the new database settings to support the third-party features.
Migrate the database to Amazon DynamoDB by using AWS Database Migration Service (AWS DMS). Customize the new database settings to support the third-party features.
Migrate the database to Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL by using AWS Database Migration Service (AWS DMS). Rewrite the application code to remove the dependency on third-party features.

questions.explanation:
Amazon RDS Custom for Oracle is the best fit because it supports Oracle Database Enterprise Edition with the BYOL licensing model and is designed for workloads that require privileged access to the database and underlying operating system for customizations or third-party features. Standard Amazon RDS for Oracle does not provide that level of access, while migrating to PostgreSQL or DynamoDB would require substantial rework and would not preserve the Oracle-specific third-party feature dependencies.

**Learn more:** [Feature availability and support for RDS Custom for Oracle](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonRDS/latest/UserGuide/custom-oracle-feature-support.html) · [Amazon RDS Custom](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonRDS/latest/UserGuide/rds-custom.html)

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],A company wants to move its on-premises MySQL database to AWS. The database receives regular imports from a client-facing application, causing a high volume of write operations. The company is concerned that this traffic might be creating performance issues in the application.  
  
How should a solutions architect design the architecture on AWS?

options.text: Provision an Amazon RDS for MySQL DB instance with Provisioned IOPS SSD storage. Monitor write operation metrics by using Amazon CloudWatch. Adjust the provisioned IOPS if necessary.

Provision an Amazon RDS for MySQL DB instance with General Purpose SSD storage. Place an Amazon ElastiCache cluster in front of the DB instance. Configure the application to query ElastiCache instead.

Provision an Amazon DocumentDB (with MongoDB compatibility) instance with a memory optimized instance type. Monitor Amazon CloudWatch for performance-related issues. Change the instance class if necessary.

Provision an Amazon Elastic File System (Amazon EFS) file system in General Purpose performance mode. Monitor Amazon CloudWatch for IOPS bottlenecks. Change to Provisioned Throughput performance mode if necessary.

questions.explanation:
Amazon RDS for MySQL with Provisioned IOPS SSD storage is the best fit for a write-intensive MySQL workload because Provisioned IOPS is designed for I/O-intensive, latency-sensitive transactional database workloads and delivers more predictable write performance than General Purpose SSD. Monitoring Amazon CloudWatch metrics and increasing provisioned IOPS as needed directly addresses sustained database write pressure. ElastiCache primarily reduces read load, Amazon DocumentDB is not a MySQL engine, and Amazon EFS is a shared file system rather than a relational database service.

**Learn more:** [Amazon RDS DB instance storage](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonRDS/latest/UserGuide/CHAP_Storage.html) · [Recommendations from Amazon RDS reference](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonRDS/latest/UserGuide/USERRecommendationsManage.RecommendationReference.html)

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],A company is deploying a new public web application on AWS. The application will run behind an Application Load Balancer (ALB).  
  
The application must be encrypted at the edge by using an SSL/TLS certificate that is issued by an external certificate authority (CA). The certificate must be rotated every year before it expires.  
  
What should a solutions architect do to meet these requirements?

options.text: Use AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) to issue an SSL/TLS certificate. Apply the certificate to the ALB. Use the managed renewal feature to automatically rotate the certificate.

Use AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) to issue an SSL/TLS certificate. Import the key material from the certificate. Apply the certificate to the ALUse the managed renewal feature to automatically rotate the certificate.

Use AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) Private Certificate Authority to issue an SSL/TLS certificate from the root CA. Apply the certificate to the ALB. Use the managed renewal feature to automatically rotate the certificate.

Use AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) to import an SSL/TLS certificate. Apply the certificate to the ALB. Use Amazon EventBridge (Amazon CloudWatch Events) to send a notification when the certificate is nearing expiration. Rotate the certificate manually.

questions.explanation:
When a certificate must come from an external CA, the certificate should be imported into AWS Certificate Manager and associated with the ALB. ACM managed renewal applies to Amazon-issued certificates, not imported third-party certificates. For imported certificates, AWS recommends monitoring expiration and renewing/reimporting the certificate manually before it expires; EventBridge notifications can be used to alert on upcoming expiration. That makes the imported-certificate workflow the only option that satisfies both the external-CA requirement and annual rotation.

**Learn more:** [Import certificates into AWS Certificate Manager - AWS Certificate Manager](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/acm/latest/userguide/import-certificate.html) · [Managed certificate renewal in AWS Certificate Manager - AWS Certificate Manager](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/acm/latest/userguide/managed-renewal.html)

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],A company must retain application log files for a critical application for 10 years.  
  
The application team regularly accesses logs from the past month for troubleshooting, but logs older than 1 month are rarely accessed.  
  
The application generates more than 10 TB of logs per month.  
  
Which storage option meets these requirements **MOST cost-effectively**?

options.text: Store the logs in Amazon S3. Use AWS Backup to move logs more than 1 month old to S3 Glacier Deep Archive.
Store the logs in Amazon S3. Use S3 Lifecycle policies to move logs more than 1 month old to S3 Glacier Deep Archive.
Store the logs in Amazon CloudWatch Logs. Use AWS Backup to move logs more than 1 month old to S3 Glacier Deep Archive.
Store the logs in Amazon CloudWatch Logs. Use Amazon S3 Lifecycle policies to move logs more than 1 month old to S3 Glacier Deep Archive.

questions.explanation:
Amazon S3 is the appropriate long-term storage service for very large log volumes, and Amazon S3 Lifecycle rules can automatically transition objects older than 1 month to the S3 Glacier Deep Archive storage class for the lowest-cost archival retention. This matches the pattern of frequent access for recent logs and rare access for older logs. AWS Backup is not used to move active S3 objects between S3 storage classes, and Amazon S3 Lifecycle policies do not operate on data stored in CloudWatch Logs.

**Learn more:** [Transitioning objects using Amazon S3 Lifecycle - Amazon S3](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/lifecycle-transition-general-considerations.html) · [Managing the lifecycle of objects - Amazon S3](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/object-lifecycle-mgmt.html)

A financial services company runs a web application on AWS. The application uses an Amazon API Gateway Regional API endpoint to let users retrieve current stock prices. The company’s security team has observed an increase in API requests. The security team is worried that HTTP flood attacks could take the application offline.  
  
A solutions architect must design a solution to protect the application from this type of attack.  
  
Which solution meets these requirements with the **LEAST operational overhead**?

options.text: Create an Amazon CloudFront distribution in front of the API Gateway Regional API endpoint with a maximum TTL of 24 hours.
Create a Regional AWS WAF web ACL with a rate-based rule. Associate the web ACL with the API Gateway stage.
Use Amazon CloudWatch metrics to monitor the Count metric and alert the security team when the predefined rate is reached.

Create an Amazon CloudFront distribution with Lambda@Edge in front of the API Gateway Regional API endpoint. Create an AWS Lambda function to block requests from IP addresses that exceed the predefined rate.

questions.explanation:
AWS WAF rate-based rules are designed to detect and automatically limit unusually high request rates from sources such as individual IP addresses, which is an effective control for HTTP flood attacks at Layer 7. For an Amazon API Gateway Regional REST API, a Regional AWS WAF web ACL can be associated directly with the API Gateway stage, providing native protection without building and maintaining custom logic. This is lower operational overhead than deploying CloudFront with Lambda@Edge and custom rate-limiting code, and it provides actual mitigation rather than only monitoring.

**Learn more:** [Using rate-based rule statements in AWS WAF](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/waf/latest/developerguide/waf-rule-statement-type-rate-based.html) · [Use AWS WAF to protect your REST APIs in API Gateway](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/apigateway/latest/developerguide/apigateway-control-access-aws-waf.html)

A company runs a multi-tier application on several Amazon EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group. An Amazon RDS for Oracle instance serves as the data layer and uses Oracle-specific PL/SQL functions. Application traffic has been steadily rising. As a result, the EC2 instances are becoming overloaded, and the RDS instance is running out of storage. The Auto Scaling group has no scaling metrics configured and specifies only the minimum healthy instance count.  
  
The company expects traffic to keep increasing at a steady but unpredictable rate before it eventually levels off.  
  
What should a solutions architect do to make sure the system can automatically scale for the increased traffic? **(Choose two.)**

options.text: Configure storage Auto Scaling on the RDS for Oracle instance.
Migrate the database to Amazon Aurora to use Auto Scaling storage.
Configure an alarm on the RDS for Oracle instance for low free storage space.
Configure the Auto Scaling group to use the average CPU as the scaling metric.
Configure the Auto Scaling group to use the average free memory as the scaling metric.

questions.explanation:
Amazon RDS for Oracle supports storage autoscaling, which automatically increases allocated storage when free space runs low and is intended for workloads with unpredictable growth, so enabling storage Auto Scaling addresses the database storage bottleneck. For the EC2 tier, Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling supports target tracking based on `ASGAverageCPUUtilization`, allowing the group to add or remove instances automatically as average CPU load changes. An alarm on low storage space only provides notification, not automatic scaling, and migrating to Aurora would not preserve Oracle-specific PL/SQL compatibility. Memory is not the standard predefined scaling metric here, while average CPU utilization is explicitly supported for Auto Scaling target tracking.

**Learn more:** [Managing capacity automatically with Amazon RDS storage autoscaling](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonRDS/latest/UserGuide/USER_PIOPS.Autoscaling.html) · [Target tracking scaling policies for Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/autoscaling/ec2/userguide/as-scaling-target-tracking.html)

A company currently operates an on-premises stock-trading application on Microsoft Windows Server and wants to migrate the application to the AWS Cloud.  
  
The company must design a highly available solution that delivers low-latency access to block storage across multiple Availability Zones.  
  
Which solution meets these requirements with the **LEAST** implementation effort?

options.text: Configure a Windows Server cluster that spans two Availability Zones on Amazon EC2 instances. Install the application on both cluster nodes. Use Amazon FSx for Windows File Server as shared storage between the two cluster nodes.

Configure a Windows Server cluster that spans two Availability Zones on Amazon EC2 instances. Install the application on both cluster nodes. Use Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) General Purpose SSD (gp3) volumes as storage attached to the EC2 instances. Set up application-level replication to sync data from one EBS volume in one Availability Zone to another EBS volume in the second Availability Zone.

Deploy the application on Amazon EC2 instances in two Availability Zones. Configure one EC2 instance as active and the second EC2 instance in standby mode. Use an Amazon FSx for NetApp ONTAP Multi-AZ file system to access the data by using Internet Small Computer Systems Interface (iSCSI) protocol.

Deploy the application on Amazon EC2 instances in two Availability Zones. Configure one EC2 instance as active and the second EC2 instance in standby mode. Use Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) Provisioned IOPS SSD (io2) volumes as storage attached to the EC2 instances. Set up Amazon EBS level replication to sync data from one io2 volume in one Availability Zone to another io2 volume in the second Availability Zone.

questions.explanation:
Amazon FSx for NetApp ONTAP Multi-AZ provides managed high availability across Availability Zones, including synchronous replication to a standby file server and automatic failover. It supports iSCSI, which supplies block storage to Windows EC2 instances. Amazon EBS volumes are scoped to a single Availability Zone and cannot provide native shared, cross-AZ block storage or EBS-level cross-AZ replication.

**Learn more:** [Accessing your FSx for ONTAP data](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/fsx/latest/ONTAPGuide/supported-fsx-clients.html) · [Availability, durability, and deployment options for FSx for ONTAP](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/fsx/latest/ONTAPGuide/high-availability-AZ.html)

A company is planning the disaster recovery (DR) strategy for its production application. The application uses a MySQL database on an Amazon Aurora cluster in the `us-east-1` Region. The company selected the `us-west-1` Region as the DR Region.  
  
The company's target recovery point objective (RPO) is **5 minutes**, and its target recovery time objective (RTO) is **20 minutes**. The company also wants to minimize configuration changes.  
  
Which solution will meet these requirements with the **MOST operational efficiency**?

options.text: Create an Aurora read replica in us-west-1 similar in size to the production application's Aurora MySQL cluster writer instance.
Convert the Aurora cluster to an Aurora global database. Configure managed failover.
Create a new Aurora cluster in us-west-1 that has Cross-Region Replication.
Create a new Aurora cluster in us-west-1. Use AWS Database Migration Service (AWS DMS) to sync both clusters.

questions.explanation:
Amazon Aurora Global Database is the most operationally efficient DR solution for an Aurora MySQL database that must fail over to another Region with minimal data loss and fast recovery. Aurora Global Database replicates at the storage layer across Regions with replication lag typically measured in seconds, and AWS documents cross-Region recovery times in the order of minutes, which satisfies a 5-minute RPO and 20-minute RTO. It is also the most natural fit when minimizing configuration changes because an existing Aurora cluster can be used as the primary cluster of a global database and managed switchover or failover is built in.

**Learn more:** [Using switchover or failover in Amazon Aurora Global Database](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonRDS/latest/AuroraUserGuide/aurora-global-database-disaster-recovery.html) · [Using Amazon Aurora Global Database](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonRDS/latest/AuroraUserGuide/aurora-global-database.html)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],A company's application runs on Amazon EC2 instances and uses AWS Lambda functions in an event-driven architecture. The company uses nonproduction development environments in a different AWS account to test new features before deploying those features to production.  
  
The production instances have constant utilization because customers are in different time zones. The company uses the nonproduction instances only during business hours on weekdays. The company does not use the nonproduction instances on weekends. The company wants to optimize the cost of running its application on AWS.  
  
Which solution will meet these requirements **MOST cost-effectively**?

options.text: Use On-Demand Instances for the production instances. Use Dedicated Hosts for the nonproduction instances on weekends only.
Use Reserved Instances for the production instances and the nonproduction instances. Shut down the nonproduction instances when not in use.
Use Compute Savings Plans for the production instances. Use On-Demand Instances for the nonproduction instances. Shut down the nonproduction instances when not in use.
Use Dedicated Hosts for the production instances. Use EC2 Instance Savings Plans for the nonproduction instances.

questions.explanation:
Compute Savings Plans are the best fit for the production workload because the usage is steady and the plan applies discounted pricing to both Amazon EC2 and AWS Lambda, which matches the architecture. For the nonproduction environment, On-Demand Instances are better because the instances are needed only intermittently during weekday business hours, and shutting them down when idle avoids paying for unused capacity. Reserved commitments for the nonproduction fleet or Dedicated Hosts would cost more than necessary for that limited schedule.

**Learn more:** [Compute Savings Plans and Reserved Instances - Savings Plans](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/savingsplans/latest/userguide/sp-ris.html) · [Savings Plans types - Savings Plans](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/savingsplans/latest/userguide/plan-types.html)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],A company keeps its data on premises. The volume of data is increasing beyond the company's available capacity.  
  
The company wants to migrate its data from the on-premises environment to an Amazon S3 bucket. The company requires a solution that will automatically validate the integrity of the data after the transfer.  
  
Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Order an AWS Snowball Edge device. Configure the Snowball Edge device to perform the online data transfer to an S3 bucket
Deploy an AWS DataSync agent on premises. Configure the DataSync agent to perform the online data transfer to an S3 bucket.
Create an Amazon S3 File Gateway on premises Configure the S3 File Gateway to perform the online data transfer to an S3 bucket
Configure an accelerator in Amazon S3 Transfer Acceleration on premises. Configure the accelerator to perform the online data transfer to an S3 bucket.

questions.explanation:
AWS DataSync is designed for online data transfer from on-premises storage to AWS storage services, including Amazon S3. It uses checksum verification to validate data integrity during transfer and can perform additional verification at the end of the task by comparing checksums calculated at the source and destination. That directly satisfies the requirement for automatic integrity validation after the transfer. Snowball Edge is primarily used for edge or offline large-scale data movement, S3 File Gateway provides file-based access to S3 rather than migration validation workflows, and S3 Transfer Acceleration improves transfer speed but does not provide the required automatic end-to-end verification behavior.

**Learn more:** [Configuring how AWS DataSync verifies data integrity - AWS DataSync](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/datasync/latest/userguide/configure-data-verification-options.html) · [Checking object integrity in Amazon S3 - Amazon S3 User Guide](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/checking-object-integrity.html)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],A payment processing company records all voice communications with its customers and stores the audio files in an Amazon S3 bucket.  
  
The company needs to capture the text from the audio files. The company must remove from the text any personally identifiable information (PII) that belongs to customers.  
  
What should a solutions architect do to meet these requirements?

options.text: Process the audio files by using Amazon Kinesis Video Streams. Use an AWS Lambda function to scan for known PII patterns.
When an audio file is uploaded to the S3 bucket, invoke an AWS Lambda function to start an Amazon Textract task to analyze the call recordings.

Configure an Amazon Transcribe transcription job with PII redaction turned on. When an audio file is uploaded to the S3 bucket, invoke an AWS Lambda function to start the transcription job. Store the output in a separate S3 bucket.

Create an Amazon Connect contact flow that ingests the audio files with transcription turned on. Embed an AWS Lambda function to scan for known PII patterns. Use Amazon EventBridge to start the contact flow when an audio file is uploaded to the S3 bucket.

questions.explanation:
Amazon Transcribe is the AWS service designed to transcribe audio files into text, and its content redaction feature can automatically redact PII in the transcript output. An S3 event can invoke AWS Lambda to start a batch transcription job for each uploaded recording, and the redacted transcript can be written to a separate S3 bucket. Amazon Textract does not process audio, and the other options do not provide the direct managed speech-to-text plus PII-redaction capability required.

**Learn more:** [Redacting or identifying personally identifiable information - Amazon Transcribe](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/transcribe/latest/dg/pii-redaction.html) · [Redacting PII in your batch job - Amazon Transcribe](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/transcribe/latest/dg/pii-redaction-batch.html)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],A company runs its web application on AWS by using seven Amazon EC2 instances. The company requires that DNS queries return the IP addresses of all healthy EC2 instances.  
  
Which policy should be used to meet this requirement?

options.text: Simple routing policy
Latency routing policy
Multivalue routing policy
Geolocation routing policy

questions.explanation:
Amazon Route 53 multivalue routing returns multiple values, such as several EC2 instance IP addresses, in response to DNS queries and can check the health of each resource so that only healthy records are returned. That directly matches the requirement to return the IP addresses of all healthy EC2 instances. Latency and geolocation policies select records based on network latency or user location, and simple routing does not provide the same health-aware multivalue behavior.

**Learn more:** [Multivalue answer routing - Route 53](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/Route53/latest/DeveloperGuide/routing-policy-multivalue.html) · [Choosing a routing policy](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/Route53/latest/DeveloperGuide/routing-policy.html)

A company plans to use an Amazon DynamoDB table for data storage and is focused on optimizing cost.  
  
The table will be unused during most mornings. In the evenings, read and write traffic will often be unpredictable. When traffic spikes happen, they will occur very quickly.  
  
What should a solutions architect recommend?

options.text: Create a DynamoDB table in on-demand capacity mode.
Create a DynamoDB table with a global secondary index.
Create a DynamoDB table with provisioned capacity and auto scaling.
Create a DynamoDB table in provisioned capacity mode, and configure it as a global table.

questions.explanation:
Amazon DynamoDB on-demand capacity mode is the best fit for a workload that has long idle periods, unpredictable evening traffic, and sudden fast spikes. On-demand uses pay-per-request pricing, so there is no charge for unused provisioned throughput during quiet periods, and AWS documentation specifically recommends it for variable workloads with unpredictable request timing and traffic spikes. Provisioned capacity with auto scaling is less cost-efficient for this pattern and can be slower to respond to sudden spikes.

**Learn more:** [DynamoDB on-demand capacity mode - Amazon DynamoDB](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/amazondynamodb/latest/developerguide/on-demand-capacity-mode.html) · [Evaluate your DynamoDB table's capacity mode - Amazon DynamoDB](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/amazondynamodb/latest/developerguide/CostOptimization_TableCapacityMode.html)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],A company’s website is used to sell products to the public. The site runs on Amazon EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group behind an Application Load Balancer (ALB). There is also an Amazon CloudFront distribution, and AWS WAF is being used to protect against SQL injection attacks. The ALB is the origin for the CloudFront distribution. A recent review of security logs revealed an external malicious IP that needs to be blocked from accessing the website.  
  
What should a solutions architect do to protect the application?

options.text: Modify the network ACL on the CloudFront distribution to add a deny rule for the malicious IP address.
Modify the configuration of AWS WAF to add an IP match condition to block the malicious IP address.
Modify the network ACL for the EC2 instances in the target groups behind the ALB to deny the malicious IP address.
Modify the security groups for the EC2 instances in the target groups behind the ALB to deny the malicious IP address.

questions.explanation:
AWS WAF can block requests by source IP address by using an IP-based match rule, and it integrates with Amazon CloudFront and Application Load Balancer. Because the traffic is coming through CloudFront and the application is already protected by AWS WAF, the correct control is to add the malicious address to an AWS WAF IP match condition so the request is blocked before it reaches the origin. CloudFront distributions do not have editable network ACLs, and security groups cannot create deny rules for EC2 instances.

**Learn more:** [AWS WAF or AWS Shield? AWS Decision Guide](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/pdfs/decision-guides/latest/waf-or-shield/waf-or-shield.pdf?did=wp_card) · [How Amazon CloudFront works with IAM](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonCloudFront/latest/DeveloperGuide/security_iam_service-with-iam.html)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],A company sells ringtones made from clips of popular songs. The ringtone files are stored in Amazon S3 Standard and are at least 128 KB in size. The company has millions of files, but downloads are rare for ringtones older than 90 days. The company needs to reduce storage costs while keeping the most frequently accessed files readily available for users.  
  
Which action should the company take to meet these requirements in the **MOST cost-effective** way?

options.text: Configure S3 Standard-Infrequent Access (S3 Standard-IA) storage for the initial storage tier of the objects.
Move the files to S3 Intelligent-Tiering and configure it to move objects to a less expensive storage tier after 90 days.
Configure S3 inventory to manage objects and move them to S3 Standard-Infrequent Access (S3 Standard-1A) after 90 days.
Implement an S3 Lifecycle policy that moves the objects from S3 Standard to S3 Standard-Infrequent Access (S3 Standard-1A) after 90 days.

questions.explanation:
An Amazon S3 Lifecycle rule that transitions objects from S3 Standard to S3 Standard-IA after 90 days is the most cost-effective fit for a known access pattern: frequent access early, then infrequent access later. S3 Standard-IA is designed for infrequently accessed data that still requires millisecond retrieval, and Amazon S3 supports lifecycle transitions from S3 Standard to S3 Standard-IA. S3 Intelligent-Tiering is better when access patterns are unknown or changing, but it adds monitoring and automation charges per object, which is less economical for millions of objects when the 90-day cutoff is already known. S3 Inventory only reports on objects and does not move them.

**Learn more:** [Transitioning objects using Amazon S3 Lifecycle](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/lifecycle-transition-general-considerations.html) · [How S3 Intelligent-Tiering works](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/intelligent-tiering-overview.html)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],A company has a website hosted on AWS. The website sits behind an Application Load Balancer (ALB) that is configured to handle HTTP and HTTPS separately. The company wants all requests to the website to be forwarded so that the requests use HTTPS.  
  
What should a solutions architect do to meet this requirement?

options.text: Update the ALB's network ACL to accept only HTTPS traffic.
Create a rule that replaces the HTTP in the URL with HTTPS.
Create a listener rule on the ALB to redirect HTTP traffic to HTTPS.
Replace the ALB with a Network Load Balancer configured to use Server Name Indication (SNI).

questions.explanation:
Application Load Balancer listener rules support a **redirect** action that can send HTTP requests to HTTPS, typically from port 80 to port 443 while preserving the host, path, and query string. Network ACLs can only allow or deny traffic and cannot perform redirects, and Network Load Balancer SNI does not address HTTP-to-HTTPS redirection.

**Learn more:** [Action types for listener rules - Elastic Load Balancing](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/elasticloadbalancing/latest/application/rule-action-types.html) · [Add a listener rule for your Application Load Balancer - Elastic Load Balancing](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/elasticloadbalancing/latest/application/add-rule.html)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],A finance company uses an on-premises search application to gather streaming data from several producers. The application delivers real-time updates for search and visualization capabilities.  
  
The company plans to migrate to AWS and wants an AWS-native solution.  
  
Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Use Amazon EC2 instances to ingest and process the data streams to Amazon S3 buckets tor storage. Use Amazon Athena to search the data. Use Amazon Managed Grafana to create visualizations.
Use Amazon EMR to ingest and process the data streams to Amazon Redshift for storage. Use Amazon Redshift Spectrum to search the data. Use Amazon QuickSight to create visualizations.

Use Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS) to ingest and process the data streams to Amazon DynamoDB for storage. Use Amazon CloudWatch to create graphical dashboards to search and visualize the data.
Use Amazon Kinesis Data Streams to ingest and process the data streams to Amazon OpenSearch Service. Use OpenSearch Service to search the data. Use Amazon QuickSight to create visualizations.

questions.explanation:
Amazon Kinesis Data Streams provides real-time ingestion and processing of streaming data, and Amazon OpenSearch Service is designed for near-real-time indexing and search. Amazon QuickSight can visualize data from OpenSearch Service, so this architecture satisfies the required streaming, search, and visualization capabilities.

**Learn more:** [What is Amazon OpenSearch Service?](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/opensearch-service/latest/developerguide/what-is.html) · [What is Amazon Kinesis Data Streams?](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/streams/latest/dev/introduction.html)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],A company wants to run its experimental workloads in the AWS Cloud. The company has a budget for cloud spending. The company's CFO is concerned about cloud spending accountability for each department. The CFO wants to receive a notification when spending reaches 60% of the budget threshold.  
  
Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Use cost allocation tags on AWS resources to label owners. Create usage budgets in AWS Budgets. Add an alert threshold to receive notification when spending exceeds 60% of the budget.
Use AWS Cost Explorer forecasts to determine resource owners. Use AWS Cost Anomaly Detection to create alert threshold notifications when spending exceeds 60% of the budget.
Use cost allocation tags on AWS resources to label owners. Use AWS Support API on AWS Trusted Advisor to create alert threshold notifications when spending exceeds 60% of the budget.
Use AWS Cost Explorer forecasts to determine resource owners. Create usage budgets in AWS Budgets. Add an alert threshold to receive notification when spending exceeds 60% of the budget.

questions.explanation:
Cost allocation tags provide departmental accountability by labeling AWS resources with attributes such as owner, cost center, or department so costs can be tracked back to the responsible group. AWS Budgets is the AWS service designed to create cost or usage budgets and send alerts when a threshold is reached, including at 60% of the budget. Cost Explorer can analyze and forecast costs, but it does not determine resource owners, and Trusted Advisor is not the mechanism for budget-threshold notifications.

**Learn more:** [Using user-defined cost allocation tags - AWS Billing](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/awsaccountbilling/latest/aboutv2/custom-tags.html) · [Cost allocation tags - Best Practices for Tagging AWS Resources](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/whitepapers/latest/tagging-best-practices/cost-allocation-tags.html)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],A company is building an ecommerce application that will include a load-balanced front end, a container-based application, and a relational database.  
  
A solutions architect must design a highly available solution that runs with as little manual intervention as possible.  
  
Which solutions satisfy these requirements? **(Choose two.)**

options.text: Create an Amazon RDS DB instance in Multi-AZ mode.
Create an Amazon RDS DB instance and one or more replicas in another Availability Zone.
Create an Amazon EC2 instance-based Docker cluster to handle the dynamic application load.
Create an Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) cluster with a Fargate launch type to handle the dynamic application load.
Create an Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) cluster with an Amazon EC2 launch type to handle the dynamic application load.

questions.explanation:
Amazon RDS Multi-AZ is the correct relational database choice for high availability because RDS automatically provisions and maintains a synchronous standby in a different Availability Zone and can fail over automatically. By contrast, RDS read replicas are intended mainly for read scaling, not as the primary high-availability mechanism. For the container tier, Amazon ECS with the Fargate launch type is the best fit for minimal operational effort because AWS manages the underlying compute infrastructure, avoiding the host management required by EC2-based container clusters.

**Learn more:** [Multi-AZ DB instance deployments for Amazon RDS](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonRDS/latest/UserGuide/Concepts.MultiAZSingleStandby.html) · [Working with DB instance read replicas](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonRDS/latest/UserGuide/USER_ReadRepl.html)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],To satisfy security requirements, a company must encrypt all of its application data in transit while communicating with an Amazon RDS for MySQL DB instance. A recent security audit found that encryption at rest is enabled by using AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS), but encryption in transit is not enabled.  
  
What should a solutions architect do to meet the security requirements?

options.text: Enable IAM database authentication on the database.
Provide self-signed certificates. Use the certificates in all connections to the RDS instance.
Take a snapshot of the RDS instance. Restore the snapshot to a new instance with encryption enabled.
Download AWS-provided root certificates. Provide the certificates in all connections to the RDS instance.

questions.explanation:
Amazon RDS for MySQL encrypts data in transit by using SSL/TLS for client connections. AWS provides the CA/root certificates for RDS, and clients should use those certificates when connecting so the connection is encrypted and the server certificate can be validated. IAM database authentication does not by itself enable transport encryption, and creating a new encrypted instance from a snapshot only addresses encryption at rest, not in-transit protection.

**Learn more:** [SSL/TLS support for MySQL DB instances on Amazon RDS](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonRDS/latest/UserGuide/MySQL.Concepts.SSLSupport.html) · [Using SSL/TLS to encrypt a connection to a DB instance or cluster](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonRDS/latest/UserGuide/UsingWithRDS.SSL.html)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],A company runs an Oracle database on premises. As part of the company’s migration to AWS, the company wants to upgrade the database to the most recent available version.  
  
The company also wants to set up disaster recovery (DR) for the database. The company needs to minimize the operational overhead for normal operations and DR setup. The company also needs to maintain access to the database's underlying operating system.  
  
Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Migrate the Oracle database to an Amazon EC2 instance. Set up database replication to a different AWS Region.
Migrate the Oracle database to Amazon RDS for Oracle. Activate Cross-Region automated backups to replicate the snapshots to another AWS Region.
Migrate the Oracle database to Amazon RDS Custom for Oracle. Create a read replica for the database in another AWS Region.
Migrate the Oracle database to Amazon RDS for Oracle. Create a standby database in another Availability Zone.

questions.explanation:
RDS Custom for Oracle provides limited operating system access to the database server, which is required by the question. A cross-Region read replica for RDS Custom satisfies the disaster recovery requirement. Standard RDS for Oracle does not provide OS access, and running Oracle on EC2 would require substantially more administration for patches, backups, and DR configuration. Aurora read replicas provide faster replication with lower lag.

**Learn more:** [Amazon RDS Custom](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonRDS/latest/UserGuide/rds-custom.html) · [Working with Oracle replicas for RDS Custom for Oracle](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonRDS/latest/UserGuide/custom-rr.html)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],A company wants to run a gaming application on Amazon EC2 instances that are part of an Auto Scaling group in the AWS Cloud. The application will transmit data by using UDP packets. The company wants to ensure that the application can scale out and in as traffic increases and decreases.  
  
What should a solutions architect do to meet these requirements?

options.text: Attach a Network Load Balancer to the Auto Scaling group.
Attach an Application Load Balancer to the Auto Scaling group.
Deploy an Amazon Route 53 record set with a weighted policy to route traffic appropriately.
Deploy a NAT instance that is configured with port forwarding to the EC2 instances in the Auto Scaling group.

questions.explanation:
A Network Load Balancer is the correct service because it load balances at Layer 4 and supports UDP traffic, and it can be attached to an Auto Scaling group so instances are automatically registered and deregistered as the group scales. An Application Load Balancer is for HTTP/HTTPS application-layer traffic, not UDP. Weighted Route 53 records do not replace a load balancer for distributing UDP traffic across changing EC2 targets, and a NAT instance with port forwarding is not the appropriate scalable inbound load-balancing design. ([docs.aws.amazon.com](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/autoscaling/ec2/userguide/autoscaling-load-balancer.html?utm_source=openai))

**Learn more:** [Use Elastic Load Balancing to distribute incoming application traffic in your Auto Scaling group](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/autoscaling/ec2/userguide/autoscaling-load-balancer.html) · [Elastic Load Balancing API Reference - Welcome](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/elasticloadbalancing/latest/APIReference/Welcome.html)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],A company deploys Amazon EC2 instances that run in a VPC. The EC2 instances load source data into Amazon S3 buckets so the data can be processed later. Under compliance requirements, the data must not be sent across the public internet. Servers in the company's on-premises data center will consume the output from an application that runs on the EC2 instances.  
  
Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Deploy an interface VPC endpoint for Amazon EC2. Create an AWS Site-to-Site VPN connection between the company and the VPC.
Deploy a gateway VPC endpoint for Amazon S3. Set up an AWS Direct Connect connection between the on-premises network and the VPC.
Set up an AWS Transit Gateway connection from the VPC to the S3 buckets. Create an AWS Site-to-Site VPN connection between the company and the VPC.
Set up proxy EC2 instances that have routes to NAT gateways. Configure the proxy EC2 instances to fetch S3 data and feed the application instances.

questions.explanation:
A gateway VPC endpoint for S3 enables private connectivity from VPC resources to S3 without requiring internet gateways or NAT devices. AWS Direct Connect establishes a dedicated connection from on-premises infrastructure directly to AWS infrastructure, using a private virtual interface to access the VPC over private IP addresses instead of the public internet. Together, these provide end-to-end private connectivity.

**Learn more:** [Gateway endpoints for Amazon S3](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/privatelink/vpc-endpoints-s3.html) · [What is AWS Direct Connect?](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/directconnect/latest/UserGuide/Welcome.html)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],A company is planning to store confidential data in Amazon S3. For compliance reasons, the data must be encrypted at rest. Encryption key usage must be logged for auditing, and the keys must be rotated every year.  
  
Which solution satisfies these requirements and is the **MOST operationally efficient**?

options.text: Server-side encryption with customer-provided keys (SSE-C)
Server-side encryption with Amazon S3 managed keys (SSE-S3)
Server-side encryption with AWS KMS keys (SSE-KMS) with manual rotation
Server-side encryption with AWS KMS keys (SSE-KMS) with automatic rotation

questions.explanation:
Server-side encryption with AWS KMS keys (SSE-KMS) is the best fit because AWS KMS provides auditable key usage through AWS logging integrations and supports automatic rotation of customer managed symmetric keys on a yearly schedule by default. That meets the encryption-at-rest, auditability, and annual-rotation requirements while minimizing operational overhead compared with manual rotation or customer-supplied keys.

**Learn more:** [Rotate AWS KMS keys - AWS Key Management Service](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/kms/latest/developerguide/rotate-keys.html) · [Enable automatic key rotation - AWS Key Management Service](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/kms/latest/developerguide/rotating-keys-enable.html)

options.text: Run the EC2 instances in a spread placement group.
Group the EC2 instances in separate accounts.
Configure the EC2 instances with dedicated tenancy.
Configure the EC2 instances with shared tenancy.

questions.explanation:
A spread placement group ensures each EC2 instance runs on separate underlying physical hardware, preventing hardware sharing among the nodes in the group. This minimizes correlated failures during parallel processing. Dedicated tenancy isolates from other AWS customers but does not prevent instances within the same account from sharing physical hardware, failing to meet the stated requirement.

**Learn more:** [Placement groups for your EC2 instances](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSEC2/latest/UserGuide/placement-groups.html)

An ecommerce company runs applications in AWS accounts that are part of an organization in AWS Organizations. The applications use Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL databases across all the accounts. The company must prevent malicious activity and identify abnormal failed and incomplete login attempts to the databases.  
  
Which solution will meet these requirements in the **MOST operationally efficient** way?

options.text: Attach service control policies (SCPs) to the root of the organization to identity the failed login attempts.
Enable the Amazon RDS Protection feature in Amazon GuardDuty for the member accounts of the organization.
Publish the Aurora general logs to a log group in Amazon CloudWatch Logs. Export the log data to a central Amazon S3 bucket.
Publish all the Aurora PostgreSQL database events in AWS CloudTrail to a central Amazon S3 bucket.

questions.explanation:
Amazon GuardDuty RDS Protection is the managed AWS feature designed to monitor Aurora PostgreSQL and other supported RDS login activity directly and detect anomalous patterns, including failed and incomplete login attempts, then generate security findings. Because it can be enabled for member accounts in an AWS Organizations environment, it provides centralized, purpose-built detection with far less operational overhead than collecting logs and creating custom analytics. SCPs control AWS API permissions rather than database logins, and AWS CloudTrail records AWS API activity rather than native Aurora PostgreSQL authentication attempts.

**Learn more:** [GuardDuty RDS Protection - Amazon GuardDuty](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/guardduty/latest/ug/rds-protection.html) · [GuardDuty RDS Protection finding types - Amazon GuardDuty](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/guardduty/latest/ug/findings-rds-protection.html)
