lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],A company performs monthly maintenance on its AWS infrastructure. During these maintenance activities, the company needs to rotate the credentials for its Amazon RDS for MySQL databases across multiple AWS Regions.  
  
Which solution will meet these requirements with the **LEAST operational overhead**?

options.text: Store the credentials as secrets in AWS Secrets Manager. Use multi-Region secret replication for the required Regions. Configure Secrets Manager to rotate the secrets on a schedule.

Store the credentials as secrets in AWS Systems Manager by creating a secure string parameter. Use multi-Region secret replication for the required Regions. Configure Systems Manager to rotate the secrets on a schedule.

Store the credentials in an Amazon S3 bucket that has server-side encryption (SSE) enabled. Use Amazon EventBridge (Amazon CloudWatch Events) to invoke an AWS Lambda function to rotate the credentials.

Encrypt the credentials as secrets by using AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) multi-Region customer managed keys. Store the secrets in an Amazon DynamoDB global table. Use an AWS Lambda function to retrieve the secrets from DynamoDB. Use the RDS API to rotate the secrets.

questions.explanation:
AWS Secrets Manager is the managed AWS service designed for database credentials. It can automatically rotate Amazon RDS for MySQL secrets on a schedule, and multi-Region secret replication replicates the primary secret to other Regions; when rotation is enabled on the primary secret, the updated secret value propagates to the replica secrets. This provides the required cross-Region credential management with the least custom implementation and administration compared with using Parameter Store, Amazon S3, or DynamoDB plus Lambda.

**Learn more:** [Replicate AWS Secrets Manager secrets across Regions](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/secretsmanager/latest/userguide/replicate-secrets.html) · [Password management with Amazon RDS and AWS Secrets Manager](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonRDS/latest/UserGuide/rds-secrets-manager.html)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],A company has deployed an Amazon RDS for MySQL DB instance. Most database connections come from serverless applications. Application traffic to the database varies significantly at random intervals. During periods of high demand, users report that their applications receive database connection rejection errors.  
  
Which solution will resolve this issue with the **LEAST operational overhead**?

options.text: Create a proxy in RDS Proxy. Configure the users’ applications to use the DB instance through RDS Proxy.
Deploy Amazon ElastiCache for Memcached between the users’ applications and the DB instance.
Migrate the DB instance to a different instance class that has higher I/O capacity. Configure the users’ applications to use the new DB instance.
Configure Multi-AZ for the DB instance. Configure the users’ applications to switch between the DB instances.

questions.explanation:
Amazon RDS Proxy is designed for serverless and event-driven applications that generate large numbers of short-lived, bursty connections. It maintains a pool of database connections, multiplexes many application connections onto fewer backend DB connections, and helps absorb unpredictable surges without exhausting the MySQL instance’s connection limits. That directly addresses connection rejection errors while remaining a fully managed service, so it has less operational overhead than redesigning with caching or resizing the database.

**Learn more:** [Amazon RDS Proxy - Amazon Relational Database Service](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonRDS/latest/UserGuide/rds-proxy.html) · [Common usage scenarios - Amazon Relational Database Service](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonRDS/latest/UserGuide/rds-proxy-best-practices.usage-scenarios.html)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],A company's software development team requires an Amazon RDS Multi-AZ cluster. The RDS cluster will function as the backend for an on-premises desktop client. The desktop client needs direct connectivity to the RDS cluster.  
  
The company must enable the development team to connect to the cluster with the client while the team is in the office.  
  
Which solution delivers the required connectivity **MOST securely**?

options.text: Create a VPC and two public subnets. Create the RDS cluster in the public subnets. Use AWS Site-to-Site VPN with a customer gateway in the company's office.
Create a VPC and two private subnets. Create the RDS cluster in the private subnets. Use AWS Site-to-Site VPN with a customer gateway in the company's office.
Create a VPC and two private subnets. Create the RDS cluster in the private subnets. Use RDS security groups to allow the company's office IP ranges to access the cluster.
Create a VPC and two public subnets. Create the RDS cluster in the public subnets. Create a cluster user for each developer. Use RDS security groups to allow the users to access the cluster.

questions.explanation:
An RDS cluster in private subnets is not exposed to the public internet. An AWS Site-to-Site VPN securely extends the office private network into the VPC, enabling the on-premises desktop clients to reach the private RDS cluster directly. RDS documentation identifies Site-to-Site VPN as a private-network access option for non-public RDS deployments, and private access reduces exposure to external threats.

**Learn more:** [Scenarios for accessing a DB instance in a VPC](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonRDS/latest/UserGuide/USER_VPC.Scenarios.html) · [Setting up public or private access in Amazon RDS](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonRDS/latest/gettingstartedguide/security-public-private.html)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],A company has a web application for travel ticketing. The application uses a database that runs in a single data center in North America. The company wants to expand the application to support a global user base and must deploy the application in multiple AWS Regions. Average latency for updates to the reservation database must be less than 1 second.  
  
The company wants separate deployments of its web platform in multiple Regions. However, it must keep a single primary reservation database that is globally consistent.  
  
Which solution should a solutions architect recommend to meet these requirements?

options.text: Convert the application to use Amazon DynamoDB. Use a global table for the center reservation table. Use the correct Regional endpoint in each Regional deployment.
Migrate the database to an Amazon Aurora MySQL database. Deploy Aurora Read Replicas in each Region. Use the correct Regional endpoint in each Regional deployment for access to the database.
Migrate the database to an Amazon RDS for MySQL database. Deploy MySQL read replicas in each Region. Use the correct Regional endpoint in each Regional deployment for access to the database.

Migrate the application to an Amazon Aurora Serverless database. Deploy instances of the database to each Region. Use the correct Regional endpoint in each Regional deployment to access the database. Use AWS Lambda functions to process event streams in each Region to synchronize the databases.

questions.explanation:
Amazon DynamoDB global tables provide a single logical table replicated across multiple AWS Regions with local Regional endpoints for the application. AWS documentation states that global tables replicate writes across Regions, and in multi-Region eventual consistency mode the changes are typically replicated within a second. By contrast, Amazon RDS for MySQL and Aurora cross-Region read replicas are asynchronous read replicas, not a globally consistent multi-Region primary write solution, and a custom Lambda-based synchronization design does not provide the required managed consistency model.

**Learn more:** [Global tables - multi-active, multi-Region replication - Amazon DynamoDB](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/amazondynamodb/latest/developerguide/GlobalTables.html) · [DynamoDB read consistency - Amazon DynamoDB](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/amazondynamodb/latest/developerguide/HowItWorks.ReadConsistency.html)

A company has an organization in AWS Organizations with all features enabled.  
  
The company requires that all API calls and logins in any existing or new AWS account be audited. The company needs a managed solution to avoid additional work and to minimize costs. The company also needs visibility into when any AWS account is not compliant with the AWS Foundational Security Best Practices (FSBP) standard.  
  
Which solution meets these requirements with the **LEAST operational overhead**?

options.text: Deploy an AWS Control Tower environment in the Organizations management account. Enable AWS Security Hub and AWS Control Tower Account Factory in the environment.
Deploy an AWS Control Tower environment in a dedicated Organizations member account. Enable AWS Security Hub and AWS Control Tower Account Factory in the environment.
Use AWS Managed Services (AMS) Accelerate to build a multi-account landing zone (MALZ). Submit an RFC to self-service provision Amazon GuardDuty in the MALZ.
Use AWS Managed Services (AMS) Accelerate to build a multi-account landing zone (MALZ). Submit an RFC to self-service provision AWS Security Hub in the MALZ.

questions.explanation:
AWS Control Tower is the lowest-overhead managed multi-account governance solution for an AWS Organizations environment because it automatically establishes landing-zone logging with an organization-level AWS CloudTrail trail that records actions and events for the management account and all member accounts. AWS Security Hub is the service that assesses accounts against the AWS Foundational Security Best Practices (FSBP) standard and can centralize that posture information across the organization. A Control Tower landing zone must be deployed from the Organizations management account, so using a dedicated member account for that purpose is not the correct design. GuardDuty detects threats, but it does not provide FSBP compliance evaluation; Security Hub does. Therefore, deploying AWS Control Tower in the management account and enabling AWS Security Hub best satisfies the auditing and FSBP requirements with minimal operational effort.

**Learn more:** [About logging in AWS Control Tower](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/controltower/latest/userguide/about-logging.html) · [AWS Foundational Security Best Practices standard in Security Hub CSPM](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/securityhub/latest/userguide/fsbp-standard.html)

A company runs tests on an application that uses an Amazon DynamoDB table. The tests run for 4 hours once each week. The company knows how many read and write operations per second the application performs against the table during the tests. The company does not currently use DynamoDB for any other use case. A solutions architect needs to optimize the table's costs.  
  
Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Choose on-demand mode. Update the read and write capacity units appropriately.
Choose provisioned mode. Update the read and write capacity units appropriately.
Purchase DynamoDB reserved capacity for a 1-year term.
Purchase DynamoDB reserved capacity for a 3-year term.

questions.explanation:
Because the company already knows the exact read and write throughput its tests generate and the workload follows a predictable weekly schedule, DynamoDB provisioned capacity mode lets it set read and write capacity units to match that known demand, and even adjust or schedule capacity down between test windows, at a fraction of the per-request cost of on-demand mode. On-demand capacity mode is designed for traffic that is unpredictable or not well understood in advance, which does not describe a workload whose throughput requirements are already known, so it is the more expensive option here despite its convenience for idle periods.

**Learn more:** [Read/write capacity mode - Amazon DynamoDB](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/amazondynamodb/latest/developerguide/HowItWorks.ReadWriteCapacityMode.html) · [Optimize costs by scheduling provisioned capacity for Amazon DynamoDB](https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/database/optimize-costs-by-scheduling-provisioned-capacity-for-amazon-dynamodb/)

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],A company has an application that delivers marketing services to stores. Some of the files can be larger than 200 GB.  
  
Recently, the company found that some stores uploaded files containing personally identifiable information (PII) that should not have been included. The company wants administrators to be alerted if PII is shared again. The company also wants to automate remediation.  
  
What should a solutions architect do to meet these requirements with the **LEAST** development effort?

options.text: Use an Amazon S3 bucket as a secure transfer point. Use Amazon Inspector to scan the objects in the bucket. If objects contain PII, trigger an S3 Lifecycle policy to remove the objects that contain PII.

Use an Amazon S3 bucket as a secure transfer point. Use Amazon Macie to scan the objects in the bucket. If objects contain PII, use Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS) to trigger a notification to the administrators to remove the objects that contain PII.

Implement custom scanning algorithms in an AWS Lambda function. Trigger the function when objects are loaded into the bucket. If objects contain PII, use Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS) to trigger a notification to the administrators to remove the objects that contain PII.

Implement custom scanning algorithms in an AWS Lambda function. Trigger the function when objects are loaded into the bucket. If objects contain PII, use Amazon Simple Email Service (Amazon SES) to trigger a notification to the administrators and trigger an S3 Lifecycle policy to remove the meats that contain PII.

questions.explanation:
Amazon Macie is the AWS-managed service specifically designed to discover and classify sensitive data including PII in S3 objects. Using Macie requires zero custom development and can be integrated with SNS for automated alerting when PII is detected. While it requires administrator action for remediation, this remains the minimal-development-effort solution compared to building custom scanning logic.

Which solution meets these requirements **MOST** cost-effectively?

options.text: Use AWS Budgets to download data for the past 3 months into a .csv file. Look up the desired information.
Load AWS Cost and Usage Reports into an Amazon RDS DB instance. Run SQL queries to get the desired information.
Tag all the AWS resources with a key for cost and a value of the application's name. Activate cost allocation tags. Use Cost Explorerto get the desired information.

Tag all the AWS resources with a key for cost and a value of the application's name. Use the AWS Billing and Cost Management console todownload bills for the past 3 months. Look up the desired information.

questions.explanation:
User-defined cost allocation tags can associate each resource’s charges with its application. After the tags are activated in Billing and Cost Management, AWS Cost Explorer can group and analyze costs by the tag value, providing application-level cost breakdowns without operating a separate database and SQL-query solution.

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],A company uses AWS Organizations with all features enabled and runs multiple Amazon EC2 workloads in the `ap-southeast-2` Region. The company has a service control policy (SCP) that prevents any resources from being created in any other Region. A security policy requires the company to encrypt all data at rest.  
  
An audit discovers that employees have created Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) volumes for EC2 instances without encrypting the volumes. The company wants any new EC2 instances that any IAM user or root user launches in `ap-southeast-2` to use encrypted EBS volumes. The company wants a solution that will have minimal effect on employees who create EBS volumes.  
  
Which combination of steps will meet these requirements? **(Choose two.)**

options.text: In the Amazon EC2 console, select the EBS encryption account attribute and define a default encryption key.

Create an IAM permission boundary. Attach the permission boundary to the root organizational unit (OU). Define the boundary to deny the ec2:CreateVolume action when the ec2:Encrypted condition equals false.
Create an SCP. Attach the SCP to the root organizational unit (OU). Define the SCP to deny the ec2:CreateVolume action whenthe ec2:Encrypted condition equals false.
Update the IAM policies for each account to deny the ec2:CreateVolume action when the ec2:Encrypted condition equals false.
In the Organizations management account, specify the Default EBS volume encryption setting.

questions.explanation:
Amazon EBS encryption by default is a Region-specific account setting that automatically encrypts new EBS volumes, including volumes created when EC2 instances are launched, using either the default AWS managed key or a specified customer managed KMS key. Setting the EBS encryption account attribute and defining the default encryption key therefore ensures new instance launches in `ap-southeast-2` use encrypted volumes with minimal user impact. An AWS Organizations SCP can provide an organization-wide guardrail by denying `ec2:CreateVolume` when the `ec2:Encrypted` condition is `false`, which helps enforce the policy across member accounts, including actions attempted by the account root user. Permission boundaries cannot be attached to an OU, and per-account IAM policy updates are broader operationally and do not restrict the root user. There is no Organizations-wide management-account setting that centrally turns on default EBS encryption for all accounts.

**Learn more:** [Enable Amazon EBS encryption by default - Amazon EBS](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/ebs/latest/userguide/encryption-by-default.html) · [EnableEbsEncryptionByDefault - Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud API Reference](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSEC2/latest/APIReference/API_EnableEbsEncryptionByDefault.html)

A company is building a new machine learning (ML) model solution on AWS. The models are created as independent microservices that retrieve approximately 1 GB of model data from Amazon S3 during startup and load that data into memory. Users access the models by using an asynchronous API. Users can submit a single request or a batch of requests and can specify where the results should be delivered.  
  
The company offers models to hundreds of users. Usage patterns for the models are irregular. Some models might not be used for days or weeks. Other models might receive batches of thousands of requests at one time.  
  
Which design should a solutions architect recommend to meet these requirements?

options.text: Direct the requests from the API to a Network Load Balancer (NLB). Deploy the models as AWS Lambda functions that are invoked by the NLB.

Direct the requests from the API to an Application Load Balancer (ALB). Deploy the models as Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) services that read from an Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) queue. Use AWS App Mesh to scale the instances of the ECS cluster based on the SQS queue size.

Direct the requests from the API into an Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) queue. Deploy the models as AWS Lambda functions that are invoked by SQS events. Use AWS Auto Scaling to increase the number of vCPUs for the Lambda functions based on the SQS queue size.

Direct the requests from the API into an Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) queue. Deploy the models as Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) services that read from the queue. Enable AWS Auto Scaling on Amazon ECS for both the cluster and copies of the service based on the queue size.

questions.explanation:
An Amazon SQS queue is the correct front end for an asynchronous, bursty request pattern because it decouples request submission from processing and buffers large batches safely. Amazon ECS is a better fit than AWS Lambda for model-serving microservices that must download about 1 GB of data at startup and keep it loaded in memory, because ECS tasks can run as long-lived containers and scale out when demand rises, then scale back in when idle. AWS documentation for Amazon ECS recommends queue depth as the proper scaling metric for asynchronous job processors, and ECS supports both service auto scaling and cluster auto scaling so the number of tasks and the underlying capacity can grow and shrink with the SQS backlog.

**Learn more:** [Optimizing Amazon ECS service auto scaling](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonECS/latest/developerguide/capacity-autoscaling-best-practice.html) · [Automatically scale your Amazon ECS service](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonECS/latest/developerguide/service-auto-scaling.html)

A company's application is experiencing performance problems. The application is stateful and must complete in-memory tasks on Amazon EC2 instances. The company used AWS CloudFormation to deploy the infrastructure and used the M5 EC2 instance family. As traffic increased, application performance declined. Users are reporting delays when they try to access the application.  
  
Which solution will resolve these issues in the **MOST operationally efficient** way?

options.text: Replace the EC2 instances with T3 EC2 instances that run in an Auto Scaling group. Make the changes by using the AWS Management Console.

Modify the CloudFormation templates to run the EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group. Increase the desired capacity and the maximum capacity of the Auto Scaling group manually when an increase is necessary.

Modify the CloudFormation templates. Replace the EC2 instances with R5 EC2 instances. Use Amazon CloudWatch built-in EC2 memory metrics to track the application performance for future capacity planning.

Modify the CloudFormation templates. Replace the EC2 instances with R5 EC2 instances. Deploy the Amazon CloudWatch agent on the EC2 instances to generate custom application latency metrics for future capacity planning.

questions.explanation:
For a stateful application that must perform work in memory, the most effective and operationally efficient fix is to move from the M5 general-purpose family to the R5 memory-optimized family by updating the AWS CloudFormation templates. R5 instances are designed for workloads that process large data sets in memory, which directly addresses the performance bottleneck. Future capacity planning should use Amazon CloudWatch agent–published custom metrics, because Amazon EC2 does not provide built-in memory utilization metrics; operating system memory metrics require the CloudWatch agent. Managing the change in CloudFormation preserves infrastructure as code and is more efficient than making manual console changes.

**Learn more:** [Amazon EC2 instance types](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/ec2/latest/instancetypes/instance-types.html) · [Specifications for Amazon EC2 memory optimized instances](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/ec2/latest/instancetypes/mo.html)

options.text: Update the bucket policy to deny if the PutObject does not have an s3:x-amz-acl header set.
Update the bucket policy to deny if the PutObject does not have an s3:x-amz-acl header set to private.
Update the bucket policy to deny if the PutObject does not have an aws:SecureTransport header set to true.
Update the bucket policy to deny if the PutObject does not have an x-amz-server-side-encryption header set.

questions.explanation:
Amazon S3 bucket policies can enforce encryption for uploads by denying `s3:PutObject` requests that do not include a server-side encryption request header. The ACL headers control access settings, and `aws:SecureTransport` only requires TLS for data in transit. The encryption-specific enforcement is the `x-amz-server-side-encryption` header, which AWS documents as a condition key used to require encrypted object uploads.

**Learn more:** [Examples of Amazon S3 bucket policies](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/example-bucket-policies.html) · [Bucket policy examples using condition keys](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/amazon-s3-policy-keys.html)

A company uses Amazon S3 as its data lake. The company has a new partner that must use SFTP to upload data files. A solutions architect needs to implement a highly available SFTP solution that minimizes operational overhead.  
  
Which solution will satisfy these requirements?

options.text: Use AWS Transfer Family to configure an SFTP-enabled server with a publicly accessible endpoint. Choose the S3 data lake as the destination.
Use Amazon S3 File Gateway as an SFTP server. Expose the S3 File Gateway endpoint URL to the new partner. Share the S3 File Gateway endpoint with the new partner.

Launch an Amazon EC2 instance in a private subnet in a VPInstruct the new partner to upload files to the EC2 instance by using a VPN. Run a cron job script, on the EC2 instance to upload files to the S3 data lake.

Launch Amazon EC2 instances in a private subnet in a VPC. Place a Network Load Balancer (NLB) in front of the EC2 instances. Create an SFTP listener port for the NLB. Share the NLB hostname with the new partner. Run a cron job script on the EC2 instances to upload files to the S3 data lake.

questions.explanation:
AWS Transfer Family is the AWS-managed file transfer service for SFTP, and it can use Amazon S3 directly as the backend storage. It provides an SFTP-enabled server endpoint without requiring the company to build and operate its own EC2-based transfer infrastructure, which is why it best meets the requirements for high availability and minimal operational overhead. Amazon S3 File Gateway is designed to present S3 through NFS or SMB file interfaces rather than as the managed SFTP service for partner uploads.

**Learn more:** [Getting started with AWS Transfer Family server endpoints](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/transfer/latest/userguide/getting-started.html) · [AWS Transfer Family Documentation](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/transfer/)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],A company's application receives data from multiple data sources. The data size varies and is expected to grow over time. The current maximum size is **700 KB**. The data volume and data size continue to increase as additional data sources are added.  
  
The company decides to use **Amazon DynamoDB** as the application's primary database. A solutions architect must identify a solution that can handle the large data sizes.  
  
Which solution will meet these requirements in the **MOST operationally efficient** way?

options.text: Create an AWS Lambda function to filter the data that exceeds DynamoDB item size limits. Store the larger data in an Amazon DocumentDB (with MongoDB compatibility) database.
Store the large data as objects in an Amazon S3 bucket. In a DynamoDB table, create an item that has an attribute that points to the S3 URL of the data.
Split all incoming large data into a collection of items that have the same partition key. Write the data to a DynamoDB table in a single operation by using the BatchWriteItem API operation.
Create an AWS Lambda function that uses gzip compression to compress the large objects as they are written to a DynamoDB table.

questions.explanation:
Amazon DynamoDB has a maximum item size of 400 KB, so payloads that are already as large as 700 KB cannot be stored directly as single items. AWS recommends storing large attribute values or items as objects in Amazon S3 and storing the S3 object identifier or URL in the DynamoDB item. This pattern handles continued growth while keeping DynamoDB as the primary database and avoids the extra operational overhead of adding another database engine or implementing complex item-splitting logic.

**Learn more:** [Best practices for storing large items and attributes in DynamoDB](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/amazondynamodb/latest/developerguide/bp-use-s3-too.html) · [Constraints in Amazon DynamoDB](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/amazondynamodb/latest/developerguide/Constraints.html)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],A company runs a dynamic web application on two Amazon EC2 instances. The company has its own SSL certificate, and that certificate is installed on each instance to handle SSL termination.  
  
Traffic has increased recently, and the operations team found that SSL encryption and decryption is causing the web servers' compute capacity to reach its maximum limit.  
  
What should a solutions architect do to improve the application's performance?

options.text: Create a new SSL certificate using AWS Certificate Manager (ACM). Install the ACM certificate on each instance.
Create an Amazon S3 bucket Migrate the SSL certificate to the S3 bucket. Configure the EC2 instances to reference the bucket for SSL termination.
Create another EC2 instance as a proxy server. Migrate the SSL certificate to the new instance and configure it to direct connections to the existing EC2 instances.
Import the SSL certificate into AWS Certificate Manager (ACM). Create an Application Load Balancer with an HTTPS listener that uses the SSL certificate from ACM.

questions.explanation:
To improve performance, SSL/TLS termination should be offloaded from the EC2 instances to an Application Load Balancer. AWS allows an existing certificate to be imported into AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) and associated with an ALB HTTPS listener. The load balancer then terminates and decrypts client connections before routing requests to the EC2 targets, which removes the CPU-intensive encryption and decryption work from the web servers and is the AWS-recommended design for this use case.

**Learn more:** [SSL certificates for your Application Load Balancer - Elastic Load Balancing](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/elasticloadbalancing/latest/application/https-listener-certificates.html) · [Create an HTTPS listener for your Application Load Balancer - Elastic Load Balancing](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/elasticloadbalancing/latest/application/create-https-listener.html)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],A company needs to give its employees secure access to confidential and sensitive files. The company wants to make sure that only authorized users can access the files. The files must be downloaded securely to the employees’ devices.  
  
The files are stored on an on-premises Windows file server. However, because remote usage has increased, the file server is running out of capacity.  
  
Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Migrate the file server to an Amazon EC2 instance in a public subnet. Configure the security group to limit inbound traffic to the employees’ IP addresses.
Migrate the files to an Amazon FSx for Windows File Server file system. Integrate the Amazon FSx file system with the on-premises Active Directory. Configure AWS Client VPN.
Migrate the files to Amazon S3, and create a private VPC endpoint. Create a signed URL to allow download.
Migrate the files to Amazon S3, and create a public VPC endpoint. Allow employees to sign on with AWS IAM Identity Center (AWS Single Sign-On).

questions.explanation:
Amazon FSx for Windows File Server is the AWS service designed to replace a Windows file server while preserving SMB-based file access, Microsoft Active Directory authentication, and Windows ACL authorization. Joining the FSx file system to the on-premises Active Directory lets employees use existing AD identities, and file/folder permissions continue to enforce access only for authorized users. Using AWS Client VPN provides a secure remote path for employees to download files to their devices. AWS documentation states that FSx for Windows File Server supports AD-based authentication and Windows ACLs, and that on-premises environments can securely access FSx over VPN-connected private networking.

**Learn more:** [What is FSx for Windows File Server?](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/fsx/latest/WindowsGuide/what-is.html) · [Best practices for FSx for Windows File Server](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/fsx/latest/WindowsGuide/windows-best-practices.html)

A company has moved an application to Amazon EC2 Linux instances. One of these EC2 instances runs several 1-hour tasks on a schedule. These tasks were developed by different teams and do not share a common programming language. The company is concerned about performance and scalability while these tasks run on a single instance. A solutions architect needs to implement a solution to address these concerns.  
  
Which solution will meet these requirements with the **LEAST operational overhead**?

options.text: Use AWS Batch to run the tasks as jobs. Schedule the jobs by using Amazon EventBridge (Amazon CloudWatch Events).
Convert the EC2 instance to a container. Use AWS App Runner to create the container on demand to run the tasks as jobs.
Copy the tasks into AWS Lambda functions. Schedule the Lambda functions by using Amazon EventBridge (Amazon CloudWatch Events).
Create an Amazon Machine Image (AMI) of the EC2 instance that runs the tasks. Create an Auto Scaling group with the AMI to run multiple copies of the instance.

questions.explanation:
AWS Batch is the best fit for scheduled, long-running batch workloads because it is designed to run jobs in queues, handle scheduling and scaling, and supports scheduled submission through Amazon EventBridge. It also avoids the language constraint because the jobs do not need to be rewritten into a single runtime model. AWS Lambda is not suitable for 1-hour tasks because a Lambda function can run for only up to 900 seconds (15 minutes). Managing multiple EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group would add more operational work than using a managed batch service.

**Learn more:** [Tutorial: Create a scheduled AWS Batch job - AWS Batch](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/batch/latest/userguide/scheduled-batch-job.html) · [Configure Lambda function timeout - AWS Lambda](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/lambda/latest/dg/configuration-timeout.html)

A company hosts a database on an Amazon RDS instance that is deployed across multiple Availability Zones. The company periodically runs a script against the database to report new entries that have been added to the database. The script negatively affects the performance of a critical application.  
  
The company needs to improve application performance at minimal cost.  
  
Which solution will meet these requirements with the **LEAST operational overhead**?

options.text: Add functionality to the script to identify the instance that has the fewest active connections. Configure the script to read from that instance to report the total new entries.
Create a read replica of the database. Configure the script to query only the read replica to report the total new entries.
Instruct the development team to manually export the new entries for the day in the database at the end of each day.
Use Amazon ElastiCache to cache the common queries that the script runs against the database.

questions.explanation:
For an Amazon RDS Multi-AZ DB instance, the standby replica is for high availability and failover and cannot serve read traffic. To offload a reporting script that performs read-only queries, the appropriate solution is to create an RDS read replica and direct the script to query that replica. AWS documentation specifically describes read replicas as a way to reduce load on the primary DB instance for read-heavy and business reporting workloads, which improves application performance with low operational overhead.

**Learn more:** [Multi-AZ DB instance deployments for Amazon RDS](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonRDS/latest/UserGuide/Concepts.MultiAZSingleStandby.html) · [Working with Multi-AZ read replica deployments with MySQL](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonRDS/latest/UserGuide/USER_MySQL.Replication.ReadReplicas.MultiAZ.html)

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],A company provides a food delivery service that is expanding quickly. Because of this growth, the company’s order processing system has scaling issues during peak traffic hours. The existing architecture includes the following:  
  
- A group of Amazon EC2 instances that run in an Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling group to collect orders from the application  
- Another group of EC2 instances that run in an Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling group to fulfill orders  
  
The order collection process happens quickly, but the order fulfillment process can take longer. Data must not be lost because of a scaling event.  
  
A solutions architect must make sure that both the order collection process and the order fulfillment process can scale correctly during peak traffic hours. The solution must optimize utilization of the company’s AWS resources.  
  
Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Use Amazon CloudWatch metrics to monitor the CPU of each instance in the Auto Scaling groups. Configure each Auto Scaling group’s minimum capacity according to peak workload values.

Use Amazon CloudWatch metrics to monitor the CPU of each instance in the Auto Scaling groups. Configure a CloudWatch alarm to invoke an Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS) topic that creates additional Auto Scaling groups on demand.

Provision two Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) queues: one for order collection and another for order fulfillment. Configure the EC2 instances to poll their respective queue. Scale the Auto Scaling groups based on notifications that the queues send.

Provision two Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) queues: one for order collection and another for order fulfillment. Configure the EC2 instances to poll their respective queue. Create a metric based on a backlog per instance calculation. Scale the Auto Scaling groups based on this metric.

questions.explanation:
Amazon SQS should be used to decouple the fast order-collection tier from the slower order-fulfillment tier so messages remain durable while worker instances scale independently. For EC2 Auto Scaling with SQS workloads, the correct scaling signal is backlog per instance, which measures queue depth relative to the number of in-service instances and lets capacity track actual pending work efficiently. CPU-based scaling does not reflect queue backlog well, and setting minimum capacity for peak load wastes resources.

**Learn more:** [Scaling policy based on Amazon SQS - Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/autoscaling/ec2/userguide/as-using-sqs-queue.html) · [Create a target tracking scaling policy using metric math - Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/autoscaling/ec2/userguide/ec2-auto-scaling-target-tracking-metric-math.html)

A company runs a multiplayer gaming application on AWS. The company needs the application to read data with sub-millisecond latency and to perform one-time queries on historical data.  
  
Which solution will satisfy these requirements with the **LEAST operational overhead**?

options.text: Use Amazon RDS for data that is frequently accessed. Run a periodic custom script to export the data to an Amazon S3 bucket.

Store the data directly in an Amazon S3 bucket. Implement an S3 Lifecycle policy to move older data to S3 Glacier Deep Archive for long-term storage. Run one-time queries on the data in Amazon S3 by using Amazon Athena.

Use Amazon DynamoDB with DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) for data that is frequently accessed. Export the data to an Amazon S3 bucket by using DynamoDB table export. Run one-time queries on the data in Amazon S3 by using Amazon Athena.

Use Amazon DynamoDB for data that is frequently accessed. Turn on streaming to Amazon Kinesis Data Streams. Use Amazon Kinesis Data Firehose to read the data from Kinesis Data Streams. Store the records in an Amazon S3 bucket.

questions.explanation:
Amazon DynamoDB with DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) is designed for extremely fast reads, providing microsecond to sub-millisecond latency for frequently accessed data. DynamoDB can also export table data directly to Amazon S3 by using the managed export feature, and Amazon Athena can run SQL queries against data in S3 for occasional historical analysis. This combination meets both requirements while avoiding custom export code and avoiding the extra operational complexity of a streaming pipeline.

**Learn more:** [DynamoDB data export to Amazon S3: how it works](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/amazondynamodb/latest/developerguide/S3DataExport.HowItWorks.html) · [Integrating DynamoDB with Amazon S3](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/amazondynamodb/latest/developerguide/S3forDynamoDB.html)

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],A 4-year-old media company uses the AWS Organizations **all features** feature set to organize its AWS accounts.  
  
According to the company's finance team, billing information in the member accounts must not be accessible to anyone, including the root user of the member accounts.  
  
Which solution will satisfy these requirements?

options.text: Add all finance team users to an IAM group. Attach an AWS managed policy named Billing to the group.
Attach an identity-based policy to deny access to the billing information to all users, including the root user.
Create a service control policy (SCP) to deny access to the billing information. Attach the SCP to the root organizational unit (OU).
Convert from the Organizations all features feature set to the Organizations consolidated billing feature set.

questions.explanation:
A service control policy (SCP) can centrally restrict permissions for AWS Organizations member accounts, and SCPs affect all users and roles in those attached accounts, including the account root user. Because the organization already uses the all features set, it can use SCPs. Attaching an SCP with an explicit deny for billing access at the root organizational unit ensures the restriction applies throughout the member accounts. IAM identity-based policies do not provide this organization-wide control over the member account root user, and consolidated billing would remove SCP support rather than enforce the requirement.

**Learn more:** [Service control policies (SCPs) - AWS Organizations](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/organizations/latest/userguide/orgs_manage_policies_scps.html) · [Enabling all features for an organization with AWS Organizations](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/organizations/latest/userguide/orgs_manage_org_support-all-features.html)

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],A company is building a mobile game that sends score updates to a backend processor and then publishes results to a leaderboard.  
  
A solutions architect must design a solution that can:  
  
- handle large traffic spikes,  
- process the mobile game updates in the order they are received, and  
- store the processed updates in a highly available database.  
  
The company also wants to reduce the management overhead required to maintain the solution.  
  
What should the solutions architect do to meet these requirements?

options.text: Push score updates to Amazon Kinesis Data Streams. Process the updates in Kinesis Data Streams with AWS Lambda. Store the processed updates in Amazon DynamoDB.
Push score updates to Amazon Kinesis Data Streams. Process the updates with a fleet of Amazon EC2 instances set up for Auto Scaling. Store the processed updates in Amazon Redshift.

Push score updates to an Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS) topic. Subscribe an AWS Lambda function to the SNS topic to process the updates. Store the processed updates in a SQL database running on Amazon EC2.

Push score updates to an Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) queue. Use a fleet of Amazon EC2 instances with Auto Scaling to process the updates in the SQS queue. Store the processed updates in an Amazon RDS Multi-AZ DB instance.

questions.explanation:
Amazon Kinesis Data Streams is built for high-throughput streaming workloads and supports ordered consumption of records within a shard. AWS Lambda can process records directly from Kinesis without managing servers, which reduces operational overhead. Amazon DynamoDB is a fully managed, multi-AZ highly available database and is well suited for low-latency leaderboard storage. The other options either increase administration by requiring Amazon EC2 management, use a database that is a poorer fit for this access pattern, or do not provide the needed ordering guarantees in the form described.

**Learn more:** [Process Amazon Kinesis Data Streams records with Lambda](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/lambda/latest/dg/services-kinesis-create.html) · [Tutorial: Using Lambda with Kinesis Data Streams](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/lambda/latest/dg/with-kinesis-example.html)

A company has a multi-tier payment processing application that runs on virtual machines (VMs). Communication between the tiers happens asynchronously through a third-party middleware solution that guarantees exactly-once delivery.  
  
The company needs a solution that requires the least amount of infrastructure management. The solution must guarantee exactly-once delivery for application messaging.  
  
Which combination of actions will meet these requirements? **(Choose two.)**

options.text: Use AWS Lambda for the compute layers in the architecture.
Use Amazon EC2 instances for the compute layers in the architecture.
Use Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS) as the messaging component between the compute layers.
Use Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) FIFO queues as the messaging component between the compute layers.
Use containers that are based on Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS) for the compute layers in the architecture.

questions.explanation:
AWS Lambda best fits the compute requirement because it is a serverless compute service that lets the company run application tiers without provisioning or managing servers. Amazon SQS FIFO queues satisfy the messaging requirement because FIFO queues provide exactly-once processing semantics and preserve message ordering, making them the appropriate managed replacement for middleware that guarantees exactly-once message delivery.

**Learn more:** [AWS Lambda Documentation](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/lambda/) · [Amazon SQS FIFO queues - Amazon Simple Queue Service](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSSimpleQueueService/latest/SQSDeveloperGuide/sqs-fifo-queues.html)

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],A company runs an Amazon RDS for MySQL instance. To get ready for end-of-year processing, the company added a read replica to handle additional read-only queries from its reporting tool. CPU usage on both the read replica and the primary instance was 60%.  
  
After the end-of-year activities finish, the read replica has steady CPU usage of 25%, while the primary instance continues to have steady CPU usage of 60%. The company wants to rightsize the database while still providing sufficient performance for future growth.  
  
Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Delete the read replica Do not make changes to the primary instance
Resize the read replica to a smaller instance size Do not make changes to the primary instance
Resize the read replica to a larger instance size Resize the primary instance to a smaller instance size
Delete the read replica Resize the primary instance to a larger instance

questions.explanation:
Amazon RDS read replicas offload read-only and reporting workloads from the primary DB instance. Retaining the replica preserves that read capacity, while its sustained 25% CPU utilization indicates excess compute capacity that can be reduced. The primary instance remains at 60% CPU utilization, so it should not be downsized.

**Learn more:** [Working with DB instance read replicas](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonRDS/latest/UserGuide/USER_ReadRepl.html) · [Scaling and high availability in Amazon RDS](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonRDS/latest/gettingstartedguide/scaling-ha.html)

A company keeps its application logs in an Amazon CloudWatch Logs log group. A new policy requires that all application logs be stored in Amazon OpenSearch Service (Amazon Elasticsearch Service) in near-real time.  
  
Which solution will meet this requirement with the **LEAST operational overhead**?

options.text: Configure a CloudWatch Logs subscription to stream the logs to Amazon OpenSearch Service (Amazon Elasticsearch Service).
Create an AWS Lambda function. Use the log group to invoke the function to write the logs to Amazon OpenSearch Service (Amazon Elasticsearch Service).

Create an Amazon Kinesis Data Firehose delivery stream. Configure the log group as the delivery streams sources. Configure Amazon OpenSearch Service (Amazon Elasticsearch Service) as the delivery stream's destination.

Install and configure Amazon Kinesis Agent on each application server to deliver the logs to Amazon Kinesis Data Streams. Configure Kinesis Data Streams to deliver the logs to Amazon OpenSearch Service (Amazon Elasticsearch Service).

questions.explanation:
Amazon CloudWatch Logs supports subscription filters that can stream log data directly to Amazon OpenSearch Service in near real time. This is the lowest-overhead option because it uses a native integration between the log group and the OpenSearch domain, without requiring custom AWS Lambda code, separate Kinesis delivery infrastructure, or agents on each server. Firehose and Lambda can work, but they introduce extra components to operate that are not needed for this requirement.

**Learn more:** [Real-time processing of log data with subscriptions - Amazon CloudWatch Logs](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonCloudWatch/latest/logs/Subscriptions.html) · [Streaming CloudWatch Logs data to Amazon OpenSearch Service - Amazon CloudWatch Logs](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonCloudWatch/latest/logs/CWL_OpenSearch_Stream.html)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],A company wants to use high-performance computing (HPC) infrastructure on AWS for financial risk modeling. The company’s HPC workloads run on Linux. Each HPC workflow runs on hundreds of Amazon EC2 Spot Instances, is short-lived, and produces thousands of output files that are ultimately stored in persistent storage for analytics and for long-term future use.  
  
The company needs a cloud storage solution that allows copying on-premises data to long-term persistent storage so the data is available for processing by all EC2 instances. The solution must also provide a high-performance file system that is integrated with persistent storage to read and write datasets and output files.  
  
Which combination of AWS services meets these requirements?

options.text: Amazon FSx for Lustre integrated with Amazon S3
Amazon FSx for Windows File Server integrated with Amazon S3
Amazon S3 Glacier integrated with Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS)
Amazon S3 bucket with a VPC endpoint integrated with an Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) General Purpose SSD (gp2) volume

questions.explanation:
Amazon FSx for Lustre is the AWS managed high-performance Lustre file system built for Linux HPC workloads such as financial modeling, and it is natively integrated with Amazon S3 as persistent storage. This lets on-premises data be copied into S3 for durable long-term storage, while EC2 compute nodes access the same datasets through the fast shared FSx for Lustre file system and export output files back to S3.

**Learn more:** [What is Amazon FSx for Lustre?](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/fsx/latest/LustreGuide/what-is.html) · [Using data repositories with Amazon FSx for Lustre](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/fsx/latest/LustreGuide/fsx-data-repositories.html)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],A company runs a highly available web application on Amazon EC2 instances behind an Application Load Balancer. The company uses Amazon CloudWatch metrics.  
  
As traffic to the web application increases, some EC2 instances become overloaded with many outstanding requests. The CloudWatch metrics show that, for some EC2 instances, both the number of requests processed and the time required to receive responses are higher than for other EC2 instances. The company does not want new requests forwarded to EC2 instances that are already overloaded.  
  
Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Use the round robin routing algorithm based on the RequestCountPerTarget and ActiveConnectionCount CloudWatch metrics.
Use the least outstanding requests algorithm based on the RequestCountPerTarget and ActiveConnectionCount CloudWatch metrics.
Use the round robin routing algorithm based on the RequestCount and TargetResponseTime CloudWatch metrics.
Use the least outstanding requests algorithm based on the RequestCount and TargetResponseTime CloudWatch metrics.

questions.explanation:
Application Load Balancer's **least outstanding requests** routing algorithm sends requests to the healthy target with the lowest number of in-progress requests, which is exactly what is needed when some EC2 instances are already overloaded. AWS documentation states that round robin distributes requests evenly in sequence, while least outstanding requests is intended for cases where request complexity varies or targets differ in processing load. That makes the least outstanding requests option the correct choice, and the per-target metrics `RequestCountPerTarget` and `ActiveConnectionCount` best match the overloaded-target condition described.

**Learn more:** [Edit target group attributes for your Application Load Balancer - Elastic Load Balancing](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/elasticloadbalancing/latest/application/edit-target-group-attributes.html) · [Target groups for your Application Load Balancers - Elastic Load Balancing](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/elasticloadbalancing/latest/application/load-balancer-target-groups.html)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],A company uses AWS Organizations to manage multiple AWS accounts for different departments. The management account has an Amazon S3 bucket that stores project reports. The company wants to restrict access to this S3 bucket so that only users from accounts within the AWS Organizations organization can access it.  
  
Which solution satisfies these requirements with the **LEAST** operational overhead?

options.text: Add the aws PrincipalOrgID global condition key with a reference to the organization ID to the S3 bucket policy.
Create an organizational unit (OU) for each department. Add the aws:PrincipalOrgPaths global condition key to the S3 bucket policy.
Use AWS CloudTrail to monitor the CreateAccount, InviteAccountToOrganization, LeaveOrganization, and RemoveAccountFromOrganization events. Update the S3 bucket policy accordingly.
Tag each user that needs access to the S3 bucket. Add the aws:PrincipalTag global condition key to the S3 bucket policy.

questions.explanation:
The `aws:PrincipalOrgID` global condition key is designed for resource-based policies such as Amazon S3 bucket policies and lets the bucket allow access only when the requesting principal belongs to the specified AWS Organization. This avoids listing individual account IDs and automatically accommodates accounts that are added to or removed from the organization, which is the lowest-overhead way to enforce organization-wide access control.

**Learn more:** [Managing access permissions for an organization with AWS Organizations](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/organizations/latest/userguide/orgs_permissions_overview.html) · [Examples of Amazon S3 bucket policies](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/example-bucket-policies.html)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],A company has a large dataset for its online advertising business that is stored in an Amazon RDS for MySQL DB instance in a single Availability Zone.  
  
The company wants business reporting queries to run without affecting write operations on the production DB instance.  
  
Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Deploy RDS read replicas to process the business reporting queries.
Scale out the DB instance horizontally by placing it behind an Elastic Load Balancer.
Scale up the DB instance to a larger instance type to handle write operations and queries.
Deploy the DB instance in multiple Availability Zones to process the business reporting queries.

questions.explanation:
Amazon RDS read replicas are designed to offload read-heavy traffic from the primary DB instance. For MySQL, reporting and business intelligence queries can be directed to a read replica so the production writer handles transactional writes with less contention. Multi-AZ deployments improve availability and failover, but they are not intended to scale read workloads for reporting. Increasing instance size only adds capacity without separating reporting reads from production writes, and an Elastic Load Balancer is not used to horizontally scale a single RDS database instance.

**Learn more:** [Working with DB instance read replicas for Amazon RDS](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonRDS/latest/UserGuide/USER_ReadRepl.html) · [Amazon RDS Multi-AZ deployments](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonRDS/latest/UserGuide/Concepts.MultiAZ.html)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],A weather forecasting company continuously gathers temperature readings from multiple sensors. An existing data-ingestion process collects and aggregates the readings into larger Apache Parquet files. The process then encrypts the files by using client-side encryption with KMS managed keys (CSE-KMS). Finally, it writes the files to an Amazon S3 bucket, using separate prefixes for each calendar day.  
  
The company needs to run occasional SQL queries against the data to obtain sample moving averages for a particular calendar day.  
  
Which solution will meet these requirements **MOST cost-effectively**?

options.text: Configure Amazon Athena to read the encrypted files. Run SQL queries on the data directly in Amazon S3.
Use Amazon S3 Select to run SQL queries on the data directly in Amazon S3.
Configure Amazon Redshift to read the encrypted files. Use Redshift Spectrum and Redshift query editor v2 to run SQL queries on the data directly in Amazon S3.
Configure Amazon EMR Serverless to read the encrypted files. Use Apache SparkSQL to run SQL queries on the data directly in Amazon S3.

questions.explanation:
Amazon Athena can read CSE-KMS-encrypted datasets in Amazon S3 when its table definition identifies the CSE-KMS encryption configuration and KMS key. Athena runs SQL directly against the Parquet files without persistent cluster capacity, and daily prefixes can be represented as partitions to restrict each query to the required day and reduce data scanned. This makes it well suited to infrequent analysis.

**Learn more:** [Create tables based on encrypted datasets in Amazon S3](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/athena/latest/ug/creating-tables-based-on-encrypted-datasets-in-s3.html)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],A company runs a batch application on Amazon EC2 instances. The application includes a backend with multiple Amazon RDS databases. The application is generating a high volume of reads on the databases. A solutions architect must decrease the number of database reads while ensuring high availability.  
  
What should the solutions architect do to meet this requirement?

options.text: Add Amazon RDS read replicas.
Use Amazon ElastiCache for Redis.
Use Amazon Route 53 DNS caching
Use Amazon ElastiCache for Memcached.

questions.explanation:
Amazon ElastiCache for Redis can cache frequently requested data in memory so the application reads from the cache instead of repeatedly querying Amazon RDS, which reduces database read load. ElastiCache for Redis also supports replication across Availability Zones with automatic failover for high availability. By contrast, RDS read replicas help scale read traffic but the reads still go to a database engine, and Memcached does not provide the same built-in high-availability replication and failover model as Redis. Official AWS documentation describes ElastiCache as an in-memory cache for reducing backend database load and documents Redis replication groups with Multi-AZ and automatic failover, while RDS documentation states that read replicas are for scaling read-heavy workloads rather than eliminating database reads.

**Learn more:** [Amazon ElastiCache Documentation](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/elasticache/) · [High availability using replication groups - Amazon ElastiCache](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonElastiCache/latest/dg/Replication.html)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],A company runs an ecommerce website on Amazon EC2 instances behind an Application Load Balancer (ALB) in an Auto Scaling group. The website is having performance problems because of a high request rate from illegitimate external systems with changing IP addresses. The security team is concerned about possible DDoS attacks against the website. The company needs to block the illegitimate incoming requests while minimizing impact on legitimate users.  
  
What should a solutions architect recommend?

options.text: Deploy Amazon Inspector and associate it with the ALB.
Deploy AWS WAF, associate it with the ALB, and configure a rate-limiting rule.
Deploy rules to the network ACLs associated with the ALB to block the incomingtraffic.
Deploy Amazon GuardDuty and enable rate-limiting protection when configuring GuardDuty.

questions.explanation:
AWS WAF is designed to protect web applications on resources such as Application Load Balancers, and its rate-based rules can detect and block requests that exceed a defined rate. That makes it the best fit for stopping abusive high-rate web requests, even when the source IPs vary, while reducing disruption to normal traffic. Amazon Inspector performs vulnerability assessment rather than traffic filtering, GuardDuty detects suspicious activity rather than enforcing ALB rate limiting, and network ACLs are subnet-level controls that are not well suited to dynamic application-layer request filtering for this scenario.

**Learn more:** [AWS WAF Documentation](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/waf/) · [Using rate-based rule statements in AWS WAF](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/waf/latest/developerguide/waf-rule-statement-type-rate-based.html)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],A company is worried that the two NAT instances currently in use might no longer support the traffic required by the company’s application.  
  
A solutions architect wants to implement a solution that is:  
  
- highly available  
- fault tolerant  
- automatically scalable  
  
What should the solutions architect recommend?

options.text: Remove the two NAT instances and replace them with two NAT gateways in the same Availability Zone.
Use Auto Scaling groups with Network Load Balancers for the NAT instances in different Availability Zones.
Remove the two NAT instances and replace them with two NAT gateways in different Availability Zones.
Replace the two NAT instances with Spot Instances in different Availability Zones and deploy a Network Load Balancer.

questions.explanation:
AWS NAT gateways are managed by AWS and provide better scalability and availability than NAT instances. For a resilient multi-AZ design, AWS recommends creating a NAT gateway in each Availability Zone and routing each subnet to the NAT gateway in the same Availability Zone so that an AZ failure does not remove outbound internet access for resources in other AZs. That makes replacing the NAT instances with two NAT gateways in different Availability Zones the correct solution.

**Learn more:** [NAT gateway basics - Amazon VPC](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/userguide/nat-gateway-basics.html) · [Compare NAT gateways and NAT instances - Amazon VPC](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/userguide/vpc-nat-comparison.html)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],A global company runs its workloads on AWS. The company's application uses Amazon S3 buckets across AWS Regions for sensitive data storage and analysis. The company stores millions of objects in multiple S3 buckets daily. The company wants to identify all S3 buckets that are not versioning-enabled.  
  
Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Use Amazon S3 Storage Lens to identify all S3 buckets that are not versioning-enabled across Regions.
Enable IAM Access Analyzer for S3 to identify all S3 buckets that are not versioning-enabled across Regions.
Create an S3 Multi-Region Access Point to identify all S3 buckets that are not versioning-enabled across Regions.

questions.explanation:
Amazon S3 Storage Lens is the correct service because it provides S3 visibility across accounts, buckets, and Regions, and includes metrics for buckets with S3 Versioning enabled so administrators can identify buckets that do not have versioning turned on. IAM Access Analyzer for S3 focuses on bucket access findings such as public or shared access, not versioning configuration, and S3 Multi-Region Access Points are for routing requests to underlying buckets across Regions rather than auditing bucket versioning settings.

**Learn more:** [Using S3 Storage Lens to protect your data - Amazon S3](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/storage-lens-data-protection.html) · [Amazon S3 Storage Lens metrics glossary - Amazon S3](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/storage_lens_metrics_glossary.html)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],A company has two applications:  
  
- a sender application that sends messages with payloads to be processed  
- a processing application that is intended to receive the messages with payloads  
  
The company wants to use an AWS service to manage messages between the two applications. The sender application can send about 1,000 messages each hour. The messages might take as long as 2 days to be processed. If the messages fail to process, they must be retained so they do not affect the processing of any remaining messages.  
  
Which solution meets these requirements and is the **MOST operationally efficient**?

options.text: Set up an Amazon EC2 instance running a Redis database. Configure both applications to use the instance. Store, process, and delete the messages, respectively.
Use an Amazon Kinesis data stream to receive the messages from the sender application. Integrate the processing application with the Kinesis Client Library (KCL).
Integrate the sender and processor applications with an Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) queue. Configure a dead-letter queue to collect the messages that failed to process.
Subscribe the processing application to an Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS) topic to receive notifications to process. Integrate the sender application to write to the SNS topic.

questions.explanation:
Amazon SQS is the AWS service designed for decoupling a sender and a processor with durable, asynchronous message queuing. SQS can retain messages for up to 14 days, so a 2-day processing window is supported, and an SQS dead-letter queue can hold messages that fail processing so they are removed from the main processing flow and do not interfere with other messages. This is also more operationally efficient than managing an EC2/Redis solution, and it is a better fit than SNS pub/sub or Kinesis streaming for a simple one-producer, one-consumer work-queue pattern.

**Learn more:** [What is Amazon Simple Queue Service?](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSSimpleQueueService/latest/SQSDeveloperGuide/welcome.html) · [Configuring queue parameters using the Amazon SQS console](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSSimpleQueueService/latest/SQSDeveloperGuide/sqs-configure-queue-parameters.html)

A company is getting ready to build a new data platform that will ingest real-time streaming data from multiple sources. The company must transform the data before writing it to Amazon S3. The company also needs the ability to use SQL to query the transformed data.  
  
Which solutions will meet these requirements? **(Choose two.)**

options.text: Use Amazon Kinesis Data Streams to stream the data. Use Amazon Kinesis Data Analytics to transform the data. Use Amazon Kinesis Data Firehose to write the data to Amazon S3. Use Amazon Athena to query the transformed data from Amazon S3.

Use Amazon Managed Streaming for Apache Kafka (Amazon MSK) to stream the data. Use AWS Glue to transform the data and to write the data to Amazon S3. Use Amazon Athena to query the transformed data from Amazon S3.

Use AWS Database Migration Service (AWS DMS) to ingest the data. Use Amazon EMR to transform the data and to write the data to Amazon S3. Use Amazon Athena to query the transformed data from Amazon S3.

Use Amazon Managed Streaming for Apache Kafka (Amazon MSK) to stream the data. Use Amazon Kinesis Data Analytics to transform the data and to write the data to Amazon S3. Use the Amazon RDS query editor to query the transformed data from Amazon S3.

Use Amazon Kinesis Data Streams to stream the data. Use AWS Glue to transform the data. Use Amazon Kinesis Data Firehose to write the data to Amazon S3. Use the Amazon RDS query editor to query the transformed data from Amazon S3.

questions.explanation:
Amazon Athena is designed to run SQL queries against data stored in Amazon S3, so solutions that end with Athena satisfy the SQL-query requirement for transformed S3 data. Amazon Kinesis Data Analytics can perform SQL-based processing on streaming data, and Amazon Kinesis Data Firehose can deliver the transformed stream to Amazon S3, which makes the Kinesis-based pipeline valid. AWS Glue streaming ETL can consume streaming data from sources such as Amazon MSK or Amazon Kinesis Data Streams, transform that data, and write it to Amazon S3, where Athena can query it. The Amazon RDS query editor does not query files in Amazon S3; it queries RDS/Aurora databases instead.

**Learn more:** [Streaming ETL jobs in AWS Glue](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/glue/latest/dg/add-job-streaming.html) · [AWS Glue Streaming concepts](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/glue/latest/dg/glue-streaming-concepts.html)

options.text: Implement an Amazon ElastiCache for Redis cluster between the application and the DB cluster.
Add an additional read replica to the DB cluster.
Configure Aurora Auto Scaling for the Aurora read replicas.
Modify the DB cluster to have multiple writer instances.

questions.explanation:
Using Amazon ElastiCache for Redis offloads frequently repeated read queries from Aurora by serving the results from in-memory cache instead of repeatedly hitting the DB cluster. AWS documentation explicitly positions ElastiCache query-result caching for read-heavy applications that execute the same queries repeatedly. Aurora read replicas and Aurora Auto Scaling increase read capacity, but they still scale out database instances rather than eliminating repeated database reads, so they are typically less cost-effective for this pattern. Multiple writer instances are intended for write availability or write scaling scenarios, not for reducing repeated read traffic.

**Learn more:** [Caching database query results - Amazon ElastiCache](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonElastiCache/latest/dg/caching-database-query-results.html) · [Amazon Aurora Auto Scaling with Aurora Replicas - Amazon Aurora](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonRDS/latest/AuroraUserGuide/Aurora.Integrating.AutoScaling.html)

A manufacturing company runs its report-generation application on AWS. The application produces each report in about 20 minutes. It is built as a monolith that runs on a single Amazon EC2 instance. The application requires frequent updates to its tightly coupled modules. As the company adds new features, the application becomes difficult to maintain.  
  
Whenever the company patches a software module, the application has downtime. After any interruption, report generation must start over from the beginning. The company wants to redesign the application so that it is flexible, scalable, and can be improved gradually. The company also wants to minimize application downtime.  
  
Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Run the application on AWS Lambda as a single function with maximum provisioned concurrency.
Run the application on Amazon EC2 Spot Instances as microservices with a Spot Fleet default allocation strategy.
Run the application on Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) as microservices with service auto scaling.
Run the application on AWS Elastic Beanstalk as a single application environment with an all-at-once deployment strategy.

questions.explanation:
Running the application on Amazon ECS as microservices with service auto scaling best matches the need for flexibility, scalability, and incremental improvement. Microservices let the company separate tightly coupled modules into independently deployable services, which reduces the impact of updates and improves maintainability. Amazon ECS Service Auto Scaling can automatically adjust the number of tasks based on demand. The other options conflict with the requirements: a single AWS Lambda function cannot run a 20-minute report because Lambda functions are limited to 900 seconds, EC2 Spot Instances can be interrupted and are not recommended for inflexible or fault-intolerant workloads, and an Elastic Beanstalk all-at-once deployment takes all instances out of service during deployment.

**Learn more:** [Configure Lambda function timeout - AWS Lambda](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/lambda/latest/dg/configuration-timeout.html) · [Best practices for Amazon EC2 Spot](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSEC2/latest/UserGuide/spot-best-practices.html)

A company keeps multiple Amazon Machine Images (AMIs) in an AWS account for launching its Amazon EC2 instances. The AMIs include critical data and configurations required for the company’s operations. The company wants to implement a solution that can recover accidentally deleted AMIs quickly and efficiently.  
  
Which solution will meet these requirements with the **LEAST operational overhead**?

options.text: Create Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) snapshots of the AMIs. Store the snapshots in a separate AWS account.
Copy all AMIs to another AWS account periodically.
Create a retention rule in Recycle Bin.
Upload the AMIs to an Amazon S3 bucket that has Cross-Region Replication.

questions.explanation:
Amazon Recycle Bin can retain deleted EBS-backed AMIs according to a retention rule and allows them to be restored directly before the retention period expires. This provides fast recovery from accidental deletion with minimal administration compared with manually copying AMIs or snapshots to another account on an ongoing basis. AWS documentation also notes that accidentally deregistered EBS-backed AMIs can be restored from Recycle Bin within the allowed retention period.

**Learn more:** [Recover deleted EBS volumes, EBS snapshots, and EBS-backed AMIs with Recycle Bin](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/ebs/latest/userguide/recycle-bin.html) · [Recover deleted AMIs from the Recycle Bin](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/ebs/latest/userguide/recycle-bin-working-with-amis.html)

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],A company is moving an on-premises application to AWS and wants to use Amazon Redshift as the solution.  
  
Which use cases are appropriate for Amazon Redshift in this scenario? **(Choose three.)**

options.text: Supporting data APIs to access data with traditional, containerized, and event-driven applications
Supporting client-side and server-side encryption
Building analytics workloads during specified hours and when the application is not active
Caching data to reduce the pressure on the backend database
Scaling globally to support petabytes of data and tens of millions of requests per minute
Creating a secondary replica of the cluster by using the AWS Management Console

questions.explanation:
Amazon Redshift is designed for analytic data warehousing workloads. It supports the Redshift Data API for SQL access from traditional, containerized, and event-driven applications; it supports both data-in-transit and data-at-rest protection, including client-side and server-side encryption; and provisioned clusters can be paused, resumed, and scheduled for workloads that run only during specific hours. It is not intended to be an application cache, a globally distributed high-request operational database, or a service whose normal pattern is creating a secondary replica cluster from the console.

**Learn more:** [Using the Amazon Redshift Data API - Amazon Redshift](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/redshift/latest/mgmt/data-api.html) · [Data encryption - Amazon Redshift](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/redshift/latest/mgmt/security-encryption.html)

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],A company plans to create an Amazon EMR cluster that several teams will use. The company needs to ensure that each team’s big data workloads can access only the AWS services that the team needs to interact with. The company does not want the workloads to be able to access Instance Metadata Service Version 2 (IMDSv2) on the cluster’s underlying EC2 instances.  
  
Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Configure interface VPC endpoints for each AWS service that the teams need. Use the required interface VPC endpoints to submit the big data workloads.
Create EMR runtime roles. Configure the cluster to use the runtime roles. Use the runtime roles to submit the big data workloads.
Create an EC2 IAM instance profile that has the required permissions for each team. Use the instance profile to submit the big data workloads.
Create an EMR security configuration that has the EnableApplicationScopedIAMRole option set to false. Use the security configuration to submit the big data workloads.

questions.explanation:
Amazon EMR runtime roles provide workload-level IAM permissions, so each team can submit jobs with a role that permits access only to its required AWS services. Runtime roles also prevent applications from using IMDSv2 to obtain the underlying EC2 instance profile’s credentials.

**Learn more:** [Runtime roles for Amazon EMR steps](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/emr/latest/ManagementGuide/emr-steps-runtime-roles.html)
