A company has an application that uses Docker containers in its local data center. The application runs on a container host that keeps persistent data in a volume on the host, and the container instances use that stored persistent data.  
  
The company wants to migrate the application to a fully managed service because it does not want to manage any servers or storage infrastructure.  
  
Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Use Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS) with self-managed nodes. Create an Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) volume attached to an Amazon EC2 instance. Use the EBS volume as a persistent volume mounted in the containers.

Use Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) with an AWS Fargate launch type. Create an Amazon Elastic File System (Amazon EFS) volume. Add the EFS volume as a persistent storage volume mounted in the containers.
Use Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) with an AWS Fargate launch type. Create an Amazon S3 bucket. Map the S3 bucket as a persistent storage volume mounted in the containers.

Use Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) with an Amazon EC2 launch type. Create an Amazon Elastic File System (Amazon EFS) volume. Add the EFS volume as a persistent storage volume mounted in the containers.

questions.explanation:
Amazon ECS with the AWS Fargate launch type provides a serverless container platform, so the company does not manage container hosts or other server infrastructure. For persistent data mounted into containers, Amazon EFS is the appropriate storage service because ECS supports EFS volumes for Fargate tasks and documents EFS as persistent storage for ECS tasks. By contrast, EKS with self-managed nodes and ECS with the EC2 launch type still require instance management.

**Learn more:** [Storage options for Amazon ECS tasks](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonECS/latest/developerguide/using_data_volumes.html) · [Maintain nodes yourself with self-managed nodes - Amazon EKS](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/eks/latest/userguide/worker.html)

A company has a mobile chat application that uses Amazon DynamoDB as its data store. Users want new messages to be readable with the lowest possible latency. A solutions architect must design the best solution while requiring minimal changes to the application.  
  
Which method should the solutions architect choose?

options.text: Configure Amazon DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) for the new messages table. Update the code to use the DAX endpoint.
Add DynamoDB read replicas to handle the increased read load. Update the application to point to the read endpoint for the read replicas.
Double the number of read capacity units for the new messages table in DynamoDB. Continue to use the existing DynamoDB endpoint.
Add an Amazon ElastiCache for Redis cache to the application stack. Update the application to point to the Redis cache endpoint instead of DynamoDB.

questions.explanation:
Amazon DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) is the best choice because it is a fully managed, in-memory cache built specifically for DynamoDB that can reduce read latency from milliseconds to microseconds while preserving the existing DynamoDB API model. That makes it the lowest-latency option with the least application rework compared with adding a general-purpose Redis cache. Increasing read capacity improves scale, not read latency, and DynamoDB does not use the kind of read-replica endpoint described in the replica option.

**Learn more:** [Amazon DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) – Developer Guide](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/amazondynamodb/latest/developerguide/DAX.html) · [What is Amazon DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX)?](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/amazondynamodb/latest/developerguide/DAX.propoerty.html)

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],A company is designing a new multi-tier web application that includes the following components:  
  
- Web and application servers that run on Amazon EC2 instances in Auto Scaling groups  
- An Amazon RDS DB instance for data storage  
  
A solutions architect must restrict access to the application servers so that only the web servers can reach them.  
  
Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Deploy AWS PrivateLink in front of the application servers. Configure the network ACL to allow only the web servers to access the application servers.
Deploy a VPC endpoint in front of the application servers. Configure the security group to allow only the web servers to access the application servers.

Deploy a Network Load Balancer with a target group that contains the application servers' Auto Scaling group. Configure the network ACL to allow only the web servers to access the application servers.

Deploy an Application Load Balancer with a target group that contains the application servers' Auto Scaling group. Configure the security group to allow only the web servers to access the application servers.

questions.explanation:
In a multi-tier AWS design, access from one tier to another should be restricted with security groups, not network ACLs. A security group on the application tier can allow inbound traffic only from the web tier’s security group, which works cleanly with Auto Scaling groups because the rule follows the group rather than individual instance IP addresses. Placing the application tier behind an Application Load Balancer with a target group for the application servers is a standard way to expose that tier while keeping direct access limited to the approved source tier.

**Learn more:** [Security group rules - Amazon Virtual Private Cloud](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/userguide/security-group-rules.html) · [Security group rules for different use cases - Amazon EC2](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSEC2/latest/UserGuide/security-group-rules-reference.html)

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],A company runs a critical business application on Amazon EC2 instances behind an Application Load Balancer. The EC2 instances run in an Auto Scaling group and access an Amazon RDS DB instance.  
  
The design failed an operational review because the EC2 instances and the DB instance are all in a single Availability Zone. A solutions architect must revise the design to use a second Availability Zone.  
  
Which solution will make the application highly available?

options.text: Provision a subnet in each Availability Zone. Configure the Auto Scaling group to distribute the EC2 instances across both Availability Zones. Configure the DB instance with connections to each network.

Provision two subnets that extend across both Availability Zones. Configure the Auto Scaling group to distribute the EC2 instances across both Availability Zones. Configure the DB instance with connections to each network.
Provision a subnet in each Availability Zone. Configure the Auto Scaling group to distribute the EC2 instances across both Availability Zones. Configure the DB instance for Multi-AZ deployment.

Provision a subnet that extends across both Availability Zones. Configure the Auto Scaling group to distribute the EC2 instances across both Availability Zones. Configure the DB instance for Multi-AZ deployment.

questions.explanation:
A highly available design in this scenario requires the compute tier to run across multiple Availability Zones and the database tier to use Amazon RDS Multi-AZ. In AWS, each subnet resides in exactly one Availability Zone, so the architecture needs one subnet in each AZ and the Auto Scaling group configured to distribute EC2 instances across both. For the database, Multi-AZ deployment is the RDS feature that provides a synchronous standby in a different Availability Zone for failover. Simply adding network connections does not make the DB highly available, and a subnet cannot extend across Availability Zones.

**Learn more:** [Auto Scaling benefits for application architecture - Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/autoscaling/ec2/userguide/auto-scaling-benefits.html) · [Add an Availability Zone - Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/autoscaling/ec2/userguide/as-add-az-console.html)

A company wants to deploy its containerized application workloads to a VPC across three Availability Zones. The company needs a solution that is highly available across Availability Zones. The solution must require minimal changes to the application.  
  
Which solution will meet these requirements with the **LEAST operational overhead**?

options.text: Use Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS). Configure Amazon ECS Service Auto Scaling to use target tracking scaling. Set the minimum capacity to 3. Set the task placement strategy type to spread with an Availability Zone attribute.
Use Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS) self-managed nodes. Configure Application Auto Scaling to use target tracking scaling. Set the minimum capacity to 3.
Use Amazon EC2 Reserved Instances. Launch three EC2 instances in a spread placement group. Configure an Auto Scaling group to use target tracking scaling. Set the minimum capacity to 3.
Use an AWS Lambda function. Configure the Lambda function to connect to a VPC. Configure Application Auto Scaling to use Lambda as a scalable target. Set the minimum capacity to 3.

questions.explanation:
Amazon ECS is the lowest-overhead choice because it is a managed container orchestration service that can keep a minimum number of tasks running and distribute service tasks evenly across Availability Zones by using the `spread` placement strategy on `attribute:ecs.availability-zone`. ECS service auto scaling also supports target tracking scaling for the service’s desired task count. By contrast, Amazon EKS with self-managed nodes requires significantly more cluster and node administration, EC2 instances with a placement group do not provide managed container orchestration and a spread placement group does not solve cross-Availability-Zone container scheduling, and Lambda is not the right scaling model for this container workload pattern. ([docs.aws.amazon.com](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonECS/latest/developerguide/task-placement-strategies.html?utm_source=openai))

**Learn more:** [Use strategies to define Amazon ECS task placement](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonECS/latest/developerguide/task-placement-strategies.html) · [Example Amazon ECS task placement strategies](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonECS/latest/developerguide/strategy-examples.html)

A company runs a three-tier application in a VPC. The database tier uses an Amazon RDS for MySQL DB instance.  
  
The company plans to migrate the RDS for MySQL DB instance to an Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL DB cluster. The company needs a solution that replicates the data changes that occur during the migration to the new database.  
  
Which combination of steps will meet these requirements? **(Choose two.)**

options.text: Use AWS Database Migration Service (AWS DMS) Schema Conversion to transform the database objects.
Use AWS Database Migration Service (AWS DMS) Schema Conversion to create an Aurora PostgreSQL read replica on the RDS for MySQL DB instance.
Configure an Aurora MySQL read replica for the RDS for MySQL DB instance.
Define an AWS Database Migration Service (AWS DMS) task with change data capture (CDC) to migrate the data.
Promote the Aurora PostgreSQL read replica to a standalone Aurora PostgreSQL DB cluster when the replica lag is zero.

questions.explanation:
Migrating from MySQL to Aurora PostgreSQL is a heterogeneous database migration, so the schema must be converted to PostgreSQL-compatible objects rather than replicated as a read replica. AWS DMS Schema Conversion is designed to transform source schema objects for the target engine, and an AWS DMS migration task using change data capture (CDC) replicates ongoing source changes during migration. Aurora read replica promotion applies to RDS for MySQL to Aurora MySQL, not to Aurora PostgreSQL.

**Learn more:** [Using DMS Schema Conversion - AWS Database Migration Service](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/dms/latest/userguide/schema-conversion.html) · [Creating tasks for ongoing replication using AWS DMS](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/dms/latest/userguide/CHAP_Task.CDC.html)

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],A company is designing a web application that uses an internet-facing Application Load Balancer (ALB).  
  
The company requires the ALB to accept HTTPS web traffic from the public internet. The ALB must forward only HTTPS traffic to web application servers hosted on Amazon EC2 instances over port 443. The ALB must conduct HTTPS health checks of the web application servers on port 8443.  
  
Which combination of security-group configurations associated with the ALB will satisfy these requirements? (Choose three.)

options.text: Allow HTTPS inbound traffic from 0.0.0.0/0 for port 443.
Allow all outbound traffic to 0.0.0.0/0 for port 443.
Allow HTTPS outbound traffic to the web application instances for port 443.
Allow HTTPS inbound traffic from the web application instances for port 443.
Allow HTTPS outbound traffic to the web application instances for the health check on port 8443.
Allow HTTPS inbound traffic from the web application instances for the health check on port 8443.

questions.explanation:
An internet-facing ALB security group must allow inbound client traffic on its HTTPS listener port (443). It must allow outbound traffic to the instance security group on both the instance listener port (443) and the configured health-check port (8443). AWS recommends separate outbound rules for the instance listener and health-check ports.

**Learn more:** [Security groups for your Application Load Balancer](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/elasticloadbalancing/latest/application/load-balancer-update-security-groups.html) · [Health checks for Application Load Balancer target groups](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/elasticloadbalancing/latest/application/target-group-health-checks.html)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],A company must transfer 600 TB of data from its on-premises network-attached storage (NAS) system to the AWS Cloud. The transfer must be completed within 2 weeks. The data is sensitive and must be encrypted in transit. The company’s internet connection supports an upload speed of 100 Mbps.  
  
Which solution meets these requirements **MOST cost-effectively**?

options.text: Use Amazon S3 multi-part upload functionality to transfer the files over HTTPS.
Create a VPN connection between the on-premises NAS system and the nearest AWS Region. Transfer the data over the VPN connection.
Use the AWS Snow Family console to order several AWS Snowball Edge Storage Optimized devices. Use the devices to transfer the data to Amazon S3.
Set up a 10 Gbps AWS Direct Connect connection between the company location and the nearest AWS Region. Transfer the data over a VPN connection into the Region to store the data in Amazon S3.

questions.explanation:
AWS Snowball Edge Storage Optimized is designed for large-scale offline data transfers into AWS and can be used to move data to Amazon S3 without depending on a limited internet uplink. With only 100 Mbps of upload bandwidth, sending 600 TB over the network would take far longer than 2 weeks, so internet-based options such as multipart upload over HTTPS or a VPN do not satisfy the timeline. A new 10 Gbps AWS Direct Connect connection could provide sufficient bandwidth, but it is generally a more expensive choice for a one-time bulk migration. Snowball Edge devices are available in Storage Optimized 210 TB configurations, support encrypted data transfer, and ordering several devices in parallel is the most cost-effective way to meet the deadline for this volume of data.

**Learn more:** [What is Snowball Edge? - AWS Snowball Edge Developer Guide](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/snowball/latest/developer-guide/whatisedge.html) · [AWS Snowball Pricing](https://aws.amazon.com/snowball/pricing/)

A company recently deployed Linux-based application instances on Amazon EC2 in a private subnet and a Linux-based bastion host on an Amazon EC2 instance in a public subnet of a VPC.  
  
A solutions architect needs to connect from the on-premises network, through the company's internet connection, to the bastion host and to the application servers. The solutions architect must ensure that the security groups for all the EC2 instances allow this access.  
  
Which combination of steps should the solutions architect take to meet these requirements? **(Choose two.)**

options.text: Replace the current security group of the bastion host with one that only allows inbound access from the application instances.
Replace the current security group of the bastion host with one that only allows inbound access from the internal IP range for the company.
Replace the current security group of the bastion host with one that only allows inbound access from the external IP range for the company.
Replace the current security group of the application instances with one that allows inbound SSH access from only the private IP address of the bastion host.
Replace the current security group of the application instances with one that allows inbound SSH access from only the public IP address of the bastion host.

questions.explanation:
For a bastion host in a public subnet, the inbound SSH rule should permit the company's public-facing external IP range, because traffic arriving over the internet is sourced from those external addresses. The private application instances should allow inbound SSH only from the bastion host's private IP address, because communication from the bastion host to instances in the private subnet occurs over the VPC using private addressing. AWS documentation for bastion-host access patterns describes allowing inbound SSH to the bastion from the local network's public IP range and allowing inbound SSH to the private instance from the bastion host's private IP (or bastion security group).

**Learn more:** [NAT gateway use cases - Amazon Virtual Private Cloud](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/userguide/nat-gateway-scenarios.html) · [Security group rules for different use cases - Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSEC2/latest/UserGuide/security-group-rules-reference.html)

A company must set up a real-time data ingestion architecture for its application. The company requires:  
  
- an API  
- a process that transforms data while the data is streaming  
- a storage solution for the data  
  
Which solution will meet these requirements with the **LEAST operational overhead**?

options.text: Deploy an Amazon EC2 instance to host an API that sends data to an Amazon Kinesis data stream. Create an Amazon Kinesis Data Firehose delivery stream that uses the Kinesis data stream as a data source. Use AWS Lambda functions to transform the data. Use the Kinesis Data Firehose delivery stream to send the data to Amazon S3.
Deploy an Amazon EC2 instance to host an API that sends data to AWS Glue. Stop source/destination checking on the EC2 instance. Use AWS Glue to transform the data and to send the data to Amazon S3.

Configure an Amazon API Gateway API to send data to an Amazon Kinesis data stream. Create an Amazon Kinesis Data Firehose delivery stream that uses the Kinesis data stream as a data source. Use AWS Lambda functions to transform the data. Use the Kinesis Data Firehose delivery stream to send the data to Amazon S3.
Configure an Amazon API Gateway API to send data to AWS Glue. Use AWS Lambda functions to transform the data. Use AWS Glue to send the data to Amazon S3.

questions.explanation:
Using Amazon API Gateway for the API avoids managing servers, and API Gateway can integrate with Amazon Kinesis Data Streams for record ingestion. Amazon Data Firehose can use a Kinesis data stream as its source, invoke an AWS Lambda function to transform streaming records, and then deliver the transformed data to Amazon S3. This provides the required API, streaming transformation, and storage with less operational effort than running an API on Amazon EC2 or introducing AWS Glue into the ingestion path for this use case.

**Learn more:** [Tutorial: Create a REST API as an Amazon Kinesis proxy - Amazon API Gateway](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/apigateway/latest/developerguide/integrating-api-with-aws-services-kinesis.html) · [Transform source data in Amazon Data Firehose - Amazon Data Firehose](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/firehose/latest/dev/data-transformation.html)

A company wants to migrate an Oracle database to AWS. The database consists of a single table that contains millions of high-resolution geographic information systems (GIS) images, and each image is identified by a geographic code.  
  
When a natural disaster occurs, tens of thousands of images are updated every few minutes. Each geographic code has a single associated image, or row.  
  
The company wants a solution that is highly available and scalable during these events.  
  
Which solution meets these requirements **MOST cost-effectively**?

options.text: Store the images and geographic codes in a database table. Use Oracle running on an Amazon RDS Multi-AZ DB instance.
Store the images in Amazon S3 buckets. Use Amazon DynamoDB with the geographic code as the key and the image S3 URL as the value.
Store the images and geographic codes in an Amazon DynamoDB table. Configure DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) during times of high load.
Store the images in Amazon S3 buckets. Store geographic codes and image S3 URLs in a database table. Use Oracle running on an Amazon RDS Multi-AZ DB instance.

questions.explanation:
For large binary objects such as high-resolution images, the cost-effective AWS design is to store the images in Amazon S3 and keep only metadata or the S3 object reference in DynamoDB. DynamoDB is a fully managed, highly available key-value database that scales to high request rates, and using the geographic code as the partition key matches the one-image-per-code access pattern. Oracle on Amazon RDS Multi-AZ provides availability but is less cost-effective and less naturally scalable for this large-object, burst-update workload. DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) is mainly for faster reads, so it does not solve a write-heavy update pattern.

**Learn more:** [Best practices for storing large items and attributes in DynamoDB](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/amazondynamodb/latest/developerguide/bp-use-s3-too.html) · [Best practices - Modeling data with Amazon DynamoDB](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/prescriptive-guidance/latest/dynamodb-data-modeling/best-practices.html)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],A company’s production environment uses Amazon EC2 On-Demand Instances that run continuously from Monday through Saturday. The instances must operate for only 12 hours on Sunday and cannot tolerate interruptions. The company wants to optimize production-environment costs.  
  
Which solution will satisfy these requirements in the **MOST** cost-effective way?

options.text: Purchase Scheduled Reserved Instances for the EC2 instances that run for only 12 hours on Sunday. Purchase Standard Reserved Instances for the EC2 instances that run constantly between Monday and Saturday.

Purchase Convertible Reserved Instances for the EC2 instances that run for only 12 hours on Sunday. Purchase Standard Reserved Instances for the EC2 instances that run constantly between Monday and Saturday.
Use Spot Instances for the EC2 instances that run for only 12 hours on Sunday. Purchase Standard Reserved Instances for the EC2 instances that run constantly between Monday and Saturday.
Use Spot Instances for the EC2 instances that run for only 12 hours on Sunday. Purchase Convertible Reserved Instances for the EC2 instances that run constantly between Monday and Saturday.

questions.explanation:
For a fixed, recurring 12-hour weekly workload, Scheduled Reserved Instances were designed to provide reserved EC2 capacity on a defined schedule without the interruption risk of Spot Instances. Standard Reserved Instances provide a larger discount than Convertible Reserved Instances for the stable instances that run continuously from Monday through Saturday, when exchange flexibility is not required. AWS now states that Scheduled Instances can no longer be purchased, so this combination represents the legacy product-model answer.

**Learn more:** [Reserved Instances for Amazon EC2 overview](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSEC2/latest/UserGuide/ec2-reserved-instances.html) · [Purchase Scheduled Instances command reference](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/cli/v1/reference/ec2/purchase-scheduled-instances.html)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],A company wants to use an Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL DB cluster to simplify time-consuming database administrative tasks for production database workloads.  
  
The company wants to ensure that its database is highly available and will provide automatic failover support in most scenarios in less than 40 seconds.  
  
The company wants to offload reads off of the primary instance and keep costs as low as possible.  
  
Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Use an Amazon RDS Multi-AZ DB instance deployment. Create one read replica and point the read workload to the read replica.
Use an Amazon RDS Multi-AZ DB duster deployment Create two read replicas and point the read workload to the read replicas.
Use an Amazon RDS Multi-AZ DB instance deployment. Point the read workload to the secondary instances in the Multi-AZ pair.
Use an Amazon RDS Multi-AZ DB cluster deployment Point the read workload to the reader endpoint.

questions.explanation:
An Amazon RDS Multi-AZ DB cluster deployment is the best fit because it provides a writer instance plus readable reader instances across three Availability Zones, supports automatic failover typically in under 35 seconds, and includes a reader endpoint that routes read-only connections to the reader instances. That satisfies the availability, failover, and read-scaling requirements without adding extra read replicas that would increase cost. In contrast, a standard Multi-AZ DB instance deployment uses a standby that does not serve read traffic.

**Learn more:** [Failing over a Multi-AZ DB cluster for Amazon RDS](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonRDS/latest/UserGuide/multi-az-db-clusters-concepts-failover.html) · [Connecting to a Multi-AZ DB cluster for Amazon RDS](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonRDS/latest/UserGuide/multi-az-db-clusters-concepts-connection-management.html)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],A solutions architect is designing a new VPC layout.  
  
There are:  
  
- two public subnets for the load balancer,  
- two private subnets for web servers, and  
- two private subnets for MySQL.  
  
The web servers use only HTTPS. The solutions architect has already created a security group for the load balancer that allows port 443 from `0.0.0.0/0`.  
  
Company policy requires that each resource has only the minimum access needed to perform its tasks.  
  
Which additional configuration strategy should the solutions architect use to meet these requirements?

options.text: Create a security group for the web servers and allow port 443 from 0.0.0.0/0. Create a security group for the MySQL servers and allow port 3306 from the web servers security group.
Create a network ACL for the web servers and allow port 443 from 0.0.0.0/0. Create a network ACL for the MySQL servers and allow port 3306 from the web servers security group.
Create a security group for the web servers and allow port 443 from the load balancer. Create a security group for the MySQL servers and allow port 3306 from the web servers security group.
Create a network ACL for the web servers and allow port 443 from the load balancer. Create a network ACL for the MySQL servers and allow port 3306 from the web servers security group.

questions.explanation:
The least-privilege design is to use security groups so each tier allows traffic only from the tier that must reach it. AWS guidance for load balancers is to configure the instance security group to accept traffic only from the load balancer, and EC2 security groups support using another security group as the source. That means the web servers should allow TCP 443 from the load balancer’s security group, and the MySQL servers should allow TCP 3306 from the web servers’ security group. The network ACL choices are not appropriate here because network ACLs are stateless subnet filters and do not use security groups as rule sources.

**Learn more:** [Security groups for your Application Load Balancer - Elastic Load Balancing](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/en_en/elasticloadbalancing/latest/application/load-balancer-update-security-groups.html) · [Infrastructure security in Elastic Load Balancing - Elastic Load Balancing](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/elasticloadbalancing/latest/userguide/infrastructure-security.html)

A company runs Amazon EC2 instances and stores data on Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) volumes. The company must ensure that all data at rest is encrypted by using AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS). The company must also be able to control rotation of the encryption keys.  
  
Which solution meets these requirements with the **LEAST** operational overhead?

options.text: Create a customer managed key. Use the key to encrypt the EBS volumes.
Use an AWS managed key to encrypt the EBS volumes. Use the key to configure automatic key rotation.
Create an external KMS key with imported key material. Use the key to encrypt the EBS volumes.
Use an AWS owned key to encrypt the EBS volumes.

questions.explanation:
Amazon EBS can use a customer managed AWS KMS key for volume encryption, and customer managed symmetric KMS keys let the customer control key rotation settings. AWS managed keys rotate automatically but their rotation is not customer-configurable, and AWS owned keys do not provide customer control. Using imported key material creates additional lifecycle and rotation work, so it has higher operational overhead than a standard customer managed key created in AWS KMS.

**Learn more:** [How Amazon EBS encryption works](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/ebs/latest/userguide/how-ebs-encryption-works.html) · [Rotate AWS KMS keys](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/kms/latest/developerguide/rotate-keys.html)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],A company operates multiple Amazon RDS DB instances in a development AWS account. Every instance is tagged to identify it as a development resource. The company requires the development DB instances to run on a schedule only during business hours.  
  
Which solution meets these requirements with the **LEAST** operational overhead?

options.text: Create an Amazon CloudWatch alarm to identify RDS instances that need to be stopped. Create an AWS Lambda function to start and stop the RDS instances.
Create an AWS Trusted Advisor report to identify RDS instances to be started and stopped. Create an AWS Lambda function to start and stop the RDS instances.
Create AWS Systems Manager State Manager associations to start and stop the RDS instances.
Create an Amazon EventBridge rule that invokes AWS Lambda functions to start and stop the RDS instances.

questions.explanation:
Amazon EventBridge can run scheduled rules on recurring cron or rate expressions and invoke AWS Lambda. Lambda can identify the tagged development RDS DB instances and start or stop them through the Amazon RDS API, providing centralized automated scheduling without alarms, reports, or per-instance Systems Manager management. [Tutorial: Schedule an AWS Lambda function](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/eventbridge/latest/userguide/eb-run-lambda-schedule.html)

**Learn more:** [Tutorial: Schedule an AWS Lambda function](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/eventbridge/latest/userguide/eb-run-lambda-schedule.html) · [Instance Scheduler on AWS architecture](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/solutions/latest/instance-scheduler-on-aws/architecture.html)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],An online learning company is moving to the AWS Cloud. The company stores its student records in a PostgreSQL database. It needs a solution in which the data is available and online across multiple AWS Regions at all times.  
  
Which solution will meet these requirements with the **LEAST** operational overhead?

options.text: Migrate the PostgreSQL database to a PostgreSQL cluster on Amazon EC2 instances.
Migrate the PostgreSQL database to an Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL DB instance with the Multi-AZ feature turned on.
Migrate the PostgreSQL database to an Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL DB instance. Create a read replica in another Region.
Migrate the PostgreSQL database to an Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL DB instance. Set up DB snapshots to be copied to another Region.

questions.explanation:
Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL with a read replica in another AWS Region provides managed cross-Region replication and keeps the database available in multiple Regions with less administration than self-managing PostgreSQL on Amazon EC2. RDS Multi-AZ deployments are designed for high availability within a single AWS Region, not across Regions, and cross-Region snapshot copies are for backup and disaster recovery rather than an always-online database target. Therefore, creating an Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL DB instance and adding a cross-Region read replica is the lowest-overhead option that meets the multi-Region availability requirement.

**Learn more:** [Creating a read replica in a different AWS Region - Amazon RDS](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonRDS/latest/UserGuide/USER_ReadRepl.XRgn.html) · [Working with read replicas for Amazon RDS](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonRDS/latest/UserGuide/USER_ReadRepl.html)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],A company operates multiple workloads on virtual machines (VMs) in an on-premises data center. The company is growing rapidly, but the on-premises data center cannot scale quickly enough to satisfy business needs. The company wants to migrate the workloads to AWS.  
  
The migration is time-sensitive. The company wants to use a lift-and-shift strategy for non-critical workloads.  
  
Which combination of steps meets these requirements? (Choose three.)

options.text: Use the AWS Schema Conversion Tool (AWS SCT) to collect data about the VMs.
Use AWS Application Migration Service. Install the AWS Replication Agent on the VMs.
Complete the initial replication of the VMs. Launch test instances to perform acceptance tests on the VMs.
Stop all operations on the VMs. Launch a cutover instance.
Use AWS App2Container (A2C) to collect data about the VMs.
Use AWS Database Migration Service (AWS DMS) to migrate the VMs.

questions.explanation:
AWS Application Migration Service supports lift-and-shift server migrations by using the AWS Replication Agent to replicate source servers. After initial synchronization completes, test instances can be launched for acceptance testing. During the cutover window, source-server operations are stopped before launching cutover instances to complete the migration.

**Learn more:** [AWS Application Migration Service migration workflow](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/mgn/latest/ug/migration-workflow-gs.html)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],A solutions architect must design a highly available application with web, application, and database tiers. HTTPS content delivery needs to occur as close to the edge as possible, with the lowest delivery latency.  
  
Which solution satisfies these requirements and is **MOST secure**?

options.text: Configure a public Application Load Balancer (ALB) with multiple redundant Amazon EC2 instances in public subnets. Configure Amazon CloudFront to deliver HTTPS content using the public ALB as the origin.

Configure a public Application Load Balancer with multiple redundant Amazon EC2 instances in private subnets. Configure Amazon CloudFront to deliver HTTPS content using the EC2 instances as the origin.

Configure a public Application Load Balancer (ALB) with multiple redundant Amazon EC2 instances in private subnets. Configure Amazon CloudFront to deliver HTTPS content using the public ALB as the origin.

Configure a public Application Load Balancer with multiple redundant Amazon EC2 instances in public subnets. Configure Amazon CloudFront to deliver HTTPS content using the EC2 instances as the origin.

questions.explanation:
Amazon CloudFront provides HTTPS delivery from edge locations, minimizing latency for end users. For the origin, using an Application Load Balancer is more secure and architecturally appropriate than exposing individual EC2 instances, because the load balancer fronts redundant targets and supports restricting origin access through CloudFront. The most secure option given is the one with the ALB as the CloudFront origin and the EC2 instances placed in private subnets, so the instances are not publicly reachable while the application still remains highly available behind the load balancer.

**Learn more:** [Restrict access to Application Load Balancers - Amazon CloudFront](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonCloudFront/latest/DeveloperGuide/restrict-access-to-load-balancer.html) · [Use various origins with CloudFront distributions - Amazon CloudFront](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonCloudFront/latest/DeveloperGuide/DownloadDistS3AndCustomOrigins.html)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],A solutions architect must deliver an automated solution for a company's compliance policy stating that security groups cannot contain a rule that permits SSH from `0.0.0.0/0`. The company must be notified if the policy is ever violated. A solution is required as soon as possible.  
  
What should the solutions architect do to satisfy these requirements with the **LEAST operational overhead**?

options.text: Write an AWS Lambda script that monitors security groups for SSH being open to 0.0.0.0/0 addresses and creates a notification every time it finds one.
Enable the restricted-ssh AWS Config managed rule and generate an Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS) notification when a noncompliant rule is created.

Create an IAM role with permissions to globally open security groups and network ACLs. Create an Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS) topic to generate a notification every time the role is assumed by a user.

Configure a service control policy (SCP) that prevents non-administrative users from creating or editing security groups. Create a notification in the ticketing system when a user requests a rule that needs administrator permissions.

questions.explanation:
AWS Config provides the managed rule **restricted-ssh**, which evaluates security groups for unrestricted SSH access and marks them noncompliant when SSH is allowed from `0.0.0.0/0` or `::/0`. AWS Config can publish compliance change notifications to Amazon SNS, so this meets both the detection and notification requirements with minimal implementation and maintenance effort compared with building a custom AWS Lambda solution.

**Learn more:** [restricted-ssh - AWS Config](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/config/latest/developerguide/restricted-ssh.html) · [Notifications that AWS Config Sends to an Amazon SNS topic - AWS Config](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/config/latest/developerguide/notifications-for-AWS-Config.html)

options.text: Configure Lambda provisioned concurrency.
Increase the timeout of the Lambda functions.
Increase the memory of the Lambda functions.
Configure Lambda SnapStart.

questions.explanation:
AWS Lambda SnapStart is the best fit because it is supported for Java 11 and is specifically intended to reduce function startup latency by minimizing initialization time, which is the main cause of cold starts. AWS documentation distinguishes SnapStart from provisioned concurrency by recommending provisioned concurrency for workloads with strict latency requirements, while SnapStart improves startup performance without keeping execution environments pre-initialized and therefore is generally more cost-effective for this scenario.

**Learn more:** [Improving startup performance with Lambda SnapStart - AWS Lambda](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/lambda/latest/dg/snapstart.html) · [Configuring provisioned concurrency for a function - AWS Lambda](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/lambda/latest/dg/provisioned-concurrency.html)

A solutions architect is using Amazon S3 to design the storage architecture for a new digital media application.  
  
The media files must be resilient to the loss of an Availability Zone. Some files are accessed often, while other files are accessed rarely in an unpredictable pattern. The solutions architect must minimize the costs of storing and retrieving the media files.  
  
Which storage option meets these requirements?

options.text: S3 Standard
S3 Intelligent-Tiering
S3 Standard-Infrequent Access (S3 Standard-IA)
S3 One Zone-Infrequent Access (S3 One Zone-IA)

questions.explanation:
S3 Intelligent-Tiering is the best fit because it is designed for data with unknown, changing, or unpredictable access patterns and automatically moves objects between frequent and lower-cost infrequent tiers to optimize storage cost. It also supports multi-Availability Zone resilience, unlike S3 One Zone-IA, and avoids the mismatch of putting frequently accessed objects into S3 Standard-IA, which is meant for infrequent access and includes retrieval charges. AWS documentation describes S3 Intelligent-Tiering as the recommended storage class for unpredictable access patterns and notes that, unlike One Zone classes, it is resilient to the loss of an Availability Zone.

**Learn more:** [Managing storage costs with Amazon S3 Intelligent-Tiering](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/intelligent-tiering.html) · [Understanding and managing Amazon S3 storage classes](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/storage-class-intro.html)

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],A company has a data ingestion workflow that consists of the following:  
  
- An Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS) topic for notifications about new data deliveries  
- An AWS Lambda function to process the data and record metadata  
  
The company notices that the ingestion workflow sometimes fails because of network connectivity issues. When one of these failures happens, the Lambda function does not ingest the related data unless the company manually reruns the job.  
  
Which combination of actions should a solutions architect take to make sure that the Lambda function ingests all data going forward? **(Choose two.)**

options.text: Deploy the Lambda function in multiple Availability Zones.
Create an Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) queue, and subscribe it to the SNS topic.
Increase the CPU and memory that are allocated to the Lambda function.
Increase provisioned throughput for the Lambda function.
Modify the Lambda function to read from an Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) queue.

questions.explanation:
Using Amazon SQS between Amazon SNS and AWS Lambda adds durable buffering so notifications are retained even if processing cannot succeed immediately. Amazon SNS can deliver messages to an SQS subscription, and Lambda can consume from SQS through an event source mapping. For SQS event sources, Lambda retries failed invocations with backoff, which makes transient connectivity problems far less likely to cause permanently missed ingestions. Increasing Lambda size or throughput does not solve message durability, and deploying Lambda in multiple Availability Zones does not change this event-delivery pattern.

**Learn more:** [Subscribing an Amazon SQS queue to an Amazon SNS topic](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sns/latest/dg/subscribe-sqs-queue-to-sns-topic.html) · [Using Lambda with Amazon SQS](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/lambda/latest/dg/with-sqs.html)

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],An ecommerce company is seeing increased user traffic. The company’s store runs on Amazon EC2 instances as a two-tier web application with a web tier and a separate database tier. As traffic grows, the company observes that the architecture is causing significant delays in sending timely marketing and order confirmation emails to users. The company wants to reduce the time spent resolving complex email delivery issues and to minimize operational overhead.  
  
What should a solutions architect do to meet these requirements?

options.text: Create a separate application tier using EC2 instances dedicated to email processing.
Configure the web instance to send email through Amazon Simple Email Service (Amazon SES).
Configure the web instance to send email through Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS).
Create a separate application tier using EC2 instances dedicated to email processing. Place the instances in an Auto Scaling group.

questions.explanation:
Amazon SES is the AWS managed service designed for sending both marketing and transactional email at scale, so integrating the web instance with SES offloads email infrastructure management and delivery complexity while reducing operational overhead. Amazon SNS email is intended for simple notifications and internal alerts, not customized marketing or order-confirmation workflows, and building separate EC2 email-processing tiers would add administration instead of removing it.

**Learn more:** [Amazon Simple Email Service Documentation](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/ses/) · [Set up email sending with Amazon SES](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/ses/latest/dg/send-email.html)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],A company wants to build a scalable key management infrastructure to support developers who need to encrypt data in their applications.  
  
What should a solutions architect do to reduce the operational burden?

options.text: Use multi-factor authentication (MFA) to protect the encryption keys.
Use AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) to protect the encryption keys.
Use AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) to create, store, and assign the encryption keys.
Use an IAM policy to limit the scope of users who have access permissions to protect the encryption keys.

questions.explanation:
AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) is the AWS-managed service designed for centralized creation, storage, control, and use of encryption keys for application data. It is built to scale, integrates with applications and many AWS services, and reduces operational overhead because AWS manages the underlying key infrastructure and hardware security modules. MFA and IAM can help control access, but they do not provide the key management system itself, and AWS Certificate Manager is intended for managing SSL/TLS certificates rather than general-purpose data encryption keys.

**Learn more:** [AWS Key Management Service Documentation](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/kms/) · [AWS Key Management Service overview](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/kms/latest/developerguide/overview.html)

A company has an application that runs on a single Amazon EC2 instance. The application uses a MySQL database that runs on the same EC2 instance. The company needs a highly available and automatically scalable solution to handle increased traffic.  
  
Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Deploy the application to EC2 instances that run in an Auto Scaling group behind an Application Load Balancer. Create an Amazon Redshift cluster that has multiple MySQL-compatible nodes.
Deploy the application to EC2 instances that are configured as a target group behind an Application Load Balancer. Create an Amazon RDS for MySQL cluster that has multiple instances.
Deploy the application to EC2 instances that run in an Auto Scaling group behind an Application Load Balancer. Create an Amazon Aurora Serverless MySQL cluster for the database layer.
Deploy the application to EC2 instances that are configured as a target group behind an Application Load Balancer. Create an Amazon ElastiCache for Redis cluster that uses the MySQL connector.

questions.explanation:
A highly available and automatically scalable web tier on AWS is typically built with Amazon EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group behind an Application Load Balancer. For the database tier, the requirement is still MySQL plus automatic scaling and high availability. Amazon Aurora Serverless for MySQL-compatible workloads provides on-demand autoscaling capacity and supports highly available cluster configurations, making it the best fit. Amazon Redshift is an analytics data warehouse rather than a MySQL OLTP replacement, and ElastiCache for Redis is a cache, not a relational MySQL database.

**Learn more:** [Use Elastic Load Balancing to distribute incoming application traffic in your Auto Scaling group](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/autoscaling/ec2/userguide/autoscaling-load-balancer.html) · [Using Aurora serverless](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonRDS/latest/AuroraUserGuide/aurora-serverless-v2.html)

A company is designing the architecture for a new mobile app that uses the AWS Cloud. The company uses organizational units (OUs) in AWS Organizations to manage its accounts. The company needs to tag Amazon EC2 instances with data sensitivity, using the values `sensitive` and `nonsensitive`. IAM identities must be unable to delete a tag or create instances without a tag.  
  
Which combination of steps meets these requirements? (Choose two.)

options.text: In Organizations, create a new tag policy that specifies the data sensitivity tag key and the required values. Enforce the tag values for the EC2 instances. Attach the tag policy to the appropriate OU.

In Organizations, create a new service control policy (SCP) that specifies the data sensitivity tag key and the required tag values. Enforce the tag values for the EC2 instances. Attach the SCP to the appropriate OU.
Create a tag policy to deny running instances when a tag key is not specified. Create another tag policy that prevents identities from deleting tags. Attach the tag policies to the appropriate OU.

Create a service control policy (SCP) to deny creating instances when a tag key is not specified. Create another SCP that prevents identities from deleting tags. Attach the SCPs to the appropriate OU.
Create an AWS Config rule to check if EC2 instances use the data sensitivity tag and the specified values. Configure an AWS Lambda function to delete the resource if a noncompliant resource is found.

questions.explanation:
AWS Organizations tag policies standardize a tag key and its permitted values, and enforcement can prevent EC2 tagging operations that use noncompliant values. Tag-policy enforcement alone does not prevent creation of untagged resources. Service control policies can explicitly deny `ec2:RunInstances` when the required request tag is absent and deny `ec2:DeleteTags`, thereby preventing untagged instance creation and tag removal across the targeted OU.

**Learn more:** [Enforce tagging consistency — AWS Organizations](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/organizations/latest/userguide/orgs_manage_policies_tag-policies-enforcement.html) · [Grant permission to tag Amazon EC2 resources during creation](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSEC2/latest/UserGuide/supported-iam-actions-tagging.html)

A company runs its application on multiple Amazon EC2 instances in a VPC. The company creates a separate Amazon S3 bucket for each customer to store that customer’s relevant information in Amazon S3.  
  
The company must ensure that the application running on the EC2 instances can securely access only S3 buckets that belong to the company’s AWS account.  
  
Which solution meets these requirements with the **LEAST operational overhead**?

options.text: Create a gateway endpoint for Amazon S3 that is attached to the VPC. Update the IAM instance profile policy to provide access to only the specific buckets that the application needs.
Create a NAT gateway in a public subnet with a security group that allows access to only Amazon S3. Update the route tables to use the NAT Gateway.
![](https://cdn.examcademy.com/images/questions/1784025988561-ckwbi3aj.png)
![](https://cdn.examcademy.com/images/questions/1784025991900-r0b30b3e.png)

questions.explanation:
An Amazon S3 gateway VPC endpoint keeps S3 traffic private without requiring a NAT gateway. A Deny policy using the `aws:ResourceAccount` condition key blocks access to buckets not owned by the company’s AWS account, while allowing access to every company-owned customer bucket without continually updating a policy as buckets are created. AWS documents this condition key specifically for restricting IAM or VPC endpoint access to buckets owned by a specified account.

**Learn more:** [Bucket policy examples using condition keys — Amazon S3 User Guide](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/amazon-s3-policy-keys.html) · [Gateway endpoints for Amazon S3 — Amazon VPC User Guide](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/privatelink/vpc-endpoints-s3.html)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],A company runs an application on multiple Amazon EC2 instances. The application reads messages from an Amazon SQS queue, writes to an Amazon RDS table, and then deletes the message from the queue. Occasional duplicate records are discovered in the RDS table. The SQS queue itself does not contain duplicate messages.  
  
What should a solutions architect do to make sure the messages are processed only once?

options.text: Use the CreateQueue API call to create a new queue.
Use the AddPermission API call to add appropriate permissions.
Use the ReceiveMessage API call to set an appropriate wait time.
Use the ChangeMessageVisibility API call to increase the visibility timeout.

questions.explanation:
When a message is received from an SQS queue, it becomes hidden from other consumers for the visibility-timeout period. If message processing takes longer than the timeout, the message becomes visible again and can be received and processed by another consumer, causing duplicates. Using ChangeMessageVisibility to increase the visibility timeout keeps the message hidden until processing completes and the message is deleted.

**Learn more:** [ChangeMessageVisibility - Amazon SQS API Reference](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSSimpleQueueService/latest/APIReference/API_ChangeMessageVisibility.html) · [Amazon SQS visibility timeout](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSSimpleQueueService/latest/SQSDeveloperGuide/sqs-visibility-timeout.html)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],A company needs to reduce its Amazon S3 storage costs for an application that creates many files that cannot be recreated. Each file is about 5 MB and is stored in Amazon S3 Standard storage.  
  
The company must retain the files for 4 years before they can be deleted. The files must be immediately accessible. The files are accessed frequently during the first 30 days after object creation, but they are rarely accessed after the first 30 days.  
  
Which solution will meet these requirements in the **MOST** cost-effective way?

options.text: Create an S3 Lifecycle policy to move the files to S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval 30 days after object creation. Delete the files 4 years after object creation.
Create an S3 Lifecycle policy to move the files to S3 One Zone-Infrequent Access (S3 One Zone-IA) 30 days after object creation. Delete the files 4 years after object creation.
Create an S3 Lifecycle policy to move the files to S3 Standard-Infrequent Access (S3 Standard-IA) 30 days after object creation. Delete the files 4 years after object creation.

Create an S3 Lifecycle policy to move the files to S3 Standard-Infrequent Access (S3 Standard-IA) 30 days after object creation. Move the files to S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval 4 years after object creation.

questions.explanation:
S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval is the best fit because it provides millisecond, immediate access for long-lived data that is rarely accessed, and AWS documents that it has lower storage cost than S3 Standard-IA for this type of access pattern. S3 Standard-IA also provides immediate access, but it is typically more expensive for long-term, very infrequently accessed retention. S3 One Zone-IA is less appropriate because the files cannot be recreated and One Zone-IA stores data in only a single Availability Zone. S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval does not meet the immediate-access requirement because archived objects must be restored before access.

**Learn more:** [Understanding S3 Glacier storage classes for long-term data storage](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/glacier-storage-classes.html) · [Understanding and managing Amazon S3 storage classes](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/storage-class-intro.html)

A company is developing a new application that uses a serverless architecture. The architecture will include an Amazon API Gateway REST API and AWS Lambda functions to handle incoming requests.  
  
The company needs to add a service that can send messages received from the API Gateway REST API to multiple target Lambda functions for processing. The service must provide message filtering so that the target Lambda functions receive only the messages they require.  
  
Which solution meets these requirements with the **LEAST** operational overhead?

options.text: Send the requests from the API Gateway REST API to an Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS) topic. Subscribe Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) queues to the SNS topic. Configure the target Lambda functions to poll the different SQS queues.
Send the requests from the API Gateway REST API to Amazon EventBridge. Configure EventBridge to invoke the target Lambda functions.
Send the requests from the API Gateway REST API to Amazon Managed Streaming for Apache Kafka (Amazon MSK). Configure Amazon MSK to publish the messages to the target Lambda functions.
Send the requests from the API Gateway REST API to multiple Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) queues. Configure the target Lambda functions to poll the different SQS queues.

questions.explanation:
Amazon EventBridge uses event-pattern rules to filter incoming events based on event content and route each matching event to one or more targets, including AWS Lambda functions. This provides direct serverless fanout and content-based routing without the queues, Lambda polling configuration, or cluster management required by the other approaches.

**Learn more:** [Rules in Amazon EventBridge](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/eventbridge/latest/userguide/eb-rules.html) · [Event bus targets in Amazon EventBridge](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/eventbridge/latest/userguide/eb-targets.html)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],A solutions architect must design a system to store client case files. The files are important core company assets, and the number of files will increase over time.  
  
The files must be accessible concurrently from multiple application servers running on Amazon EC2 instances. The solution must provide built-in redundancy.  
  
Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Amazon Elastic File System (Amazon EFS)
Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS)
Amazon S3 Glacier Deep Archive
AWS Backup

questions.explanation:
Amazon Elastic File System (Amazon EFS) is the AWS managed file storage service built for shared access, allowing multiple Amazon EC2 instances to read and write the same file system concurrently. EFS is elastic so storage grows as files are added, and it is designed with redundant storage across multiple Availability Zones in a Region, which satisfies the redundancy requirement. Amazon EBS is block storage and Multi-Attach has narrower constraints, S3 Glacier Deep Archive is for archival data that is not directly accessed, and AWS Backup is for backup orchestration rather than primary shared storage. ([docs.aws.amazon.com](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/efs/latest/ug/how-it-works.html?utm_source=openai))

**Learn more:** [How Amazon EFS works - Amazon Elastic File System](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/efs/latest/ug/how-it-works.html) · [Best practices for using Amazon EFS volumes with Amazon ECS](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonECS/latest/developerguide/efs-best-practices.html)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],An ecommerce company operates several internal applications across multiple AWS accounts and uses AWS Organizations to manage those accounts.  
  
A security appliance in the company's networking account must inspect interactions among applications in different AWS accounts.  
  
Which solution satisfies these requirements?

options.text: Deploy a Network Load Balancer (NLB) in the networking account to send traffic to the security appliance. Configure the application accounts to send traffic to the NLB by using an interface VPC endpoint in the application accounts.
Deploy an Application Load Balancer (ALB) in the application accounts to send traffic directly to the security appliance.

Deploy a Gateway Load Balancer (GWLB) in the networking account to send traffic to the security appliance. Configure the application accounts to send traffic to the GWLB by using an interface GWLB endpoint in the application accounts.
Deploy an interface VPC endpoint in the application accounts to send traffic directly to the security appliance.

questions.explanation:
A Gateway Load Balancer is purpose-built to deploy and scale virtual security appliances for transparent traffic inspection. Gateway Load Balancer endpoints in the application accounts provide private cross-VPC and cross-account connectivity to the Gateway Load Balancer and its registered security appliance targets in the networking account; routing can direct the application traffic through the inspection path.

**Learn more:** [What is a Gateway Load Balancer?](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/elasticloadbalancing/latest/gateway/introduction.html) · [Access virtual appliances through AWS PrivateLink](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/privatelink/vpce-gateway-load-balancer.html)

A company is developing an ecommerce application and must store sensitive customer information. The company needs to allow customers to complete purchase transactions on the website. The company also must ensure that sensitive customer data is protected, including from database administrators.  
  
Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Store sensitive data in an Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) volume. Use EBS encryption to encrypt the data. Use an IAM instance role to restrict access.
Store sensitive data in Amazon RDS for MySQL. Use AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) client-side encryption to encrypt the data.
Store sensitive data in Amazon S3. Use AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) server-side encryption to encrypt the data. Use S3 bucket policies to restrict access.
Store sensitive data in Amazon FSx for Windows Server. Mount the file share on application servers. Use Windows file permissions to restrict access.

questions.explanation:
A transactional ecommerce application needs a relational database service such as Amazon RDS for MySQL. To protect sensitive fields even from database administrators, the sensitive data must be encrypted before it reaches the database, so the database stores only ciphertext. AWS documentation distinguishes this client-side, data-level encryption from standard Amazon RDS encryption at rest, which is transparent to the database engine and primarily protects the underlying storage. Because client-side encryption prevents the database and its administrators from seeing plaintext, this is the only option that satisfies both the transaction-processing requirement and the requirement to protect data from DB admins.

**Learn more:** [Encrypting Amazon RDS resources - Amazon RDS](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonRDS/latest/UserGuide/Overview.Encryption.html) · [Encryption - AWS Prescriptive Guidance](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/prescriptive-guidance/latest/aws-kms-best-practices/data-protection-encryption.html)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],A company runs an ecommerce application on Amazon EC2 instances behind an Application Load Balancer. The instances run in an Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling group across multiple Availability Zones. The Auto Scaling group scales based on CPU utilization metrics. The ecommerce application stores the transaction data in a MySQL 8.0 database that is hosted on a large EC2 instance.  
  
The database performance degrades rapidly as application load increases. The application processes more read requests than write transactions. The company wants a solution that will automatically scale the database to meet demand from unpredictable read workloads while maintaining high availability.  
  
Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Use Amazon Redshift with a single node for leader and compute functionality.
Use Amazon RDS with a Single-AZ deployment Configure Amazon RDS to add reader instances in a different Availability Zone.
Use Amazon Aurora with a Multi-AZ deployment. Configure Aurora Auto Scaling with Aurora Replicas.
Use Amazon ElastiCache for Memcached with EC2 Spot Instances.

questions.explanation:
Amazon Aurora is appropriate for a read-heavy MySQL-compatible workload that needs both high availability and automatic scaling of read capacity. Aurora Replicas are dedicated reader instances that scale read operations, and Aurora Auto Scaling can automatically add or remove Aurora Replicas in response to workload changes. Aurora also supports Multi-AZ high availability, and reader instances can be promoted during failover. By contrast, Redshift is a data warehouse rather than an OLTP MySQL replacement, Single-AZ RDS does not satisfy the high-availability requirement for the main deployment, and ElastiCache does not replace the relational database for transaction storage.

**Learn more:** [Amazon Aurora Auto Scaling with Aurora Replicas](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonRDS/latest/AuroraUserGuide/Aurora.Integrating.AutoScaling.html?icmpid=docs_as_landing) · [Replication with Amazon Aurora](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/en_en/AmazonRDS/latest/AuroraUserGuide/Aurora.Replication.html)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],A company runs an application on AWS Lambda functions that are invoked by an Amazon API Gateway API. The Lambda functions store customer data in an Amazon Aurora MySQL database. Whenever the company upgrades the database, the Lambda functions cannot establish database connections until the upgrade finishes. As a result, customer data is not captured for some of the events.  
  
A solutions architect must design a solution that stores customer data created during database upgrades.  
  
Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Provision an Amazon RDS proxy to sit between the Lambda functions and the database. Configure the Lambda functions to connect to the RDS proxy.
Increase the run time of the Lambda functions to the maximum. Create a retry mechanism in the code that stores the customer data in the database.
Persist the customer data to Lambda local storage. Configure new Lambda functions to scan the local storage to save the customer data to the database.
Store the customer data in an Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) FIFO queue. Create a new Lambda function that polls the queue and stores the customer data in the database.

questions.explanation:
An Amazon SQS FIFO queue provides durable message storage that decouples the API/Lambda ingestion layer from the Aurora database layer. Customer data can be written to the queue while the database is unavailable during an upgrade, and a Lambda function can later poll the queue and persist the messages to Aurora when connectivity is restored. AWS documentation describes SQS as a way to decouple components and buffer requests, and Lambda natively supports polling SQS queues as an event source. By contrast, RDS Proxy improves connection pooling and resilience to failovers and maintenance events, but it does not provide durable buffering of write events while the database is unavailable.

**Learn more:** [Using Lambda with Amazon SQS - AWS Lambda](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/lambda/latest/dg/with-sqs.html) · [Amazon SQS, Amazon SNS, or EventBridge? - AWS Decision Guide](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/pdfs/decision-guides/latest/sns-or-sqs-or-eventbridge/sns-or-sqs-or-eventbridge.pdf)

A company recently migrated a monolithic application to an Amazon EC2 instance and Amazon RDS. The application’s modules are tightly coupled. Its current design allows the application to run on only one EC2 instance.  
  
The company has observed high CPU utilization on the EC2 instance during periods of peak use. This high CPU utilization is associated with degraded Amazon RDS read-request performance. The company needs to reduce the high CPU utilization and improve read-request performance.  
  
Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Resize the EC2 instance to an EC2 instance type that has more CPU capacity. Configure an Auto Scaling group with a minimum and maximum size of 1. Configure an RDS read replica for read requests.

Resize the EC2 instance to an EC2 instance type that has more CPU capacity. Configure an Auto Scaling group with a minimum and maximum size of 1. Add an RDS read replica and redirect all read/write traffic to the replica.
Configure an Auto Scaling group with a minimum size of 1 and maximum size of 2. Resize the RDS DB instance to an instance type that has more CPU capacity.

Resize the EC2 instance to an EC2 instance type that has more CPU capacity. Configure an Auto Scaling group with a minimum and maximum size of 1. Resize the RDS DB instance to an instance type that has more CPU capacity.

questions.explanation:
A larger EC2 instance provides more CPU capacity for the single-instance application. Keeping the Auto Scaling group at a minimum and maximum of one preserves the application’s single-instance constraint. An RDS read replica can serve read-only requests, offloading read traffic from the primary DB instance and improving read performance; read/write traffic must remain directed to the primary. AWS documents that read replicas are read-only copies and that routing application read queries to them reduces load on the primary database instance.

**Learn more:** [Working with DB instance read replicas](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonRDS/latest/UserGuide/USER_ReadRepl.html)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],A company runs an application that receives data from thousands of geographically distributed remote devices that use UDP. The application processes the data immediately and sends a message back to the device when necessary. No data is stored.  
  
The company needs a solution that minimizes latency for data transmission from the devices. The solution must also provide rapid failover to another AWS Region.  
  
Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Configure an Amazon Route 53 failover routing policy. Create a Network Load Balancer (NLB) in each of the two Regions. Configure the NLB to invoke an AWS Lambda function to process the data.

Use AWS Global Accelerator. Create a Network Load Balancer (NLB) in each of the two Regions as an endpoint. Create an Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) cluster with the Fargate launch type. Create an ECS service on the cluster. Set the ECS service as the target for the NLProcess the data in Amazon ECS.

Use AWS Global Accelerator. Create an Application Load Balancer (ALB) in each of the two Regions as an endpoint. Create an Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) cluster with the Fargate launch type. Create an ECS service on the cluster. Set the ECS service as the target for the ALB. Process the data in Amazon ECS.

Configure an Amazon Route 53 failover routing policy. Create an Application Load Balancer (ALB) in each of the two Regions. Create an Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) cluster with the Fargate launch type. Create an ECS service on the cluster. Set the ECS service as the target for the ALB. Process the data in Amazon ECS.

questions.explanation:
AWS Global Accelerator is the best fit because it is designed to improve performance for TCP and UDP traffic by routing users onto the AWS global network and directing traffic to the optimal healthy regional endpoint. For UDP traffic, the load balancer must be a Network Load Balancer, because NLB supports UDP listeners and targets, whereas an Application Load Balancer does not support UDP. Route 53 failover is DNS-based and therefore not the fastest option for rapid failover. Using Global Accelerator with NLB endpoints in two Regions and processing the traffic in Amazon ECS on Fargate meets the latency and cross-Region failover requirements.

**Learn more:** [What is AWS Global Accelerator?](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/global-accelerator/latest/dg/what-is-global-accelerator.html) · [How AWS Global Accelerator works](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/global-accelerator/latest/dg/introduction-how-it-works.html)
