lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],A company needs to ingest and handle large amounts of streaming data that its application generates. The application runs on Amazon EC2 instances and sends data to Amazon Kinesis Data Streams, which is configured with default settings. Every other day, the application consumes the data and writes the data to an Amazon S3 bucket for business intelligence (BI) processing. The company observes that Amazon S3 is not receiving all the data that the application sends to Kinesis Data Streams.  
  
What should a solutions architect do to resolve this issue?

options.text: Update the Kinesis Data Streams default settings by modifying the data retention period.
Update the application to use the Kinesis Producer Library (KPL) to send the data to Kinesis Data Streams.
Update the number of Kinesis shards to handle the throughput of the data that is sent to Kinesis Data Streams.
Turn on S3 Versioning within the S3 bucket to preserve every version of every object that is ingested in the S3 bucket.

questions.explanation:
Amazon Kinesis Data Streams retains records for 24 hours by default. Because the application reads the stream only every other day, some records expire before they are consumed and written to Amazon S3. Increasing the Kinesis Data Streams data retention period allows the consumer to read older records before they are removed. AWS documentation states that retention is 24 hours by default and can be increased up to 365 days. In contrast, using KPL improves producer behavior, adding shards increases stream throughput, and S3 Versioning only preserves multiple versions of objects already written to S3.

**Learn more:** [Change the data retention period - Amazon Kinesis Data Streams](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/streams/latest/dev/kinesis-extended-retention.html) · [Quotas and limits - Amazon Kinesis Data Streams](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/streams/latest/dev/service-sizes-and-limits.html)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],A company uses a fleet of Amazon EC2 instances to ingest data from on-premises data sources. The data is in JSON format, and ingestion rates can be as high as 1 MB/s. If an EC2 instance is rebooted, data that is in flight is lost. The company's data science team wants to query the ingested data in near real time.  
  
Which solution provides near-real-time querying of the data, is scalable, and minimizes data loss?

options.text: Publish data to Amazon Kinesis Data Streams, Use Kinesis Data Analytics to query the data.
Publish data to Amazon Kinesis Data Firehose with Amazon Redshift as the destination. Use Amazon Redshift to query the data.
Store ingested data in an EC2 instance store. Publish data to Amazon Kinesis Data Firehose with Amazon S3 as the destination. Use Amazon Athena to query the data.
Store ingested data in an Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) volume. Publish data to Amazon ElastiCache for Redis. Subscribe to the Redis channel to query the data.

questions.explanation:
Amazon Kinesis Data Streams is designed for durable real-time streaming ingestion and can scale throughput by using shards, with each shard supporting 1 MB/s writes. Kinesis Data Analytics for SQL applications can continuously process and query streaming records in near real time. This combination removes dependence on ephemeral EC2 memory or storage for in-flight data and best satisfies the requirements for scalability, near-real-time querying, and minimal data loss.

**Learn more:** [Create and manage Kinesis data streams](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/streams/latest/dev/working-with-streams.html) · [What Is Amazon Kinesis Data Analytics for SQL Applications?](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/kinesisanalytics/latest/dev/what-is.html)

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],A company has a data ingestion workflow that includes the following components:  
  
- An Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS) topic that receives notifications about new data deliveries  
- An AWS Lambda function that processes and stores the data  
  
The ingestion workflow sometimes fails because of network connectivity issues. When a failure happens, the related data is not ingested unless the company manually reruns the job.  
  
What should a solutions architect do to ensure that all notifications are eventually processed?

options.text: Configure the Lambda function for deployment across multiple Availability Zones.
Modify the Lambda function's configuration to increase the CPU and memory allocations for the function.
Configure the SNS topic’s retry strategy to increase both the number of retries and the wait time between retries.
Configure an Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) queue as the on-failure destination. Modify the Lambda function to process messages in the queue.

questions.explanation:
To ensure eventual processing, failed notifications must be stored durably so they can be retried later instead of being lost when the Lambda processing attempt fails. An Amazon SQS queue used as a failure destination provides that buffer: failed events are retained in the queue, and the Lambda function can then process messages from the queue until they succeed. AWS documentation also notes that SNS retry behavior for AWS-managed endpoints such as Lambda is predefined, while undeliverable or failed processing records should be retained by using a dead-letter or failure destination rather than relying only on retries.

**Learn more:** [Amazon SNS message delivery retries - Amazon Simple Notification Service](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sns/latest/dg/sns-message-delivery-retries.html) · [Capturing records of Lambda asynchronous invocations - AWS Lambda](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/lambda/latest/dg/invocation-async-retain-records.html)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],A company runs an application on a large fleet of Amazon EC2 instances. The application reads from and writes entries to an Amazon DynamoDB table. The DynamoDB table keeps increasing in size continuously, but the application requires only the data from the most recent 30 days.  
  
The company needs a solution that minimizes cost and development effort.  
  
Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Use an AWS CloudFormation template to deploy the complete solution. Redeploy the CloudFormation stack every 30 days, and delete the original stack.

Use an EC2 instance that runs a monitoring application from AWS Marketplace. Configure the monitoring application to use Amazon DynamoDB Streams to store the timestamp when a new item is created in the table. Use a script that runs on the EC2 instance to delete items that have a timestamp that is older than 30 days.
Configure Amazon DynamoDB Streams to invoke an AWS Lambda function when a new item is created in the table. Configure the Lambda function to delete items in the table that are older than 30 days.

Extend the application to add an attribute that has a value of the current timestamp plus 30 days to each new item that is created in the table. Configure DynamoDB to use the attribute as the TTL attribute.

questions.explanation:
Amazon DynamoDB Time to Live (TTL) is the native, cost-effective way to remove items that are no longer needed. The application can write a per-item expiration attribute set to the current time plus 30 days, and DynamoDB can use that attribute as the TTL field to delete expired items automatically. This avoids extra EC2 instances, monitoring software, custom cleanup scripts, or Lambda-based deletion logic, so it best minimizes both cost and development effort.

**Learn more:** [Using time to live (TTL) in DynamoDB](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/amazondynamodb/latest/developerguide/TTL.html) · [Computing time to live (TTL) in DynamoDB](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/amazondynamodb/latest/developerguide/time-to-live-ttl-before-you-start.html)

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],A solutions architect is designing an application.  
  
The application will run on Amazon EC2 instances in private subnets across multiple Availability Zones in a VPC. The EC2 instances will frequently access large files that contain confidential information. These files are stored in Amazon S3 buckets for processing. The solutions architect must optimize the network architecture to minimize data transfer costs.  
  
What should the solutions architect do to meet these requirements?

options.text: Create a gateway endpoint for Amazon S3 in the VPC. In the route tables for the private subnets, add an entry for the gateway endpoint.
Create a single NAT gateway in a public subnet. In the route tables for the private subnets, add a default route that points to the NAT gateway.
Create an AWS PrivateLink interface endpoint for Amazon S3 in the VPIn the route tables for the private subnets, add an entry for the interface endpoint.

Create one NAT gateway for each Availability Zone in public subnets. In each of the route tables for the private subnets, add a default route that points to the NAT gateway in the same Availability Zone.

questions.explanation:
An Amazon S3 gateway VPC endpoint is the lowest-cost way for EC2 instances in private subnets to access S3 privately. It routes S3 traffic over the AWS network without using an internet gateway or NAT gateway, and AWS documents that gateway endpoints for S3 have no additional charge. Associating the private-subnet route tables with the gateway endpoint ensures the instances send S3 traffic through that endpoint instead of through paid NAT infrastructure.

**Learn more:** [Gateway endpoints for Amazon S3 - Amazon Virtual Private Cloud](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/privatelink/vpc-endpoints-s3.html) · [Gateway endpoints - Amazon Virtual Private Cloud](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/privatelink/gateway-endpoints.html)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],A company plans to run a set of Amazon EC2 instances that connect to an Amazon Aurora database. The company has created an AWS CloudFormation template to deploy the EC2 instances and the Aurora DB cluster. The company wants the instances to authenticate to the database securely, and it does not want to manage static database credentials.  
  
Which solution satisfies these requirements with the **LEAST** operational effort?

options.text: Create a database user with a user name and password. Add parameters for the database user name and password to the CloudFormation template. Pass the parameters to the EC2 instances when the instances are launched.

Create a database user with a user name and password. Store the user name and password in AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store. Configure the EC2 instances to retrieve the database credentials from Parameter Store.

Configure the DB cluster to use IAM database authentication. Create a database user to use with IAM authentication. Associate a role with the EC2 instances to allow applications on the instances to access the database.

Configure the DB cluster to use IAM database authentication with an IAM user. Create a database user that has a name that matches the IAM user. Associate the IAM user with the EC2 instances to allow applications on the instances to access the database.

questions.explanation:
Amazon Aurora IAM database authentication is designed for this use case because it allows applications to connect by using short-lived authentication tokens instead of stored database passwords. AWS documentation specifically notes that applications running on Amazon EC2 can use credentials from the EC2 instance profile for greater security, and IAM access is granted by attaching the appropriate `rds-db:connect` permission to a role. This removes the need to maintain static database credentials while keeping operational overhead low.

**Learn more:** [IAM database authentication - Amazon Aurora](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonRDS/latest/AuroraUserGuide/UsingWithRDS.IAMDBAuth.html) · [Creating and using an IAM policy for IAM database access - Amazon Aurora](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/en_en/AmazonRDS/latest/AuroraUserGuide/UsingWithRDS.IAMDBAuth.IAMPolicy.html)

A company has an Amazon S3 data lake governed by AWS Lake Formation. The company wants to build a visualization in Amazon QuickSight by joining data in the data lake with operational data stored in an Amazon Aurora MySQL database.  
  
The company wants to enforce column-level authorization so that the marketing team can access only a subset of columns in the database.  
  
Which solution will meet these requirements with the **LEAST operational overhead**?

options.text: Use Amazon EMR to ingest the data directly from the database to the QuickSight SPICE engine. Include only the required columns.

Use AWS Glue Studio to ingest the data from the database to the S3 data lake. Attach an IAM policy to the QuickSight users to enforce column-level access control. Use Amazon S3 as the data source in QuickSight.

Use AWS Glue Elastic Views to create a materialized view for the database in Amazon S3. Create an S3 bucket policy to enforce column-level access control for the QuickSight users. Use Amazon S3 as the data source in QuickSight.

Use a Lake Formation blueprint to ingest the data from the database to the S3 data lake. Use Lake Formation to enforce column-level access control for the QuickSight users. Use Amazon Athena as the data source in QuickSight.

questions.explanation:
AWS Lake Formation provides fine-grained column-level access control for data in an S3 data lake, and Amazon Athena is one of the integrated query engines that enforces those Lake Formation permissions. Amazon QuickSight can query Athena data sources that are governed by Lake Formation, so the low-overhead approach is to ingest the Aurora MySQL data into the Lake Formation-managed S3 data lake and let Athena perform the join and Lake Formation enforce column-level permissions. Lake Formation blueprints are designed to ingest relational database sources such as Aurora into the data lake, making this the most operationally efficient option.

**Learn more:** [Data filtering and cell-level security in Lake Formation](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/lake-formation/latest/dg/data-filtering.html) · [Using AWS Lake Formation with Amazon Athena](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/lake-formation/latest/dg/athena-lf.html)

A company has an AWS Lambda function that requires read access to an Amazon S3 bucket in the same AWS account.  
  
Which solution will meet these requirements in the **MOST secure** manner?

options.text: Apply an S3 bucket policy that grants read access to the S3 bucket.
Apply an IAM role to the Lambda function. Apply an IAM policy to the role to grant read access to the S3 bucket.
Embed an access key and a secret key in the Lambda function’s code to grant the required IAM permissions for read access to the S3 bucket.
Apply an IAM role to the Lambda function. Apply an IAM policy to the role to grant read access to all S3 buckets in the account.

questions.explanation:
The most secure solution is to assign the Lambda function an IAM execution role and attach an identity-based policy that grants only the required read permissions for the specific S3 bucket. AWS Lambda uses execution roles for a function to access other AWS services, and AWS recommends least-privilege permissions. Using long-term access keys in code is not secure, and granting access to all buckets is overly permissive. A bucket policy can allow access, but for same-account function-to-service access, a tightly scoped execution role is the standard least-privilege design.

**Learn more:** [Managing permissions in AWS Lambda](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/lambda/latest/dg/lambda-permissions.html) · [Defining Lambda function permissions with an execution role](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/lambda/latest/dg/lambda-intro-execution-role.html)

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],A company runs several business applications in three separate VPCs in the `us-east-1` Region. The applications must be able to communicate across the VPCs. The applications also must consistently send hundreds of gigabytes of data each day to a latency-sensitive application running in a single on-premises data center.  
  
A solutions architect must design a network connectivity solution that maximizes cost-effectiveness.  
  
Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Configure three AWS Site-to-Site VPN connections from the data center to AWS. Establish connectivity by configuring one VPN connection for each VPC.
Launch a third-party virtual network appliance in each VPC. Establish an IPsec VPN tunnel between the data center and each virtual appliance.
Set up three AWS Direct Connect connections from the data center to a Direct Connect gateway in us-east-1. Establish connectivity by configuring each VPC to use one of the Direct Connect connections.

Set up one AWS Direct Connect connection from the data center to AWS. Create a transit gateway, and attach each VPC to the transit gateway. Establish connectivity between the Direct Connect connection and the transit gateway.

questions.explanation:
AWS Transit Gateway provides interconnectivity for multiple VPCs through VPC attachments, and AWS Direct Connect can be associated to a transit gateway through a Direct Connect gateway and transit virtual interface so one dedicated connection can serve multiple VPCs in the same Region. That satisfies the need for VPC-to-VPC communication and provides more consistent, lower-latency, high-throughput on-premises connectivity than VPN-based options. Using three separate Direct Connect links would meet the connectivity need but would not maximize cost-effectiveness when one Direct Connect connection can be shared through the transit gateway design.

**Learn more:** [Direct Connect gateways - AWS Direct Connect](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/directconnect/latest/UserGuide/direct-connect-gateways-intro.html) · [Direct Connect gateways and Transit Gateway associations - AWS Direct Connect](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/directconnect/latest/UserGuide/direct-connect-transit-gateways.html)

A bicycle-sharing company is building a multi-tier architecture to monitor the location of its bicycles during peak operating hours. The company wants to use these data points in its existing analytics platform. A solutions architect must identify the most viable multi-tier option to support this architecture. The data points must be accessible from the REST API.  
  
Which action meets these requirements for storing and retrieving location data?

options.text: Use Amazon Athena with Amazon S3.
Use Amazon API Gateway with AWS Lambda.
Use Amazon QuickSight with Amazon Redshift.
Use Amazon API Gateway with Amazon Kinesis Data Analytics.

questions.explanation:
Amazon API Gateway with AWS Lambda is the best fit because API Gateway natively provides REST API endpoints, and Lambda supplies the compute tier to process requests and store or fetch the bicycle location records. This matches a multi-tier design in which clients access location data through a REST API while the application logic can also send the same data to downstream analytics services. Athena and QuickSight are analytics and visualization services rather than REST-facing application tiers, and Kinesis Data Analytics is intended for stream analytics instead of direct REST-based data storage and retrieval. Official AWS documentation states that API Gateway is used to create and deploy REST APIs and that Lambda can be invoked directly by API Gateway for request handling.

**Learn more:** [Amazon API Gateway Documentation](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/apigateway/) · [Lambda integrations for REST APIs in API Gateway](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/apigateway/latest/developerguide/set-up-lambda-integrations.html)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],An ecommerce company is building a distributed application that uses several serverless functions and AWS services to complete order-processing tasks. These tasks require manual approvals as part of the workflow.  
  
A solutions architect must design an architecture for the order-processing application. The solution must be able to combine multiple AWS Lambda functions into responsive serverless applications. The solution must also orchestrate data and services that run on Amazon EC2 instances, containers, or on-premises servers.  
  
Which solution will meet these requirements with the **LEAST operational overhead**?

options.text: Use AWS Step Functions to build the application.
Integrate all the application components in an AWS Glue job.
Use Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) to build the application.
Use AWS Lambda functions and Amazon EventBridge events to build the application.

questions.explanation:
AWS Step Functions is designed for workflow orchestration across multiple AWS Lambda functions and other AWS services, and AWS documentation specifically calls out conditional workflows and human approvals as a strong fit. It also supports integrating tasks that run beyond Lambda, including containers and externally hosted workers, which covers Amazon EC2-, container-, and on-premises-based processing with minimal operational management compared with building custom orchestration from SQS or EventBridge. AWS Glue is an ETL service rather than a general application workflow orchestrator.

**Learn more:** [Orchestrating Lambda functions with Step Functions](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/lambda/latest/dg/with-step-functions.html) · [Deploying a workflow that waits for human approval in Step Functions](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/step-functions/latest/dg/tutorial-human-approval.html)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],A company operates all of its business applications in the AWS Cloud. The company uses AWS Organizations to manage multiple AWS accounts.  
  
A solutions architect must review every permission granted to IAM users to identify IAM users that have more permissions than necessary.  
  
Which solution satisfies these requirements with the **LEAST** administrative overhead?

options.text: Use Network Access Analyzer to review all access permissions in the company's AWS accounts.
Create an AWS CloudWatch alarm that activates when an IAM user creates or modifies resources in an AWS account.
Use AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) Access Analyzer to review all the company’s resources and accounts.
Use Amazon Inspector to find vulnerabilities in existing IAM policies.

questions.explanation:
IAM Access Analyzer can create an organization-wide unused-access analyzer that continuously reviews IAM users and roles. It uses access activity and last-accessed information to identify unused service- and action-level permissions, enabling least-privilege remediation with centralized administration.

**Learn more:** [Using AWS Identity and Access Management Access Analyzer](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/what-is-access-analyzer.html) · [Create an IAM Access Analyzer unused access analyzer](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/access-analyzer-create-unused.html)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],A company is building a mobile gaming application in a single AWS Region. The app runs on multiple Amazon EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group, and the company stores application data in Amazon DynamoDB.  
  
The application communicates between users and servers by using **TCP** and **UDP** traffic, and it will be used globally. The company wants to provide the **lowest possible latency** for all users.  
  
Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Use AWS Global Accelerator to create an accelerator. Create an Application Load Balancer (ALB) behind an accelerator endpoint that uses Global Accelerator integration and listening on the TCP and UDP ports. Update the Auto Scaling group to register instances on the ALB.

Use AWS Global Accelerator to create an accelerator. Create a Network Load Balancer (NLB) behind an accelerator endpoint that uses Global Accelerator integration and listening on the TCP and UDP ports. Update the Auto Scaling group to register instances on the NLB.

Create an Amazon CloudFront content delivery network (CDN) endpoint. Create a Network Load Balancer (NLB) behind the endpoint and listening on the TCP and UDP ports. Update the Auto Scaling group to register instances on the NLB. Update CloudFront to use the NLB as the origin.

Create an Amazon CloudFront content delivery network (CDN) endpoint. Create an Application Load Balancer (ALB) behind the endpoint and listening on the TCP and UDP ports. Update the Auto Scaling group to register instances on the ALB. Update CloudFront to use the ALB as the origin.

questions.explanation:
AWS Global Accelerator is the correct global entry point for non-HTTP application traffic because it improves performance for worldwide users by routing traffic onto the AWS global network and supports both TCP and UDP listeners. The load balancer behind it must be a Network Load Balancer, because NLB operates at Layer 4 and supports TCP and UDP traffic to the EC2 instances. Application Load Balancer is not appropriate for UDP workloads, and CloudFront is for HTTP/HTTPS content delivery rather than generic TCP/UDP application transport.

**Learn more:** [What is AWS Global Accelerator?](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/global-accelerator/latest/dg/what-is-global-accelerator.html) · [How AWS Global Accelerator works](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/global-accelerator/latest/dg/introduction-how-it-works.html)

A company is building a new application on AWS. The application includes:  
  
- an Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) cluster  
- an Amazon S3 bucket that stores application assets  
- an Amazon RDS for MySQL database that stores the application's dataset  
  
The dataset contains sensitive information. The company wants to make sure that **only the ECS cluster** can access the data in the RDS for MySQL database and the data in the S3 bucket.  
  
Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Create a new AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) customer managed key to encrypt both the S3 bucket and the RDS for MySQL database. Ensure that the KMS key policy includes encrypt and decrypt permissions for the ECS task execution role.

Create an AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) AWS managed key to encrypt both the S3 bucket and the RDS for MySQL database. Ensure that the S3 bucket policy specifies the ECS task execution role as a user.

Create an S3 bucket policy that restricts bucket access to the ECS task execution role. Create a VPC endpoint for Amazon RDS for MySQL. Update the RDS for MySQL security group to allow access from only the subnets that the ECS cluster will generate tasks in.

Create a VPC endpoint for Amazon RDS for MySQL. Update the RDS for MySQL security group to allow access from only the subnets that the ECS cluster will generate tasks in. Create a VPC endpoint for Amazon S3. Update the S3 bucket policy to allow access from only the S3 VPC endpoint.

questions.explanation:
Restricting Amazon S3 access to only the ECS cluster's network path requires a gateway VPC endpoint for S3 with a bucket policy that allows requests only from that endpoint, while a VPC endpoint plus a security group scoped to the ECS tasks' subnets restricts Amazon RDS for MySQL access to traffic originating from the ECS cluster. This purely network-based enforcement is consistent across both resources and does not depend on the ECS task execution role, which AWS reserves for pulling container images and writing logs rather than for granting application-level access to data stores, so solutions built around that role do not actually satisfy the exclusivity requirement. Encrypting the data with a KMS key (as in the other options) protects data at rest but does not, by itself, restrict which network paths or principals can call the S3 or RDS APIs.

**Learn more:** [Controlling access from VPC endpoints with bucket policies](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/example-bucket-policies-vpc-endpoint.html) · [Amazon ECS task execution IAM role](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonECS/latest/developerguide/task_execution_IAM_role.html)

A company experienced a breach that affected several applications in its on-premises data center. The attacker exploited vulnerabilities in the custom applications running on the servers. The company is now migrating its applications to Amazon EC2 instances and wants to implement a solution that actively scans the EC2 instances for vulnerabilities and sends a report detailing the findings.  
  
Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Deploy AWS Shield to scan the EC2 instances for vulnerabilities. Create an AWS Lambda function to log any findings to AWS CloudTrail.
Deploy Amazon Macie and AWS Lambda functions to scan the EC2 instances for vulnerabilities. Log any findings to AWS CloudTrail.
Turn on Amazon GuardDuty. Deploy the GuardDuty agents to the EC2 instances. Configure an AWS Lambda function to automate the generation and distribution of reports that detail the findings.
Turn on Amazon Inspector. Deploy the Amazon Inspector agent to the EC2 instances. Configure an AWS Lambda function to automate the generation and distribution of reports that detail the findings.

questions.explanation:
Amazon Inspector is the AWS service designed to continuously assess Amazon EC2 instances for software vulnerabilities and unintended network exposure, and it creates detailed findings that can be exported as reports. Those findings can also be routed through Amazon EventBridge to AWS Lambda for automated generation and distribution workflows. AWS Shield is for DDoS protection, Amazon Macie is for sensitive data discovery, and Amazon GuardDuty focuses on threat detection rather than EC2 vulnerability assessment. The Amazon Inspector documentation states that it scans EC2 instances, produces findings when vulnerabilities are detected, and supports exporting findings reports.

**Learn more:** [What is Amazon Inspector?](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/inspector/latest/user/what-is-inspector.html) · [Scanning Amazon EC2 instances with Amazon Inspector](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/inspector/latest/user/scanning-ec2.html)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],A company has deployed a self-managed DNS service on AWS. The solution includes the following:  
  
- Amazon EC2 instances in different AWS Regions  
- Endpoints of a standard accelerator in AWS Global Accelerator  
  
The company wants to protect the solution from DDoS attacks.  
  
What should a solutions architect do to meet this requirement?

options.text: Subscribe to AWS Shield Advanced. Add the accelerator as a resource to protect.
Subscribe to AWS Shield Advanced. Add the EC2 instances as resources to protect.
Create an AWS WAF web ACL that includes a rate-based rule. Associate the web ACL with the accelerator.
Create an AWS WAF web ACL that includes a rate-based rule. Associate the web ACL with the EC2 instances.

questions.explanation:
AWS Shield Advanced is the AWS service designed for enhanced DDoS protection, and AWS Global Accelerator **standard accelerators** are supported resources that can be directly protected. Amazon EC2 instances are not protected by adding the instances themselves unless protection is applied through associated Elastic IP addresses, which is not described here. AWS WAF rate-based rules are for HTTP(S) application-layer inspection and are not the primary control for protecting this self-managed DNS architecture behind Global Accelerator.

**Learn more:** [List of resources that AWS Shield Advanced protects](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/waf/latest/developerguide/ddos-protections-by-resource-type.html) · [CreateProtection - AWS Shield Advanced](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/waf/latest/DDOSAPIReference/API_CreateProtection.html)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],A company runs a two-tier image-processing application. The application uses two Availability Zones, and each Availability Zone has:  
  
- one public subnet  
- one private subnet  
  
An Application Load Balancer (ALB) for the web tier uses the public subnets. Amazon EC2 instances for the application tier use the private subnets.  
  
Users report that the application is performing more slowly than expected. A security audit of the web server log files shows that the application is receiving millions of illegitimate requests from a small number of IP addresses. A solutions architect must fix the immediate performance issue while the company investigates a more permanent solution.  
  
What should the solutions architect recommend to meet this requirement?

options.text: Modify the inbound security group for the web tier. Add a deny rule for the IP addresses that are consuming resources.
Modify the network ACL for the web tier subnets. Add an inbound deny rule for the IP addresses that are consuming resources.
Modify the inbound security group for the application tier. Add a deny rule for the IP addresses that are consuming resources.
Modify the network ACL for the application tier subnets. Add an inbound deny rule for the IP addresses that are consuming resources.

questions.explanation:
In Amazon VPC, security groups support only allow rules, not deny rules, so blocking specific abusive source IP addresses cannot be done with a security group. A network ACL operates at the subnet level and supports ordered allow and deny rules, which makes it the appropriate immediate control to block traffic from those IP addresses before it reaches resources in the internet-facing web tier subnets. Because the malicious requests are entering through the public-facing web tier path, the deny rule should be applied to the network ACL associated with the web tier subnets.

**Learn more:** [Security group rules - Amazon VPC](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/userguide/security-group-rules.html) · [Infrastructure security in Amazon VPC](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/userguide/infrastructure-security.html)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],A company uses Amazon EC2 instances to host its internal systems. During a deployment operation, an administrator attempts to use the AWS CLI to terminate an EC2 instance, but receives a 403 (Access Denied) error.  
  
The administrator is using an IAM role with the following IAM policy attached:  
  
![Question Image](https://cdn.examcademy.com/images/questions/1783644236871-i5uq3hht.png)  
  
What is causing the request to fail?

options.text: The EC2 instance has a resource-based policy with a Deny statement.
The principal has not been specified in the policy statement.
The
The request to terminate the EC2 instance does not originate from the CIDR blocks 192.0.2.0/24 or 203.0.113.0/24.

questions.explanation:
The policy contains both an `Allow` and an explicit `Deny` for `ec2:TerminateInstances`. The `Deny` uses the `NotIpAddress` condition on `aws:SourceIp`, so any terminate request originating from an IP address outside `192.0.2.0/24` or `203.0.113.0/24` is denied. In AWS policy evaluation, an explicit deny overrides an allow, which causes the 403 Access Denied response. In an identity-based policy, a `Principal` element is not required because the attached role is the principal.

**Learn more:** [How AWS enforcement code logic evaluates requests to allow or deny access](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/reference_policies_evaluation-logic_policy-eval-denyallow.html) · [AWS: Denies access to AWS based on the source IP](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/reference_policies_examples_aws_deny-ip.html)

options.text: Configure the security group for the web servers to allow inbound traffic on port 443 from 0.0.0.0/0. Configure the security group for the DB instance to allow inbound traffic on port 3306 from the security group of the web servers.

Configure the security group for the web servers to allow inbound traffic on port 443 from the IP addresses of the customers. Configure the security group for the DB instance to allow inbound traffic on port 3306 from the security group of the web servers.

Configure the security group for the web servers to allow inbound traffic on port 443 from the IP addresses of the customers. Configure the security group for the DB instance to allow inbound traffic on port 3306 from the IP addresses of the customers.

Configure the security group for the web servers to allow inbound traffic on port 443 from 0.0.0.0/0. Configure the security group for the DB instance to allow inbound traffic on port 3306 from 0.0.0.0/0.

questions.explanation:
A public web tier that must be reachable by worldwide users with changing IP addresses needs an inbound HTTPS rule on port 443 from `0.0.0.0/0`. The RDS for MySQL database should not allow direct internet access; instead, its security group should allow inbound MySQL traffic on port 3306 only from the web tier's security group. AWS documentation explicitly describes allowing web access from any IPv4 address for HTTPS and allowing RDS access by specifying the EC2 security group as the source for the database port.

**Learn more:** [Security group rules for different use cases - Amazon EC2](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSEC2/latest/UserGuide/security-group-rules-reference.html) · [Determining who can connect to your Amazon RDS DB instance - Amazon RDS](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonRDS/latest/gettingstartedguide/security-groups.html)

A company has applications hosted on Amazon EC2 instances with IPv6 addresses. The applications must initiate communications with other external applications by using the internet. However, the company’s security policy states that no external service can initiate a connection to the EC2 instances.  
  
What should a solutions architect recommend to resolve this issue?

options.text: Create a NAT gateway and make it the destination of the subnet's route table
Create an internet gateway and make it the destination of the subnet's route table
Create a virtual private gateway and make it the destination of the subnet's route table
Create an egress-only internet gateway and make it the destination of the subnet's route table

questions.explanation:
For IPv6 workloads in Amazon VPC, an egress-only internet gateway provides outbound internet access while preventing unsolicited inbound connections from the internet. AWS documents that it allows outbound communication over IPv6 from instances in a VPC to the internet and prevents internet hosts from initiating an IPv6 connection to those instances. The subnet route table should send IPv6 internet traffic, typically `::/0`, to the egress-only internet gateway.

**Learn more:** [Enable outbound IPv6 traffic using an egress-only internet gateway - Amazon VPC](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/userguide/egress-only-internet-gateway.html) · [Example routing options - Amazon VPC](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/userguide/route-table-options.html)

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],A gaming company plans to launch a new internet-facing application in multiple AWS Regions. The application will use the TCP and UDP protocols for communication. The company requires high availability and minimum latency for users worldwide.  
  
Which combination of actions should a solutions architect take to meet these requirements? **(Choose two.)**

options.text: Create internal Network Load Balancers in front of the application in each Region.
Create external Application Load Balancers in front of the application in each Region.
Create an AWS Global Accelerator accelerator to route traffic to the load balancers in each Region.
Configure Amazon Route 53 to use a geolocation routing policy to distribute the traffic.
Configure Amazon CloudFront to handle the traffic and route requests to the application in each Region

questions.explanation:
Network Load Balancer supports both TCP and UDP protocols required for gaming applications; Application Load Balancer only supports HTTP/HTTPS. AWS Global Accelerator provides anycast static IP addresses and routes traffic across the AWS backbone to the regional endpoint with the lowest latency, reducing end-user latency and improving availability. This combination is specifically designed for multi-region gaming and real-time applications.

**Learn more:** [How AWS Global Accelerator works](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/global-accelerator/latest/dg/introduction-how-it-works.html) · [Endpoints for standard accelerators](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/global-accelerator/latest/dg/about-endpoints.html)

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],A company runs a three-tier web application that uses a PostgreSQL database. The database stores metadata for documents. The company searches that metadata for key terms to retrieve documents that it reviews in a monthly report. The documents themselves are stored in Amazon S3. The documents are typically written once, but they are updated often.  
  
The reporting process currently takes a few hours when it uses relational queries. The reporting process must not block document updates or the addition of new documents. A solutions architect needs to implement a solution to accelerate the reporting process.  
  
Which solution will meet these requirements with the **LEAST** amount of change to the application code?

options.text: Set up a new Amazon DocumentDB (with MongoDB compatibility) cluster that includes a read replica. Scale the read replica to generate the reports.
Set up a new Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL DB cluster that includes an Aurora Replica. Issue queries to the Aurora Replica to generate the reports.
Set up a new Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL Multi-AZ DB instance. Configure the reporting module to query the secondary RDS node so that the reporting module does not affect the primary node.
Set up a new Amazon DynamoDB table to store the documents. Use a fixed write capacity to support new document entries. Automatically scale the read capacity to support the reports.

questions.explanation:
Using a PostgreSQL-compatible read replica for reporting offloads the long-running read workload from the primary database so writes and new inserts can continue without being affected. Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL with an Aurora Replica is designed to serve read traffic from replicas while keeping PostgreSQL compatibility, so the reporting module can be redirected with minimal code change compared with moving to a different database model. A standard RDS for PostgreSQL Multi-AZ DB instance does not allow queries against its standby node, so it does not solve the reporting-offload requirement. DocumentDB and DynamoDB would require significantly larger application and data-model changes because they are not drop-in replacements for a relational PostgreSQL reporting workload.

**Learn more:** [Configuring and managing a Multi-AZ deployment for Amazon RDS](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonRDS/latest/UserGuide/Concepts.MultiAZ.html) · [Read replica configuration with PostgreSQL](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonRDS/latest/UserGuide/USER_PostgreSQL.Replication.ReadReplicas.Configuration.html)

A solutions architect is designing a new hybrid architecture to extend a company's on-premises infrastructure to AWS. The company requires a highly available connection with consistent low latency to an AWS Region. The company needs to minimize costs and is willing to accept slower traffic if the primary connection fails.  
  
What should the solutions architect do to meet these requirements?

options.text: Provision an AWS Direct Connect connection to a Region. Provision a VPN connection as a backup if the primary Direct Connect connection fails.
Provision a VPN tunnel connection to a Region for private connectivity. Provision a second VPN tunnel for private connectivity and as a backup if the primary VPN connection fails.
Provision an AWS Direct Connect connection to a Region. Provision a second Direct Connect connection to the same Region as a backup if the primary Direct Connect connection fails.

Provision an AWS Direct Connect connection to a Region. Use the Direct Connect failover attribute from the AWS CLI to automatically create a backup connection if the primary Direct Connect connection fails.

questions.explanation:
AWS Direct Connect is designed for dedicated hybrid connectivity and provides a more consistent network experience with low latency than internet-based VPN connectivity. To keep costs down while still providing failover, the appropriate design is to use Direct Connect as the primary path and an AWS Site-to-Site VPN as the backup path. AWS documentation also notes that VPN can be used for redundancy with Direct Connect, whereas adding a second Direct Connect connection would raise cost, and VPN-only connectivity would not meet the consistent low-latency primary-connection requirement.

**Learn more:** [Direct Connect Documentation](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/directconnect/) · [Configure a Direct Connect Classic connection - AWS Direct Connect](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/directconnect/latest/UserGuide/toolkit-classic.html)

A company runs its applications on Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL in the us-east-1 Region. The company also uses machine learning (ML) models to forecast annual revenue from near-real-time reports. The reports are generated by using the same RDS for PostgreSQL database. Database performance slows during business hours. The company needs to improve database performance.  
  
Which solution will meet these requirements **MOST cost-effectively**?

options.text: Create a cross-Region read replica. Configure the reports to be generated from the read replica.
Activate Multi-AZ DB instance deployment for RDS for PostgreSQL. Configure the reports to be generated from the standby database.
Use AWS Data Migration Service (AWS DMS) to logically replicate data to a new database. Configure the reports to be generated from the new database.
Create a read replica in us-east-1. Configure the reports to be generated from the read replica.

questions.explanation:
An Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL read replica in the same Region can serve the read-only reporting workload, offloading those queries from the primary database while retaining near-real-time asynchronous replication. A Multi-AZ DB instance standby cannot serve read traffic, and a cross-Region replica or separate database replicated by AWS DMS adds unnecessary cost and complexity.

**Learn more:** [Working with read replicas for Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonRDS/latest/UserGuide/USER_PostgreSQL.Replication.ReadReplicas.html) · [Multi-AZ DB instance deployments for Amazon RDS](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonRDS/latest/UserGuide/Concepts.MultiAZSingleStandby.html)

A company's security team asks that network traffic be captured in VPC Flow Logs. The logs will be accessed frequently for 90 days and then accessed only intermittently.  
  
What should a solutions architect do to satisfy these requirements when configuring the logs?

options.text: Use Amazon CloudWatch as the target. Set the CloudWatch log group with an expiration of 90 days
Use Amazon Kinesis as the target. Configure the Kinesis stream to always retain the logs for 90 days.
Use AWS CloudTrail as the target. Configure CloudTrail to save to an Amazon S3 bucket, and enable S3 Intelligent-Tiering.
Use Amazon S3 as the target. Enable an S3 Lifecycle policy to transition the logs to S3 Standard-Infrequent Access (S3 Standard-IA) after 90 days.

questions.explanation:
Amazon VPC Flow Logs can be delivered to Amazon S3, and S3 Lifecycle rules can automatically transition objects to a lower-cost storage class based on age. Because the logs need frequent access for the first 90 days and only intermittent access after that, storing them in S3 and transitioning them to S3 Standard-IA after 90 days is the best fit. CloudWatch Logs expiration would remove the data, CloudTrail is not a destination for VPC Flow Logs, and Kinesis is not the correct target for this use case according to current AWS documentation.

**Learn more:** [Logging IP traffic using VPC Flow Logs - Amazon VPC](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/userguide/flow-logs.html) · [Transitioning objects using Amazon S3 Lifecycle - Amazon S3](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/lifecycle-transition-general-considerations.html)

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],The following IAM policy is attached to an IAM group, and this is the only policy applied to the group.  
  
![Question Image](https://cdn.examcademy.com/images/questions/1783644185061-v0d30bys.png)  
  
What effective IAM permissions does this policy grant to members of the group?

options.text: Group members are permitted any Amazon EC2 action within the us-east-1 Region. Statements after the Allow permission are not applied.
Group members are denied any Amazon EC2 permissions in the us-east-1 Region unless they are logged in with multi-factor authentication (MFA).

Group members are allowed the ec2:StopInstances and ec2:TerminateInstances permissions for all Regions when logged in with multi-factor authentication (MFA). Group members are permitted any other Amazon EC2 action.

Group members are allowed the ec2:StopInstances and ec2:TerminateInstances permissions for the us-east-1 Region only when logged in with multi-factor authentication (MFA). Group members are permitted any other Amazon EC2 action within the us-east-1 Region.

questions.explanation:
The first statement allows all Amazon EC2 actions only when the request is for the `us-east-1` Region. The second statement adds an explicit deny for `ec2:StopInstances` and `ec2:TerminateInstances` when MFA is not present. In AWS policy evaluation, an explicit deny overrides any allow, so those two actions are blocked unless the user is authenticated with MFA. Because the only allow is scoped to `us-east-1`, all other EC2 actions are permitted only in `us-east-1`, and no EC2 permissions are granted in other Regions.

**Learn more:** [Amazon EC2: Allows full EC2 access within a specific Region, programmatically and in the console](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/reference_policies_examples_ec2_region.html) · [Example policies to control access the Amazon EC2 API](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSEC2/latest/UserGuide/ExamplePolicies_EC2.html)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],A company has applications that run on Amazon EC2 instances. The EC2 instances connect to Amazon RDS databases by using an IAM role that has associated policies. The company wants to use AWS Systems Manager to patch the EC2 instances without disrupting the running applications.  
  
Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Create a new IAM role. Attach the AmazonSSMManagedInstanceCore policy to the new IAM role. Attach the new IAM role to the EC2 instances and the existing IAM role.
Create an IAM user. Attach the AmazonSSMManagedInstanceCore policy to the IAM user. Configure Systems Manager to use the IAM user to manage the EC2 instances.
Enable Default Host Configuration Management in Systems Manager to manage the EC2 instances.
Remove the existing policies from the existing IAM role. Add the AmazonSSMManagedInstanceCore policy to the existing IAM role.

questions.explanation:
AWS Systems Manager can manage and patch EC2 instances through Default Host Management Configuration, which automatically configures instances as managed nodes and supplies the permissions needed for Systems Manager without requiring you to remove or replace the IAM permissions the applications already use. Removing the existing role policies would break the applications’ access to Amazon RDS, and creating a second role for the same instance is not the intended model because EC2 uses a single instance profile. An IAM user is also not how Systems Manager should be configured for EC2 instance management.

**Learn more:** [Managing EC2 instances automatically with Default Host Management Configuration - AWS Systems Manager](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/systems-manager/latest/userguide/fleet-manager-default-host-management-configuration.html) · [Adjusting Systems Manager settings - AWS Systems Manager](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/systems-manager/latest/userguide/settings-overview.html)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],A company operates a shopping application that uses Amazon DynamoDB to store customer information. In the event of data corruption, a solutions architect must design a solution that achieves:  
  
- a recovery point objective (RPO) of 15 minutes  
- a recovery time objective (RTO) of 1 hour  
  
What should the solutions architect recommend to meet these requirements?

options.text: Configure DynamoDB global tables. For RPO recovery, point the application to a different AWS Region.
Configure DynamoDB point-in-time recovery. For RPO recovery, restore to the desired point in time.
Export the DynamoDB data to Amazon S3 Glacier on a daily basis. For RPO recovery, import the data from S3 Glacier to DynamoDB.
Schedule Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) snapshots for the DynamoDB table every 15 minutes. For RPO recovery, restore the DynamoDB table by using the EBS snapshot.

questions.explanation:
Amazon DynamoDB point-in-time recovery (PITR) is the feature intended to recover from accidental writes, deletes, or corruption by restoring a table to a specific earlier time. DynamoDB PITR provides continuous backups with per-second granularity, and the latest restorable time is typically about 5 minutes before the current time, which satisfies a 15-minute RPO. The restore operation creates a new table, making PITR the correct recovery mechanism for corruption. Global tables improve multi-Region availability but replicate corrupted data, daily Glacier exports cannot meet a 15-minute RPO, and Amazon EBS snapshots do not apply to DynamoDB table recovery.

**Learn more:** [Enable point-in-time recovery in DynamoDB - Amazon DynamoDB](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/amazondynamodb/latest/developerguide/PointInTimeRecovery_Howitworks.html) · [Restore a table in DynamoDB - Amazon DynamoDB](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/amazondynamodb/latest/developerguide/pointintimerecovery_restores.html)

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],A company stores raw collected data in an Amazon S3 bucket. The data is used for several kinds of analytics on behalf of the company's customers. The analytics requested determine the access pattern for the S3 objects.  
  
The company cannot predict or control the access pattern. The company wants to reduce its S3 costs.  
  
Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Use S3 replication to transition infrequently accessed objects to S3 Standard-Infrequent Access (S3 Standard-IA)
Use S3 Lifecycle rules to transition objects from S3 Standard to Standard-Infrequent Access (S3 Standard-IA)
Use S3 Lifecycle rules to transition objects from S3 Standard to S3 Intelligent-Tiering
Use S3 Inventory to identify and transition objects that have not been accessed from S3 Standard to S3 Intelligent-Tiering

questions.explanation:
Amazon S3 Intelligent-Tiering is the recommended storage class for data with unknown, changing, or unpredictable access patterns, including analytics workloads, because it automatically moves objects between access tiers to optimize cost without operational overhead. AWS also supports using S3 Lifecycle rules to transition objects from S3 Standard directly to S3 Intelligent-Tiering, making that the correct cost-optimization approach here.

**Learn more:** [Managing storage costs with Amazon S3 Intelligent-Tiering](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/intelligent-tiering.html) · [Using S3 Intelligent-Tiering](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/using-intelligent-tiering.html)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],A company has an application that runs on several Amazon EC2 instances. Each EC2 instance has multiple Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) data volumes attached to it. The application's EC2 instance configuration and data must be backed up every night. The application must also be recoverable in a different AWS Region.  
  
Which solution will meet these requirements in the **MOST operationally efficient** way?

options.text: Write an AWS Lambda function that schedules nightly snapshots of the application’s EBS volumes and copies the snapshots to a different Region.
Create a backup plan by using AWS Backup to perform nightly backups. Copy the backups to another Region. Add the application’s EC2 instances as resources.
Create a backup plan by using AWS Backup to perform nightly backups. Copy the backups to another Region. Add the application’s EBS volumes as resources.
Write an AWS Lambda function that schedules nightly snapshots of the application's EBS volumes and copies the snapshots to a different Availability Zone.

questions.explanation:
AWS Backup can protect Amazon EC2 instances as a resource type, and an EC2 backup includes the instance's root volume, attached EBS data volumes, and some instance configuration settings. A backup plan can run on a nightly schedule and copy recovery points to another AWS Region, which satisfies both the backup and cross-Region recovery requirements with the least operational overhead. Backing up only EBS volumes misses the EC2 instance configuration, and a custom AWS Lambda snapshot solution is less operationally efficient than using the managed AWS Backup service.

**Learn more:** [How AWS Backup works with supported AWS services](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/aws-backup/latest/devguide/working-with-supported-services.html) · [Amazon EBS and AWS Backup](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/aws-backup/latest/devguide/multi-volume-crash-consistent.html)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],An Amazon EC2 administrator created the following policy and associated it with an IAM group that contains several users:  
  
![Question Image](https://cdn.examcademy.com/images/questions/1783639762864-d1xzck1n.png)  
  
What is the effect of this policy?

options.text: Users can terminate an EC2 instance in any AWS Region except us-east-1.
Users can terminate an EC2 instance with the IP address 10.100.100.1 in the us-east-1 Region.
Users can terminate an EC2 instance in the us-east-1 Region when the user's source IP is 10.100.100.254.
Users cannot terminate an EC2 instance in the us-east-1 Region when the user's source IP is 10.100.100.254.

questions.explanation:
The policy has an Allow statement for ec2:TerminateInstances when the source IP is in the 10.100.100.0/24 CIDR range, and a Deny statement for all ec2:* actions when the region is not us-east-1. The IP address 10.100.100.254 falls within the allowed CIDR block. Therefore, users can terminate EC2 instances in us-east-1 when their source IP is in the allowed range. This combines both conditions (region and source IP).

**Learn more:** [IAM JSON policy elements: Condition](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/reference_policies_elements_condition.html) · [AWS global condition context keys (aws:SourceIp)](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/reference_policies_condition-keys.html)

A company operates its media-rendering application on premises. To lower storage costs, the company has moved all data to Amazon S3. The on-premises rendering application requires low-latency access to storage.  
  
The company must design a storage solution for the application that maintains the required application performance.  
  
Which storage solution meets these requirements in the **MOST** cost-effective manner?

options.text: Use Mountpoint for Amazon S3 to access the data in Amazon S3 for the on-premises application.
Configure an Amazon S3 File Gateway to provide storage for the on-premises application.
Copy the data from Amazon S3 to Amazon FSx for Windows File Server. Configure an Amazon FSx File Gateway to provide storage for the on-premises application.
Configure an on-premises file server. Use the Amazon S3 API to connect to S3 storage. Configure the application to access the storage from the on-premises file server.

questions.explanation:
Amazon S3 File Gateway presents Amazon S3 objects to on-premises applications through standard NFS or SMB file shares and uses transparent local caching to provide low-latency access to recently accessed data. It preserves Amazon S3 as the primary durable storage layer, avoiding the cost and operational overhead of copying the data into Amazon FSx or maintaining a custom local file-server integration.

**Learn more:** [What is Amazon S3 File Gateway - AWS Storage Gateway](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/filegateway/latest/files3/what-is-file-s3.html) · [How Amazon S3 File Gateway works - AWS Storage Gateway](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/filegateway/latest/files3/file-gateway-concepts.html)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],A company operates a highly available SFTP service. The SFTP service uses two Amazon EC2 Linux instances with elastic IP addresses to accept traffic from trusted IP sources on the internet. The SFTP service is backed by shared storage that is attached to the instances. User accounts are created and managed as Linux users on the SFTP servers.  
  
The company wants a serverless option that provides high IOPS performance and highly configurable security. The company also wants to maintain control over user permissions.  
  
Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Create an encrypted Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) volume. Create an AWS Transfer Family SFTP service with a public endpoint that allows only trusted IP addresses. Attach the EBS volume to the SFTP service endpoint. Grant users access to the SFTP service.

Create an encrypted Amazon Elastic File System (Amazon EFS) volume. Create an AWS Transfer Family SFTP service with elastic IP addresses and a VPC endpoint that has internet-facing access. Attach a security group to the endpoint that allows only trusted IP addresses. Attach the EFS volume to the SFTP service endpoint. Grant users access to the SFTP service.

Create an Amazon S3 bucket with default encryption enabled. Create an AWS Transfer Family SFTP service with a public endpoint that allows only trusted IP addresses. Attach the S3 bucket to the SFTP service endpoint. Grant users access to the SFTP service.

Create an Amazon S3 bucket with default encryption enabled. Create an AWS Transfer Family SFTP service with a VPC endpoint that has internal access in a private subnet. Attach a security group that allows only trusted IP addresses. Attach the S3 bucket to the SFTP service endpoint. Grant users access to the SFTP service.

questions.explanation:
AWS Transfer Family provides the serverless managed SFTP service, and Amazon EFS is the appropriate backend when you need shared file storage with POSIX-style permissions that map well to Linux-style user access control. AWS Transfer Family supports only Amazon S3 or Amazon EFS as storage backends, not Amazon EBS. For restricting internet access to trusted IP ranges, the correct design is a VPC-hosted internet-facing endpoint with security groups, and Transfer Family can use Elastic IP addresses on that endpoint. This combination satisfies the requirements for serverless SFTP, shared high-performance storage, configurable network security, and continued control over per-user permissions.

**Learn more:** [Configure storage to use with AWS Transfer Family servers](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/transfer/latest/userguide/configure-storage.html) · [Working with service-managed users - AWS Transfer Family](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/transfer/latest/userguide/service-managed-users.html)

A solutions architect must review a company's Amazon S3 buckets to identify personally identifiable information (PII). The company stores the PII data in the `us-east-1` Region and `us-west-2` Region.  
  
Which solution will meet these requirements with the **LEAST operational overhead**?

options.text: Configure Amazon Macie in each Region. Create a job to analyze the data that is in Amazon S3.
Configure AWS Security Hub for all Regions. Create an AWS Config rule to analyze the data that is in Amazon S3.
Configure Amazon Inspector to analyze the data that is in Amazon S3.
Configure Amazon GuardDuty to analyze the data that is in Amazon S3.

questions.explanation:
Amazon Macie is the AWS service built to discover and classify sensitive data such as PII in Amazon S3. It can run sensitive data discovery jobs against S3 buckets and produce findings when it detects PII. Because Macie is a Regional service, it must be enabled in each Region that contains the target buckets, so using Macie in both `us-east-1` and `us-west-2` satisfies the requirement with minimal administration. AWS Security Hub and AWS Config do not scan S3 object contents for PII, Amazon Inspector is for vulnerability management, and GuardDuty is for threat detection rather than content inspection.

**Learn more:** [Discovering sensitive data with Macie - Amazon Macie](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/macie/latest/user/data-classification.html) · [Storing and retaining sensitive data discovery results - Amazon Macie](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/macie/latest/user/discovery-results-repository-s3.html)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],A company uses Amazon FSx for NetApp ONTAP in its primary AWS Region for CIFS and NFS file shares. Applications running on Amazon EC2 instances access the file shares. The company needs a storage disaster recovery (DR) solution in a secondary Region. The replicated data in the secondary Region must be accessible by using the same protocols as in the primary Region.  
  
Which solution will meet these requirements with the **LEAST operational overhead**?

options.text: Create an AWS Lambda function to copy the data to an Amazon S3 bucket. Replicate the S3 bucket to the secondary Region.
Create a backup of the FSx for ONTAP volumes by using AWS Backup. Copy the volumes to the secondary Region. Create a new FSx for ONTAP instance from the backup.
Create an FSx for ONTAP instance in the secondary Region. Use NetApp SnapMirror to replicate data from the primary Region to the secondary Region.
Create an Amazon Elastic File System (Amazon EFS) volume. Migrate the current data to the volume. Replicate the volume to the secondary Region.

questions.explanation:
Amazon FSx for NetApp ONTAP natively supports SMB/CIFS and NFS file access, and NetApp SnapMirror is the ONTAP replication technology designed for disaster recovery between ONTAP systems, including across AWS Regions. Deploying an FSx for ONTAP file system in the secondary Region and using SnapMirror preserves the same file protocols at the DR site while providing managed, storage-level replication with less operational effort than backup-and-restore workflows. S3 replication does not provide CIFS/NFS shares, and Amazon EFS does not support SMB/CIFS.

**Learn more:** [What is Amazon FSx for NetApp ONTAP?](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/fsx/latest/ONTAPGuide/what-is-fsx-ontap.html) · [Disaster recovery support with NetApp SnapMirror](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/fsx/latest/ONTAPGuide/snapmirror-overview.html)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],A global ecommerce company operates its critical workloads on AWS. The workloads use an Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL DB instance configured for a Multi-AZ deployment.  
  
Customers have reported application timeouts during database failovers. The company requires a resilient solution that reduces failover time.  
  
Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Create an Amazon RDS Proxy. Assign the proxy to the DB instance.
Create a read replica for the DB instance. Move the read traffic to the read replica.
Enable Performance Insights. Monitor the CPU load to identify the timeouts.
Take regular automatic snapshots. Copy the automatic snapshots to multiple AWS Regions.

questions.explanation:
Amazon RDS Proxy improves application resilience during Multi-AZ DB instance failovers by bypassing DNS caching delays, automatically directing traffic to the new database instance, and retaining idle application connections. AWS states that RDS Proxy can reduce failover times by up to 66% for RDS Multi-AZ DB instances.

**Learn more:** [Planning where to use RDS Proxy](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonRDS/latest/UserGuide/rds-proxy-planning.html) · [RDS Proxy concepts and terminology](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonRDS/latest/UserGuide/rds-proxy.howitworks.html)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],A company wants to migrate its on-premises application to AWS. The application produces output files that range in size from tens of gigabytes to hundreds of terabytes. The application data must be stored in a standard file system structure. The company wants a solution that scales automatically, is highly available, and requires minimal operational overhead.  
  
Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Migrate the application to run as containers on Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS). Use Amazon S3 for storage.
Migrate the application to run as containers on Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS). Use Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) for storage.
Migrate the application to Amazon EC2 instances in a Multi-AZ Auto Scaling group. Use Amazon Elastic File System (Amazon EFS) for storage.
Migrate the application to Amazon EC2 instances in a Multi-AZ Auto Scaling group. Use Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) for storage.

questions.explanation:
Amazon EFS is the AWS storage service designed for shared file storage with a standard file system interface. A Regional EFS file system stores data redundantly across multiple Availability Zones and supports concurrent access from multiple EC2 instances, which aligns with a Multi-AZ Auto Scaling deployment. EFS also scales storage automatically as data grows, minimizing administration. By contrast, Amazon S3 is object storage rather than a standard file system, and Amazon EBS is block storage limited to attachment within a single Availability Zone, so those options do not satisfy the file system and high-availability requirements.

**Learn more:** [Creating EFS file systems - Amazon Elastic File System](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/efs/latest/ug/creating-using-create-fs.html) · [Features of Amazon EFS - Amazon Elastic File System](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/efs/latest/ug/features.html)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],A company has a financial application that generates reports. The reports average 50 KB in size and are stored in Amazon S3. The reports are frequently accessed during the first week after they are produced and must be retained for several years. The reports must be retrievable within 6 hours.  
  
Which solution meets these requirements **MOST cost-effectively**?

options.text: Use S3 Standard. Use an S3 Lifecycle rule to transition the reports to S3 Glacier after 7 days.
Use S3 Standard. Use an S3 Lifecycle rule to transition the reports to S3 Standard-Infrequent Access (S3 Standard-IA) after 7 days.
Use S3 Intelligent-Tiering. Configure S3 Intelligent-Tiering to transition the reports to S3 Standard-Infrequent Access (S3 Standard-IA) and S3 Glacier.
Use S3 Standard. Use an S3 Lifecycle rule to transition the reports to S3 Glacier Deep Archive after 7 days.

questions.explanation:
S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval standard retrieval completes within 3–5 hours, satisfying the 6-hour retrieval requirement. Transitioning 50 KB reports to Glacier after 7 days is cost-effective for long-term retention. S3 Glacier Deep Archive's 12-hour standard retrieval exceeds the time window. S3 Intelligent-Tiering incurs overhead without benefit for small objects below the 128 KB efficiency threshold.

**Learn more:** [Transitioning objects using Amazon S3 Lifecycle](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/lifecycle-transition-general-considerations.html)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],A company runs analytics software on Amazon EC2 instances. The software accepts job requests from users to process data that has been uploaded to Amazon S3.  
  
Users report that some submitted data is not being processed. Amazon CloudWatch reveals that the EC2 instances have a consistent CPU utilization at or near 100%.  
  
The company wants to improve system performance and scale the system based on user load.  
  
What should a solutions architect do to meet these requirements?

options.text: Create a copy of the instance. Place all instances behind an Application Load Balancer.
Create an S3 VPC endpoint for Amazon S3. Update the software to reference the endpoint.
Stop the EC2 instances. Modify the instance type to one with a more powerful CPU and more memory. Restart the instances.
Route incoming requests to Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS). Configure an EC2 Auto Scaling group based on queue size. Update the software to read from the queue.

questions.explanation:
For CPU-bound, asynchronous job processing, the correct architecture is to decouple incoming work with Amazon SQS and let EC2 worker instances process messages from the queue. An EC2 Auto Scaling group can then scale horizontally based on queue backlog or backlog per instance, which matches user-driven demand more accurately than simply resizing one instance or placing workers behind a load balancer. AWS documentation specifically describes scaling EC2 Auto Scaling groups for SQS-based workloads and recommends using queue backlog per instance as the scaling signal.

**Learn more:** [Scaling policy based on Amazon SQS - Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/autoscaling/ec2/userguide/as-using-sqs-queue.html) · [Target tracking scaling policies for Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/autoscaling/ec2/userguide/as-scaling-target-tracking.html)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],A company needs to extract the names of ingredients from recipe records that are stored as text files in an Amazon S3 bucket. A web application will use the ingredient names to query an Amazon DynamoDB table and determine a nutrition score.  
  
The application can handle non-food records and errors. The company does not have any employees who have machine learning knowledge to develop this solution.  
  
Which solution will meet these requirements **MOST cost-effectively**?

options.text: Use S3 Event Notifications to invoke an AWS Lambda function when PutObject requests occur. Program the Lambda function to analyze the object and extract the ingredient names by using Amazon Comprehend. Store the Amazon Comprehend output in the DynamoDB table.

Use an Amazon EventBridge rule to invoke an AWS Lambda function when PutObject requests occur. Program the Lambda function to analyze the object by using Amazon Forecast to extract the ingredient names. Store the Forecast output in the DynamoDB table.

Use S3 Event Notifications to invoke an AWS Lambda function when PutObject requests occur. Use Amazon Polly to create audio recordings of the recipe records. Save the audio files in the S3 bucket. Use Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS) to send a URL as a message to employees. Instruct the employees to listen to the audio files and calculate the nutrition score. Store the ingredient names in the DynamoDB table.

Use an Amazon EventBridge rule to invoke an AWS Lambda function when a PutObject request occurs. Program the Lambda function to analyze the object and extract the ingredient names by using Amazon SageMaker. Store the inference output from the SageMaker endpoint in the DynamoDB table.

questions.explanation:
Amazon Comprehend is the AWS service designed to analyze text and extract entities, including custom entities when needed, so it fits a text-based ingredient-extraction workflow without requiring the company to build and manage its own machine learning models. S3 Event Notifications can invoke AWS Lambda when new objects are created, making this a simple serverless pipeline. Amazon Forecast is for time-series prediction, Amazon Polly is for text-to-speech, and Amazon SageMaker would require a more complex ML build/deploy approach than necessary for a team without ML expertise. The most cost-effective solution is therefore the serverless S3-to-Lambda design that uses Amazon Comprehend for extraction.

**Learn more:** [Custom entity recognition - Amazon Comprehend](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/comprehend/latest/dg/custom-entity-recognition.html) · [Entities - Amazon Comprehend](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/comprehend/latest/dg/how-entities.html)
